title: Plasma Lens
problem:
# III. Plasma Lens

The physics of the intense particle beams has a great impact not only on the basic research but also the applications in medicine and industry. The plasma lens is a device to provide an ultra-strong final focus at the end of the linear colliders. To appreciate the possibilities of the plasma lens it is quite natural to compare this with the usual magnetic and electrostatic lenses. In magnetic lenses, focusing capability is proportional to the magnetic field gradient. The practical upper limit of the quadrupole focusing lens is in the order of $10^{2}\mathrm{T / m}$ , while for plasma lens having density of $10^{17}\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ , its focusing capability is equivalent to a magnetic field gradient of $3\times 10^{6}\mathrm{T / m}$ (about four orders of magnitude more than that of a magnetic quadrupole lens).

In what follows, we will illuminate why the intense relativistic particle beams could produce self-focusing beams and do not blow themselves apart in free space.

sub_problems.problem: (a) Consider a long cylindrical electron beam of uniform number density $n$ and average speed $\nu$ (both quantities in laboratory frame). Derive the expression for the electric field at a point at distance $r$ from the central axis of the beam using classical electromagnetics.
sub_problems.solution:
By cylindrical symmetry, the electric field is purely radial and depends only on the distance $r$ from the axis. Choose a coaxial Gaussian cylinder of radius $r$ and length $\ell$.

The electric flux through the curved surface is
\[
\Phi_E = E(r)\,(2\pi r\ell),
\]
since the field is perpendicular to the curved surface and parallel to the end caps, so the end-cap contributions vanish.

The charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface is
\[
Q_{\text{enc}} = -ne\, (\pi r^2\ell),
\]
because the beam has uniform number density $n$ and each electron carries charge $-e$.

Gauss's law gives
\[
E(r)\,(2\pi r\ell)=\frac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}
= -\frac{ne\,\pi r^2\ell}{\varepsilon_0}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
E(r)= -\frac{ne}{2\varepsilon_0}\,r.
\]
So the electric field vector is
\[
\boxed{\mathbf{E}(r)= -\frac{ne}{2\varepsilon_0}\,r\,\hat{\mathbf r}}.
\]
The field points radially inward, toward the beam axis.

knowledge_points.name: Gauss's law
knowledge_points.description: Integral form ∮ E·dA = Q_enc/ε0 is used to relate the electric flux through a closed surface to the enclosed charge, enabling direct calculation of the electric field for symmetric charge distributions.

knowledge_points.name: cylindrical symmetry
knowledge_points.description: The beam is infinitely long and uniform, so the electric field is purely radial and depends only on the distance r from the axis, simplifying the flux integral.

knowledge_points.name: uniform volume charge density
knowledge_points.description: The electron number density n is constant, giving a uniform charge density ρ = -ne, which makes the enclosed charge proportional to the volume inside the Gaussian surface.

knowledge_points.name: electron charge
knowledge_points.description: Each electron carries charge -e, so the total charge enclosed is -ne times the volume, determining the sign and magnitude of the field.

knowledge_points.name: Gaussian surface selection
knowledge_points.description: A coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length ℓ is chosen to exploit symmetry: the field is perpendicular to the curved side and parallel to the end caps, making the flux evaluation trivial.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Derive the expression for the magnetic field at the same point as in a).
sub_problems.solution:
Using Ampres law for a long, cylindrically symmetric beam, choose a circular Amperian loop of radius $r$ centered on the beam axis. The magnetic field is tangential and constant on the loop, so
\[
\oint \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{l}=B_\theta(2\pi r)=\mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}.
\]
For a beam with uniform number density $n$, charge $q$, and speed $v$, the enclosed current is
\[
I_{\text{enc}} = n q v\,\pi r^2.
\]
Therefore,
\[
B_\theta(2\pi r)=\mu_0 n q v\,\pi r^2,
\]
which gives
\[
B_\theta(r)=\frac{\mu_0 n q v}{2}\,r.
\]
The direction is azimuthal around the beam axis, with sign determined by the charge and current direction. Thus the magnetic field at the same point is
\[
\boxed{B_\theta(r)=\frac{\mu_0 n q v}{2}\,r}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Ampère's law
knowledge_points.description: Relates the line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop to the total current passing through the loop; used here to find B from the enclosed current of the electron beam.

knowledge_points.name: cylindrical symmetry Amperian loop
knowledge_points.description: Choosing a circular Amperian loop coaxial with the beam exploits cylindrical symmetry so that B is constant in magnitude and tangential along the loop, simplifying the line integral to B·2πr.

knowledge_points.name: current density
knowledge_points.description: The current enclosed by the Amperian loop is the product of charge density (nq), drift velocity v, and cross-sectional area πr²; needed to compute I_enc for a uniform beam.

knowledge_points.name: uniform beam density
knowledge_points.description: The electron beam is assumed to have uniform number density n across its cross-section, making the enclosed current simply proportional to r².

knowledge_points.name: steady current
knowledge_points.description: The beam current is treated as steady (DC), so Ampère's law in its magnetostatic form applies without displacement current correction.

sub_problems.problem: (c) What is then the net outward force on the electron in the electron beam passing that point?
sub_problems.solution:
For an electron beam with number density $n$, the electric field produced by the beam at radius $r$ gives an outward electric force on an electron of magnitude
\[\nF_E= eE = \frac{n e^2 r}{2\varepsilon_0}.
\]\nThe beam current also produces a magnetic field, which gives an inward magnetic force of magnitude
\[\nF_B = e v B = \frac{\mu_0 n e^2 r v^2}{2}.
\]\nTherefore the net outward force on the electron is
\[
\vec F = \left(\frac{n e^2 r}{2\varepsilon_0} - \frac{\mu_0 n e^2 r v^2}{2}\right)\hat r.
\]\nUsing $c^{-2}=\mu_0\varepsilon_0$, this becomes
\[
\vec F = \frac{n e^2 r}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)\hat r.
\]\nHence the net outward force is \(\boxed{\vec F=\frac{n e^2 r}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)\hat r}\).

knowledge_points.name: Lorentz force law
knowledge_points.description: Gives the total electromagnetic force on a point charge: F = q(E + v × B). Here it is used to sum the outward electric force and inward magnetic force on a beam electron.

knowledge_points.name: electric force on a charge
knowledge_points.description: The force due to an electric field on a charge q is F_E = qE. Used to convert the known electric field from part (a) into the outward force component.

knowledge_points.name: magnetic force on a moving charge
knowledge_points.description: The magnetic component of the Lorentz force is F_B = q v × B, with magnitude qvB when v is perpendicular to B. Used to convert the known magnetic field from part (b) into the inward force component.

knowledge_points.name: electromagnetic wave speed relation
knowledge_points.description: The identity c^{-2} = μ₀ ε₀ relates the vacuum permittivity, permeability, and speed of light. Used to simplify the net force expression into a form showing the (1 - v²/c²) factor.

knowledge_points.name: point particle in macroscopic fields
knowledge_points.description: The electron is treated as a point charge experiencing the smooth macroscopic E and B fields derived from the continuous beam distribution, ignoring discrete particle effects.

sub_problems.problem:
(d) Assuming that the expression obtained in c) is applicable at relativistic velocities, what will be the force on the electron as $\nu$ approaches speed of light $c$ , where

$$c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{0} \mu_{0}}} ? \tag{}$$
sub_problems.solution:
For an electron moving with speed $v$ in the beam, the transverse force from the electric and magnetic fields is of the form found in part (c). If this expression is extended to the relativistic limit, then as $v \to c$ the magnetic force grows to match the electric force in magnitude and opposite direction. Hence the net force tends to zero:
\[\nF_r \to 0 \qquad (v \to c).
\]\nTherefore, the electron experiences no net radial force in the ultrarelativistic limit, because the electric and magnetic forces cancel. Final answer: $\boxed{0}$.

knowledge_points.name: prior net force expression
knowledge_points.description: The net radial force on an electron in the beam derived in part (c) is assumed to remain valid at relativistic speeds. This expression contains both electric and magnetic contributions.

knowledge_points.name: Lorentz force law
knowledge_points.description: The total electromagnetic force on a moving charge is the sum of electric and magnetic parts. In the relativistic limit, the magnetic force on a charge moving at speed v in its own beam's fields becomes equal and opposite to the electric force.

knowledge_points.name: relativistic limit
knowledge_points.description: As the electron speed approaches the speed of light c, the magnetic force magnitude approaches the electric force magnitude, leading to cancellation of the net transverse force.

knowledge_points.name: speed of light definition
knowledge_points.description: The speed of light c is given by 1/sqrt(epsilon_0 mu_0), linking the vacuum permittivity and permeability constants that appear in the electric and magnetic field expressions.

sub_problems.problem: (e) If the electron beam of radius $R$ enters into a plasma of uniform density $n_0 < n$ (the plasma is an ionized gas of ions and electrons with equal charge density), what will be the net force on the stationary plasma ion at distance $r'$ outside the electron beam long after the beam entering the plasma. You may assume that the density of the plasma ions remains constant and the cylindrical symmetry is maintained.
sub_problems.solution:
Since the plasma particles are stationary, their velocity is zero, so there is no magnetic force on them. The net force is purely electrostatic:
\[
\mathbf F = q\mathbf E.
\]

For a cylindrically symmetric charge distribution, the radial electric field at a point a distance $r'$ from the axis, outside the electron beam, is the sum of the field from the beam electrons and the field from the uniform plasma ions.

The electron beam of radius $R$ has charge density $-ne$, so for $r'>R$ its enclosed charge per unit length is
\[
\lambda_{\rm beam}=-ne\,\pi R^2.
\]
Hence its field is
\[
E_{\rm beam}(r')=\frac{\lambda_{\rm beam}}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r'}
=-\frac{neR^2}{2\varepsilon_0 r'}.
\]
The uniform ion background of density $n_0$ contributes, inside radius $r'$, an enclosed charge per unit length
\[
\lambda_{\rm ion}=n_0 e\,\pi r'^2,
\]
so
\[
E_{\rm ion}(r')=\frac{\lambda_{\rm ion}}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r'}
=\frac{n_0 e r'}{2\varepsilon_0}.
\]
Therefore the total radial electric field is
\[
E_{r'}=-\frac{neR^2}{2\varepsilon_0 r'}+\frac{n_0 e r'}{2\varepsilon_0}.
\]
So the force on a stationary plasma ion ($q=+e$) is
\[
F_{r'}=eE_{r'}
=-\frac{ne^2R^2}{2\varepsilon_0 r'}+\frac{n_0e^2r'}{2\varepsilon_0}.
\]
For a stationary plasma electron ($q=-e$), the force is the opposite:
\[
F_{r'}=-eE_{r'}
=\frac{ne^2R^2}{2\varepsilon_0 r'}-\frac{n_0e^2r'}{2\varepsilon_0}.
\]
Thus the ions are pulled inward and the electrons are pushed outward; there is no magnetic-force cancellation because the plasma particles are at rest.

Final answer: \boxed{F_{r'}=e\left(-\frac{neR^2}{2\varepsilon_0 r'}+\frac{n_0 e r'}{2\varepsilon_0}\right)\ \text{for an ion}}

knowledge_points.name: stationary plasma particles
knowledge_points.description: The plasma ions and electrons are at rest in the lab frame, so they experience no magnetic force (v=0). This is stated in the problem and used to reduce the net force to purely electrostatic.

knowledge_points.name: Lorentz force law
knowledge_points.description: The force on a charged particle is q(E + v×B). Because plasma particles are stationary, the magnetic term vanishes, leaving F = qE.

knowledge_points.name: Gauss's law in integral form
knowledge_points.description: Used to compute the radial electric field from a cylindrically symmetric charge distribution: E = λ_enclosed/(2πε₀r). Applied separately to the electron beam and the uniform ion background.

knowledge_points.name: cylindrical symmetry maintained
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that cylindrical symmetry is maintained after the beam enters the plasma, allowing the use of Gauss's law with radial dependence only.

knowledge_points.name: uniform plasma ion density
knowledge_points.description: The plasma ion density n₀ is constant and uniform, as stated in the problem. This gives a uniform positive background charge density for the electrostatic calculation.

knowledge_points.name: superposition of electric fields
knowledge_points.description: The total electric field outside the beam is the sum of the field from the electron beam (negative line charge) and the field from the uniform ion background (positive volume charge).

knowledge_points.name: electron beam charge density from earlier parts
knowledge_points.description: The electron beam has uniform number density n and charge density -ne, and its radius is R. These quantities are imported from the problem setup and earlier sub-problems to compute the beam's enclosed charge per unit length.

sub_problems.problem: (f) After long enough time, what is the net force on an electron at distance $r$ from the central axis of the beam in the plasma, assuming $\nu \rightarrow c$ provided that the density of the plasma ions remains constant and the cylindrical symmetry is maintained?
sub_problems.solution:
For a cylindrical beam of electrons in a plasma, the beams own charge produces an outward electric force, while the beam current produces an inward magnetic force. For a particle at distance $r$ from the axis, the combined self-force from the beam is proportional to
\[
\frac{n e^2 r}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)\hat r,
\]
where $n$ is the beam density.

The uniform ion background in the plasma contributes an additional electrostatic force on the electron, which is inward:
\[
-\frac{n_0 e^2 r}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat r,
\]
where $n_0$ is the ion density.

Thus the total force is
\[
\vec F=\frac{n e^2 r}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)\hat r-\frac{n_0 e^2 r}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat r.
\]
In the ultrarelativistic limit $v\to c$, the first term vanishes, so the net force becomes
\[
\vec F\approx -\frac{n_0 e^2 r}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat r.
\]
Therefore the electron experiences an inward radial force toward the beam axis:
\[
\boxed{\vec F=-\frac{n_0 e^2 r}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat r}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: ultra-relativistic limit
knowledge_points.description: The problem explicitly states v → c, which makes the beam's self-force term proportional to (1 - v²/c²) vanish, leaving only the plasma ion background force.

knowledge_points.name: cylindrical symmetry maintained
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that cylindrical symmetry is maintained, which justifies using radial electric fields that depend only on distance r from the axis and applying Gauss's law in cylindrical geometry.

knowledge_points.name: constant plasma ion density
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that the density of plasma ions remains constant, so the ion background charge density n₀ is fixed and provides a static inward electric force on electrons.

knowledge_points.name: prior self-force expression
knowledge_points.description: The solution imports the combined electric and magnetic self-force on a beam electron derived in part (c) and its relativistic form from part (d), which is proportional to (1 - v²/c²).

knowledge_points.name: prior ion force expression
knowledge_points.description: The solution imports the electrostatic force on a stationary plasma ion from part (e), which is inward and proportional to n₀, and applies it to an electron by charge sign reversal.

knowledge_points.name: superposition of forces
knowledge_points.description: The total force on the electron is the vector sum of the beam self-force (which vanishes at v → c) and the force from the uniform ion background.

title: Measure the mass in the weightless state
problem:
# Theoretical competition – Problem No.1 Measure the mass in the weightless state

In the spacecraft orbiting the Earth, there is weightless state, so that one cannot use ordinary instruments to measure the weight and then to deduce the mass of the astronaut. Skylab 2 and some other spacecrafts are supplied with a Body Mass Measurement Device which consists of a chair attached to one end of a spring. The other end of the spring is attached to a fixed point of the spacecraft. The axis of the spring passes through the center of mass of the craft. The force constant (the hardness) of the spring is $k =605.6 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$ .

1. When the craft is fixed on the pad, the chair (without person) oscillates with the period $T_{0} =1.28195$ s.

Calculate the mass $m_0$ of the chair .

2. When the craft orbits the Earth the astronaut straps himself into the chair and measures the period $T$ of the chair oscillations. He obtains $T' =2.33044 \, \text{s}$ , then calculates roughly his mass. He feels some doubt and tries to find the true value of his mass. He measures again the period of oscillation of the chair (without person), and find $T_0' =1.27395 \, \text{s}$ .

What is the true value of the astronaut's mass and the craft's mass?

Note: The mass of the spring is negligible and the astronaut is floating.
solution:
For a mass $m$ on a spring of force constant $k$, the oscillation period is
\[T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}.

### 1) Mass of the chair
With the craft fixed on the pad, the chair alone oscillates with period $T_0$, so
\[m_0=\frac{kT_0^2}{4\pi^2}.
\]Substituting $k=605.6\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and $T_0=1.28195\,\mathrm{s}$ gives
\[m_0\approx 25.21\,\mathrm{kg}.

### 2) Mass of the craft and astronaut
When the craft is free in space, the spring connects two moving masses: the chair of mass $m_0$ and the craft of mass $M$. Their relative oscillation is governed by the reduced mass
\[
\mu=\frac{m_0M}{m_0+M}.
\]Thus, for the chair alone in orbit,
\[T_0'=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0}{k}},\qquad \mu_0=\frac{m_0M}{m_0+M},
\]and for the chair plus astronaut,
\[T'=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{k}},\qquad \mu=\frac{mM}{m+M},
\]where $m$ is the total mass of chair + astronaut.
From the two chair-only periods,
\[
\frac{m_0}{\mu_0}=\left(\frac{T_0}{T_0'}\right)^2.
\]So
\[M=\frac{m_0}{\left(\frac{T_0}{T_0'}\right)^2-1}
\approx \frac{25.21}{\left(\frac{1.28195}{1.27395}\right)^2-1}
\approx 2.00\times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}.
\]
Now use $T'$ to find the total mass $m$ of chair plus astronaut:
\[
\mu=\frac{kT'^2}{4\pi^2}\approx 83.31\,\mathrm{kg}.
\]Since $\mu=\dfrac{mM}{m+M}$,
\[m=\frac{\mu M}{M-\mu}\approx 86.93\,\mathrm{kg}.
\]Therefore the astronaut’s mass is
\[m- m_0 \approx 86.93-25.21=61.72\,\mathrm{kg}.
\]
Final answer: the craft has mass \boxed{2.00\times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}}, and the astronaut has mass \boxed{61.72\,\mathrm{kg}}.

knowledge_points.description: The period of a mass m oscillating on a spring of constant k with the other end fixed is T = 2π√(m/k). Used in part 1 to find m0 and as a special case of the two-body system when one mass is effectively infinite.

title: Compression and expansion of a two gases system
problem:
# Theoretical Competition-Problem No. 3

# Compression and expansion of a two gases system

A cylinder is divided in two compartments with a mobile partition NM. The compartment

in the left is limited by the fond of the cylinder and the partition NM (Figure 1). This compartment contains one mole of water vapor. The compartment in the right is limited by the partition NM and a mobile piston AB. This compartment contains one mole of nitrogen gas $(\mathrm{N}_2)$ .

At first, the volumes and temperatures of the gases in two compartments are equal. The partition NM is well heat conductive. His heat capacity is very small and can be neglected.

Figure 1

The specific volume of liquid water is negligible in comparison with the specific volume of water vapor at the same temperature.

The specific latent heat of vaporization $L$ is defined as the amount of heat that must be delivered to one unit of mass of substance to convert it from liquid state to vapor at the same temperature. For water at $T_0=373\mathrm{K}$ , $L =2250\mathrm{kJ / kg}$ .

1. Suppose that the piston and the wall of the cylinder are heat conductive, the partition NM can slide freely without friction. The initial state of the gases in the cylinder is defined as follows:

Pressure $p_1=0.5$ atm.; total volume $V_1=2V_0$ ; temperature $T_1=373$ K.

The piston AB slowly compresses the gases in a quasi-static (quasi-equilibrium) and isothermal process to the final volume $V_{\mathrm{F}} = V_{0} /4$

sub_problems.problem:
(a) Draw the $p(V)$ curve, that is the curve representing the dependence of pressure $p$ on the total volume $V$ of both gases in the cylinder at temperature $T_{1}$ . Calculate the coordinates of important points of the curve.

Gas constant: $R =8.31$ J/mol.K or $R =0.0820$ L.atm./mol.K

1 atm. $=101.3\mathrm{kPa}$

Under the pressure $p_0=1$ atm., water boils at the temperature $T_0=373 \, \mathrm{K}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Because the partition is frictionless and thermally conductive, the two compartments always have the same temperature and the same pressure \(p\). The process is isothermal at \(T_1=373\ \mathrm{K}\).
\nFirst find \(V_0\) from the initial state of one mole of nitrogen in the right compartment:
\[\nV_0=\frac{RT_1}{p_1}=\frac{8.31\times 373}{0.5\times 1.013\times 10^5}
=0.0612\ \mathrm{m^3}=61.2\ \mathrm{dm^3}.
\]\nSo the initial total volume is \(2V_0=122.4\ \mathrm{dm^3}\).

### 1) Before condensation of water vapor\nAs long as the water remains entirely in the vapor state, each side contains one mole of ideal gas at the same \(p,T\). Hence
\[\nV_{\mathrm{N_2}}=\frac{RT_1}{p},\qquad V_{\mathrm{H_2O}}=\frac{RT_1}{p}.
\]\nTherefore the total volume is
\[\nV=\frac{2RT_1}{p}.
\]\nUsing \(V_0=RT_1/p_1\) and \(p_1=0.5\ \mathrm{atm}\), this becomes
\[
 p=\frac{V_0}{V}\,\mathrm{atm}.
\]\nThis branch runs from \((V,p)=(2V_0,0.5\ \mathrm{atm})\) to \((V_0,1\ \mathrm{atm})\).

### 2) Condensation plateau\nAt \(T_1=373\ \mathrm{K}\), water boils at \(p_0=1\ \mathrm{atm}\). So when the pressure reaches \(1\ \mathrm{atm}\), the water vapor starts to condense and the pressure stays at the saturation value \(1\ \mathrm{atm}\) while compression continues.
\nFor nitrogen at \(1\ \mathrm{atm}\),
\[\nV_{\mathrm{N_2}}=\frac{RT_1}{p_0}=\frac{V_0}{2}.
\]\nThus, while water is condensing,
\[
 p=1\ \mathrm{atm},\qquad V_0/2 \le V \le V_0.
\]\nThe left compartment volume shrinks from \(V_0/2\) to \(0\) as liquid water forms.

### 3) After all water has condensed\nOnce all water is liquid, its volume is negligible, and only nitrogen determines the pressure:
\[
 pV=RT_1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad p=\frac{RT_1}{V}=\frac{V_0}{2V}\,\mathrm{atm}.
\]\nThis branch starts from \((V,p)=(V_0/2,1\ \mathrm{atm})\) and goes to the final state \(V_F=V_0/4\):
\[
 p_F=\frac{V_0}{2(V_0/4)}=2\ \mathrm{atm}.
\]

### Important points on the \(p(V)\) curve
\[
(2V_0,\,0.5\ \mathrm{atm}),\qquad (V_0,\,1\ \mathrm{atm}),\qquad (V_0/2,\,1\ \mathrm{atm}),\qquad (V_0/4,\,2\ \mathrm{atm}).
\]\nWith \(V_0=61.2\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), these are
\[

sub_problems.problem:
(b) Calculate the work done by the piston in the process of gases compressing.

$$\int \frac{d V}{V} = \ln V$$
sub_problems.solution:
The compression can be divided into three quasi-static stages.
\nFrom the initial state,
\[\np_1(2V_0)=2RT_1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad p_1V_0=RT_1.
\]

**Stage 1: \(2V_0 \to V_0\)**\nThe system is compressed isothermally while both gases are still in the gaseous state. Since there are two moles in total,
\[\np=\frac{2RT_1}{V}.
\]\nHence the work done by the piston on the gases is
\[\nA_{12}=-\int_{2V_0}^{V_0} p\,dV
=\int_{V_0}^{2V_0}\frac{2RT_1}{V}\,dV
=2RT_1\ln 2.
\]

**Stage 2: \(V_0 \to V_0/2\)**\nDuring this stage the pressure stays constant at \(2p_1\), so
\[\nA_{23}=2p_1\left(V_0-\frac{V_0}{2}\right)=p_1V_0=RT_1.
\]

**Stage 3: \(V_0/2 \to V_0/4\)**\nOnly one mole of gas remains, so the isothermal relation is
\[\np=\frac{RT_1}{V}.
\]\nTherefore,
\[\nA_{34}=-\int_{V_0/2}^{V_0/4}p\,dV
=\int_{V_0/4}^{V_0/2}\frac{RT_1}{V}\,dV
=RT_1\ln 2.
\]
\nThus the total work done by the piston is
\[\nA=A_{12}+A_{23}+A_{34}=(2\ln 2+1+\ln 2)RT_1=(1+3\ln 2)RT_1.
\]\nWith \(R=8.31\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\) and \(T_1=373\,\mathrm{K}\),
\[\nRT_1\approx 3.10\times 10^3\,\mathrm{J},
\]\nso
\[\nA\approx 9.55\times 10^3\,\mathrm{J}=9.55\,\mathrm{kJ}.
\]
\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{9.55\,\mathrm{kJ}}\).

title: Specific heat of free electron gas at constant volume
problem:
# Theoretical Problem 3

# 3A. Average contribution of each electron to specific heat of free electron gas at constant volume

sub_problems.problem:
(1) According to the classical physics the conduction electrons in metals constitute free electron gas like an ideal gas. In thermal equilibrium their average energy relates to temperature, therefore they contribute to the specific heat. The average contribution of each electron to the specific heat of free electron gas at constant volume is defined as

$$c_{V} = \frac{d \bar{E}}{d T}, \tag{1}$$

where $\overline{E}$ is the average energy of each electron. However the value of the specific heat at constant volume is a constant, independent of temperature. Please calculate $\overline{E}$ and the average contribution of each electron to the specific heat at constant volume $c_{V}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a classical free electron gas, each electron has 3 translational degrees of freedom. By the equipartition theorem, each quadratic degree of freedom contributes $\tfrac{1}{2}k_B T$ to the average energy. Hence the average energy per electron is
\[
\overline{E}=\frac{3}{2}k_B T.
\]\nTherefore the average contribution of each electron to the specific heat at constant volume is
\[
 c_V=\frac{d\overline{E}}{dT}=\frac{3}{2}k_B.
\]\nSo,
\[
\boxed{\overline{E}=\frac{3}{2}k_B T,\qquad c_V=\frac{3}{2}k_B}.
\]

knowledge_points.description: The problem instructs to treat conduction electrons as a classical ideal gas, which justifies using the equipartition theorem and ignoring quantum effects.

knowledge_points.description: A point particle (or monatomic ideal gas) has three translational degrees of freedom corresponding to motion in x, y, z directions.

knowledge_points.name: equipartition theorem
knowledge_points.description: In classical statistical mechanics, each quadratic degree of freedom contributes (1/2)k_B T to the average energy at thermal equilibrium.

title: Pancharatnam Phase
problem:
# Pancharatnam Phase

This problem deals with the two beam phenomena associated with light, its interference, polarization and superposition. The particular context of the problem was studied by the Indian physicist S. Pancharatnam (1934-1969).

S. Pancharatnam (1934-1969)

Consider the experimental set up as shown in Fig. (1). Two coherent monochromatic light beams (marked as beam 1 and 2), travelling in the $z$ direction, are incident on two narrow slits and separated by a distance $d$ ( $S_{1}S_{2} = d$ ). After passing through the slits the two beams interfere and the pattern is observed on the screen $S$ . The distance between the slits and the screen is $D$ and $D \gg d$ . Assume that the width of each slit $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ is much smaller than the wavelength of light.

Figure 1

III.1. Let the beams 1 and 2 be linearly polarized at $z =0$ . The corresponding electric field vectors are given by

$$\vec{E}_{1} = \hat{\imath} E_{0} \cos (\omega t) \tag{1a}$$

$$\vec{E}_{2} = \mathrm{i} E_{0} \cos (\omega t) \tag{1b}$$

where $\hat{t}$ is the unit vector along the $x$ -axis, $\omega$ is angular frequency of light and $E_0$ is the amplitude. Find the expression for the intensity of the light $I(\theta)$ , that will be observed on the screen where $\theta$ is the angle shown in Fig. (1). Express your answer in terms of $\theta, d, E_0, c$ and $\omega$ where $c$ is the speed of light. Also, note that the intensity is proportional to the time average of the square of the electric field. Here you make take the proportionality constant to be $\beta$ . You may ignore the attenuation in the magnitude of the electric fields with distance from the slits to any point on the screen.

III.2. A perfectly transparent glass slab of thickness $w$ and refractive index $\mu$ is

introduced in the path of beam 1 before the slits. Find the expression for the intensity of the light $I(\theta)$ that will be observed on the screen. Express your answer in terms of $\theta, d, E_0, c, \omega, \mu$ and $w$ .

III.3. An optical device (known as quarter wave plate (QWP)) is introduced in the path of beam 1, before the slits, replacing the glass slab. This device changes the polarization of the beam from the linear polarization state

$$\vec{E}_{1} = \hat{\imath} E_{0} \cos (\omega t)$$

to a circular polarization state which is given by

$$\vec{E}_{1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} [ \hat{\imath} E_{0} \cos (\omega t) + \hat{\jmath} E_{0} \sin (\omega t) ] \tag{2}$$

where $\hat{J}$ is the unit vector along the $y$ -axis.

Assume that the device does not introduce any additional path difference and that it is perfectly transparent. Note that the tip of the electric field vector traces a circle as time elapses and hence, the beam is said to be circularly polarized. We assume that the angle $\theta$ is small enough so that intensity from slit one does not depend on the angle $\theta$ even for $j$ polarization.

III.3.a. Find the expression for the intensity $I(\theta)$ of the light that will be observed on the screen. Express your answer in terms of $\theta, d, E_0, c$ and $\omega$ .
III.3.b. What is the maximum intensity $(I_{\max})$ ?
III.3.c. What is the minimum intensity $(I_{\min})$ ?

III.4.

Figure 2

Now, consider the experimental setup (see Fig. (2)) in which the beam 1 is subjected to

- the device (QWP) described in part 3 and,
- a linear polarizer (marked as I), between $z = a$ and $z = b$ which allows only the component of the electric field parallel to an axis ( $i'$ ) to pass through. The

unit vector $t'$ is defined as

$$\hat{t}^{\prime} = \hat{t} \cos \gamma + \hat{j} \sin \gamma$$

and,

- another linear polarizer (marked as II) between $z = b$ and $z = c$ which polarizes the beam back to $\hat{t}$ direction.

Thus the beam 1 is back to its original state of polarization. Assume that the polarizers do not introduce any path difference and are perfectly transparent.

III.4.a. Write down the expression for the electric field of beam 1 after the first polarizer at $z = b$ [E1(z = b)].
III.4.b. Write down the expression for the electric field of beam 1 after the second polarizer at $z = c$ [E1(z=c)].
III.4.c. What is the phase difference $(\alpha)$ between the two beams at the slits?

The most general type of polarization is elliptical polarization. A convenient way of expressing elliptical polarization is to consider it as a superposition of two orthogonal linearly polarized components i.e.

$$\vec{E} = \hat{\iota}^{\prime} E_{0} \cos e \cos (\omega t) + \hat{\jmath}^{\prime} E_{0} \sin e \sin (\omega t) \tag{3}$$

where $\hat{t}^{\prime}$ and $\hat{f}^{\prime}$ and this state of polarization are depicted in Fig. 3.

Figure 3

The tip of the electric field vector traces an ellipse as time elapses. Here $e$ represents the ellipticity and is given by

$$\tan e = \frac{\text{Semi - minoraxisoftheellipse}}{\text{Semi - majoraxisoftheellipse}}$$

Linear polarization (Eqs. (1)) and circular polarization (Eq. (2)) are special cases of elliptical polarization (Eq. (3)). The two parameters $\gamma (\in [0,\pi ])$ and $e(\in [-\pi /4,\pi /4])$ completely describe the state of polarization.

The polarization state can also be represented by a point on a sphere of unit radius called the Poincare sphere. The polarization of the beam described in Eq. (3) is represented by a point $P$ on the Poincare sphere (see Fig. 4), then latitude $\angle PCD =2e$ and longitude $\angle ACD =2\gamma$ . Here $C$ is the center.

Figure 4

III.5. Consider a point on the equator of the Poincare sphere.

III.5.a. Write down the electric field $(\vec{E}_{\mathrm{Eq}})$ corresponding to this point.

III.5.b. What is its state of polarization?

III.6. Consider a point at the north pole of the Poincare sphere.

III.6.a Write down the electric field $(\vec{E}_{\mathrm{NP}})$ corresponding to this point.

III.6.b What is its state of polarization?

III.7. Now, consider the three polarization states of beam 1 as given in part 4. Let the initial polarization (at $z =0$ ) be represented by a point $A_{1}$ on the Poincaré sphere; after the optical device, let the state (at $z = a$ ) be represented by point $A_{2}$ and after the first polarizer (say, at $z = b$ ), the state be represented by point $A_{3}$ . At $z = c$ , the polarization returns to its original state which is represented by $A_{1}$ . Locate these points $(A_{1}, A_{2},$ and $A_{3}$ ) on the Poincaré sphere.

III.8. If these three points $(A_{1}, A_{2}$ , and $A_{3}$ from the part (III.7)) are joined by great circles on the sphere, a triangle on the surface of the sphere is obtained (Note: A great circle is a circle on the sphere whose center coincides with the center of the sphere). The phase difference $\alpha$ obtained in part 4 and the area $S$ of the curved surface enclosed by the triangle are related to each other. Relate $S$ to $\alpha$ .

This relationship is general and was obtained by Pancharatnam and the phase difference is called the Pancharatnam phase.
solution:
III.1. The path difference between the two beams at angle \(\theta\) is \(d\sin\theta\), so the phase difference is
\[
\delta=\omega\Delta t=\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}.
\]
Hence
\[
I(\theta)=\beta\overline{|\mathbf E_1+\mathbf E_2|^2}
=\beta E_0^2\bigl(1+\cos\delta\bigr)
=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\cos\left(\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}\right)\right].
\]

III.2. A glass slab of thickness \(w\) and refractive index \(\mu\) adds optical path \((\mu-1)w\). Therefore
\[
\delta=\frac{\omega}{c}\Bigl(d\sin\theta-(\mu-1)w\Bigr),
\]
and
\[
I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\cos\left(\frac{\omega}{c}\bigl(d\sin\theta-(\mu-1)w\bigr)\right)\right].
\]

III.3. After the QWP, beam 1 is circularly polarized while beam 2 remains linearly polarized. Only the component of beam 1 parallel to beam 2 interferes, giving
\[
I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos\delta\right],
\qquad
\delta=\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}.
\]
Thus
\[
I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos\left(\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}\right)\right].
\]
So
\[
I_{\max}=\beta E_0^2\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right),
\qquad
I_{\min}=\beta E_0^2\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right).
\]

III.4. After the QWP, beam 1 is
\[
\mathbf E=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\hat{\mathbf i}\cos\omega t+\hat{\mathbf j}\sin\omega t\bigr).
\]
With \(\hat{\mathbf i}'=\hat{\mathbf i}\cos\gamma+\hat{\mathbf j}\sin\gamma\), the first polarizer gives
\[
\mathbf E_1(z=b)=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\cos(\omega t-kb-\gamma)\,\hat{\mathbf i}'.
\]
The second polarizer returns the beam to the \(\hat{\mathbf i}\) direction:
\[
\mathbf E_1(z=c)=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\cos\gamma\,\cos(\omega t-kc-\gamma)\,\hat{\mathbf i}.
\]
Since beam 2 at the slits is \(\mathbf E_2=E_0\cos(\omega t-kc)\hat{\mathbf i}\), the relative phase shift is
\[
\alpha=\gamma.
\]

III.5. A point on the equator corresponds to \(e=0\), i.e. linear polarization:
\[
\mathbf E_{\mathrm{Eq}}=E_0\hat{\mathbf i}'\cos(\omega t).
\]
Its state of polarization is linear.

III.6. A point at the north pole corresponds to \(e=\pi/4\), i.e. circular polarization:
\[
\mathbf E_{\mathrm{NP}}=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\hat{\mathbf i}\cos\omega t+\hat{\mathbf j}\sin\omega t\bigr).
\]
Its state of polarization is circular.

III.7. On the Poincaré sphere, \(A_1\) is the initial linear polarization along \(\hat{\mathbf i}\) on the equator; \(A_2\) is the north pole (circular polarization); \(A_3\) is the linear polarization along \(\hat{\mathbf i}'\) on the equator, at longitude \(2\gamma\).

III.8. The spherical triangle \(A_1A_2A_3\) encloses area \(S=2\gamma\), while the Pancharatnam phase is \(\alpha=\gamma\). Therefore
\[
\alpha=\frac{S}{2}
\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad
S=2\alpha.
\]
Thus the final relation is \(\boxed{\alpha=S/2}\).
answer: \boxed{I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\cos\left(\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}\right)\right]},\ \boxed{I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\cos\left(\frac{\omega}{c}\bigl(d\sin\theta-(\mu-1)w\bigr)\right)\right]},\ \boxed{I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos\left(\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}\right)\right]},\ \boxed{I_{\max}=\beta E_0^2\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)},\ \boxed{I_{\min}=\beta E_0^2\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)},\ \boxed{\alpha=\gamma},\ \boxed{\mathbf E_{\mathrm{Eq}}=E_0\hat{\mathbf i}'\cos(\omega t)},\ \boxed{\mathbf E_{\mathrm{NP}}=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}(\hat{\mathbf i}\cos\omega t+\hat{\mathbf j}\sin\omega t)},\ \boxed{A_1:\text{ equator at }\gamma=0,\ A_2:\text{ north pole,}\ A_3:\text{ equator at longitude }2\gamma},\ \boxed{S=2\alpha}

III.5.a. Write down the electric field $(\vec{E}_{\mathrm{Eq}})$ corresponding to this point.

III.5.b. What is its state of polarization?

III.6. Consider a point at the north pole of the Poincare sphere.

III.6.a Write down the electric field $(\vec{E}_{\mathrm{NP}})$ corresponding to this point.

III.6.b What is its state of polarization?

III.7. Now, consider the three polarization states of beam 1 as given in part 4. Let the initial polarization (at $z =0$ ) be represented by a point $A_{1}$ on the Poincaré sphere; after the optical device, let the state (at $z = a$ ) be represented by point $A_{2}$ and after the first polarizer (say, at $z = b$ ), the state be represented by point $A_{3}$ . At $z = c$ , the polarization returns to its original state which is represented by $A_{1}$ . Locate these points $(A_{1}, A_{2},$ and $A_{3}$ ) on the Poincaré sphere.

III.8. If these three points $(A_{1}, A_{2}$ , and $A_{3}$ from the part (III.7)) are joined by great circles on the sphere, a triangle on the surface of the sphere is obtained (Note: A great circle is a circle on the sphere whose center coincides with the center of the sphere). The phase difference $\alpha$ obtained in part 4 and the area $S$ of the curved surface enclosed by the triangle are related to each other. Relate $S$ to $\alpha$ .

This relationship is general and was obtained by Pancharatnam and the phase difference is called the Pancharatnam phase.
sub_problems.solution:
III.1. The path difference between the two beams at angle \(\theta\) is \(d\sin\theta\), so the phase difference is
\[
\delta=\omega\Delta t=\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}.
\]
Hence
\[
I(\theta)=\beta\overline{|\mathbf E_1+\mathbf E_2|^2}
=\beta E_0^2\bigl(1+\cos\delta\bigr)
=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\cos\left(\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}\right)\right].
\]

III.2. A glass slab of thickness \(w\) and refractive index \(\mu\) adds optical path \((\mu-1)w\). Therefore
\[
\delta=\frac{\omega}{c}\Bigl(d\sin\theta-(\mu-1)w\Bigr),
\]
and
\[
I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\cos\left(\frac{\omega}{c}\bigl(d\sin\theta-(\mu-1)w\bigr)\right)\right].
\]

III.3. After the QWP, beam 1 is circularly polarized while beam 2 remains linearly polarized. Only the component of beam 1 parallel to beam 2 interferes, giving
\[
I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos\delta\right],
\qquad
\delta=\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}.
\]
Thus
\[
I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos\left(\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}\right)\right].
\]
So
\[
I_{\max}=\beta E_0^2\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right),
\qquad
I_{\min}=\beta E_0^2\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right).
\]

III.4. After the QWP, beam 1 is
\[
\mathbf E=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\hat{\mathbf i}\cos\omega t+\hat{\mathbf j}\sin\omega t\bigr).
\]
With \(\hat{\mathbf i}'=\hat{\mathbf i}\cos\gamma+\hat{\mathbf j}\sin\gamma\), the first polarizer gives
\[
\mathbf E_1(z=b)=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\cos(\omega t-kb-\gamma)\,\hat{\mathbf i}'.
\]
The second polarizer returns the beam to the \(\hat{\mathbf i}\) direction:
\[
\mathbf E_1(z=c)=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\cos\gamma\,\cos(\omega t-kc-\gamma)\,\hat{\mathbf i}.
\]
Since beam 2 at the slits is \(\mathbf E_2=E_0\cos(\omega t-kc)\hat{\mathbf i}\), the relative phase shift is
\[
\alpha=\gamma.
\]

III.5. A point on the equator corresponds to \(e=0\), i.e. linear polarization:
\[
\mathbf E_{\mathrm{Eq}}=E_0\hat{\mathbf i}'\cos(\omega t).
\]
Its state of polarization is linear.

III.6. A point at the north pole corresponds to \(e=\pi/4\), i.e. circular polarization:
\[
\mathbf E_{\mathrm{NP}}=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\hat{\mathbf i}\cos\omega t+\hat{\mathbf j}\sin\omega t\bigr).
\]
Its state of polarization is circular.

III.7. On the Poincaré sphere, \(A_1\) is the initial linear polarization along \(\hat{\mathbf i}\) on the equator; \(A_2\) is the north pole (circular polarization); \(A_3\) is the linear polarization along \(\hat{\mathbf i}'\) on the equator, at longitude \(2\gamma\).

III.8. The spherical triangle \(A_1A_2A_3\) encloses area \(S=2\gamma\), while the Pancharatnam phase is \(\alpha=\gamma\). Therefore
\[
\alpha=\frac{S}{2}
\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad
S=2\alpha.
\]
Thus the final relation is \(\boxed{\alpha=S/2}\).
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\cos\left(\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}\right)\right]},\ \boxed{I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\cos\left(\frac{\omega}{c}\bigl(d\sin\theta-(\mu-1)w\bigr)\right)\right]},\ \boxed{I(\theta)=\beta E_0^2\left[1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos\left(\frac{\omega d\sin\theta}{c}\right)\right]},\ \boxed{I_{\max}=\beta E_0^2\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)},\ \boxed{I_{\min}=\beta E_0^2\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)},\ \boxed{\alpha=\gamma},\ \boxed{\mathbf E_{\mathrm{Eq}}=E_0\hat{\mathbf i}'\cos(\omega t)},\ \boxed{\mathbf E_{\mathrm{NP}}=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt2}(\hat{\mathbf i}\cos\omega t+\hat{\mathbf j}\sin\omega t)},\ \boxed{A_1:\text{ equator at }\gamma=0,\ A_2:\text{ north pole,}\ A_3:\text{ equator at longitude }2\gamma},\ \boxed{S=2\alpha}
