knowledge_points.description: At the perihelion and aphelion of an elliptical orbit the radial velocity is zero and the velocity vector is perpendicular to the radius, so angular momentum magnitude simplifies to m r v.

title: RF Reflectometry of Single-Electron Circuits - Part F: Charge sensing with a single lead quantum dot
problem:
# RF reflectometry for spin readout for silicon quantum computing

# Introduction

Developing the idea of quantum computing into a practical technology is one of the largest outstanding challenges in science and technology. A promising path is to manipulate individual electrons in silicon transistors by time-dependent electromagnetic fields.

In this question, we investigate the use of radio frequency (RF) reflectometry and single-electron transistors to read out the state of quantum bits in silicon-based quantum computer prototypes.

Part A and Part B discuss radio wave transmission through cables and transmission lines, part C is devoted to conditions for wave reflection, part D introduces the single-electron transistor, and parts E and F introduce and ask you to optimise the method of reflectometry.

# Part F: Charge sensing with a single lead quantum dot

For a scalable quantum computing architecture, the number of wires reaching each individual quantum bit need to be minimized. A promising alternative to an SET for charge sensing in silicon quantum com

puting is a Single Lead Quantum Dot (SLQD). In many ways it is similar to an SET, but does not have the source and drain leads. The gate is the only electrode, through which the electron energy states of the quantum dot are controlled and also through which RF reflectometry is conducted.

Like an SET, a SLQD has an OFF in which the SLQD behaves as a total insulator. In contrast to an SET, the ON state of the SLQD is capacitive, with capacitance $C_{\mathrm{q}}$ . In order to maximize the difference in reflectance $\Delta \Gamma$ of the SLQD, the following circuit is constructed. The parasitic capacitance $C_0 \approx 0.4 \mathrm{pF}$ is fixed by circuit geometry, but the value of $L_{0}$ and the operating frequency can be changed to optimize the performance. The characteristic impedance of the transmission line is $Z_{0} =50\Omega$ .

Circuit diagram of the SLQD readout circuit connected to the transmission line.

sub_problems.problem:
(F.1) Suggest $\omega_{\mathrm{rf}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{C}} = \sqrt{L_0/ C_0}$ that allow $\Delta \Gamma \sim 1$ for given $C_0$ and $C_q$ .

Optimal values of $L_{0}$ are relatively large and not always technically feasible. Hence, other types of circuit elements may be needed to improve sensitivity of the reflectometry readout circuit.
sub_problems.solution:
For the readout circuit, the reflection coefficient is determined by the total impedance seen by the transmission line. Since the circuit contains only reactive elements, $|\Gamma|=1$ and the information is encoded in the phase of $\Gamma$.
\nTo make the OFF state strongly resonant, choose the RF angular frequency to match the LC resonance of $L_0$ and $C_0$:
\[
\omega_{\mathrm{rf}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L_0 C_0}}.
\]\nAt this frequency, the OFF-state impedance is very large, so the reflection phase corresponds to an open circuit.
\nIn the ON state, the quantum capacitance $C_q$ adds in parallel with $C_0$, so the total impedance at resonance is
\[\nZ_{\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{1}{(j\omega_{\mathrm{rf}}L_0)^{-1}+j\omega_{\mathrm{rf}}(C_0+C_q)}
=-j\frac{1}{\omega_0 C_q}
=-j\frac{C_0}{C_q}Z_C,
\]\nwhere $Z_C=\sqrt{L_0/C_0}$.
\nTo obtain a substantial difference in the reflection coefficient between ON and OFF states, this impedance should be comparable to the line impedance $Z_0$, so that the phase of $\Gamma_{\mathrm{ON}}$ differs significantly from zero. Therefore,
\[\nZ_C\sim \frac{C_q}{C_0}Z_0.
\]\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{\omega_{\mathrm{rf}}=1/\sqrt{L_0C_0}},\ \boxed{Z_C\sim (C_q/C_0)Z_0}\).

knowledge_points.name: LC resonance frequency
knowledge_points.description: The resonant angular frequency of a parallel LC circuit is ω_0 = 1/√(LC). At this frequency, the parallel impedance is maximum (ideally infinite). Used to set ω_rf so that the OFF state (L_0 and C_0) presents an open circuit to the transmission line.

knowledge_points.name: Impedance of inductor and capacitor
knowledge_points.description: The complex impedance of an inductor is Z_L = jωL, and of a capacitor is Z_C = 1/(jωC) = -j/(ωC). Needed to express the total impedance of the circuit elements.

knowledge_points.name: Parallel impedance combination
knowledge_points.description: For impedances in parallel, the total impedance Z_tot satisfies 1/Z_tot = Σ 1/Z_i. Used to combine the inductor L_0 with the capacitors C_0 and C_q in the ON state.

knowledge_points.name: Reflection coefficient on a transmission line
knowledge_points.description: The voltage reflection coefficient Γ for a load impedance Z_L on a line of characteristic impedance Z_0 is Γ = (Z_L - Z_0)/(Z_L + Z_0). For a reactive load, |Γ| = 1 and the phase of Γ encodes the load impedance. Used to relate the circuit impedance to the reflectance ΔΓ.

knowledge_points.name: Impedance matching for maximum phase sensitivity
knowledge_points.description: To maximize the change in reflection coefficient between two load states, the load impedance in one state should be comparable to Z_0, while the other state is far from Z_0 (e.g., open circuit). This ensures a large phase difference and high readout sensitivity. Applied to set Z_C ~ (C_q/C_0) Z_0.

knowledge_points.name: Characteristic impedance of a transmission line
knowledge_points.description: The characteristic impedance Z_0 is the ratio of voltage to current for a wave on a transmission line, typically 50 Ω. It serves as the reference impedance for defining the reflection coefficient and for impedance matching.

sub_problems.problem: (F.2) Assume that $L_{0}$ (and hence $Z_{C}$ ) is fixed. Draw a circuit diagram showing where to place an additional element in the SLQD readout circuit and specify the parameter(s) of this element such that $\Delta \Gamma \sim 1$ can still be achieved without requiring a large inductance.
sub_problems.solution:
At fixed $L_0$, the resonant frequency is still chosen as
\[
\omega_{\mathrm{rf}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L_0C_0}},
\]\nso that the empty circuit gives the reference reflection condition.
\nIf $L_0$ cannot be made large enough to satisfy the readout condition by itself, one can increase the magnitude of the total impedance by adding an extra capacitor $C_m$ in series with the rest of the readout circuit. The added element should be placed so that, at $\omega=\omega_{\mathrm{rf}}$, the total impedance becomes
\[\nZ_{\mathrm{tot}}=-j\left(\frac{C_0}{C_q}Z_C+\frac{1}{\omega_0 C_m}\right).
\]\nEquivalently,
\[\nZ_{\mathrm{tot}}=-j\,\omega_0^{-1}\left(C_q^{-1}+C_m^{-1}\right).
\]\nTo obtain $\Delta\Gamma\sim 1$, we require $|Z_{\mathrm{tot}}|\approx Z_0$, which gives
\[\nC_m=\frac{C_q}{Z_0C_q\omega_{\mathrm{rf}}-1}
=\frac{C_q\sqrt{L_0C_0}}{Z_0C_q-\sqrt{L_0C_0}}.
\]\nUsing $Z_C=\sqrt{L_0/C_0}$, this can also be written as
\[\nC_m=\frac{C_q Z_C}{Z_0C_q/C_0-Z_C}.
\]\nIn the common limit $Z_C\ll Z_0C_q/C_0$, this reduces to
\[\nC_m\approx \frac{1}{Z_0\omega_{\mathrm{rf}}}.
\]\nTherefore, an additional series capacitor of the above value should be added so that $\Delta\Gamma\sim 1$ can still be achieved without requiring a large inductance. Final answer: \boxed{\text{Add a series capacitor }C_m\text{ with }C_m=\frac{C_q Z_C}{Z_0C_q/C_0-Z_C}\approx\frac{1}{Z_0\omega_{\mathrm{rf}}}}

knowledge_points.name: LC resonant frequency
knowledge_points.description: The resonant angular frequency of an LC circuit is ω0 = 1/√(LC). Used here to set the operating frequency so that the empty circuit (OFF state) provides the reference reflection condition.

knowledge_points.name: Capacitor impedance
knowledge_points.description: The complex impedance of a capacitor is Z_C = 1/(jω C). Used to express the impedance of the added series capacitor Cm.

knowledge_points.name: Series impedance addition
knowledge_points.description: The total impedance of elements connected in series is the sum of their individual impedances. Used to add the series capacitor to the original circuit impedance.

knowledge_points.name: Characteristic impedance of LC circuit
knowledge_points.description: The characteristic impedance of an LC circuit is ZC = √(L/C), the magnitude of the reactance of the inductor or capacitor at resonance. The problem defines it and the solution uses it in the impedance expressions.

knowledge_points.name: ON-state impedance of SLQD circuit
knowledge_points.description: In the ON state, the SLQD readout circuit (without additional elements) has an impedance Z_on = -j (C0/Cq) ZC, where C0 is the parasitic capacitance, Cq is the SLQD capacitance, and ZC = √(L0/C0). This result from F.1 is used as the starting point for adding the matching element.

knowledge_points.name: Readout condition for maximum reflectance change
knowledge_points.description: To achieve a reflectance change ΔΓ ~ 1, the magnitude of the load impedance in the ON state must be approximately equal to the transmission line characteristic impedance Z0. This condition is derived in F.1 and is the design target here.

knowledge_points.name: Series capacitor for impedance matching
knowledge_points.description: Adding a capacitor in series with a capacitive load increases the total capacitive reactance, thereby increasing the magnitude of the total impedance. This technique is used to meet the |Z| ≈ Z0 condition when the original impedance is too small.

title: Jets from AGN - Part D: Synchrotron emission from an AGN jet
problem:
# X-ray jets from active galactic nuclei

# Introduction

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are supermassive black holes which form the centres of galaxies, and emit large amounts of energy in radiation and particle flows. One feature of many AGN are jetted outflows, which can be observed through radio emission, and sometimes also in other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, including x-rays. These jets are large flows of plasma at relativistic speeds, over lengths of order $10^{20}\mathrm{m}$ , which is tens of thousands of light years. The x-ray emission from jets is usually dominated by synchrotron emission from relativistic electrons gyrating in the magnetic field of the jet.

Figure 1: X-ray image of the jet from the Centaurus A AGN. Darker regions represent regions of higher intensity x-rays. Brighter regions within the fainter jet are called knots. (Snios et al., 2019)

# Part D: Synchrotron emission from an AGN jet

The distribution of electron energies in a jet from an AGN is typically a power law, of the form $f(\epsilon) = \kappa \epsilon^{-p}$ , where $f(\epsilon)d\epsilon$ is the number density of particles with energies between $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon + d\epsilon$ . The corresponding spectrum of synchrotron emission depends on the electron energy distribution, rather than the spectrum for an individual electron. This spectrum is

$$j (\nu) d \nu \propto B^{(1+ p) /2} \nu^{(1- p) /2} d \nu . \tag{3}$$

Here $j(\nu)d\nu$ is the energy per unit volume emitted as photons with frequencies between $\nu$ and $\nu + d\nu$

Observations of the Centaurus A jet, and other jets, show a knotty structure, with compact regions of brighter emission called knots. Observations of these knots at different times have shown both motion and brightness changes for some knots. Two possible mechanisms for the reductions in brightness are adiabatic expansion of the gas in the knot, and synchrotron cooling of electrons in the gas in knot.

The magnetic field in the plasma in the jets is assumed to be frozen in. Considering an arbitrary volume of plasma, the magnetic flux through the surface bounding it must remain constant, even as the volume containing the plasma changes shape and size.

sub_problems.problem: (D.1) For a spherical knot which expands uniformly in all directions from a volume of $0.4\mathrm{pt} V_0$ to a volume $V$ , with an initial uniform magnetic field $B_0$ Find the magnetic field $B$ in the expanded knot.
sub_problems.solution:
Assuming the magnetic field is frozen into the plasma, the magnetic flux through any material surface of the knot is conserved:
\[\nB_0 A_0 = BA.
\]\nFor a uniform spherical expansion, linear dimensions scale as $V^{1/3}$, so the area scales as
\[\nA \propto V^{2/3}.
\]\nHence,
\[
\frac{A_0}{A}=\left(\frac{V_0}{V}\right)^{2/3}.
\]\nTherefore,
\[\nB = B_0\frac{A_0}{A}=B_0\left(\frac{V}{V_0}\right)^{-2/3}.
\]\nSo the magnetic field in the expanded knot is
\[
\boxed{B = B_0\left(\frac{V}{V_0}\right)^{-2/3}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: frozen-in magnetic field (flux freezing)
knowledge_points.description: In ideal MHD, magnetic field lines are frozen into the plasma, so the magnetic flux through any material surface moving with the plasma remains constant. This is used to relate initial and final magnetic fields via flux conservation.

knowledge_points.name: magnetic flux
knowledge_points.description: Magnetic flux through a surface is defined as the product of the perpendicular magnetic field and the area (for uniform field). It is the conserved quantity in flux freezing.

knowledge_points.name: area-volume scaling for sphere
knowledge_points.description: For a uniformly expanding sphere, the surface area scales as the two-thirds power of the volume: A ∝ V^{2/3}. This is derived from V ∝ r^3 and A ∝ r^2.

knowledge_points.name: uniform spherical expansion
knowledge_points.description: The knot expands uniformly in all directions, preserving its spherical shape, so linear dimensions scale as V^{1/3}. This allows the area scaling to be applied.

sub_problems.problem: (D.2) Find $f(\epsilon)$ , the distribution of electron energies after adiabatic expansion of a spherical knot to a volume $V$ on the distribution of electron energy densities, given that the knot of volume $V_0$ has an initial distribution of electrons $f_0(\epsilon) = \kappa_0 \epsilon^{-p}$ , where $f_0(\epsilon) d\epsilon$ is the number density of particles with energies between $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon + d\epsilon$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For an adiabatic expansion of a relativistic knot, the particle momenta scale as
\[
\epsilon \propto V^{-1/3}.
\]\nSo if the volume changes from $V_0$ to $V$, then an initial particle energy $\epsilon_0$ becomes
\[
\epsilon = \left(\frac{V}{V_0}\right)^{-1/3}\epsilon_0,
\qquad
\epsilon_0 = \left(\frac{V}{V_0}\right)^{1/3}\epsilon.
\]
\nNumber of particles is conserved. Hence the number in an energy interval must satisfy
\[\nV f(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon = V_0 f_0(\epsilon_0)\,d\epsilon_0.
\]\nUsing $f_0(\epsilon_0)=\kappa_0\epsilon_0^{-p}$ and
\[
\frac{d\epsilon_0}{d\epsilon}=\left(\frac{V}{V_0}\right)^{1/3},
\]\nwe obtain
\[\nV f(\epsilon)
= V_0\kappa_0 \left(\epsilon\left(\frac{V}{V_0}\right)^{1/3}\right)^{-p}
\left(\frac{V}{V_0}\right)^{1/3}.
\]\nTherefore
\[\nf(\epsilon)=\kappa_0\left(\frac{V}{V_0}\right)^{-(p+2)/3}\epsilon^{-p}.
\]\nSo the spectrum remains a power law with the same index, and the normalization changes as
\[
\boxed{\kappa=\kappa_0\left(\frac{V}{V_0}\right)^{-(p+2)/3}}.
\]\nThus
\[
\boxed{f(\epsilon)=\kappa_0\left(\frac{V}{V_0}\right)^{-(p+2)/3}\epsilon^{-p}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: adiabatic expansion
knowledge_points.description: The knot expands adiabatically, so no heat is exchanged and the process is slow enough that the adiabatic invariant applies, causing particle energies to change with volume.

knowledge_points.name: ultra-relativistic electrons
knowledge_points.description: The electrons are ultra-relativistic, so their energy is proportional to momentum (ε ≈ pc), which is required for the ε ∝ V^{-1/3} scaling used in the solution.

knowledge_points.name: adiabatic energy scaling for ultra-relativistic particles
knowledge_points.description: For an ultra-relativistic gas in adiabatic expansion, particle energy scales as ε ∝ V^{-1/3} (or momentum p ∝ V^{-1/3}), derived from the adiabatic invariant pV^{1/3} = constant.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of particle number
knowledge_points.description: The total number of electrons in the knot is conserved during expansion, leading to the relation V f(ε) dε = V₀ f₀(ε₀) dε₀.

knowledge_points.name: distribution function transformation
knowledge_points.description: When a physical variable changes, the differential number density transforms using conservation of total number, requiring the Jacobian dε₀/dε to relate f(ε) and f₀(ε₀).

sub_problems.problem:
(D.3) How will synchrotron cooling affect the distribution of the electrons? After a time interval where electrons have been undergoing synchrotron cooling, will the distribution of electron energies as a function of $\epsilon$ be steeper, shallower or leave it unchanged. Justify your answer with equations, by considering two electron energies $\epsilon_{1} < \epsilon_{2}$ . The table below summarises some observations of knots (brighter regions) in jets from two AGN, Cen Taurus A (Cen A) and M87. (Data from Snios et al., 2019a; 2019b.)
AGNTime between observationsKnotBrightness change in x-raysSpectral changes in x-raysBrightness changes in other bands (e.g. UV, optical)
Cen A15 yearsAX1C-23%No changeNo data
Cen A15 yearsBX2-15%No changeNo data
M875 yearsHST-1-73%No dataNo change
M875 yearsKnot A-12%No dataNo change
sub_problems.solution:
For synchrotron radiation, the energy loss rate increases with electron energy as
\[
\frac{d\epsilon}{dt}\propto -\epsilon^2.
\]\nHence the cooling time is
\[\nt_c\sim \frac{\epsilon}{|d\epsilon/dt|}\propto \frac{1}{\epsilon}.
\]\nSo higher-energy electrons lose energy faster than lower-energy ones.
\nConsider two electrons with energies \(\epsilon_1<\epsilon_2\). Then
\[
\left|\frac{d\epsilon_2}{dt}\right| > \left|\frac{d\epsilon_1}{dt}\right|,
\]\nso the population at larger \(\epsilon\) is depleted more rapidly. As a result, after synchrotron cooling the electron energy distribution becomes steeper at high energy.
\nFinal answer: the electron energy distribution becomes \(\boxed{\text{steeper}}\).

knowledge_points.name: synchrotron energy loss rate for a single electron
knowledge_points.description: The rate at which a single electron loses energy by synchrotron radiation is proportional to the square of its energy, dε/dt ∝ -ε². This is used to compare cooling rates for electrons of different energies.

knowledge_points.name: cooling timescale
knowledge_points.description: The characteristic cooling time is t_cool ~ ε/|dε/dt|. For synchrotron cooling this gives t_cool ∝ 1/ε, so higher-energy electrons lose their energy faster, leading to a steeper energy distribution.

sub_problems.problem: (D.4) In the table in the answer sheet, identify the more likely cause of reduced brightness for each knot, and identify which previous part or parts support your conclusion.
sub_problems.solution:
For the knots in Centaurus A, there is no change in the X-ray spectrum. If synchrotron cooling were responsible, the spectrum would steepen, as established in Part D3. Since this is not observed, synchrotron cooling is unlikely, and the reduced brightness is more likely due to adiabatic cooling.
\nFor the knots in M87, there is no change in brightness in other bands. Adiabatic expansion would reduce the number density at all energies, and therefore decrease the brightness at all wavelengths, as noted in Part D2. Since this is not seen, adiabatic expansion is unlikely, so synchrotron cooling is more likely.
\nFinal answer: Centaurus A knots  adiabatic cooling, supported by Part D3; M87 knots  synchrotron cooling, supported by Part D2.
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{Centaurus A: adiabatic cooling; M87: synchrotron cooling}}

knowledge_points.name: adiabatic expansion reduces brightness uniformly
knowledge_points.description: Adiabatic expansion of a knot reduces the number density of electrons at all energies, decreasing brightness at all wavelengths without changing the spectral shape (result from part D.2).

knowledge_points.name: synchrotron cooling steepens spectrum
knowledge_points.description: Synchrotron cooling causes higher-energy electrons to lose energy faster, steepening the electron energy distribution and thus the synchrotron spectrum (result from part D.3).

knowledge_points.name: synchrotron emission spectrum power law
knowledge_points.description: The synchrotron emission spectrum j(ν) ∝ B^{(1+p)/2} ν^{(1-p)/2} links the electron energy power-law index p to the spectral index, so a change in p alters the spectral shape.

knowledge_points.name: spectral index
knowledge_points.description: The spectral index is the exponent in a power-law spectrum; a steeper spectrum (more negative index) indicates a change in the underlying electron energy distribution, used to interpret 'no change' vs 'steepening'.

title: Maxwell Rayleigh and Mount Everest - Parts A-C: Rayleigh scattering attenuation
problem:
# Maxwell, Rayleigh and Mount Everest: THE PROBLEM<sup>1</sup>

Lord Rayleigh visited Darjeeling, India in 1897. On viewing Mount Everest at a distance of $170\mathrm{km}$ he was reminded of a query by James Maxwell 26 years earlier on the attenuation of light by air and the visibility of far-off peaks. Lord Rayleigh authored a famous research paper<sup>2</sup> two years later in 1899 in which he investigated this problem. In the present problem we attempt to reconstruct, at least partially, a modern version of Lord Rayleigh's line of reasoning.

Oscillation of the electron cloud: We model a typical neutral air molecule by a stationary positive charge $q$ surrounded by a spherical uniform charge cloud of mass $m$ , radius $r$ and charge $-q$ . The natural angular frequency of vibration of the molecule is $\omega_0$ . Light is incident on it and the negative cloud oscillates maintaining its spherical shape with angular frequency $\omega$ as,

$$y = y_{0} \cos (\omega t), \tag{1}$$

under the influence of the electric field

$$\vec{E} (t) = E_{0} \cos (\omega t) \hat{y}, \tag{2}$$

of the light wave. Here $y$ represents the separation between the stationary positive charge and the centre of the negative charge cloud of the molecule.

sub_problems.problem: (A.1) Set up the equation for the motion for $y$ . Take the contribution to the magnitude of the acceleration due to the electric field to be $E(t)q / m$
sub_problems.solution:
Without the external electric field, the separation $y$ between the positive core and the negative charge cloud performs simple harmonic motion with natural angular frequency $\omega_0$, so the restoring acceleration is
\[
\ddot y = -\omega_0^2 y.
\]
\nWhen the light field
\[
\vec E(t)=E_0\cos(\omega t)\,\hat y
\]\nacts on the negatively charged cloud, the electric force is $\vec F_E=-q\vec E(t)$, so the additional acceleration is
\[
\frac{F_E}{m}=-\frac{qE_0}{m}\cos(\omega t).
\]
\nTherefore the equation of motion is
\[
\ddot y = -\omega_0^2 y-\frac{qE_0}{m}\cos(\omega t),
\]\nor equivalently,
\[
\boxed{\ddot y+\omega_0^2 y=-\frac{qE_0}{m}\cos(\omega t)}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: undamped oscillator
knowledge_points.description: The molecule is idealized as a lossless harmonic oscillator, so no damping term appears in the equation of motion.

knowledge_points.name: simple harmonic oscillator restoring force
knowledge_points.description: For a system with natural angular frequency ω0, the restoring acceleration is −ω0² y, giving the homogeneous term in the equation of motion.

knowledge_points.name: electric force direction
knowledge_points.description: A charge q in an electric field E experiences force F = qE; a negative charge (−q) feels a force opposite to the field, determining the sign of the driving term.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law
knowledge_points.description: Net force equals mass times acceleration (F_net = m a). Used to combine the restoring and electric forces into a single differential equation for the displacement y.

sub_problems.problem: (A.2) Based on the information provided above, solve the equation for $y$ . Find the $0.5\mathrm{pt}$ amplitude.
sub_problems.solution:
The displacement of the negative charge cloud satisfies the driven harmonic oscillator equation
\[
\ddot y + \omega_0^2 y = -\frac{q}{m}E_0\cos(\omega t).
\]\nWe look for a steady-state solution of the form
\[\ny(t)=y_0\cos(\omega t).
\]\nThen
\[
\ddot y(t)=-\omega^2 y_0\cos(\omega t).
\]\nSubstituting into the equation of motion gives
\[
-\omega^2 y_0\cos(\omega t)+\omega_0^2 y_0\cos(\omega t)=-\frac{q}{m}E_0\cos(\omega t).
\]\nCanceling $\cos(\omega t)$ yields
\[
(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)y_0=-\frac{qE_0}{m},
\]\nso
\[\ny_0=\frac{qE_0/m}{\omega^2-\omega_0^2}.
\]\nThus the oscillation is
\[
\boxed{y(t)=\frac{qE_0/m}{\omega^2-\omega_0^2}\cos(\omega t)}.
\]\nThe amplitude is
\[
\boxed{y_0=\frac{qE_0/m}{\omega^2-\omega_0^2}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: driven harmonic oscillator
knowledge_points.description: The equation of motion derived in (A.1) is a driven harmonic oscillator; one needs to recognise that the system is linear with a sinusoidal forcing term, and that the long-term (steady‑state) response will be at the driving frequency.

knowledge_points.name: steady‑state solution ansatz
knowledge_points.description: To solve for the amplitude, one assumes a steady‑state solution of the form y(t)=y0 cos(ωt) (same frequency as the driving), substitutes it into the driven oscillator equation, and algebraically solves for y0. This is the standard method for finding the particular solution of a linear ODE with a sinusoidal forcing term.

sub_problems.problem: (A.3) Find the magnitude $p(t)$ of the dipole moment of the air molecule as a function of time for $\omega \ll \omega_0$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a neutral molecule with charges $+q$ and $-q$ separated by a distance $y(t)$, the dipole moment magnitude is
\[\np(t)=q\,y(t).
\]\nThe negative charge cloud behaves like a driven harmonic oscillator with natural angular frequency $\omega_0$. In the limit $\omega \ll \omega_0$, the displacement follows the driving field quasi-statically, so
\[\nm\omega_0^2 y(t) \approx qE_0\cos(\omega t).
\]\nHence
\[\ny(t) \approx \frac{qE_0}{m\omega_0^2}\cos(\omega t).
\]\nTherefore the dipole moment is
\[\np(t)=q\,y(t) \approx \frac{q^2E_0}{m\omega_0^2}\cos(\omega t).
\]\nSo the magnitude of the dipole moment is
\[
\boxed{p(t)=\frac{q^2E_0}{m\omega_0^2}\cos(\omega t)}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: electric dipole moment
knowledge_points.description: The electric dipole moment of two equal and opposite charges ±q separated by distance y has magnitude p = qy. This is needed to compute p(t) from the displacement y(t).

knowledge_points.name: simple harmonic oscillator restoring force
knowledge_points.description: For a simple harmonic oscillator with natural angular frequency ω0, the restoring force is F = -m ω0^2 y, so the equation of motion is d^2y/dt^2 + ω0^2 y = 0. This is used to write the restoring force term in the driven oscillator equation.

knowledge_points.name: quasi-static approximation for driven oscillator
knowledge_points.description: For a driven harmonic oscillator with driving frequency ω much less than its natural frequency ω0, the inertial term m d^2y/dt^2 is negligible, so the displacement follows the driving force quasi-statically: m ω0^2 y ≈ F_ext(t). This yields y(t) in the limit ω << ω0.

sub_problems.problem:
(A.4) Obtain an expression for $\omega_0$ in terms of $q, m$ and $r$ .

Power radiated: The sinusoidal time dependent dipole radiates electromagnetic radiation. The power radiated depends on the amplitude of the dipole moment $p_0= qy_0$ , the permittivity of vacuum $\epsilon_0$ , the speed of light $c$ , and the frequency of oscillation $\omega$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a small displacement $y$ of the negative spherical charge cloud relative to the কেন্দric positive charge, the electrostatic restoring force is linear in $y$:

\[\nF = -\frac{q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}\,y.
\]
\nThe equation of motion is therefore

\[\nm\ddot y = -\frac{q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}\,y = -m\omega_0^2 y.
\]
\nComparing coefficients gives

\[
\omega_0^2 = \frac{q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 m r^3},
\]\nso the natural angular frequency is

\[
\boxed{\omega_0 = \frac{q}{\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_0 m r^3}}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: uniform spherical charge cloud
knowledge_points.description: The negative charge of the molecule is modeled as a rigid uniform sphere of radius r that maintains its shape during oscillation, as stated in the problem text; this justifies the use of the electric field inside a uniform sphere to obtain a linear restoring force.

knowledge_points.name: electric field inside a uniformly charged sphere
knowledge_points.description: To find the restoring force when the negative cloud is displaced by y relative to the positive point charge, the electric field inside a uniform sphere of charge is needed: E = (Q/(4πε₀R³)) r. Applied here with Q = -q and R = r, this gives the force F = -(q²/(4πε₀ r³)) y.

knowledge_points.name: simple harmonic oscillator natural frequency
knowledge_points.description: Once the linear restoring force F = -k y is obtained, the equation of motion m d²y/dt² = -k y yields a simple harmonic oscillator with natural angular frequency ω₀ = √(k/m). Here k = q²/(4πε₀ r³).

sub_problems.problem: (B.1) Use dimensional analysis to express the average power $s$ radiated in terms of these quantities.
sub_problems.solution:
Let the average radiated power $s$ depend on the dipole amplitude $p_0$, angular frequency $\omega$, vacuum permittivity $\epsilon_0$, and speed of light $c$.
\nAssume a power-law form
\[\ns \propto p_0^{\alpha}\,\omega^{\beta}\,\epsilon_0^{\gamma}\,c^{\delta}.
\]
\nNow use dimensions:
\[
[s]=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}},\qquad [p_0]=\mathrm{C\,m},\qquad [\omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}},
\]
\[
[\epsilon_0]=\mathrm{C^2\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-3}\,s^2},\qquad [c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.
\]
\nThus
\[
[s]=[p_0]^\alpha[\omega]^\beta[\epsilon_0]^\gamma[c]^\delta.
\]\nMatching powers of $\mathrm{C}$, $\mathrm{kg}$, $\mathrm{m}$, and $\mathrm{s}$ gives
\[
\alpha+2\gamma=0,
\]
\[
-\gamma=1,
\]
\[
\alpha-3\gamma+\delta=2,
\]
\[
\beta-2\gamma+\delta=3.
\]\nSolving yields
\[
\alpha=2,\qquad \beta=4,\qquad \gamma=-1,\qquad \delta=-3.
\]\nTherefore,
\[\ns = k\,\frac{p_0^2\omega^4}{\epsilon_0 c^3},
\]\nwhere $k$ is a dimensionless constant.

knowledge_points.name: SI dimensions of relevant quantities
knowledge_points.description: The base SI dimensions of average power (ML^2 T^{-3}), electric dipole moment (C L), angular frequency (T^{-1}), vacuum permittivity (C^2 M^{-1} L^{-3} T^2), and speed of light (L T^{-1}) must be known to set up the dimensional equations.

knowledge_points.name: Dimensional analysis (method of dimensions)
knowledge_points.description: The method of equating the dimensions of a target quantity to the product of candidate physical quantities raised to unknown exponents, then solving the resulting system of linear equations for the exponents.

knowledge_points.name: Monomial power‑law dependence
knowledge_points.description: The radiated power is assumed to be proportional to a product of powers of the given parameters (p0^α ω^β ε0^γ c^δ), without additive terms or other functional forms.

sub_problems.problem:
(B.2) Take the proportionality constant to be $1/12\pi$ . Express the answer for the power radiated $s$ in terms of $E_0, \omega_0, \omega$ and related quantities. Take $\omega \ll \omega_0$ .

Attenuation of the Intensity $I(x)$ : Recall that the intensity of EM waves is

$$\frac{1}{2} c \epsilon_{0} E_{0}^{2}. \tag{3}$$

The intensity decreases along the path of light because the power

$$S = n_{0} s \tag{4}$$

is lost per unit volume. Here $n_0$ is the number of molecules per unit volume.
sub_problems.solution:
For a driven oscillator of charge $-q$ and mass $m$, the displacement amplitude is
\[\ny_0=\frac{qE_0}{m(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)}\,.
\]\nSince $\omega\ll\omega_0$, this becomes
\[\ny_0\approx \frac{qE_0}{m\omega_0^2}.
\]\nThe oscillating dipole moment has amplitude
\[\np_0=qy_0\approx \frac{q^2E_0}{m\omega_0^2}.
\]\nUsing the given radiation formula with proportionality constant $1/12\pi$,
\[\ns=\frac{1}{12\pi}\frac{p_0^2\omega^4}{\varepsilon_0 c^3},
\]\nwe obtain
\[\ns=\frac{1}{12\pi}\frac{q^2y_0^2\omega^4}{\varepsilon_0 c^3}
\approx \frac{1}{12\pi}\frac{q^4E_0^2}{m^2\varepsilon_0 c^3}\frac{\omega^4}{\omega_0^4}.
\]\nTherefore, the radiated power is
\[
\boxed{s=\frac{1}{12\pi}\frac{q^4E_0^2}{m^2\varepsilon_0 c^3}\frac{\omega^4}{\omega_0^4}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Driven oscillator amplitude from Part A.2
knowledge_points.description: The steady-state displacement amplitude of the driven electron cloud is y0 = qE0/(m(ω0^2 - ω^2)), which for ω ≪ ω0 simplifies to y0 ≈ qE0/(mω0^2).

knowledge_points.name: Electric dipole moment
knowledge_points.description: The magnitude of the electric dipole moment for two charges ±q separated by distance y is p = q y; thus the amplitude is p0 = q y0.

knowledge_points.name: Radiated power of an oscillating electric dipole
knowledge_points.description: The average power radiated by an oscillating electric dipole with amplitude p0 and angular frequency ω is s = (1/12π) p0^2 ω^4/(ε0 c^3).

knowledge_points.name: Low-frequency limit ω ≪ ω0
knowledge_points.description: The driving light frequency ω is much smaller than the natural molecular vibration frequency ω0, so ω0^2 - ω^2 ≈ ω0^2.

sub_problems.problem: (C.1) Set up the differential equation for the intensity $I(x)$ as a function of the distance $x$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Consider a thin horizontal atmospheric slab of cross-sectional area $A$ and thickness $\Delta x$ at position $x$. If the light intensity entering the slab is $I(x)$, then the incident power is $I(x)A$, while the transmitted power at $x+\Delta x$ is $I(x+\Delta x)A$.
\nThe power lost from the beam in this slab is therefore
\[\nI(x)A-I(x+\Delta x)A.
\]\nThis loss is due to scattering by the air molecules. If the number density of molecules is $n_0$ and each molecule radiates power $s$, then the total radiated power from the slab is
\[\nn_0 s\,(A\Delta x).
\]\nEquating the two expressions gives
\[\nI(x)A-I(x+\Delta x)A=n_0 s\,(A\Delta x).
\]\nDividing by $A\Delta x$ and taking the limit $\Delta x\to 0$ yields
\[
-\frac{dI}{dx}=n_0 s,
\]\nor equivalently,
\[
\frac{dI}{dx}=-n_0 s.
\]
\nFinal answer: $\boxed{\frac{dI}{dx}=-n_0 s}$

knowledge_points.name: Intensity (power per unit area)
knowledge_points.description: Needed to relate the electromagnetic wave's energy flow to power through a cross-sectional area, enabling expressions like incident power = I(x) A.

knowledge_points.name: Infinitesimal slab energy balance
knowledge_points.description: Standard method to derive differential transport equations: consider a thin slab of thickness Δx, equate the net power leaving the slab to the total power lost inside it, and take Δx→0.

knowledge_points.name: Uniform number density
knowledge_points.description: The number density n₀ of air molecules is taken as constant along the light path, so the scattering power in the slab is simply n₀ s A Δx.

knowledge_points.name: Scattering as only attenuation mechanism
knowledge_points.description: All decrease in beam intensity is attributed to power radiated (scattered) by the molecules; no absorption or re-scattering into the forward beam is considered.

sub_problems.problem: (C.2) Obtain the expression for the intensity $I(x)$ as a function of $x$ in terms of the characteristic length scale $L$ associated with the drop in intensity. Take the initial intensity to be $I_0$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Since the scattering rate is proportional to the wave intensity, and the light intensity is proportional to the square of the electric-field amplitude, the intensity decreases exponentially with distance. Thus we write

\[
-\frac{dI}{dx}=\frac{I}{L},
\]
\nwhere the characteristic attenuation length is

\[\nL=\frac{6\pi \epsilon_0^2 m^2 c^4}{n_0 q^4}\left(\frac{\omega_0}{\omega}\right)^4.
\]
\nSolving the differential equation gives

\[\nI(x)=I_0 e^{-x/L}.
\]
\nTherefore, the intensity as a function of position is \(\boxed{I(x)=I_0 e^{-x/L}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Beer-Lambert law
knowledge_points.description: In a medium where the fractional loss of intensity per unit length is constant, the intensity decays exponentially with distance: I(x) = I_0 e^{-x/L}. This is the solution to the differential equation dI/dx = -I/L.

knowledge_points.name: attenuation length (e-folding length)
knowledge_points.description: The characteristic length L is the distance over which the intensity drops by a factor of e. It is the inverse of the attenuation coefficient and defines the scale of the exponential decay.

knowledge_points.name: initial intensity I_0
knowledge_points.description: The intensity at the starting point x = 0 is given as I_0, providing the boundary condition needed to determine the specific exponential solution.

knowledge_points.name: homogeneous medium
knowledge_points.description: The attenuation length L is constant along the path, which assumes a uniform medium with constant number density and scattering properties so that the simple exponential form holds.

sub_problems.problem:
(C.3) Take $m$ to be the mass of the electron (typically only one electron constitutes the charge cloud) and take

$$n_{0} =2.54 \times 10^{25} \mathrm{m}^{-3}, \tag{5}$$

$$\omega_{0} =1.25 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{rad} \cdot \mathrm{s}^{-1}, \tag{6}$$

$$\omega =3.25 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{rad} \cdot \mathrm{s}^{-1}. \tag{7}$$

Obtain the numerical value of $L$ in kilometers.
sub_problems.solution:
Using the expression obtained earlier,
\[\nL=\frac{6\pi\epsilon_0^2 m^2 c^4}{n_0 q^4}\left(\frac{\omega_0}{\omega}\right)^4.
\]\nSubstituting the given values \(m=m_e\), \(n_0=2.54\times10^{25}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), \(\omega_0=1.25\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\), and \(\omega=3.25\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\), we obtain
\[\nL \approx 130\,\mathrm{km}.
\]\nTherefore, the final answer is \(\boxed{130\,\mathrm{km}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Rayleigh scattering attenuation length
knowledge_points.description: The characteristic length scale L over which intensity drops due to Rayleigh scattering is given by L = (6π ε0^2 m^2 c^4)/(n0 q^4) (ω0/ω)^4, derived from the differential equation dI/dx = -I/L.

knowledge_points.name: elementary charge
knowledge_points.description: The charge magnitude q in the attenuation formula equals the elementary charge e = 1.602 × 10^{-19} C, as the oscillating charge cloud is a single electron.

knowledge_points.name: electron rest mass
knowledge_points.description: The mass m in the attenuation formula is the electron rest mass m_e = 9.109 × 10^{-31} kg, as specified in the problem.

knowledge_points.name: speed of light in vacuum
knowledge_points.description: The speed of light c = 2.998 × 10^8 m/s appears in the attenuation length expression and must be inserted numerically.

knowledge_points.name: permittivity of free space
knowledge_points.description: The vacuum permittivity ε0 = 8.854 × 10^{-12} F/m is required to evaluate the numerical value of L.

title: A ball on a turntable - Part A: Ball on turntable with constant angular velocity [1.5 points]
problem:
# Theoretical Problem 2: A ball on a turntable [10.0 points]

# Preamble

Notations and conventions: The length of a vector $\vec{A}$ is simply denoted as $A \equiv |\vec{A}|$ . It's $x, y, z$ components are denoted by $A_x, A_y, A_z$ , respectively. The time derivative of a quantity is denoted by the dot over the quantity: $\dot{\vec{A}} \equiv d\vec{A}/dt$ , $\dot{A} \equiv dA/dt$ . The unit vector along the direction of vector $\vec{A}$ is denoted as $\hat{A}$ . The unit vectors along the Cartesian coordinates are, therefore, $\hat{x}, \hat{y}$ and $\hat{z}$ . The definitions of scalar and vector products are:

$$(\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}) = (\vec{B} \cdot \vec{A}) = A_{x} B_{x} + A_{y} B_{y} + A_{z} B_{z} = A B \cos \theta$$

$$(\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) = - (\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$$

$$= (A_{y} B_{z} - A_{z} B_{y}) \hat{x} + (A_{z} B_{x} - A_{x} B_{z}) \hat{y} + (A_{x} B_{x} - A_{y} B_{x}) \hat{z}$$

$$\left| \vec{A} \times \vec{B} \right| = A B \sin \theta ,$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ . You may need the following properties of vectors and their multiplications. Triple product rules for vectors:

$$(\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \times \vec{C} = (\vec{A} \cdot \vec{C}) \vec{B} - (\vec{B} \cdot \vec{C}) \vec{A},$$

$$(\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{C} = (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) \cdot \vec{A} = (\vec{C} \times \vec{A}) \cdot \vec{B}.$$

The vector products are very useful in describing many relations in physics. For example:

$$\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r},$$

$$\vec{F}_{L o r e n t z} = Q \vec{v} \times \vec{B},$$

and, often, saves time combining three equations for vector components into a single equation.

# The statement

Figure 1. Ball rolling on the turntable without slipping

A ball of mass $m$ and radius $r$ is rolling on a horizontal turntable without slipping (see Figure 1). Its mass density has a spherical symmetry, i.e. only depends on the distance from its center. The moment of inertia of the ball is $I$ . In part B and C, where the turntable can rotate freely, the moment of inertia of the turntable is denoted as $I_d$ . The purpose of the problem is to analyze the motion and trajectory of the ball with respect to the laboratory frame. Throughout the problem, assume the turntable is large enough so that the ball does not fall off. The following notations are used:

$\Omega$ - the magnitude of the turntable angular velocity,

$\vec{\omega}$ - the spinning angular velocity of the ball with respect to its spinning axis,

$\vec{R}$ - the horizontal position of the ball center with respect to the rotation axis of the turn table,

$\vec{v}$ - the velocity of the ball at $\vec{R}$ with respect to the laboratory frame.

Assume that the initial position $\vec{R}_0 \equiv \vec{R}(0)$ and velocity $\vec{v}_0 \equiv \vec{v}(0)$ of the ball, the angular velocity of the turn table $\Omega_0 \equiv \Omega(0)$ are known. For the initial vector quantities $\vec{R}_0 \equiv \vec{R}(0)$ and $\vec{v}_0 \equiv \vec{v}(0)$ , assume that their directions are known. In addition, whenever you need to express a vector quantity, you may use $\hat{z}$ in your expression. Also, if asked to write your expression in terms of the known quantity you may use any or all of $m$ , $r$ , $I$ and $I_d$ . Unless otherwise stated, keep $I$ as general. The following notations are recommended:

$$\alpha = \frac{I}{I + m r^{2}}, \delta = \frac{I_{d}}{m r^{2}},$$

You may write the final answers as vector expressions involving cross product (vector product), dot product (scalar product) and unit vectors in axis directions.

# Part A: Ball on turntable with constant angular velocity [1.5 points]

First we start with the simplest case wherein the turntable angular velocity with respect to vertical axis $\hat{z}$ is constant, therefore $\Omega = \Omega_0$ .

sub_problems.problem: (A.1) Express the ball's velocity $\vec{v}$ in terms of $\Omega$ , $\vec{\omega}$ , $r$ and $\vec{R}$ from a kinematic constraint.
sub_problems.solution:
The velocity of the point on the ball that is in contact with the turntable must match the velocity of the corresponding point on the turntable, because there is no slipping.
The velocity of the contact point of the ball equals the translational velocity of the center plus the rotational contribution from the balls spin. If the contact point is at displacement $-r\hat{z}$ from the center, then its velocity is
\[
\vec v - \vec\omega\times (r\hat z).
\]
The turntable point at the same location has velocity
\[
\Omega\,\hat z\times \vec R.
\]
Thus the no-slip condition gives
\[
\vec v - \vec\omega\times (r\hat z)=\Omega\,\hat z\times \vec R.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\vec v=\Omega\,\hat z\times \vec R+r\,\vec\omega\times\hat z.
\]
Therefore the balls velocity is
\[
\boxed{\vec v=\Omega\,\hat z\times \vec R+r\,\vec\omega\times\hat z}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: no-slip rolling condition
knowledge_points.description: The velocity of the point on the ball in contact with the turntable must equal the velocity of the corresponding point on the turntable; this kinematic constraint is the basis for relating translational and rotational velocities.

knowledge_points.name: rigid body velocity composition
knowledge_points.description: The velocity of any point on a rigid body is the sum of the translational velocity of its center of mass and the tangential velocity due to rotation about the center, given by v_point = v_cm + ω × r_rel.

knowledge_points.name: uniform circular motion velocity
knowledge_points.description: A point fixed on a turntable rotating with constant angular velocity Ω about the vertical axis has velocity Ω ẑ × R, where R is the horizontal position vector from the rotation axis.

knowledge_points.name: vector cross product in kinematics
knowledge_points.description: Using the cross product to express rotational velocity contributions and the no-slip matching condition in vector form, avoiding separate scalar component equations.

sub_problems.problem: (A.2) Using Newton's equation and torque equation with respect to its center, find the acceleration of the ball $\vec{a} \equiv \vec{v}$ in terms of $\Omega$ , $\vec{v}$ , $r$ , $m$ and $I$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For rolling without slipping, the velocity of the contact point of the ball with the turntable equals the local velocity of the turntable surface. Hence

\[
\vec v - r\,\dot{\vec\phi}\times\hat z = \Omega\,\hat z\times\vec R,
\]
\nwhere \(\dot{\vec\phi}=\vec\omega\) is the balls angular velocity. Equivalently,

\[
\vec v = \Omega\,\hat z\times\vec R - r\,\hat z\times\vec\omega.
\]
\nSince \(\Omega\) is constant, differentiating gives

\[
\vec a = \Omega\,\hat z\times\vec v - r\,\hat z\times\dot{\vec\omega}.
\]
\nNow use Newtons second law for translation and the torque equation about the center of the ball. Let \(\vec f\) be the friction force. Then

\[\nm\vec a = \vec f,
\]
\nand the torque due to friction is

\[\nI\,\dot{\vec\omega} = (-r\hat z)\times\vec f = -r\hat z\times(m\vec a).
\]
\nTherefore

\[
\hat z\times\dot{\vec\omega} = -\frac{mr}{I}\,\hat z\times(\hat z\times\vec a).
\]
\nSince the motion is horizontal, \(\hat z\cdot\vec a=0\), so \(\hat z\times(\hat z\times\vec a)=-\vec a\). Thus

\[
\hat z\times\dot{\vec\omega} = \frac{mr}{I}\,\vec a.
\]
\nSubstituting into the differentiated rolling condition,

\[
\vec a = \Omega\,\hat z\times\vec v - r\left(\frac{mr}{I}\vec a\right),
\]
\nso

\[
\left(1+\frac{mr^2}{I}\right)\vec a = \Omega\,\hat z\times\vec v.
\]
\nHence the acceleration of the ball is

\[
\boxed{\vec a = \frac{I}{I+mr^2}\,\Omega\,\hat z\times\vec v }.
\]

knowledge_points.name: rolling without slipping constraint
knowledge_points.description: The velocity of the ball's contact point relative to the lab equals the local velocity of the turntable surface, giving the kinematic relation used to relate v, ω, Ω, and R.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law for translation
knowledge_points.description: Relates the net force (here friction) on the ball to its center-of-mass acceleration: m a = f.

knowledge_points.name: torque equation about center of mass
knowledge_points.description: Relates net torque about the ball's center to its angular acceleration: I dω/dt = r × f, used to connect friction force to spin acceleration.

knowledge_points.name: vector triple product simplification
knowledge_points.description: Uses the identity a × (b × c) = (a·c)b - (b·c)a, together with the horizontal motion condition (a_z=0), to simplify ẑ×(ẑ×a) = -a.

knowledge_points.name: horizontal motion
knowledge_points.description: The ball's acceleration has no vertical component (a_z = 0), which simplifies the triple product ẑ×(ẑ×a) to -a.

knowledge_points.name: constant turntable angular velocity
knowledge_points.description: Ω is constant in time, so its time derivative is zero when differentiating the rolling constraint to relate a and dω/dt.

sub_problems.problem: (A.3) Find the velocity $\vec{v}$ in terms of $\Omega, \vec{R}, \vec{v}_0, \vec{R}_0, r, m$ and $I$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a ball rolling without slipping on a turntable, the velocity of the balls center in the laboratory frame is related to the turntable motion and the balls spin by the rolling constraint. In this constant-$\Omega$ case, the standard result for the translational velocity can be written in terms of the initial data and the instantaneous position as

\[
\vec v = \vec v_0 + \Omega\,\hat z \times (\vec R-\vec R_0).
\]
\nUsing the rolling-without-slipping relation for a rigid sphere, the motion is consistent with the same form at all times, with the balls center following the turntable motion while maintaining the no-slip condition. Therefore the velocity is given by the expression above.
\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{\vec v = \vec v_0 + \Omega\,\hat z \times (\vec R-\vec R_0)}\).

knowledge_points.name: constant turntable angular velocity
knowledge_points.description: The turntable rotates at a fixed angular velocity Ω = Ω₀ about the vertical axis, so its motion is steady and known at all times.

knowledge_points.name: no-slip rolling constraint
knowledge_points.description: The ball rolls without slipping on the turntable surface, linking its translational velocity, spin angular velocity, and the local velocity of the turntable surface at the contact point.

knowledge_points.name: integration of constant acceleration
knowledge_points.description: The reference solution implicitly uses the result from part (A.2) that the acceleration is zero or that the velocity relation integrates to the given form; the final expression follows from integrating the equation of motion or directly from the kinematic constraint combined with constant Ω.

knowledge_points.name: velocity addition in rotating frame
knowledge_points.description: The velocity of the ball in the lab frame is the sum of its velocity relative to the turntable surface and the local velocity of the turntable surface, which is Ω × R.

knowledge_points.name: rigid sphere rolling on horizontal plane
knowledge_points.description: The ball is a rigid sphere with spherical mass symmetry, so its moment of inertia I is constant and the rolling constraint takes the standard form for a sphere on a flat surface.

sub_problems.problem: (A.4) Write an explicit solution for the trajectory of the ball given the initial conditions $0.5 \, \text{pt} \vec{v}_0$ and $\vec{R}_0$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Since the turntable rotates with constant angular velocity \(\Omega_0\hat z\), the no-slip condition for the ball on the turntable gives the kinematic relation
\[
\vec v = \dot{\vec R} = \Omega_0\,\hat z \times \vec R.
\]\nThis is the standard equation for uniform rotation of a point around the \(z\)-axis. Its solution with initial condition \(\vec R(0)=\vec R_0\) is
\[
\vec R(t)=\exp\!\left(t\,\Omega_0\,\hat z\times\right)\vec R_0,
\]\nwhich, written explicitly in vector form, is equivalent to a rotation of \(\vec R_0\) about the \(z\)-axis by angle \(\Omega_0 t\):
\[
\vec R(t)=\vec R_0\cos(\Omega_0 t)+\left(\hat z\times \vec R_0\right)\sin(\Omega_0 t)
+\hat z\,\bigl(\hat z\cdot \vec R_0\bigr)\bigl[1-\cos(\Omega_0 t)\bigr].
\]\nSince \(\vec R\) is horizontal, \(\hat z\cdot \vec R_0=0\), so the trajectory simplifies to
\[
\boxed{\vec R(t)=\vec R_0\cos(\Omega_0 t)+\left(\hat z\times \vec R_0\right)\sin(\Omega_0 t)}.
\]\nThis is the complete trajectory of the ball center in the laboratory frame.
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\vec R(t)=\vec R_0\cos(\Omega_0 t)+\left(\hat z\times \vec R_0\right)\sin(\Omega_0 t)}

knowledge_points.name: no-slip rolling on rotating turntable
knowledge_points.description: The no-slip condition between the ball and the turntable, together with the constant turntable angular velocity, yields the kinematic relation v = Ω₀ ẑ × R for the ball's center, as derived in earlier sub-problems.

knowledge_points.name: uniform circular motion differential equation
knowledge_points.description: The vector differential equation dR/dt = ω × R describes motion with constant angular velocity ω, implying the position vector rotates at constant angular speed.

knowledge_points.name: vector rotation formula
knowledge_points.description: For a vector R perpendicular to the rotation axis, the solution to dR/dt = ω × R is R(t) = R₀ cos(ωt) + (ω̂ × R₀) sin(ωt), which is the explicit trajectory of a point in uniform circular motion.

knowledge_points.name: horizontal position vector
knowledge_points.description: The ball moves on a horizontal turntable, so its position vector R lies in the horizontal plane and is perpendicular to the vertical axis ẑ, i.e., ẑ · R = 0, simplifying the rotation formula.

sub_problems.problem: (A.5) Assume this time that the ball has a uniform mass density, i.e. $I =2mr^2/5$ . Trajectory you have found is a circle and it's radius is $R_t$ . Choose its magnitude to be the same as $R_0$ . How long does it take for the ball to approach the initial spot on the table (the position on the turntable at $t =0$ ) with the closest distance?
sub_problems.solution:
For a turntable rotating with constant angular speed \(\Omega_0\), the no-slip condition gives the horizontal velocity of the balls center as
\[
\dot{\vec R}= \frac{I}{I+m r^2}\,\Omega_0\,\hat z\times \vec R.
\]\nHence the ball moves on a circle centered at the rotation axis with angular speed
\[
\omega_t=\frac{I}{I+m r^2}\,\Omega_0.
\]\nFor a uniform solid sphere,
\[\nI=\frac{2}{5}mr^2,
\qquad
\omega_t=\frac{2/5}{1+2/5}\,\Omega_0=\frac{2}{7}\Omega_0.
\]\nThe radius of the trajectory is given to be \(R_t=R_0\). The initial spot on the turntable is reached again when the ball has advanced around its circle by one full revolution relative to the laboratory frame, so the required time is the period
\[\nT=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_t}=\frac{2\pi}{(2/7)\Omega_0}=\frac{7\pi}{\Omega_0}.
\]\nTherefore, the time to return to the initial spot is \(\boxed{\dfrac{7\pi}{\Omega_0}}\).

knowledge_points.name: uniform solid sphere moment of inertia
knowledge_points.description: The problem specifies the ball has uniform mass density, so its moment of inertia about its center is I = (2/5) m r^2, which is needed to evaluate the trajectory angular speed.

knowledge_points.name: circular trajectory from prior result
knowledge_points.description: From part A.4 the ball's trajectory is a circle centered at the turntable axis with angular speed ω_t = I/(I+mr^2) Ω_0; this result is imported to compute the period.

knowledge_points.name: trajectory radius equals initial distance
knowledge_points.description: The problem states the trajectory radius R_t equals R_0, so the ball's circular path has known radius, needed to interpret 'approach the initial spot'.

knowledge_points.name: period of uniform circular motion
knowledge_points.description: The time for one full revolution in uniform circular motion is T = 2π / ω, used to find when the ball returns to the initial spot on the turntable.

knowledge_points.name: relative rotation synchronisation
knowledge_points.description: The ball 'approaches the initial spot on the table' when it completes one full revolution relative to the laboratory frame, because the turntable rotates rigidly; this reasoning identifies the required time as the ball's orbital period.

title: Staircase
problem:
The equilibrium shape of bodies in zero-gravity is determined by the minimum of their surface energy. Thus, for example, the equilibrium shape of a water droplet turns out to be spherical: the sphere has the smallest surface area among bodies of the same volume.

At low temperature, the equilibrium shape of crystals may have flat facets. The parts of the crystal surface that have a small angle $\varphi$ with the facet are in fact staircases of rare steps on this facet. The height of such steps is equal to the period of the crystal lattice $h$ .

Equilibrium surface profile $y(x)$ of a certain crystal and the corresponding microscopic staircase are shown schematically in the figure, where $n$ denotes the step number, counting from $x =0$ . The profile shape at $x > 0$ can be approximated as $y(x) = -(x / \lambda)^{3/2}h$ , where $\lambda =45\mu \mathrm{m}$ and $h =0.3\mathrm{nm}$ .

sub_problems.problem:
(b) The interaction energy $E$ of two steps depends on the distance $d$ between them as

$$E (d) = \mu d^{\nu},$$

where $\mu$ is a constant. Assume that only adjacent steps interact. Find the numerical value for the exponent $\nu$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The crystal surface consists of steps of height $h$. For the equilibrium profile
\[y(x)= -h\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{3/2},
\]the number of steps up to position $x$ is
\[n(x)=\frac{|y(x)|}{h}=\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{3/2}.
\]Hence
\[x\propto n^{2/3}.
\]The spacing between neighboring steps is therefore
\[d_n=x_{n+1}-x_n\propto \frac{dx}{dn}\propto n^{-1/3}.
\]
Now let the interaction energy of two adjacent steps separated by distance $d$ be
\[E(d)=\mu d^{\nu}.
\]If the $n$-th step is shifted by a small amount $\delta$, the change in the interaction energy of the two adjacent gaps is
\[
\epsilon_n(\delta)=\mu\Big[(d_n+\delta)^\nu-d_n^\nu+(d_{n+1}-\delta)^\nu-d_{n+1}^\nu\Big].
\]For small $\delta$,
\[
\epsilon_n(\delta)\approx \mu\nu\big(d_n^{\nu-1}-d_{n+1}^{\nu-1}\big)\delta.
\]At equilibrium, the coefficient of $\delta$ must be independent of the particular step number $n$, so
\[d_n^{\nu-1}-d_{n+1}^{\nu-1}=\text{const}.
\]Using $d_n\propto n^{-1/3}$ gives
\[n^{(1-\nu)/3}-(n+1)^{(1-\nu)/3}\approx \frac{1-\nu}{3}\,n^{(1-\nu)/3-1}.
\]For this to be independent of $n$, the exponent of $n$ must vanish:
\[
\frac{1-\nu}{3}-1=0.
\]Thus
\[
\nu=-2.
\]So the interaction energy behaves as $E(d)\propto d^{-2}$, and the required exponent is \boxed{-2}.

knowledge_points.name: staircase crystal surface
knowledge_points.description: The crystal surface is modelled as a staircase of steps of constant height h; the number of steps up to coordinate x is n(x) = |y(x)|/h.

knowledge_points.name: equilibrium surface profile
knowledge_points.description: The given macroscopic equilibrium profile is y(x) = -(x/λ)^(3/2) h, which implies x scales with step number n as x ∝ n^(2/3).

knowledge_points.name: adjacent step interaction power law
knowledge_points.description: The interaction energy between two steps separated by a distance d is E(d) = μ d^ν, and only adjacent step pairs interact.

knowledge_points.name: equilibrium step force balance
knowledge_points.description: At equilibrium the net interaction force on each step must be constant; a small displacement δ of a step changes the total energy by an amount proportional to (d_n^{ν-1} − d_{n+1}^{ν-1})δ, and this coefficient must be independent of the step index.

knowledge_points.name: finite difference to derivative approximation

title: Thread around a cylinder
problem:
One end of a thread is tied into a loop of length $L > 2\pi R$ , and a cylinder of radius $R$ is put through the loop. The coefficient of friction between the thread and the cylinder is $\mu$ . The free end of the thread is being pulled parallel to the axis of the cylinder (as shown by arrow in

the photo) while keeping the cylinder at rest. If the length of the loop is longer than a critical value, $L > L_{0}$ , the loop can slide along the cylinder without changing its shape, otherwise the friction "locks" it into a place and increasing the pulling force would eventually just break the thread. Find this critical value $L_{0}$ . The weight of the thread is to be neglected; the thread will not twist when being pulled.

It might be useful to know that

$$2 \int \sqrt{1+ x^{2}} d x = x \sqrt{1+ x^{2}} + \arcsin h x,$$

where $\operatorname{arcsinh} x \equiv \ln \left(x + \sqrt{1+ x^2}\right)$ .
solution:
Cut the cylinder along a generator through the pulled point and unfold the lateral surface into a plane. In the unfolded picture, the thread lies on a curve $z(x)$ connecting the two boundary points corresponding to one full turn around the cylinder, so the horizontal coordinate spans $x\in[-\pi R,\pi R]$.
\nConsider a small thread element with horizontal projection $\Delta x$. Let the horizontal component of the tension be $T_x$. Since the thread is in equilibrium, $T_x$ is constant along the thread.
\nFor a small element, the radial force balance on the cylinder gives the normal force
\[
\Delta N = T_x\,\frac{\Delta x}{R}.
\]\nAt the threshold of slipping, friction has magnitude
\[
\Delta f = \mu\,\Delta N = \mu T_x\,\frac{\Delta x}{R}.
\]\nBalancing forces in the $z$-direction for the element,
\[\nT_x\left.\frac{dz}{dx}\right|_{x+\Delta x}-T_x\left.\frac{dz}{dx}\right|_x-\Delta f=0.
\]\nTaking the limit $\Delta x\to 0$ gives
\[
\frac{d^2 z}{dx^2}=\frac{\mu}{R}.
\]\nUsing the boundary conditions at the pulled point, $z(0)=0$ and $z'(0)=0$, we obtain
\[
 z(x)=\frac{\mu}{2R}x^2.
\]
\nThe critical length is the arc length of this curve over one full wrap:
\[\nL_0=\int_{-\pi R}^{\pi R}\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{dz}{dx}\right)^2}\,dx
=2\int_0^{\pi R}\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\mu x}{R}\right)^2}\,dx.
\]\nWith $\xi=\mu x/R$,
\[\nL_0=\frac{R}{\mu}\,2\int_0^{\pi\mu}\sqrt{1+\xi^2}\,d\xi.
\]\nUsing
\[
2\int\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx=x\sqrt{1+x^2}+\operatorname{arcsinh}x,
\]\nwe find
\[\nL_0=\pi R\sqrt{1+(\pi\mu)^2}+\frac{R}{\mu}\operatorname{arcsinh}(\pi\mu).
\]\nTherefore the critical loop length is
\[
\boxed{L_0=\pi R\sqrt{1+(\pi\mu)^2}+\frac{R}{\mu}\operatorname{arcsinh}(\pi\mu)}.
\]\nFor $L>L_0$, the loop can slide; for $L<L_0$, friction locks it in place.

title: Thermal lens
problem:
When an intense laser beam falls onto a semitransparent plate, the transmitted light can self-focus to a point behind the plate due to the inhomogeneous heating of the material. This effect, known as thermal lensing, is observed in materials whose index of refraction increases with temperature, characterized by a positive thermo-optic coefficient $\gamma = \frac{\mathrm{dn}}{\mathrm{dT}}$ .

A semitransparent disk with radius $a =15.0\mathrm{mm}$ , thickness $b =0.2\mathrm{mm}$ and optical absorption coefficient $A =0.1$ is composed of a material having thermal conductivity $k =0.3\mathrm{Wm}^{-1}\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ and thermo-optic coefficient $\gamma =2.5 \cdot 10^{-4}\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ . The outer rim of the disk is thermally connected to a circular metallic holder (not shown in the figure) maintained at a constant temperature $T_{\mathrm{h}} =20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . A parallel laser beam of radius $\sigma =0.5\mathrm{mm}$ and power $P_{\mathrm{L}} =20\mathrm{mW}$ is incident normally onto the center of the disk. The intensity distribution is homogeneous across the cross-section of the beam.

sub_problems.problem: (b) In the vicinity of the center of the disk, the temperature profile can be represented by a quadratic function $T(r) = T_{\mathrm{c}} + mr^{2}$ . Calculate the parameters $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $m$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For steady radial heat flow through a thin disk, the absorbed laser power inside radius $r$ must be conducted through the cylindrical surface $2\pi r b$. Hence
\[
-k(2\pi r b)\frac{\mathrm d T}{\mathrm d r}=P_{\mathrm{abs}}(r).
\]
\Inside the laser spot, $0\le r\le \sigma$, the intensity is uniform,
\[\nI=\frac{P_L}{\pi\sigma^2},
\]\nso the absorbed power within radius $r$ is
\[\nP_{\mathrm{abs}}(r)=A I\pi r^2=A P_L\frac{r^2}{\sigma^2}.
\]\nSubstituting into the heat equation gives
\[
-k(2\pi r b)\frac{\mathrm d T}{\mathrm d r}=A P_L\frac{r^2}{\sigma^2},
\]\nso
\[
\frac{\mathrm d T}{\mathrm d r}=-\frac{A P_L}{2\pi k b\sigma^2}r.
\]\nIntegrating and using $T(r)=T_c+mr^2$ near the center,
\[\nT(r)=T_c-\frac{A P_L}{4\pi k b\sigma^2}r^2,
\]\ntherefore
\[\nm=-\frac{A P_L}{4\pi k b\sigma^2}.
\]\nNumerically,
\[\nm=-\frac{0.1\cdot 0.020}{4\pi(0.3)(2.0\times10^{-4})(5.0\times10^{-4})^2}
\approx -1.1\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{K\,m^{-2}}.
\]
\nOutside the beam, $\sigma\le r\le a$, the absorbed power is constant:
\[\nP_{\mathrm{abs}}(r)=A P_L.
\]\nThen
\[
-k(2\pi r b)\frac{\mathrm d T}{\mathrm d r}=A P_L,
\qquad
\frac{\mathrm d T}{\mathrm d r}=-\frac{A P_L}{2\pi k b}\frac1r.
\]\nWith the boundary condition $T(a)=T_h$, this gives
\[\nT(r)=T_h+\frac{A P_L}{2\pi k b}\ln\!\left(\frac{a}{r}\right).
\]\nMatching the two expressions at $r=\sigma$ yields
\[\nT_c-\frac{A P_L}{4\pi k b}=T_h+\frac{A P_L}{2\pi k b}\ln\!\left(\frac{a}{\sigma}\right),
\]\nso
\[\nT_c=T_h+\frac{A P_L}{4\pi k b}\left[1+2\ln\!\left(\frac{a}{\sigma}\right)\right].
\]\nUsing the data,
\[\nT_c\approx 20^\circ\mathrm C+\frac{0.1\cdot0.020}{4\pi(0.3)(2.0\times10^{-4})}\left[1+2\ln(30)\right]
\approx 41^\circ\mathrm C.
\]
\nFinal answer: $\boxed{T_c\approx 41^\circ\mathrm C}$ and $\boxed{m\approx -1.1\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{K\,m^{-2}}}$.

sub_problems.problem:
(c) Show that the beam is focused in one point and find the distance $f$ from this point to the disk. If you failed to obtain $T_{c}$ and $m$ in part b), you may use them as parameters in your final answer.

Do not consider the thermal expansion of the disk. Neglect the thermal radiation and the heat exchange between the disk and the surrounding air. Assume that the index of refraction of air is $n_{\mathrm{air}} =1$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a ray entering the disk at distance $r$ from the axis, the optical path to a point on the axis a distance $f$ behind the disk is approximately

$$s(r)\approx n(r)b+\sqrt{f^2+r^2}$$
\nbecause the bending inside the disk is small. Since $f\gg r$,

$$\sqrt{f^2+r^2}\approx f+\frac{r^2}{2f},$$
\nso

$$s(r)\approx n(r)b+f+\frac{r^2}{2f}.$$ 
\nFor all rays to meet at the same focal point, the total optical path must be the same for every $r$ in the beam. Hence $s(r)=s(0)$, which gives

$$b\bigl(n(0)-n(r)\bigr)=\frac{r^2}{2f}.$$ 
\nThe refractive index depends on temperature as $n(T)=n_0+\gamma T$, and from part (b) the temperature profile has the form

$$T(r)=T_c+mr^2,$$
\nwith $m<0$. Therefore

$$n(0)-n(r)=\gamma\bigl(T(0)-T(r)\bigr)=-\gamma mr^2=\gamma |m|r^2.$$ 
\nSubstituting into the focusing condition yields

$$b\gamma |m|r^2=\frac{r^2}{2f},$$
\nso the $r^2$ cancels and the beam indeed focuses to one point, with

$$f=\frac{1}{2\gamma b|m|}.$$ 
\nUsing the result from part (b),

$$|m|=\frac{AP}{4\pi k\sigma^2},$$
\nwe obtain

$$f=\frac{2\pi k\sigma^2}{\gamma AP}.$$ 
\nWith the given numerical values,

$$f=\frac{2\pi(0.3)(0.5\times10^{-3})^2}{(2.5\times10^{-4})(0.1)(20\times10^{-3})}\approx 0.94\,\text{m}.$$ 
\nThus the beam is focused at a point located a distance \(\boxed{0.94\,\text{m}}\) from the disk.

knowledge_points.name: optical path length
knowledge_points.description: The product of the geometric path length and the local refractive index; used to construct the total phase accrual s(r) = n(r)b + sqrt(f^2+r^2) for a ray through the disk and air to the focal point.

knowledge_points.name: equal optical path condition for focusing
knowledge_points.description: For all rays from an incoming wavefront to converge to a single point, the optical path lengths to that point must be equal; applied by setting s(r) = s(0) to derive the focusing condition.

knowledge_points.name: paraxial approximation
knowledge_points.description: Because the focal distance is large compared to the radial coordinate (f ≫ r), the distance sqrt(f^2+r^2) is expanded as f + r^2/(2f), simplifying the cancellation of the quadratic r-dependence.

knowledge_points.name: linear thermo-optic relation
knowledge_points.description: The refractive index increases linearly with temperature, n(T) = n0 + γ T, where γ = dn/dT; this converts the temperature difference T(0)-T(r) into the refractive index difference needed for the focusing equation.

knowledge_points.name: quadratic temperature profile near center
knowledge_points.description: Near the center of the disk the steady-state temperature has the form T(r) = T_c + m r^2 (with m < 0), as obtained in part (b); this provides the explicit radial dependence for the refractive index difference.

knowledge_points.name: temperature curvature coefficient relation
knowledge_points.description: The curvature parameter m satisfies |m| = AP/(4πkσ^2), relating the absorbed beam power, thermal conductivity, and beam radius; needed to express the final focal length in terms of the given numerical parameters.

knowledge_points.name: negligible ray bending inside disk
knowledge_points.description: The gradient-index refraction inside the thin disk is small, so the ray trajectory is approximated as a straight line of length b with the local index n(r); this simplifies the optical path in the disk to n(r)b.

knowledge_points.name: refractive index of air equals 1
knowledge_points.description: The surrounding medium is air with n = 1, so the geometric path in air equals the optical path; used to write the air segment as sqrt(f^2+r^2) without an extra refractive factor.

knowledge_points.name: negligible thermal expansion
knowledge_points.description: The disk thickness b remains constant during heating, as thermal expansion is not considered; this ensures the geometric path inside the disk is simply b and does not depend on temperature.

title: Sliding puck
problem:
A puck (a small disc) with radius $r$ and uniform density is moving on a horizontal plane with the velocity $v_{0}$ without rotation. The puck meets a fixed half-circular wall with a radius $R \gg r$ and starts to move along the wall. The coefficient of friction with the wall is $\mu$ , and friction with the horizontal plane is negligible.

a) Find the velocity of the puck $\nu_{e}$ when it leaves the wall.
b) Sketch the graph $\nu_{e}(\mu)$ . Indicate important features of the graph. You are encouraged to sketch the graph even if you haven't found the exact formula for $\nu_{e}$ .
solution:
As the puck moves along the fixed wall, the wall exerts a normal force that bends the trajectory and a kinetic friction force that slows the center of mass and spins the puck. Since friction with the floor is negligible, only the wall matters.

While the puck is slipping along the wall, the normal force provides the centripetal acceleration, so
\[
N=\frac{mv^2}{R}.
\]
Hence the friction force has magnitude
\[
F_f=\mu N=\mu \frac{mv^2}{R}.
\]
This friction opposes the motion, so the translational equation is
\[
m\frac{dv}{dt}=-\mu\frac{mv^2}{R}.
\]
It is convenient to use the arc length $l$ along the wall, with $dl=v\,dt$ and $l=R\varphi$. Then
\[
\frac{dv}{v}=-\mu\,d\varphi.
\]
Integrating from the start of the wall, where $v=v_0$ and $\varphi=0$, gives
\[
v(\varphi)=v_0 e^{-\mu\varphi}.
\]

The same friction force also produces a torque on the puck about its center:
\[
\tau_f=rF_f=r\mu\frac{mv^2}{R}.
\]
For a uniform disc, $I=\frac12 mr^2$, so
\[
I\frac{d\omega}{dt}=r\mu\frac{mv^2}{R}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
r\frac{d\omega}{dt}=2\mu\frac{v^2}{R}.
\]
Defining $u=r\omega$, and using $d\varphi/dt=v/R$, we get
\[
\frac{du}{d\varphi}=2\mu v_0 e^{-\mu\varphi}.
\]
With $u=0$ initially,
\[
u(\varphi)=r\omega(\varphi)=2v_0\bigl(1-e^{-\mu\varphi}\bigr).
\]

Slip stops when the contact point has zero relative velocity, i.e. when
\[
v=r\omega.
\]
Thus
\[
v_0 e^{-\mu\varphi_c}=2v_0\bigl(1-e^{-\mu\varphi_c}\bigr),
\]
so
\[
e^{-\mu\varphi_c}=\frac23,
\qquad
\mu\varphi_c=\ln\frac32.
\]
At that moment the speed is
\[
v_c=\frac23 v_0.
\]

Now compare the critical angle $\varphi_c$ with the total angle of the semicircle, $\pi$.

- If $\varphi_c\ge \pi$, i.e.
\[
\mu\pi\le \ln\frac32,
\]
then slipping continues all the way to the exit, so
\[
v_e=v_0 e^{-\mu\pi}.
\]

- If $\varphi_c\le \pi$, i.e.
\[
\mu\pi\ge \ln\frac32,
\]
then slipping ends before the puck leaves the wall. After that there is no more friction, so the speed stays constant at
\[
v_e=\frac23 v_0.
\]

Therefore,
\[
\boxed{v_e(\mu)=
\begin{cases}
 v_0 e^{-\pi\mu}, & \mu\le \dfrac{\ln(3/2)}{\pi},\\[6pt]
 \dfrac23 v_0, & \mu\ge \dfrac{\ln(3/2)}{\pi}.
\end{cases}}
\]
The graph starts at $v_e(0)=v_0$, decreases exponentially for small $\mu$, and then becomes a horizontal line at $\frac23 v_0$ once $\mu$ reaches $\frac{\ln(3/2)}{\pi}$.
