knowledge_points.name: Centripetal force equation
knowledge_points.description: For an object moving in a circle of radius R at speed v, the net radial force equals m v^2 / R. Used to express the normal force N in terms of v and R.

knowledge_points.name: Kinetic friction law
knowledge_points.description: The magnitude of kinetic friction is f_k = μ N, where μ is the coefficient of kinetic friction. Used to find the friction force from the normal force.

knowledge_points.name: Torque
knowledge_points.description: Torque about an axis is the product of force and lever arm; here friction acts at the rim, so torque = r F_f. Used to relate friction to angular acceleration.

knowledge_points.name: Moment of inertia of a uniform disc
knowledge_points.description: The moment of inertia of a uniform solid disc about its central axis is I = 1/2 m r^2. Needed to relate torque to angular acceleration.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law for rotation
knowledge_points.description: The net torque on a rigid body equals I α, where α = dω/dt. Used to derive the angular acceleration from the friction torque.

knowledge_points.name: No-slip condition
knowledge_points.description: When a round object rolls without slipping on a surface, the translational speed v and angular speed ω satisfy v = ω r. Used to find when slipping stops.

knowledge_points.name: Angular parametrization of motion
knowledge_points.description: For circular motion, use dφ = v dt / R to change the independent variable from time to angular displacement, simplifying differential equations. Used to solve for v(φ) and ω(φ).

knowledge_points.name: Center path radius R approximation
knowledge_points.description: Since R ≫ r, the puck's center trajectory is approximated as a circle of radius R, allowing use of the centripetal formula with radius R.

knowledge_points.name: Semicircular wall geometry
knowledge_points.description: The wall is a half-circle, so the total angular span is π radians. Used to determine the exit condition and integration limit.

knowledge_points.name: Negligible floor friction
knowledge_points.description: Friction with the horizontal plane is negligible, so only the wall forces affect the puck's horizontal motion.

title: Crossed wires
problem:
(a) (1 pt) Current flows through an infinite, straight, thin wire. There is an externally imposed, uniform magnetic field directed parallel to the wire. Qualitatively sketch one of the magnetic field lines.

(c) (4 pts) Let $L$ be the length of this field line between $P$ and its point of closest approach to wire $X$ . Using values $a =10\mathrm{cm}$ and $r =1.0\mathrm{mm}$ , calculate $L$ to within $20\%$ relative error.

sub_problems.problem: (a) Current flows through an infinite, straight, thin wire. There is an externally imposed, uniform magnetic field directed parallel to the wire. Qualitatively sketch one of the magnetic field lines.
sub_problems.solution:
For an infinite straight current-carrying wire, the magnetic field of the wire alone consists of closed circular loops centered on the wire, lying in planes perpendicular to the wire.
\nIf a uniform external magnetic field is added parallel to the wire, the total magnetic field at each point is the vector sum of the circular field of the wire and the uniform parallel field. Because the total field now has a component along the wire, a field line is no longer confined to a plane perpendicular to the wire.
\nTherefore the magnetic field line becomes a spiral around the wire, i.e. a helix whose axis is the wire.
\nFinal answer: \boxed{\text{a helical field line around the wire}}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{a helical field line around the wire}}

knowledge_points.name: magnetic field lines of a straight current-carrying wire
knowledge_points.description: The magnetic field due to an infinite straight wire consists of closed circular loops centered on the wire, lying in planes perpendicular to the wire. This shape is essential to combine with the external uniform field.

knowledge_points.name: superposition principle for magnetic fields
knowledge_points.description: The total magnetic field at any point is the vector sum of the fields from all sources. Here it is used to add the wire's circular field and the uniform external field.

knowledge_points.name: magnetic field line definition
knowledge_points.description: A magnetic field line is a curve whose tangent at every point is parallel to the magnetic field vector at that point. This definition is used to deduce that the combined field yields a helical line.

sub_problems.problem: (c) Let $L$ be the length of this field line between $P$ and its point of closest approach to wire $X$ . Using values $a =10\mathrm{cm}$ and $r =1.0\mathrm{mm}$ , calculate $L$ to within $20\%$ relative error.
sub_problems.solution:
The field line is tightly wound, so its length from $P$ to the point of closest approach $Q$ is much larger than both $a$ and $r$. Therefore, we may ignore the precise location of $Q$ around the nearest turn and integrate up to $x=0$.
\nFor a small displacement along the field line, let the change in the coordinate along wire $X$ be $dx$ and the corresponding arc length be $dL$. Since the field line is tangent to the magnetic field, we have

$$dx \approx \frac{B_{\parallel}}{B_{\perp}}\, dL,$$
\nwhere $B_{\parallel}$ is the component of the magnetic field along wire $X$ and $B_{\perp}$ is the component perpendicular to wire $X$.
\nFrom the previous part,

$$B_{\parallel}=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi}\,\frac{a}{a^2+x^2}.$$
\nThe perpendicular component is dominated by the field of wire $X$ itself, so

$$B_{\perp}=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi \rho}.$$
\nHence

$$dL=\frac{a^2+x^2}{a\rho}\,dx,$$
\nand the total length is

$$L=\int_0^{3a}\frac{a^2+x^2}{a\rho}\,dx.$$
\nUsing the result from part b,

$$\frac{\rho^2}{a^2+x^2}=\frac{r^2}{10a^2},$$
\nso

$$\rho=\frac{r}{\sqrt{10}a}\sqrt{a^2+x^2}.$$
\nSubstituting this into the integral gives

$$L=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{r}\int_0^{3a}\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\,dx
=\frac{\sqrt{10}a^2}{r}\int_0^3\sqrt{1+u^2}\,du,$$
\nwhere $u=x/a$.
\nNow estimate the dimensionless integral:

$$\int_0^3\sqrt{1+u^2}\,du \approx 5.6,$$
\nso

$$L\approx \frac{\sqrt{10}a^2}{r}(5.6).$$
\nWith $a=10\,\mathrm{cm}=0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ and $r=1.0\,\mathrm{mm}=1.0\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$,

$$\frac{a^2}{r}=\frac{(0.10)^2}{10^{-3}}=10\,\mathrm{m},$$
\ntherefore

$$L\approx 5.6\times \sqrt{10}\times 10\,\mathrm{m}\approx 1.8\times 10^2\,\mathrm{m}.$$
\nFinal answer: $$\boxed{L\approx 1.8\times 10^2\ \mathrm{m}}$$

knowledge_points.name: magnetic field line
knowledge_points.description: A magnetic field line is a curve everywhere tangent to the magnetic field vector; this property is used to relate the differential arc length dL to the coordinate differential dx via the ratio of the parallel and perpendicular field components.

knowledge_points.name: Biot-Savart law for infinite straight wire
knowledge_points.description: The magnetic field magnitude at a perpendicular distance ρ from an infinite straight current-carrying wire is B = μ0 I/(2πρ); used to express the perpendicular component B_⊥.

knowledge_points.name: tightly wound helix approximation
knowledge_points.description: When a magnetic field line is tightly wound (pitch much smaller than the scale of variation), the arc length element dL is approximately (B_⊥/B_∥) dx, allowing integration along the wire coordinate.

knowledge_points.name: parallel field component from part (b)
knowledge_points.description: The parallel component of the magnetic field is given by B_∥ = (μ0 I/(2π)) * a/(a^2+x^2), as derived in the previous sub-problem.

knowledge_points.name: radial distance relation from part (b)
knowledge_points.description: The relation ρ^2/(a^2+x^2) = r^2/(10a^2) from part (b) connects the radial distance ρ to the coordinate x and the parameters a and r, allowing substitution into the integral.

title: Supernova Distance and Hubble Time
problem: Consider a type Ia supernova, in a distant galaxy, which has a luminosity of $5.8 \times 10^{9} L_{\odot}$ at maximum light. Suppose you observe this supernova using your telescope and find that its brightness is $1.6 \times 10^{-7}$ times the brightness of Vega. The redshift of its host galaxy is known to be $z = 0.03$ . Calculate the distance of this galaxy (in pc) using the data of the supernova and also the Hubble time.
solution:
The relation between flux $F$ and luminosity $L$ is $F = \frac{L}{4\pi d^2}$. For Vega: $F_V = \frac{L_V}{4\pi d_V^2}$. For the supernova: $F_{SN} = \frac{L_{SN}}{4\pi d_{SN}^2}$. Given $F_{SN} = 1.6 \times 10^{-7} F_V$, we have:
\[
\frac{L_{SN}}{4\pi d_{SN}^2} = (1.6 \times 10^{-7}) \frac{L_V}{4\pi d_V^2}
\]
\[
L_{SN} d_V^2 = (1.6 \times 10^{-7}) L_V d_{SN}^2
\]
Solving for $d_{SN}$:
\[
d_{SN} = d_V \left[ \frac{1}{1.6 \times 10^{-7}} \frac{L_{SN}}{L_V} \right]^{1/2}
\]
Using $d_V = 7.76$ pc (distance to Vega), $L_V = 130 L_\odot$, and $L_{SN} = 5.8 \times 10^9 L_\odot$:
\[
d_{SN} = 7.76 \left[ \frac{1}{1.6 \times 10^{-7}} \frac{5.8 \times 10^9}{130} \right]^{1/2} \approx 1.3 \times 10^8 \text{ pc}
\]
The Hubble time $t_H$ is related to redshift and distance by $t_H = \frac{d_{SN}}{c z}$. Using $c = 1 \text{ lyr/yr}$, $1 \text{ pc} = 3.26 \text{ lyr}$:
\[
t_H = \frac{1.3 \times 10^8 \text{ pc}}{(1 \text{ lyr/yr})(0.03)} \times \frac{3.26 \text{ lyr}}{1 \text{ pc}} \approx 1.41 \times 10^{10} \text{ years}
\]
Thus the distance is $\boxed{1.3 \times 10^8 \text{ pc}}$ and the Hubble time is $\boxed{1.41 \times 10^{10} \text{ years}}$.

knowledge_points.name: Inverse-square law for flux
knowledge_points.description: Relates the observed flux F of a source to its intrinsic luminosity L and distance d: F = L/(4π d²). Used to derive the distance from the brightness ratio of the supernova and Vega.

knowledge_points.name: Type Ia supernova standard candle
knowledge_points.description: Type Ia supernovae have a known peak luminosity (here 5.8×10⁹ L_⊙), making them reliable distance indicators.

knowledge_points.name: Vega reference star parameters
knowledge_points.description: Vega has a known distance (7.76 pc) and luminosity (130 L_⊙), used to calibrate the supernova's flux.

knowledge_points.name: Hubble's law
knowledge_points.description: For small redshifts, recession velocity v ≈ c z, and Hubble's law v = H₀ d relates distance and velocity. Used to compute Hubble time from distance and redshift.

knowledge_points.name: Hubble time
knowledge_points.description: The Hubble time t_H = 1/H₀ is the inverse of the Hubble constant, and can be estimated as t_H = d/(c z) for small z.

knowledge_points.name: Parsec to light-year conversion
knowledge_points.description: 1 parsec = 3.26 light-years. Needed to convert distance to units compatible with c = 1 lyr/yr.

knowledge_points.name: Speed of light in astronomical units
knowledge_points.description: The speed of light is 1 light-year per year (c = 1 lyr/yr). Used to compute Hubble time in years.

knowledge_points.name: Euclidean distance approximation
knowledge_points.description: At redshift z=0.03, the inverse-square law holds without relativistic corrections, so luminosity distance equals proper distance.

title: Cosmic Microwave Background and Horizon Distance
problem: Measurement of the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMB) shows that its temperature is practically the same at every point in the sky to a very high degree of accuracy. Let us assume that light emitted at the moment of recombination ( $T_{r} \approx 3000\mathrm{K}$ , $t_{r} \approx 300000$ years) is only reaching us now ( $T_{o} \approx 3\mathrm{K}$ , $t_{o} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{10}$ years). Scale factor $S$ is defined as such $S_{0} = S(t = t_{o}) = 1$ and $S_{t} = S(t < t_{o}) < 1$ . Note that the radiation dominated period was between the time when the inflation stopped ( $t = 10^{-32}$ seconds) and the time when the recombination took place, while the matter dominated period started at the recombination time. During the radiation dominated period $S$ is proportional to $t^{1/2}$ , while during the matter dominated period $S$ is proportional to $t^{2/3}$ .

sub_problems.problem: (a) Estimate the horizon distances when recombination took place. Assume that temperature $T$ is proportional to $1 / S$ , where $S$ is a scale factor of the size of the Universe.
sub_problems.solution:
The horizon distance at recombination is the maximum distance that light could have traveled since the Big Bang. At recombination, the horizon distance is $X_r = c t_r$. The current angular size of this horizon is $\theta_0 = X_0 / d$, where $d = c(t_o - t_r) \approx c t_o$ (since $t_o \gg t_r$). The physical size at recombination is $X_r = S_r X_0$, where $S_r$ is the scale factor at recombination. Thus $c t_r = S_r \theta_0 c t_o$, so $\theta_0 = t_r / (S_r t_o)$. Using $T \propto 1/S$, we have $S_o / S_r = T_r / T_o$, and since $S_o = 1$, $1/S_r = T_r / T_o$. Therefore $\theta_0 = (t_r T_r) / (t_o T_o)$. Substituting $t_r = 3 \times 10^5$ yr, $T_r = 3000$ K, $t_o = 1.5 \times 10^{10}$ yr, $T_o = 3$ K gives $\theta_0 = (3 \times 10^5 \times 3000) / (1.5 \times 10^{10} \times 3) = 2 \times 10^{-2}$ rad = $1.14^\circ$. The horizon distance at recombination is $X_r = c t_r = (3 \times 10^5 \text{ yr}) \times c = 3 \times 10^5$ light-years.

\boxed{\theta_0 = 1.14^\circ}

knowledge_points.name: Horizon distance approximation
knowledge_points.description: The horizon distance at time t is approximated as the light-travel distance d_horizon = c t. Used to set the physical size of the horizon at recombination: X_r = c t_r.

knowledge_points.name: Source distance approximation
knowledge_points.description: The distance from the recombination surface to the observer is approximated by the light-travel distance d = c (t_o - t_r) ≈ c t_o. Used as the distance in the angular size calculation.

knowledge_points.name: Scale factor and proper distance
knowledge_points.description: The proper distance of a comoving object scales with the scale factor S(t): X(t) = S(t) X_0, with S_0 = 1. Used to relate the horizon size at recombination X_r to its present size X_0.

knowledge_points.name: Temperature-scale factor relation
knowledge_points.description: The temperature of the CMB is inversely proportional to the scale factor: T ∝ 1/S. Given as an assumption in the problem. Used to find the scale factor at recombination: S_r = T_o / T_r.

knowledge_points.name: Small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: For small angles, the angular size θ in radians is approximately the ratio of the physical size to the distance: θ ≈ size / distance. Used to compute the current angular size of the horizon: θ_0 = X_0 / d.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Consider two points in CMBR imprint which are currently observed at a separation angle $\alpha = 5^{\circ}$ . Could the two points communicate with each other using photon? (Answer with "YES" or "NO" and give the reason mathematically)
sub_problems.solution:
The maximum angular separation for two points to have been in causal contact at recombination is the horizon angle $\theta_0 = 1.14^\circ$. Since the observed separation $\alpha = 5^\circ > \theta_0$, the two points could not have communicated via photons at recombination. Therefore the answer is NO.

\boxed{\text{NO}}

knowledge_points.name: Particle horizon
knowledge_points.description: The particle horizon at a given cosmic time is the maximum distance light could have traveled since the Big Bang; regions separated by more than this distance could not have exchanged photons. This concept defines the limit for communication between the two CMB points.

knowledge_points.name: Horizon angle at recombination
knowledge_points.description: The particle horizon at recombination subtends a specific angle on the sky today, known as the horizon angle. Two points on the CMB separated by an angle larger than this were outside each other's horizon at recombination and thus could not have communicated via photons.

knowledge_points.name: Horizon angle value 1.14 degrees
knowledge_points.description: From part (a), the horizon angle at recombination is 1.14°. This specific numerical value is used to evaluate whether the given 5° separation allows causal contact.

sub_problems.problem: (c) Estimate the size of our Universe at the end of inflation period.
sub_problems.solution:
First, find the scale factor ratio from recombination to present. During matter domination, $S \propto t^{2/3}$, so $S_o / S_r = (t_o / t_r)^{2/3} = (1.5 \times 10^{10} / 3 \times 10^5)^{2/3} = (5 \times 10^4)^{2/3} = 1.36 \times 10^3$. The size of the universe at recombination is $R_r = R_o / (S_o/S_r) = (1.5 \times 10^{10} \text{ ly}) / (1.36 \times 10^3) = 1.11 \times 10^7$ ly. Next, from inflation end to recombination, the universe was radiation dominated, so $S \propto t^{1/2}$. The time from inflation end $t_i = 10^{-32}$ s to recombination $t_r = 3 \times 10^5$ yr = $9.46 \times 10^{12}$ s. Then $S_r / S_i = (t_r / t_i)^{1/2} = (9.46 \times 10^{12} / 10^{-32})^{1/2} = (9.46 \times 10^{44})^{1/2} = 3.08 \times 10^{22}$. The size at inflation end is $R_i = R_r / (S_r/S_i) = (1.11 \times 10^7 \text{ ly}) / (3.08 \times 10^{22}) = 3.57 \times 10^{-16}$ ly $\approx 3$ m.

\boxed{R_i \approx 3 \text{ m}}

knowledge_points.name: matter-dominated scale factor evolution
knowledge_points.description: During matter-domination the scale factor grows as S ∝ t^(2/3). Used to relate S at recombination to S today.

knowledge_points.name: radiation-dominated scale factor evolution
knowledge_points.description: During radiation-domination the scale factor grows as S ∝ t^(1/2). Used to relate S at the end of inflation to S at recombination.

knowledge_points.name: cosmic era boundaries
knowledge_points.description: The universe was radiation-dominated from the end of inflation (t=10^{-32} s) to recombination (t≈300,000 yr), and matter-dominated afterwards. This defines which S(t) relation applies in each interval.

knowledge_points.name: distance scaling with scale factor
knowledge_points.description: Physical distances (like the size of the universe) are proportional to the scale factor: R(t) ∝ S(t). This allows computing sizes at different epochs from the scale-factor ratios.

knowledge_points.name: horizon distance today ~ ct_0
knowledge_points.description: The current size of the observable universe is approximately the speed of light times the age of the universe: R_0 ≈ c t_0. The solution uses R_0 = 1.5×10^10 ly, matching the given t_0.

title: High Altitude Projectile
problem: A projectile which starts from the surface of the Earth at the sea level is launched with the initial speed of $v_{\circ} = \sqrt{(GM / R)}$ and with the projecting angle (with respect to the local horizon) of $\theta = \frac{\pi}{6}$ . $M$ and $R$ are the mass and radius of the Earth respectively. Ignore the air resistance and rotation of the Earth.

sub_problems.problem: (a) Show that the orbit of the projectile is an ellipse with a semi-major axis of $a = R$.
sub_problems.solution:
Total energy of the projectile is
$$
E = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\circ}^2 - \frac{G M m}{R} = \frac{1}{2} m \left(\frac{G M}{R}\right) - \frac{G M m}{R} = -\frac{G M m}{2R} < 0.
$$
$E<0$ means the orbit is bound (ellipse or circle). Since $\theta > 0$, the orbit is an ellipse. For an elliptical orbit, total energy is $E = -\frac{G M m}{2a}$. Equating:
$$
-\frac{G M m}{2a} = -\frac{G M m}{2R} \quad \Rightarrow \quad a = R.
$$
Thus the semi-major axis is $a = R$.

\boxed{a = R}

knowledge_points.name: total mechanical energy in gravity
knowledge_points.description: The total energy of a projectile in Earth's gravity is the sum of kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy, E = (1/2)mv^2 - GMm/r. This is needed to compute the numerical value of E for the given initial conditions.

knowledge_points.name: bound orbit condition
knowledge_points.description: A negative total mechanical energy (E < 0) indicates a bound orbit (ellipse or circle), as opposed to an unbound trajectory (parabola or hyperbola). This is used to conclude the orbit is elliptical.

knowledge_points.name: energy–semi-major axis relation
knowledge_points.description: For an elliptical Keplerian orbit, the total mechanical energy is related to the semi-major axis by E = -GMm/(2a). Equating this to the computed energy yields a = R.

knowledge_points.name: non-zero launch angle
knowledge_points.description: The launch angle θ = π/6 > 0 ensures the orbit is not purely radial, which together with E < 0 rules out a circular orbit and confirms an ellipse.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Calculate the highest altitude of the projectile with respect to the Earth surface (in the unit of the Earth radius).
sub_problems.solution:
From the geometry of the ellipse (see figure), the highest point H is at distance $CH = a$ from the center C. The distance from Earth's center O to the launch point A is $R$. In triangle OCO', $OC = CO' = R \sin\theta$. The altitude $HM = CH - CM = a - (R - R\sin\theta) = R - R + R\sin\theta = R\sin\theta = \frac{R}{2}$.

\boxed{\text{Highest altitude} = \frac{R}{2}}

knowledge_points.name: elliptical orbit with semi-major axis a=R
knowledge_points.description: The result from part (a) that the projectile's orbit is an ellipse with semi-major axis equal to Earth's radius R is used to locate the highest point H at distance a=R from the occupied focus C.

knowledge_points.name: geometry of an ellipse
knowledge_points.description: Understanding that the highest point (apoapsis) of an elliptical orbit lies on the major axis at distance a from the occupied focus, and that the ellipse is symmetric about the major axis, is needed to interpret the geometric construction in the solution.

knowledge_points.name: geometric construction from launch conditions
knowledge_points.description: The solution uses a geometric diagram where the launch point A, Earth's center O, and the vacant focus C' form a triangle with OC = C'O = R sin(theta), derived from the launch angle and the ellipse properties established in part (a).

knowledge_points.name: Earth as a point mass at center O
knowledge_points.description: The Earth is treated as a point mass located at its center O, which is one focus of the elliptical orbit; the Earth's surface is a circle of radius R centered at O.

knowledge_points.name: launch from Earth surface at distance R
knowledge_points.description: The projectile is launched from a point on the Earth's surface, so its initial distance from Earth's center O is exactly R, which is used to set the scale of the geometric construction.

sub_problems.problem: (c) What is the range of the projectile (distance between launching point and falling point) in the units of the earth radii?
sub_problems.solution:
The range is the arc length $\widehat{AB}$ along Earth's surface. From the geometry, the central angle between A and B is $2\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \pi - 2\theta$. Thus
$$
\widehat{AB} = (\pi - 2\theta) R = \left(\pi - 2\cdot\frac{\pi}{6}\right)R = \left(\pi - \frac{\pi}{3}\right)R = \frac{2\pi}{3}R.
$$

\boxed{\text{Range} = \frac{2\pi}{3}R}

knowledge_points.name: elliptical orbit with semi-major axis a=R
knowledge_points.description: The result from part (a) that the projectile's orbit is an ellipse with semi-major axis equal to Earth's radius R is used implicitly to justify that the trajectory is symmetric and that the launch and impact points lie on the same elliptical path intersecting the Earth's surface.

knowledge_points.name: Earth as a perfect sphere
knowledge_points.description: The Earth is treated as a sphere of radius R, so the arc length along the surface between launch and impact points is simply R times the central angle.

knowledge_points.name: central angle
knowledge_points.description: The angle subtended at Earth's centre by the arc between launch point A and impact point B; needed to compute the surface range as arc length.

knowledge_points.name: symmetry of elliptical orbit
knowledge_points.description: For an elliptical orbit under a central inverse-square force, the trajectory is symmetric about the semi-major axis; the launch and impact points on the Earth's surface are symmetric with respect to the line of apsides, giving the central angle as twice the complement of the launch angle.

knowledge_points.name: launch angle measured from local horizon
knowledge_points.description: The given angle θ = π/6 is measured with respect to the local horizon (tangent to Earth's surface), which determines the geometry relating the central angle to θ.

knowledge_points.name: arc length formula
knowledge_points.description: The range along the Earth's surface is computed as the arc length s = R * Δφ, where Δφ is the central angle in radians.

sub_problems.problem: (d) What is eccentricity (e) of this elliptical orbit?
sub_problems.solution:
Use the ellipse equation in polar coordinates: $r = \frac{a(1-e^2)}{1+e\cos\varphi}$. At launch point A, $r = R$, $a = R$, and the angle from the major axis is $\varphi = \frac{\pi}{2} + \theta$. Substituting:
$$
R = \frac{R(1-e^2)}{1+e\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta\right)} = \frac{R(1-e^2)}{1 - e\sin\theta}.
$$
Cancel $R$ and solve: $1 - e\sin\theta = 1 - e^2 \Rightarrow e = \sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}$.

\boxed{e = \frac{1}{2}}

knowledge_points.name: ellipse equation in polar coordinates
knowledge_points.description: The polar form r = a(1-e^2)/(1+e cos φ) relates radial distance r, semi-major axis a, eccentricity e, and true anomaly φ for an elliptical orbit with the origin at one focus. It is needed to substitute the launch conditions and solve for e.

knowledge_points.name: launch point lies on ellipse
knowledge_points.description: At the moment of launch the projectile is on the Earth's surface, so its radial coordinate r equals the Earth's radius R. This boundary condition is used to evaluate the ellipse equation.

knowledge_points.name: semi-major axis equals Earth radius
knowledge_points.description: From part (a) the orbit has semi-major axis a = R. This result is imported into the ellipse equation to reduce the number of unknowns.

knowledge_points.name: true anomaly from launch geometry
knowledge_points.description: The angle φ in the polar ellipse equation is measured from perigee. At launch the projectile's velocity direction relative to the local horizon determines φ = π/2 + θ, which is used to evaluate cos φ.

knowledge_points.name: trigonometric identity for phase shift
knowledge_points.description: cos(π/2 + θ) = -sin θ is used to simplify the denominator of the ellipse equation after substituting φ.

sub_problems.problem: (e) Find the time of flight for the projectile.
sub_problems.solution:
Use Kepler's second law: $\frac{\Delta S}{S_0} = \frac{\Delta T}{T}$, where $S_0 = \pi a b$ is the total area of the ellipse, $b = a\sqrt{1-e^2} = R\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}R$. The area swept from launch to landing is $\Delta S = S_{\triangle AOB} + \frac{S_0}{2}$. The triangle AOB has base $2ae = 2R\cdot\frac{1}{2}=R$ and height $b$, so $S_{\triangle AOB} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot R \cdot b = \frac{Rb}{2}$. Thus $\Delta S = \frac{Rb}{2} + \frac{\pi a b}{2} = b\left(\frac{R}{2} + \frac{\pi R}{2}\right) = \frac{bR}{2}(1+\pi)$. But note $a=R$, so $\Delta S = \frac{bR}{2}(1+\pi)$. Then
$$
\frac{\Delta S}{S_0} = \frac{\frac{bR}{2}(1+\pi)}{\pi R b} = \frac{1+\pi}{2\pi}.
$$
Kepler's third law gives orbital period $T = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi^2 R^3}{GM}}$. Hence
$$
\Delta T = T \cdot \frac{1+\pi}{2\pi} = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi^2 R^3}{GM}} \cdot \frac{1+\pi}{2\pi}.
$$

\boxed{\Delta T = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi^2 R^3}{GM}} \cdot \frac{1+\pi}{2\pi}}

title: Problem 5: Circumpolar star declination from Damavand
problem: The Damavand Mountain is located at the North part of Iran, in south coast of Caspian Sea. Consider an observer standing on the Damavand mountaintop (latitude $= 35^{\circ}57'\mathrm{N}$ ; longitude $= 52^{\circ}6'\mathrm{E}$ ; altitude $5.6 \times 10^{3}m$ from the mean sea level) and looking at the sky over the Caspian Sea. What is the minimum declination for a star, to be seen marginally circumpolar for this observer. Geodetic radius of the Earth at this latitude is $6370.8km$ . Surface level of the Caspian Sea is approximately equal to the mean sea level.
solution: Two effects must be considered: atmospheric refraction (34' at horizon) and horizon depression due to altitude. The horizon depression angle $\theta$ is given by $\cos\theta = \frac{R}{R+h}$, where $R = 6370.8\,\mathrm{km}$ and $h = 5.6\,\mathrm{km}$. Thus $\cos\theta = \frac{6370.8}{6370.8+5.6} \approx 0.999121$, so $\theta \approx 2^{\circ}24'$. The minimum declination for a circumpolar star is $\delta_{\mathrm{min}} = 90^{\circ} - \mathrm{latitude} - \mathrm{refraction} - \mathrm{horizon\ depression} = 90^{\circ} - 35^{\circ}57' - 34' - 2^{\circ}24' = 51^{\circ}5'$. Therefore $\boxed{\delta_{\mathrm{min}} = 51^{\circ}5'}$.

title: Ratio of Annular to Total Solar Eclipses
problem: On average, the visual diameter of the Moon is slightly less than that of the Sun, so the frequency of annular solar eclipses is slightly higher than total solar eclipses. For an observer on the Earth, the longest total solar eclipse duration is about 7.5 minutes, and the longest annular eclipse duration is about 12.5 minutes. Here, the longest duration is the time interval from the second contact to the third contact. Suppose we count the occurrences of both types of solar eclipses for a very long time, estimate the ratio of the occurrences of annular solar eclipses and total solar eclipses. Assume the orbit of the Earth to be circular and the eccentricity of the Moon's orbit is 0.0549. Count all hybrid eclipses as annular eclipses.
solution:
Let the semi-major axis of the Moon's orbit be $a$, eccentricity $e = 0.0549$, orbital period $T$. The apparent angular radius of the Moon is $r$, of the Sun is $R$. At perigee, distance $d_1 = a(1-e)$, angular radius $r_1$, linear velocity $v_1$, angular velocity $\omega_1 = v_1/d_1$. The longest total eclipse duration (from second to third contact) is $t_1 = 2(r_1 - R)/\omega_1$. At apogee, $d_2 = a(1+e)$, $r_2$, $v_2$, $\omega_2 = v_2/d_2$, and longest annular eclipse duration $t_2 = 2(R - r_2)/\omega_2$. From conservation of angular momentum, $v_2/v_1 = d_1/d_2 = (1-e)/(1+e)$. Hence
$$
\frac{t_2}{t_1} = \frac{R - r_2}{r_1 - R} \times \left(\frac{1+e}{1-e}\right)^2.
$$

During a lunar orbit, the apparent radius $r$ varies inversely with distance $d$. Since $e$ is small, assume $r$ changes linearly with time $t$ from perigee ($t=0$):
$$
r = r_2 + \frac{2(r_1 - r_2)}{T} t, \quad 0 \le t < T/2.
$$
Set $r = R$ to find the critical time $t_R$:
$$
t_R = \frac{R - r_2}{2(r_1 - r_2)} T.
$$
For $t \in (t_R, T - t_R)$, $r > R$ and central eclipses are total; the time interval is $\Delta t_T = T - 2t_R$. For $t \in [0, t_R] \cup [T - t_R, T]$, $r \le R$ and central eclipses are annular; $\Delta t_A = 2t_R$. The probability of a central eclipse occurring at any time is uniform, so the ratio of counts is
$$
\frac{f_A}{f_T} = \frac{\Delta t_A}{\Delta t_T} = \frac{2t_R}{T - 2t_R} = \frac{R - r_2}{r_1 - R} = \frac{t_2}{t_1} \Big/ \left(\frac{1+e}{1-e}\right)^2.
$$
Substituting $t_1 = 7.5$ min, $t_2 = 12.5$ min, $e = 0.0549$:
$$
\frac{R - r_2}{r_1 - R} = \frac{12.5}{7.5} \times \left(\frac{1-0.0549}{1+0.0549}\right)^2 \approx 1.6667 \times (0.8959)^2 \approx 1.6667 \times 0.8026 \approx 1.338.
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{f_A}{f_T} \approx 1.338 \approx \frac{4}{3}.
$$

\boxed{\frac{f_A}{f_T} \approx \frac{4}{3}}

title: Redshift and Distance of a QSO
problem: The observed redshift of a QSO is $z = 0.20$ , estimate its distance. The Hubble constant is $72 \, \mathrm{km} \, \mathrm{s}^{-1} \, \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ .
solution:
Recession velocity of the QSO is

$$
\frac{v}{c} = \frac{(z+1)^2 - 1}{(z+1)^2 + 1} = 0.18
$$

According to Hubble's law,

$$
v = H_0 D
$$

The distance of the QSO is

$$
D = v / H_0 = 0.18 c / 72 = 750 \, \mathrm{Mpc}
$$

\boxed{D = 750 \, \mathrm{Mpc}}

title: Resolving the Event Horizon of the Galactic Center Black Hole
problem: The Galactic Center is believed to contain a super-massive black hole with a mass $\mathrm{M} = 4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ . The astronomy community is trying to resolve its event horizon, which is a challenging task. For a non-rotating black hole, this is the Schwarzschild radius, $R_{s} = 3(M / \mathrm{M}_{\odot})$ km. Assume that we have an Earth-sized telescope (using Very Long Baseline Interferometry). What wavelengths should we adopt in order to resolve the event horizon of the black hole? The Sun is located at 8.5 kpc from the Galactic Center.
solution:
The angular size of the black hole's event horizon (diameter) at distance $L = 8.5\,\mathrm{kpc}$ is
$$
\theta_{\mathrm{BH}} = \frac{2R_s}{L}.
$$
The angular resolution of an Earth-sized telescope (diameter $D = 2R_e$, where $R_e$ is Earth's radius) is given by the diffraction limit
$$
\theta_{\mathrm{tel}} = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D} = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{2R_e}.
$$
To resolve the black hole, we require $\theta_{\mathrm{BH}} \ge \theta_{\mathrm{tel}}$. Taking the marginal case $\theta_{\mathrm{BH}} = \theta_{\mathrm{tel}}$ gives
$$
\frac{2R_s}{L} = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{2R_e} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = \frac{4R_e R_s}{1.22\,L}.
$$
Inserting $R_s = 3(M/\mathrm{M}_\odot)\,\mathrm{km} = 3\times 4\times10^6\,\mathrm{km} = 1.2\times10^7\,\mathrm{km}$, $R_e \approx 6371\,\mathrm{km}$, $L = 8.5\,\mathrm{kpc} = 8.5\times 3.086\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{km} \approx 2.623\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{km}$, we obtain
$$
\lambda \approx \frac{4 \times 6371 \times 1.2\times10^7}{1.22 \times 2.623\times10^{17}}\,\mathrm{km} \approx 9.5\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{km} = 0.95\,\mathrm{mm}.
$$
Thus the required wavelength is about $0.9\,\mathrm{mm}$, corresponding to sub-millimeter radio or far-infrared observations.

\boxed{\lambda \approx 0.9\,\mathrm{mm}}

title: Sun gravitational catastrophe!
problem:
In a gravitational catastrophe, the mass of the Sun mass decrease instantly to half of its actual value. If you consider that the actual Earth orbit is elliptical, its orbital period is $T_0 = 1$ year and the eccentricity of the Earth orbit is $e_0 = 0.0167$ .

Find the period of the Earth's orbital motion, after the gravitational catastrophe, if it occurs on: a) 3rd of July (aphelion) b) 3rd of January.

sub_problems.problem: (a) 3rd of July (aphelion)
sub_problems.solution:
At aphelion, the Earth's speed is less than the circular speed for that radius. After the mass drop, the new orbit is elliptical. Using conservation of angular momentum and energy:

Initial aphelion distance: $r_{0,\text{aph}} = a_0(1+e_0)$.
Initial speed at aphelion: $v_{0,\text{aph}} = v_0 \sqrt{\frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}}$, where $v_0 = \sqrt{\frac{GM_0}{a_0}}$.

After catastrophe, $M = M_0/2$. The new orbit has perihelion at the old aphelion: $r_{\text{per}} = r_{0,\text{aph}}$. Let the new semi-major axis be $a$ and eccentricity $e$. Then:

$r_{\text{per}} = a(1-e) = a_0(1+e_0)$.

Speed at new perihelion equals old aphelion speed: $v_{\text{per}} = v_{0,\text{aph}}$. For the new orbit, $v_{\text{per}} = v \sqrt{\frac{1+e}{1-e}}$, where $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{a}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM_0}{2a}}$.

Equating:

$\sqrt{\frac{GM_0}{2a}} \sqrt{\frac{1+e}{1-e}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM_0}{a_0}} \sqrt{\frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}}$.

Simplify: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}} \sqrt{\frac{1+e}{1-e}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a_0}} \sqrt{\frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}}$.

Square: $\frac{1}{2a} \frac{1+e}{1-e} = \frac{1}{a_0} \frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}$.

Also $a(1-e) = a_0(1+e_0)$. Solve: from $a = a_0 \frac{1+e_0}{1-e}$, substitute:

$\frac{1}{2 a_0 \frac{1+e_0}{1-e}} \frac{1+e}{1-e} = \frac{1}{a_0} \frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}$.

$\frac{1-e}{2 a_0 (1+e_0)} \frac{1+e}{1-e} = \frac{1}{a_0} \frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}$.

$\frac{1+e}{2(1+e_0)} = \frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}$.

$1+e = 2(1-e_0)$  $e = 1 - 2e_0$.

Then $a = a_0 \frac{1+e_0}{1 - (1-2e_0)} = a_0 \frac{1+e_0}{2e_0}$.

Period $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a^3}{GM}}$ with $M = M_0/2$:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a^3}{G M_0/2}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{2 a^3}{G M_0}}$.

Original period $T_0 = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a_0^3}{G M_0}}$.

Ratio: $\frac{T}{T_0} = \sqrt{2} \left(\frac{a}{a_0}\right)^{3/2} = \sqrt{2} \left(\frac{1+e_0}{2e_0}\right)^{3/2}$.

With $e_0 = 0.0167$, $\frac{1+e_0}{2e_0} \approx \frac{1.0167}{0.0334} \approx 30.44$.

$\left(30.44\right)^{3/2} = 30.44 \sqrt{30.44} \approx 30.44 \times 5.517 \approx 168.0$.

$T/T_0 \approx 1.414 \times 168.0 \approx 237.6$.

Thus $T \approx 238$ years.

\boxed{T \approx 238 \text{ years}}

sub_problems.problem: (b) 3rd of January (perihelion)
sub_problems.solution:
At perihelion, the Earth's speed is larger than the circular speed for that radius. After the mass drop, the total energy becomes positive, so the orbit is hyperbolic or parabolic. Hence the Earth escapes the Sun's gravity and there is no periodic motion; the period is infinite.

\boxed{\text{The orbit is open (hyperbolic/parabolic); the period is infinite.}}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{The orbit is open (hyperbolic/parabolic); the period is infinite.}}

knowledge_points.description: v_circ = sqrt(GM/r); provides the reference speed to compare with Earth's actual speed at perihelion.

knowledge_points.name: total mechanical energy in gravity
knowledge_points.description: E = (1/2)mv^2 - GMm/r; used to compute the new total energy after the Sun's mass halves and determine if the orbit is bound.

knowledge_points.name: escape condition
knowledge_points.description: If total mechanical energy E >= 0, the orbit is unbound (parabolic or hyperbolic) and has no finite period; used to conclude the period is infinite.

knowledge_points.name: instantaneous mass loss
knowledge_points.description: The Sun's mass decreases instantly, so Earth's position and velocity are unchanged at the moment of catastrophe; this allows using the pre-catastrophe r and v in the new energy expression.

title: Volcanic activity on Io
problem:
13. Volcanic activity on lo, whose rotation period synchronizes with its orbital period, was proposed to be the result of tidal heating mainly from Jupiter. The resultant tidal force on a body is the difference in gravitational force experienced by the near and far sides of that body due to another body. Measurements of the surface distortion of lo via satellite radar altimeter mapping indicate that the surface rises and falls by up to 100m during one-half orbit. Only the surface layers will move by this amount. Interior layers within lo will move by a smaller amount, and thus we assume that on average the entire mass of lo is moved through 50m. Assume that lo is considered as two hemispheres each treated as a point mass. Calculate the average power of the tidal heating on lo.

Hint: you can use the following approximation $\left(1 + x\right)^n \approx 1 + nx$ for small $x$ .

The mass of lo is $m_{lo} = 8.931938 \times 10^{22} \, kg$

The perijove distance is $r_{peri} = 420000\mathrm{km}$

The apojove distance is $r_{apo} = 423400\mathrm{km}$

The orbital period of Io is 152853 s

The radius of lo is $R_{\mathrm{lo}} = 1821.6 \mathrm{~km}$ .
solution:
The tidal force on one hemisphere (mass $m_{Io}/2$) located at distance $R_{Io}/2$ from the center of Io is:

$$F_{\text{tidal}} = F\left(r - \frac{R_{Io}}{2}\right) - F\left(r + \frac{R_{Io}}{2}\right)$$

$$= -\frac{G M_J \frac{m_{Io}}{2}}{\left(r - \frac{R_{Io}}{2}\right)^2} + \frac{G M_J \frac{m_{Io}}{2}}{\left(r + \frac{R_{Io}}{2}\right)^2}$$

$$= -\frac{G M_J m_{Io}}{2r^2} \left[ \frac{1}{\left(1 - \frac{R_{Io}}{2r}\right)^2} - \frac{1}{\left(1 + \frac{R_{Io}}{2r}\right)^2} \right]$$

Using $(1+x)^{-2} \approx 1 - 2x$ for small $x$:

$$F_{\text{tidal}} \approx -\frac{G M_J m_{Io}}{2r^2} \left[ \left(1 + \frac{R_{Io}}{r}\right) - \left(1 - \frac{R_{Io}}{r}\right) \right] = -\frac{G M_J m_{Io} R_{Io}}{r^3}$$

The difference in tidal force between perijove and apojove:

$$\Delta F = \left| F_{\text{tidal}}(r_{\text{peri}}) - F_{\text{tidal}}(r_{\text{apo}}) \right| = G M_J m_{Io} R_{Io} \left( \frac{1}{r_{\text{peri}}^3} - \frac{1}{r_{\text{apo}}^3} \right)$$

We need $M_J$. Using Kepler's third law for Io's orbit (assuming circular approximation with mean distance $a$):

$$a = \frac{r_{\text{peri}} + r_{\text{apo}}}{2} = \frac{420000 + 423400}{2} \, \text{km} = 421700 \, \text{km} = 4.217 \times 10^8 \, \text{m}$$

$$T = 152853 \, \text{s}$$

$$G M_J = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{T^2} = \frac{4\pi^2 (4.217 \times 10^8)^3}{(152853)^2} \approx 1.267 \times 10^{17} \, \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$$

Now compute:

$$\frac{1}{r_{\text{peri}}^3} = \frac{1}{(4.20 \times 10^8)^3} = 1.350 \times 10^{-26} \, \text{m}^{-3}$$

$$\frac{1}{r_{\text{apo}}^3} = \frac{1}{(4.234 \times 10^8)^3} = 1.317 \times 10^{-26} \, \text{m}^{-3}$$

$$\Delta F = (1.267 \times 10^{17}) (8.931938 \times 10^{22}) (1.8216 \times 10^6) (1.350 \times 10^{-26} - 1.317 \times 10^{-26})$$

$$\Delta F \approx 6.65 \times 10^{18} \, \text{N}$$

The average power is work done over half an orbit divided by half the period:

$$\bar{P} = \frac{\Delta F \cdot d}{T/2} = \frac{(6.65 \times 10^{18}) (50)}{152853/2} \approx 4.35 \times 10^{15} \, \text{W}$$

\boxed{\bar{P} = 4.35 \times 10^{15} \, \text{W}}
