knowledge_points.name: tidal force
knowledge_points.description: Tidal force is the difference in gravitational force on the near and far sides of a body; it is used to compute the net stretching force on Io.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's law of universal gravitation
knowledge_points.description: Gives the gravitational force between point masses; used to calculate forces on the two hemispheres of Io at different distances from Jupiter.

knowledge_points.name: two-hemisphere point-mass model
knowledge_points.description: Io is treated as two point masses (each half its total mass) separated by its diameter; this simplifies computing the tidal force as a difference of forces on the two points.

knowledge_points.name: average tidal displacement of Io mass
knowledge_points.description: The entire mass of Io is assumed to move on average by 50 m during one-half orbit due to tidal distortion; this value is used with the net tidal force to compute mechanical work.

knowledge_points.name: binomial approximation for small x
knowledge_points.description: The approximation (1+x)^n ≈ 1+nx for |x|≪1 simplifies the tidal force expression to a linear term in R/r, avoiding exact expansions.

knowledge_points.name: semi-major axis of elliptical orbit
knowledge_points.description: For an elliptical orbit the semi-major axis a equals (r_peri + r_apo)/2; this relation yields the mean distance needed in Kepler's third law.

knowledge_points.name: Kepler's third law
knowledge_points.description: Relates orbital period T to semi-major axis a and the gravitational parameter GM of the central body; here GM_J = 4π²a³/T² is used to obtain Jupiter's mass information from Io's orbit.

knowledge_points.name: Io mass negligible relative to Jupiter
knowledge_points.description: When applying Kepler's third law, Io's mass is neglected compared to Jupiter's mass, so the satellite is treated as a test particle.

title: True or False
problem: Determine if each of the following statements is True or False. In the Summary Answersheet, tick the correct answer (TRUE / FALSE) for each statement. No justifications are necessary for this question.

sub_problems.problem: (T1.1) In a photograph of the clear sky on a Full Moon night with a sufficiently long exposure, the colour of the sky would appear blue as in daytime.
sub_problems.solution:
The colour of the clear sky during night is the same as during daytime, since the spectrum of sunlight reflected by the Moon is almost the same as the spectrum of sunlight. Only the intensity is lower. Therefore the statement is true.
\boxed{\text{TRUE}}

knowledge_points.name: Rayleigh scattering
knowledge_points.description: The daytime sky appears blue because atmospheric molecules scatter sunlight with a strong wavelength dependence (shorter wavelengths scattered more). This same scattering process operates at night when the atmosphere is illuminated by moonlight.

knowledge_points.name: lunar spectrum matches solar spectrum
knowledge_points.description: The Moon reflects sunlight, and its reflectance in the visible range is nearly flat, so the spectrum of moonlight is essentially the same as that of sunlight, only dimmer.

knowledge_points.name: color independent of intensity
knowledge_points.description: The perceived color of scattered light depends on the spectral composition of the incident light, not its absolute intensity. A long exposure can compensate for low intensity without altering the color.

sub_problems.problem: (T1.2) An astronomer at Bhubaneswar marks the position of the Sun on the sky at 05:00 UT every day of the year. If the Earth's axis were perpendicular to its orbital plane, these positions would trace an arc of a great circle.
sub_problems.solution:
If the Earth's axis were perpendicular to its orbital plane, the celestial equator would coincide with the ecliptic and the Sun would remain along the celestial equator every day. However, as the Earth's orbit is elliptical, the true Sun would still lead or lag the mean Sun by a few minutes on different days of the year, so the positions would not trace a great circle. Therefore the statement is false.
\boxed{\text{FALSE}}

knowledge_points.name: celestial equator
knowledge_points.description: The projection of Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere; needed to understand that with a perpendicular axis it would coincide with the ecliptic.

knowledge_points.name: ecliptic
knowledge_points.description: The apparent path of the Sun on the celestial sphere over a year; needed to see that with zero obliquity the Sun would stay on the celestial equator.

knowledge_points.name: great circle
knowledge_points.description: A circle on the celestial sphere whose plane passes through the observer; the statement claims the Sun's positions trace one, which is contradicted by the equation of time.

knowledge_points.name: equation of time
knowledge_points.description: The difference between apparent solar time and mean solar time due to Earth's elliptical orbit and axial tilt; even with zero tilt, orbital eccentricity causes the Sun to lead or lag the mean Sun, so its daily positions do not trace a perfect great circle.

knowledge_points.name: Earth's axis perpendicular to orbital plane
knowledge_points.description: The hypothetical condition stated in the problem; sets the obliquity to zero so the celestial equator and ecliptic coincide.

knowledge_points.name: elliptical Earth orbit
knowledge_points.description: The Earth's orbit is not a perfect circle; this eccentricity remains even under the hypothetical perpendicular axis and causes the equation of time, breaking the great-circle trace.

sub_problems.problem: (T1.3) If the orbital period of a certain minor body around the Sun in the ecliptic plane is less than the orbital period of Uranus, then its orbit must necessarily be fully inside the orbit of Uranus.
sub_problems.solution:
The semi-major axis of the orbit of the body will be less than that of Uranus. However the minor body's orbit may have a high eccentricity, in which case it may go outside that of Uranus. Therefore the statement is false.
\boxed{\text{FALSE}}

knowledge_points.name: Kepler's third law
knowledge_points.description: Relates orbital period to semi-major axis; a shorter period than Uranus implies a smaller semi-major axis.

knowledge_points.name: orbital eccentricity
knowledge_points.description: Determines how much an orbit deviates from a circle; high eccentricity allows a body with smaller semi-major axis to cross outside Uranus's orbit at aphelion.

knowledge_points.name: Keplerian two-body motion
knowledge_points.description: The minor body and Sun are treated as a gravitationally bound two-body system obeying Kepler's laws, ignoring perturbations from other planets.

sub_problems.problem: (T1.4) The centre of mass of the solar system is inside the Sun at all times.
sub_problems.solution:
The centre of mass of the Sun-Jupiter pair is just outside the Sun. Thus, if all gas giants are on the same side of the Sun, the centre of mass of the Solar system is definitely outside the Sun. Therefore the statement is false.
\boxed{\text{FALSE}}

knowledge_points.name: centre of mass
knowledge_points.description: The weighted average position of mass in a system; needed to evaluate whether the solar system's barycentre lies inside the Sun.

knowledge_points.name: two-body centre of mass formula
knowledge_points.description: The distance of the centre of mass from the primary is proportional to the secondary's mass times separation divided by total mass; used to estimate the Sun–Jupiter barycentre location.

knowledge_points.name: Sun–Jupiter barycentre outside Sun
knowledge_points.description: The reference solution states that the centre of mass of the Sun–Jupiter pair lies just outside the Sun, which is the key fact that makes the statement false.

knowledge_points.name: planetary alignment effect
knowledge_points.description: When all gas giants lie on the same side of the Sun, their combined mass shifts the solar system's centre of mass even farther from the Sun's centre, guaranteeing it is outside the Sun.

sub_problems.problem: (T1.5) A photon is moving in free space. As the Universe expands, its momentum decreases.
sub_problems.solution:
For photons the wavelength increases when the Universe expands. Since momentum is inversely proportional to wavelength, the momentum decreases. Therefore the statement is true.
\boxed{\text{TRUE}}

knowledge_points.name: cosmological redshift
knowledge_points.description: As the Universe expands, the wavelength of freely propagating photons stretches, increasing proportionally to the cosmic scale factor.

knowledge_points.name: photon momentum-wavelength relation
knowledge_points.description: The momentum p of a photon is inversely proportional to its wavelength λ, given by p = h/λ, so an increase in wavelength leads to a decrease in momentum.

knowledge_points.name: free space propagation
knowledge_points.description: The photon is moving in free space, meaning it experiences no interactions or scattering that would alter its momentum besides the cosmological expansion effect.

title: GOTO
problem: The Gravitational-Wave Optical Transient Observer (GOTO) aims to carry out searches of optical counterparts of any Gravitational Wave (GW) sources within an hour of their detection by the LIGO and VIRGO experiments. The survey needs to cover a big area on the sky in a short time to search all possible regions constrained by the GW experiments before the optical burst signal, if any, fades away. The GOTO telescope array is composed of 4 identical reflective telescopes, each with $40\mathrm{-cm}$ diameter aperture and f-ratio of 2.5, working together to image large regions of the sky. For simplicity, we assume that the telescopes' fields-of-view (FoV) do not overlap with one another.

sub_problems.problem: (a) Calculate the projected angular size per mm at the focal plane, i.e. plate scale, of each telescope.
sub_problems.solution:
For small angular separation $\theta$, the distance at the focal plane is $S = f \theta$, where $f$ is the focal length. Hence plate scale $= \theta/S = 1/f$. The focal length $f = \text{F-ratio} \times \text{diameter} = 2.5 \times 0.40\,\mathrm{m} = 1.0\,\mathrm{m} = 1000\,\mathrm{mm}$. Therefore plate scale $= 1/1000\,\mathrm{rad/mm} = (1/1000) \times (180 \times 3600/\pi)\,\mathrm{arcsec/mm} = 206\,\mathrm{arcsec/mm} = 3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm}$.

\boxed{3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm}}

knowledge_points.name: image scale for a telescope
knowledge_points.description: For a distant object and small angular separations, the linear size s of the image on the focal plane is s = f θ, where f is the focal length and θ is the angular size in radians. This directly gives the plate scale as θ/s = 1/f.

knowledge_points.name: f-number definition
knowledge_points.description: The f-number (f-ratio) of an optical system is the ratio of the focal length f to the aperture diameter D: f-number = f/D. The problem gives the f‑ratio and diameter, so f = f‑number × D is used to find the focal length.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: The reference solution explicitly assumes small angular separations so that tanθ ≈ θ, which is needed to write s = fθ instead of s = f tanθ. This is standard for most telescopic fields.

knowledge_points.name: radian to arcminute conversion
knowledge_points.description: The plate scale initially computed in rad/mm is converted into the practical astronomical units arcmin/mm (or arcsec/mm) using 1 rad = (180/π)×3600 arcsec and 1 arcmin = 60 arcsec.

sub_problems.problem: (b) If the zero-point magnitude (i.e. the magnitude at which the count rate detected by the detector is 1 count per second) of the telescope system is $18.5\mathrm{mag}$, calculate the minimum time needed to reach 21 mag at Signal-to-Noise Ratio $(\mathrm{SNR}) = 5$ for a point source. We first assume that the noise is dominated by both the Read-Out Noise (RON) at 10 counts/pixel and the CCD dark (thermal) noise (DN) rate of 1 count/pix/minute. The CCDs used with the GOTO have a 6-micron pixel size and gain (conversion factor between photo-electron and data count) of 1. The typical seeing at the observatory site is around 1.0 arcsec. [8]
sub_problems.solution:
From part (a), plate scale $= 3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm}$. Pixel size $= 6\,\mu\mathrm{m} = 6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mm}$. Angular size per pixel $= 3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm} \times 6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mm} = 0.02064\,\mathrm{arcmin} = 1.238\,\mathrm{arcsec}$. Seeing is $1.0\,\mathrm{arcsec}$, so the star light is mostly contained within $N_{\mathrm{pix}} = 1$ pixel.

Zero-point magnitude $ZP = 18.5$, magnitude $m = 21$. Count rate $\mathrm{CR} = 10^{-(m-ZP)/2.5} = 10^{-(21-18.5)/2.5} = 10^{-1} = 0.1\,\mathrm{counts/s}$.

RON $= 10$ counts/pixel, DN $= 1$ count/pix/min $= 1/60$ counts/pix/s.

SNR $= \frac{\mathrm{CR}\times t}{\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{pix}}\mathrm{RON}^2 + N_{\mathrm{pix}}\mathrm{DN}\cdot t}} = \frac{0.1 t}{\sqrt{10^2 + (1/60)t}}$.

Set SNR $= 5$: $(0.1 t)^2 = 25(100 + t/60)$.

$0.01 t^2 = 2500 + (25/60)t$.

Multiply by 60: $0.6 t^2 = 150000 + 25 t$.

$0.6 t^2 - 25 t - 150000 = 0$.

$t = \frac{25 + \sqrt{25^2 + 4\times0.6\times150000}}{2\times0.6} = \frac{25 + \sqrt{625 + 360000}}{1.2} = \frac{25 + \sqrt{360625}}{1.2} = \frac{25 + 600.52}{1.2} = 521.27\,\mathrm{s}$.

$t \approx 521\,\mathrm{s} = 8.68\,\mathrm{minutes}$.

\boxed{521\,\mathrm{s}}

knowledge_points.name: Plate scale
knowledge_points.description: The ratio of angular size on the sky to physical size at the focal plane. Here the plate scale from part (a) is 3.44 arcmin/mm. It is used to convert the CCD pixel size (6 µm) to angular size per pixel (1.238 arcsec), which is then compared to the seeing to determine how many pixels a point source covers.

knowledge_points.name: Astronomical seeing
knowledge_points.description: The atmospheric blurring of a point source, typically measured as the FWHM of the point spread function. The problem gives a seeing of 1.0 arcsec. Combined with the pixel angular size, this determines that the star's light is mostly contained within 1 pixel.

knowledge_points.name: Pogson's magnitude equation
knowledge_points.description: The relation between magnitude difference and flux ratio: m1 - m2 = -2.5 log10(F1/F2). Used to compute the count rate from the zero-point magnitude (18.5 mag, where count rate is 1 count/s) and the target magnitude (21 mag): CR = 10^{-(21-18.5)/2.5} = 0.1 counts/s.

knowledge_points.name: CCD SNR equation for point source with read noise and dark current
knowledge_points.description: The signal-to-noise ratio formula for a point source when noise is dominated by read-out noise and dark current: SNR = (CR * t) / sqrt( N_pix * (RON^2 + DN_rate * t) ), where RON is the read-out noise per pixel (variance RON^2), DN_rate is the dark current count rate per pixel (variance = DN_rate * t due to Poisson statistics), and source photon noise is neglected. Used to set up the equation for the required exposure time.

knowledge_points.name: Noise dominated by read-out noise and dark current
knowledge_points.description: The problem explicitly states that we assume the noise is dominated by read-out noise (RON) and dark current (DN), so photon noise from the source and sky background are ignored. This justifies omitting the sqrt(CR * t) term in the SNR denominator.

knowledge_points.name: Point source contained within one pixel
knowledge_points.description: Based on the computed pixel angular size (1.238 arcsec) and the given seeing (1.0 arcsec), the star's light is assumed to be mostly contained within a single pixel, so N_pix = 1 in the SNR equation.

sub_problems.problem: (c) Normally when the exposure time is long and the source count is high then Poisson noise from the source is also significant. Determine the relation between SNR and exposure time in the case that the noise is dominated by Poisson noise of the source. Recalculate the minimum exposure time required to reach 21 mag with $\mathrm{SNR} = 5$ from part b) if Poisson noise is also taken into consideration. The Poisson noise (standard deviation) of the source is given by $\sigma_{\mathrm{source}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{Source~Count}}$ . In reality, there is also the sky background which can be important source of Poisson noise. For our purpose here, please ignore any sky background in the calculation.
sub_problems.solution:
Including source Poisson noise: $\mathrm{SNR} = \frac{\mathrm{CR}\times t}{\sqrt{\mathrm{RON}^2 + \mathrm{DN}\cdot t + \mathrm{CR}\cdot t}}$.

When Poisson noise dominates, $\mathrm{SNR} \approx \frac{\mathrm{CR}\cdot t}{\sqrt{\mathrm{CR}\cdot t}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{CR}\cdot t}$, so $\mathrm{SNR} \propto t^{1/2}$.

Now with all noises: $\mathrm{CR}=0.1$, $\mathrm{RON}=10$, $\mathrm{DN}=1/60$.

Set SNR $=5$: $(0.1 t)^2 = 25(100 + t/60 + 0.1 t)$.

$0.01 t^2 = 2500 + (25/60)t + 2.5 t$.

$0.01 t^2 = 2500 + (0.4167 + 2.5)t = 2500 + 2.9167 t$.

Multiply by 100: $t^2 = 250000 + 291.67 t$.

$t^2 - 291.67 t - 250000 = 0$.

$t = \frac{291.67 + \sqrt{291.67^2 + 4\times250000}}{2} = \frac{291.67 + \sqrt{85071 + 1000000}}{2} = \frac{291.67 + \sqrt{1085071}}{2} = \frac{291.67 + 1041.67}{2} = 666.67\,\mathrm{s}$.

$t \approx 667\,\mathrm{s} = 11.1\,\mathrm{minutes}$.

\boxed{667\,\mathrm{s}}

knowledge_points.name: Poisson noise standard deviation
knowledge_points.description: For a Poisson process, the standard deviation of the number of detected events is the square root of the expected number: σ = √N. This is used to compute the noise contribution from the source counts.

knowledge_points.name: CCD SNR equation
knowledge_points.description: For a point source with count rate CR, exposure time t, read-out noise RON, and dark noise rate DN, the signal-to-noise ratio is SNR = (CR·t) / √(RON² + DN·t + CR·t). This equation combines the independent noise variances.

knowledge_points.name: Poisson-limited SNR approximation
knowledge_points.description: When source Poisson noise dominates, the other noise terms are negligible, so SNR ≈ √(CR·t), giving the relation SNR ∝ t^{1/2}.

knowledge_points.name: imported parameters from part (b)
knowledge_points.description: The source count rate for a 21 mag point source is 0.1 counts/s, the read-out noise is 10 counts/pixel, and the dark noise rate is 1 count/pix/min = 1/60 counts/s, as derived in part (b).

knowledge_points.name: ignore sky background
knowledge_points.description: Sky background Poisson noise is ignored as instructed, so only the source Poisson noise contributes to the Poisson noise term.

sub_problems.problem: (d) The typical localisation uncertainty of the GW detector is about 100 square-degrees and we would like to cover the entire possible location of any candidate within an hour after the GW is detected. Estimate the minimum side length of the square CCD needed for each telescope in terms of the number of pixels. You may assume that the time taken for the CCD read-out and the pointing change are negligible.
sub_problems.solution:
From part (c), exposure time per pointing $= 11.1$ minutes. In 1 hour, number of pointings $= 60/11.1 \approx 5.4$, round down to 5 pointings.

Total area to cover $= 100\,\mathrm{deg}^2$. With 4 telescopes, area per pointing per telescope $= \frac{100}{5 \times 4} = 5\,\mathrm{deg}^2$. So each pointing covers a square of side $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\,\mathrm{deg}$.

Plate scale $= 3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm}$, pixel size $= 6\,\mu\mathrm{m} = 0.006\,\mathrm{mm}$. Angular size per pixel $= 3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm} \times 0.006\,\mathrm{mm} = 0.02064\,\mathrm{arcmin} = 1.2384\,\mathrm{arcsec}$.

Side length in pixels $= \frac{2.236\,\mathrm{deg} \times 60\,\mathrm{arcmin/deg}}{0.02064\,\mathrm{arcmin/pixel}} = \frac{134.16}{0.02064} \approx 6500$ pixels.

More precisely: $2.236\,\mathrm{deg} = 2.236 \times 60 = 134.16\,\mathrm{arcmin}$. Number of pixels $= 134.16 / 0.02064 = 6500$.

Alternatively using arcsec: $2.236\,\mathrm{deg} = 2.236 \times 3600 = 8049.6\,\mathrm{arcsec}$. Number of pixels $= 8049.6 / 1.2384 = 6500$.

Thus minimum CCD side length $= 6500$ pixels.

\boxed{6500\,\mathrm{pixels}}

knowledge_points.name: plate scale
knowledge_points.description: The plate scale is the angular size per unit length at the focal plane. It is needed to convert between the physical size of the detector and the angular field of view.

knowledge_points.name: field of view
knowledge_points.description: Field of view (FoV) is the angular area on the sky covered by a single detector. The required FoV per telescope is derived from the total survey area and the number of pointings.

knowledge_points.name: non-overlapping fields of view
knowledge_points.description: The telescopes' fields-of-view do not overlap, so the total area covered in one pointing is simply the sum of the individual telescope FoVs.

knowledge_points.name: exposure time per pointing
knowledge_points.description: The exposure time required per pointing is 11.1 minutes, as derived in part (c). This value dictates the maximum number of pointings that can be executed within one hour.

knowledge_points.name: CCD pixel size
knowledge_points.description: The CCD pixel size is 6 microns. Multiplying this physical size by the plate scale gives the angular size per pixel, which is used to compute the number of pixels across the required detector side.

knowledge_points.name: plate scale value
knowledge_points.description: The specific numerical plate scale is 3.44 arcmin/mm, as calculated in part (a). This value converts the angular field-of-view side length into physical dimensions on the detector.

title: Mass of the Local Group
problem:
The dynamics of M31 (Andromeda) and the Milky Way (MW) can be used to estimate the total mass of the Local Group (LG). The basic idea is that galaxies currently in a binary system were at approximately the same point in space shortly after the Big Bang. To a reasonable approximation, the mass of the local group is dominated by the masses of the MW and M31. Via Doppler shifts of the spectral lines, it was found that M31 is moving towards the MW with a speed of $118 \, \mathrm{km} \, \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ . This may be surprising, given that most galaxies are moving away from each other with the general Hubble flow. The fact that M31 is moving towards the MW is presumably because their mutual gravitational attraction has eventually reversed their initial velocities. In principle, if the pair of galaxies is well-represented by isolated point masses, their total mass may be determined by measuring their separation, relative velocity and the time since the universe began. Kahn and Woltjer (1959) used this argument to estimate the mass in the LG.

In this problem we will follow this argument through our calculation as follows.

sub_problems.problem:
(a) Consider an isolated system with negligible angular momentum of two gravitating point masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ (as observed by an inertial observer at the centre of mass). Write down the expression of the total mechanical energy $(E)$ of this system in mathematical form connecting $m_{1}, m_{2}, r_{1}, r_{2}, 
u_{1}, 
u_{2}$ , and the universal gravitational constant $G$ , where $
u_{1}$ and $
u_{2}$ are the radial velocities of $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ , respectively.
sub_problems.solution:
The total mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energies of the two masses plus the gravitational potential energy:
\[
E = \frac{1}{2} m_1 \nu_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 \nu_2^2 - \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r_1 + r_2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E = \frac{1}{2} m_1 \nu_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 \nu_2^2 - \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r_1 + r_2}}
\]

knowledge_points.name: total mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: The sum of kinetic and potential energies of a system; needed here to write the expression requested by the problem.

knowledge_points.name: kinetic energy
knowledge_points.description: Energy of motion for each point mass, given by (1/2) m v^2; required to write the kinetic terms in the energy expression.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational potential energy
knowledge_points.description: Potential energy of two point masses separated by distance r, given by -G m1 m2 / r; needed for the potential term.

knowledge_points.name: isolated two-body system
knowledge_points.description: The system consists of only two point masses with no external forces; justifies using only the mutual gravitational potential and ignoring other interactions.

knowledge_points.name: negligible angular momentum
knowledge_points.description: The problem states angular momentum is negligible, so only radial velocities appear and no rotational kinetic energy terms are needed.

knowledge_points.name: point masses
knowledge_points.description: The galaxies are treated as point particles; this justifies using the simple inverse-distance gravitational potential without extended-body corrections.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's law of gravitation
knowledge_points.description: Provides the gravitational potential energy form -G m1 m2 / r, where r is the total separation r1 + r2.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Re-write the equation in a) in terms of $r$ , $\nu$ , $\mu$ , $M$ , and $G$ , where $r \equiv r_1 + r_2$ is the separation distance between $m_1$ and $m_2$ , $\nu$ is the changing rate of the separation distance, $\mu \equiv \frac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ is the reduced mass of the system, and $M \equiv m_1 + m_2$ is the total mass of the system.

knowledge_points.name: centre-of-mass frame
knowledge_points.description: The system is described from the inertial centre-of-mass frame, which gives the relations m₁r₁ = m₂r₂ and m₁ν₁ = m₂ν₂ used to express r₁, r₂, ν₁, ν₂ in terms of r, ν, and the masses.

knowledge_points.name: total mechanical energy of two-body system
knowledge_points.description: The expression E = ½ m₁ν₁² + ½ m₂ν₂² − Gm₁m₂/r from part (a) is the starting point that must be rewritten in the new variables.

knowledge_points.name: reduced mass
knowledge_points.description: The reduced mass μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂) appears in the final simplified expression and is used to compactly write the kinetic and potential terms.

knowledge_points.name: total mass
knowledge_points.description: The total mass M = m₁+m₂ is introduced and used to express the gravitational potential term −GμM/r in the final energy formula.

knowledge_points.name: algebraic substitution using centre-of-mass relations
knowledge_points.description: The solution substitutes r₁ = (m₂/M)r, r₂ = (m₁/M)r, ν₁ = (m₂/M)ν, ν₂ = (m₁/M)ν into the energy expression and simplifies to obtain the compact form.

sub_problems.problem:
(c) Show that the equation in b) yields
\[
v ^ {2} = (2 G M) \left(\frac {1}{r} - \frac {1}{r _ {0}}\right), \text {w h e r e} r _ {0} \text {i s a n e w c o n s t a n t}.
\]
Find $r_0$ in terms of $\mu, M, G$ and $E$ .
sub_problems.solution:
From part (b): $E = \frac{\mu}{2} \left( \nu^2 - \frac{2GM}{r} \right)$. Rearranging:
\[
\nu^2 - \frac{2GM}{r} = \frac{2E}{\mu} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \nu^2 = \frac{2GM}{r} + \frac{2E}{\mu}.
\]
Write $\frac{2E}{\mu} = -\frac{2GM}{r_0}$ where $r_0$ is a positive constant (since $E<0$). Then
\[
\nu^2 = 2GM \left( \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{r_0} \right).
\]
Comparing, $\frac{2E}{\mu} = -\frac{2GM}{r_0}$ gives $r_0 = -\frac{GM\mu}{E}$.
\[
\boxed{r_0 = -\frac{GM\mu}{E}}
\]

knowledge_points.name: total mechanical energy of two-body system
knowledge_points.description: The result from part (b) gives E = (μ/2)(ν² - 2GM/r), which is the starting equation for this sub-problem.

knowledge_points.name: bound orbit (negative total energy)
knowledge_points.description: The solution assumes E < 0 so that r₀ defined via 2E/μ = -2GM/r₀ is a positive constant, consistent with a gravitationally bound system.

knowledge_points.name: introducing a constant to reparameterize energy
knowledge_points.description: The step of setting 2E/μ = -2GM/r₀ defines a new constant r₀ that absorbs the energy term, transforming the energy equation into the desired kinematic form.

sub_problems.problem:
(d) From the above parametric equations, show that an expression for $\frac{vt}{r}$ is
\[
\frac {v t}{r} = \frac {(\sin \theta) (\theta - \sin \theta)}{(1 - \cos \theta) ^ {2}}.
\]
sub_problems.solution:
From part (c): $v^2 = 2GM\left(\frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{r_0}\right)$. Substitute $r(\theta) = \frac{r_0}{2}(1-\cos\theta)$:
\[
v^2 = 2GM\left(\frac{2}{r_0(1-\cos\theta)} - \frac{1}{r_0}\right) = \frac{2GM}{r_0}\left(\frac{2 - (1-\cos\theta)}{1-\cos\theta}\right) = \frac{2GM}{r_0}\left(\frac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta}\right).
\]
Using $1+\cos\theta = 2\cos^2(\theta/2)$ and $1-\cos\theta = 2\sin^2(\theta/2)$, we get $v = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r_0}}\frac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos\theta}$ (taking positive root for $v>0$; the sign is handled by the negative value in part (e)).
Now $t(\theta) = \left(\frac{r_0^3}{8GM}\right)^{1/2}(\theta - \sin\theta)$ and $r(\theta) = \frac{r_0}{2}(1-\cos\theta)$. Then
\[
\frac{v t}{r} = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r_0}}\frac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos\theta} \cdot \left(\frac{r_0^3}{8GM}\right)^{1/2}(\theta-\sin\theta)}{\frac{r_0}{2}(1-\cos\theta)} = \frac{2}{r_0}\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r_0}\cdot\frac{r_0^3}{8GM}}\frac{(\sin\theta)(\theta-\sin\theta)}{(1-\cos\theta)^2} = \frac{2}{r_0}\cdot\frac{r_0}{2}\frac{(\sin\theta)(\theta-\sin\theta)}{(1-\cos\theta)^2}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\frac{v t}{r} = \frac{(\sin\theta)(\theta-\sin\theta)}{(1-\cos\theta)^2}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: parametric radial orbit solution
knowledge_points.description: The derivation uses the parametric form r(θ) = (r₀/2)(1−cosθ) and t(θ) = (r₀³/(8GM))^(1/2)(θ−sinθ) for a bound radial orbit, which were introduced earlier in the problem. The current step simply substitutes these expressions.

knowledge_points.name: energy integral for radial motion
knowledge_points.description: The expression v² = 2GM(1/r − 1/r₀) from part (c) is the starting point for eliminating v in terms of θ.

knowledge_points.name: half-angle trigonometric identities
knowledge_points.description: The solution uses 1+cosθ = 2cos²(θ/2) and 1−cosθ = 2sin²(θ/2) to simplify the expression for v into a compact form involving sinθ/(1−cosθ).

knowledge_points.name: algebraic substitution and simplification
knowledge_points.description: The derivation proceeds by substituting the parametric forms for r(θ), t(θ), and the simplified v(θ) into the ratio vt/r and cancelling common factors algebraically.

sub_problems.problem: (e) Now we consider $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ as the MW and M31, respectively, such that the current values of $\nu$ and $r$ are $\nu = -118\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$ and $r = 710\mathrm{kpc}$ , and $t$ may be taken to be the age of the Universe (13700 million years). Find $\theta$ using numerical iteration.
sub_problems.solution:
Convert to SI units:
\[
v = -118\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} = -1.18\times10^5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},
\]
\[
r = 710\,\mathrm{kpc} = 710\times3.0857\times10^{19}\,\mathrm{m} = 2.1908\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{m},
\]
\[
t = 13700\times10^6\,\mathrm{yr} = 1.37\times10^{10}\times3.15576\times10^7\,\mathrm{s} = 4.3233\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{s}.
\]
Compute $\frac{vt}{r}$:
\[
\frac{vt}{r} = \frac{(-1.18\times10^5)(4.3233\times10^{17})}{2.1908\times10^{22}} = -2.33.
\]
Thus we need to solve $\frac{(\sin\theta)(\theta-\sin\theta)}{(1-\cos\theta)^2} = -2.33$. The negative value indicates $\theta > \pi$. Iterating:
- $\theta = 240^\circ = 4.18879$ rad: value $\approx -1.95$
- $\theta = 244^\circ = 4.2586$ rad: value $\approx -2.24$
- $\theta = 245^\circ = 4.27606$ rad: value $\approx -2.32$
- $\theta = 246^\circ = 4.29351$ rad: value $\approx -2.40$
The value $-2.33$ lies between $245^\circ$ and $246^\circ$; interpolating gives $\theta \approx 245.2^\circ = 4.279$ rad.
\[
\boxed{\theta \approx 245^\circ \; (4.28\,\mathrm{rad})}
\]

knowledge_points.name: age of Universe as t
knowledge_points.description: The time since the Big Bang is taken as the age of the Universe (13.7 Gyr), which is used as the elapsed time t in the dynamical equation.

knowledge_points.name: parsec to meter conversion
knowledge_points.description: The distance r is given in kiloparsecs (kpc) and must be converted to meters using 1 pc = 3.0857×10^16 m for numerical evaluation.

knowledge_points.name: year to second conversion
knowledge_points.description: The time t given in years must be converted to seconds using 1 yr = 3.15576×10^7 s for consistency with SI speed units.

knowledge_points.name: negative radial velocity
knowledge_points.description: The radial velocity v is negative, indicating the galaxies are approaching each other; this leads to a negative vt/r ratio and requires θ > π in the parametric solution.

knowledge_points.name: numerical iteration
knowledge_points.description: The transcendental equation for θ is solved by guessing values, evaluating the expression, and refining the guess until the target value is matched to desired accuracy.

knowledge_points.name: parametric solution from part (d)
knowledge_points.description: The expression vt/r = (sin θ)(θ - sin θ)/(1 - cos θ)^2 derived in part (d) is used directly to relate the observables to the parameter θ.

sub_problems.problem: (f) Use the value of $\theta$ from e) to calculate the maximum distance between M31 and the MW, $r_{\mathrm{max}}$ , and hence also obtain the value of $M$ in solar masses.
sub_problems.solution:
From $r(\theta) = \frac{r_0}{2}(1-\cos\theta)$, the maximum separation occurs when $\cos\theta = -1$, i.e., $r_{\max} = r_0$. Using $r = 710\,\mathrm{kpc}$ and $\theta = 245^\circ$:
\[
r_{\max} = r_0 = \frac{2r}{1-\cos\theta} = \frac{2\times710}{1-\cos245^\circ} = \frac{1420}{1-(-0.4226)} = \frac{1420}{1.4226} \approx 998\,\mathrm{kpc}.
\]
Convert to metres: $r_{\max} = 998\times3.0857\times10^{19} = 3.0795\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{m}$.

Now use the parametric equation for time:
\[
t = \left(\frac{r_0^3}{8GM}\right)^{1/2}(\theta - \sin\theta).
\]
Solve for $M$:
\[
M = \frac{r_0^3}{8G}\left(\frac{\theta - \sin\theta}{t}\right)^2.
\]
With $\theta = 245^\circ = 4.27606$ rad, $\sin\theta = \sin245^\circ = -0.9063$, so $\theta - \sin\theta = 4.27606 - (-0.9063) = 5.18236$.
\[
M = \frac{(3.0795\times10^{22})^3}{8\times6.67\times10^{-11}}\left(\frac{5.18236}{4.3233\times10^{17}}\right)^2 = \frac{2.921\times10^{67}}{5.336\times10^{-10}}\times(1.1987\times10^{-17})^2 = 5.475\times10^{76}\times1.4369\times10^{-34} = 7.86\times10^{42}\,\mathrm{kg}.
\]
In solar masses ($M_\odot = 1.99\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$):
\[
M = \frac{7.86\times10^{42}}{1.99\times10^{30}} = 3.95\times10^{12}\,M_\odot.
\]
\[
\boxed{r_{\max} = 998\,\mathrm{kpc}},\quad \boxed{M = 3.95\times10^{12}\,M_\odot}
\]

knowledge_points.name: parametric radial equation for bound orbit
knowledge_points.description: The separation r as a function of the eccentric anomaly θ in the two-body problem: r = (r0/2)(1 - cosθ). Used to find r_max from the current r and θ by setting cosθ = -1.

knowledge_points.name: parametric time equation for bound orbit
knowledge_points.description: The time t as a function of θ in the two-body problem: t = sqrt(r0^3/(8GM)) (θ - sinθ). Used to solve for the total mass M after r0 is known.

knowledge_points.name: parsec to meter conversion
knowledge_points.description: 1 kpc = 3.0857×10^19 m, needed to convert r_max from kiloparsecs to metres for the mass formula.

knowledge_points.name: solar mass value
knowledge_points.description: 1 M_sun = 1.99×10^30 kg, used to express the total mass M in solar masses.

knowledge_points.name: age of the Universe
knowledge_points.description: The time since the Big Bang, t = 13.7 Gyr = 4.3233×10^17 s, as given in part (e), used as the elapsed time in the two-body model.

title: The Star of Bethlehem
problem:
A great conjunction is a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn for observers on Earth. Assume that Jupiter and Saturn have circular orbits in the ecliptic plane.

The time between successive conjunctions may vary slightly as viewed from the Earth. However, the average time period of the great conjunctions is the same as that of an observer at the centre of the Solar system.

sub_problems.problem: (a) Find the average great conjunction period (in years) and average heliocentric angle between two successive great conjunctions (in degrees).
sub_problems.solution:
Assume that the average Earth's orbit is at the Sun. Therefore, average great conjunction period equals to the synodic period between Jupiter and Saturn.
$$
\frac{1}{P_{\text{Synodic}}} = \frac{1}{P_{\text{Jupiter}}} - \frac{1}{P_{\text{Saturn}}}
$$
$$
\frac{1}{P_{\text{Synodic}}} = \frac{1}{11.86} - \frac{1}{29.45}
$$
$$
P_{\text{Synodic}} = 19.86 \text{ years}
$$
From average great conjunction period, in 19.86 years Jupiter and Saturn move
Heliocentric angle $= \frac{19.86}{11.86} \times 360^{\circ} = 602.7^{\circ} = 242.7^{\circ}$
in an eastward direction through the zodiac, or $360^{\circ} - 242.7^{\circ} = 117.3^{\circ}$ in a westward direction through the zodiac.
\boxed{P = 19.86\text{ years}, \theta = 242.7^{\circ}}

knowledge_points.name: Earth at Sun approximation
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that the average great conjunction period is the same as for an observer at the centre of the Solar system, so the Earth's orbital motion is neglected and the observer is treated as being at the Sun.

knowledge_points.name: synodic period
knowledge_points.description: The synodic period is the time between successive conjunctions of two planets as seen from a third body (here the Sun). The average great conjunction period equals the Jupiter-Saturn synodic period.

knowledge_points.name: synodic period formula
knowledge_points.description: For two planets orbiting the Sun, the synodic period P_syn satisfies 1/P_syn = 1/P_inner - 1/P_outer, where P_inner and P_outer are the sidereal orbital periods.

knowledge_points.name: circular orbits
knowledge_points.description: The problem explicitly states Jupiter and Saturn have circular orbits in the ecliptic plane, so constant angular speeds can be used.

knowledge_points.name: known sidereal periods
knowledge_points.description: The solution uses the known sidereal orbital periods of Jupiter (11.86 years) and Saturn (29.45 years) without deriving them.

knowledge_points.name: angular displacement from period ratio
knowledge_points.description: The heliocentric angle a planet moves in a given time is computed as (time / orbital period) × 360°, using the constant angular speed from circular motion.

sub_problems.problem: (b) The next great conjunction will be on 21st December 2020 with an elongation of $30.3^{\circ}$ East of the Sun. Suggest the constellation in which the conjunction on 21st December 2020 will occur. (Give the IAU Latin name or IAU three-letter abbreviation of the constellation, i.e. Ursa Major or UMa)

knowledge_points.name: Sun's ecliptic longitude on winter solstice
knowledge_points.description: On 21 December (winter solstice) the Sun is located in the constellation Sagittarius along the ecliptic; this is needed to establish the starting point for the angular offset.

knowledge_points.name: planets near ecliptic plane
knowledge_points.description: Jupiter and Saturn orbit near the ecliptic plane, so their conjunction also lies near the ecliptic and can be located by ecliptic longitude relative to the Sun.

knowledge_points.name: zodiac constellations equal 30-degree divisions
knowledge_points.description: The 12 zodiac constellations are approximated as equal 30-degree segments along the ecliptic, allowing conversion from elongation angle to constellation name.

knowledge_points.name: elongation
knowledge_points.description: Elongation is the angular separation between a planet (or conjunction) and the Sun as seen from Earth; the problem gives 30.3° East, meaning the conjunction is east of the Sun along the ecliptic.

knowledge_points.name: ecliptic longitude addition
knowledge_points.description: Adding the eastward elongation angle to the Sun's ecliptic longitude determines the conjunction's ecliptic longitude, which is then mapped to the corresponding zodiac constellation.

sub_problems.problem: (c) Suggest the constellation in which the great conjunctions in 7 BC occurred. (Give the IAU Latin name or IAU three-letter abbreviation of the constellation, i.e. Ursa Major or UMa)
sub_problems.solution:
The duration between 7BC and 2020 is 2026 years or 2027 years.
Each conjunction occurs on the average every 19.86 years. Therefore, the number of conjunctions between 7BC and 2020 is
Integer value of $2026 / 19.86 = 102$.
From a conjunction to its previous successive conjunction, the conjunction moves $243^{\circ}$ westwards. The position of the conjunction in 7BC is
$$102 \times 242.7^{\circ} = 24758.33^{\circ} = 278.3^{\circ}$$
westward, or equivalently $81.7^{\circ}$ eastward from the position of the conjunction in 2020. Therefore, the conjunction was in the constellation of Aries (Ari) or Pisces (Psc).
\boxed{\text{Aries (Ari) or Pisces (Psc)}}

knowledge_points.name: average conjunction period from part (a)
knowledge_points.description: The average time between successive great conjunctions (19.86 years) derived in part (a) is reused here to compute the number of conjunctions elapsed.

knowledge_points.name: heliocentric angular shift per conjunction from part (a)
knowledge_points.description: The average westward shift of the conjunction location (about 243°) derived in part (a) is reused to propagate the conjunction position backward in time.

knowledge_points.name: integer number of elapsed periods
knowledge_points.description: Dividing the total time interval by the average period and taking the integer part gives the number of full conjunction cycles between the two dates.

knowledge_points.name: modulo 360° angle reduction
knowledge_points.description: Accumulated angular displacement is reduced modulo 360° to find the net direction on the celestial circle, converting large multiples of full rotations into an equivalent angle between 0° and 360°.

knowledge_points.name: conjunction location on 21 Dec 2020
knowledge_points.description: The reference solution uses the known position (elongation and date) of the 2020 great conjunction, implicitly relying on its ecliptic longitude to anchor the backward propagation.

knowledge_points.name: zodiacal constellations
knowledge_points.description: The answer requires mapping an ecliptic longitude to one of the zodiac constellations; the student must know the approximate longitude ranges of Aries and Pisces.

sub_problems.problem: (d) During the second conjunction of the series of three conjunctions in 7 BC, suggest the constellation the Sun was in as viewed by the observer on Earth. (Give the IAU Latin name or IAU three-letter abbreviation of the constellation, i.e. Ursa Major or UMa)
sub_problems.solution:
At the second conjunction, Jupiter and Saturn had retrograde motions. For observers on the Earth, both of them were in opposition. Therefore, the sun was in the constellation of Libra (Lib) (if answer c) is Aries) or Virgo (Vir) (if answer c) is Pisces).
\boxed{\text{Libra (Lib) or Virgo (Vir)}}

knowledge_points.name: retrograde motion
knowledge_points.description: Apparent westward motion of a planet relative to the stars, caused by Earth overtaking a superior planet; indicates the planet is near opposition.

knowledge_points.name: opposition
knowledge_points.description: Configuration where a planet is opposite the Sun in the sky (ecliptic longitudes differ by 180°), with Earth between the Sun and the planet.

knowledge_points.name: second conjunction at opposition
knowledge_points.description: In a triple conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn, the middle (second) conjunction occurs when both planets are near opposition as Earth passes between them and the Sun.

knowledge_points.name: conjunction constellation from part (c)
knowledge_points.description: The great conjunction of 7 BC occurred in either Aries or Pisces, as determined in sub-problem (c); this fixes the planet's constellation at the second conjunction.

knowledge_points.name: zodiac opposite constellations
knowledge_points.description: Constellations on the ecliptic are paired opposite each other: Aries opposite Libra, Pisces opposite Virgo. At opposition, the Sun is in the opposite constellation to the planet.

title: Super Luminal Galaxies
problem: Read the statements given below and state if they are true or false:

sub_problems.problem: (a) For some galaxies the apparent recession speed exceeds the speed of light.
sub_problems.solution:
In the expanding universe, the recession velocity of a galaxy is given by Hubble's law: v = H0 d. For sufficiently large distances, v can exceed c. This is allowed because it is the expansion of space itself, not motion through space, so special relativity is not violated. Therefore the statement is true.
\boxed{\text{True}}

knowledge_points.name: Hubble's law
knowledge_points.description: The law v = H₀ d relates a galaxy's recession velocity to its distance. For sufficiently large distances, v exceeds the speed of light c.

knowledge_points.name: metric expansion allows superluminal recession
knowledge_points.description: Recession velocities arise from the expansion of space itself, not motion through space. Therefore they are not restricted by the special-relativistic speed-of-light limit, and apparent speeds can exceed c.

sub_problems.problem: (b) The velocity – Distance relation as given by Hubble cannot allow recession velocities to exceed the speed of light.
sub_problems.solution:
Hubble's law v = H0 d is linear and unbounded; for large d, v can exceed c. The statement is false.
\boxed{\text{False}}

knowledge_points.name: Hubble's law
knowledge_points.description: The linear relation v = H0 d between recession velocity v and distance d, with H0 the Hubble constant. This is the relation referred to in the statement.

knowledge_points.name: superluminal recession in Hubble's law
knowledge_points.description: Hubble's law v = H0 d is linear and unbounded, so for sufficiently large distances the recession velocity can exceed the speed of light. This directly contradicts the statement that the relation cannot allow such velocities.

sub_problems.problem: (c) Hubble-Lemaitre's law (formerly known as Hubble's Law) does not violate special relativity.
sub_problems.solution:
Special relativity prohibits objects moving through space faster than light, but Hubble's law describes the recession due to the expansion of space itself, which is not constrained by special relativity. Hence the statement is true.
\boxed{\text{True}}

knowledge_points.name: Special relativity speed limit
knowledge_points.description: Special relativity forbids any massive object or signal from moving through space faster than the speed of light, applicable locally in inertial frames.

knowledge_points.name: Hubble-Lemaître law
knowledge_points.description: Describes the linear relationship v = H₀ d for distant galaxies, linking distance to recessional velocity caused by cosmic expansion.

knowledge_points.name: Cosmological expansion of space
knowledge_points.description: The recession of galaxies is due to the metric expansion of space itself, not to motion through a static space; this distinguishes Hubble flow from local peculiar motion.

knowledge_points.name: Global expansion not restricted by special relativity
knowledge_points.description: Special relativity is a local theory that does not constrain the global expansion of the universe; recession speeds exceeding c do not violate its postulates because no information is locally transmitted faster than light.

sub_problems.problem: (d) If some galaxies would have an apparent recession speed exceeding the speed of light, then the photons from those galaxies can never reach us.
sub_problems.solution:
Photons from galaxies with recession speed > c can still reach us because the Hubble sphere is not a horizon; the expansion rate changes over time, and photons can cross into regions where recession speed is less than c. The statement is false.
\boxed{\text{False}}

knowledge_points.name: Recession velocity
knowledge_points.description: The apparent velocity of a galaxy due to the expansion of the universe; it can exceed the speed of light without violating special relativity. Needed to understand the premise of the statement.

knowledge_points.name: Hubble-Lemaitre law
knowledge_points.description: The linear relation v = H0 d between recession velocity and distance, which implies that at sufficiently large distances, recession speed exceeds c. Needed to define the Hubble sphere.

knowledge_points.name: Hubble sphere
knowledge_points.description: The distance from an observer at which the recession velocity equals the speed of light, given by d = c/H0. The solution states that this sphere is not a horizon.

knowledge_points.name: Cosmological event horizon
knowledge_points.description: The boundary in spacetime beyond which events can never be observed by a given observer. The solution contrasts this with the Hubble sphere, noting that the Hubble sphere is not a true horizon.

knowledge_points.name: Time-varying Hubble parameter
knowledge_points.description: In realistic cosmological models, the Hubble parameter H(t) changes with time, so the Hubble sphere is not a static barrier. This allows photons emitted from regions with v > c to eventually cross into regions with v < c and reach the observer.

sub_problems.problem: (e) As the expansion of Universe is accelerating, photons emitted right now from galaxies which have apparent recession speed equal to the speed of light will never reach us.
sub_problems.solution:
In an accelerating universe, the Hubble sphere shrinks relative to the comoving coordinates, so photons emitted from the Hubble sphere today may eventually reach us if the acceleration is not too strong. However, in the standard ΛCDM model, such photons do eventually reach us. The statement is false.
\boxed{\text{False}}

knowledge_points.name: Hubble sphere
knowledge_points.description: The proper distance at which the recession velocity equals the speed of light, given by d_H = c/H. The problem's condition 'apparent recession speed equal to the speed of light' defines this boundary.

knowledge_points.name: Accelerating cosmic expansion
knowledge_points.description: The expansion of the universe is accelerating, meaning the scale factor a(t) has a positive second derivative (ä > 0). The statement takes this as a premise.

knowledge_points.name: Hubble sphere shrinkage in accelerating universe
knowledge_points.description: In an accelerating universe, the Hubble sphere shrinks relative to comoving coordinates (the comoving Hubble radius c/(aH) decreases). This allows photons emitted from the Hubble sphere to later be inside it and eventually reach the observer, provided the acceleration is not too strong.

knowledge_points.name: ΛCDM model
knowledge_points.description: The standard Lambda Cold Dark Matter cosmological model, in which the acceleration history (driven by a cosmological constant) is such that photons emitted today from the Hubble sphere will eventually reach us.

title: Atmospheric Refraction
problem: Consider sunrise at Beijing $(\varphi = 40^{\circ})$ on the vernal equinox day.

sub_problems.problem: (a) Let us say $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{l}}, \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{d}}, \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{r}}$ and $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{u}}$ are distances from the centre of the undistorted disk of the Sun to the edge of the disk towards the directions left, down, right and up respectively. What will be the hierarchical relation $(<, =, >)$ between the four radii just after the sunrise?
sub_problems.solution: Atmospheric refraction near the horizon compresses the solar disk vertically, making the vertical radius smaller than the horizontal radius. The upward direction is less compressed than the downward direction because the lower edge is closer to the horizon. Thus the radii satisfy: $r_d < r_u < r_l = r_r$.

knowledge_points.name: atmospheric refraction
knowledge_points.description: Bending of light rays as they pass through Earth's atmosphere due to a gradient in refractive index; near the horizon this effect is strongest and compresses the apparent shape of celestial objects.

knowledge_points.name: vertical compression of solar disk
knowledge_points.description: Atmospheric refraction near the horizon compresses the Sun's image primarily in the vertical direction, making the vertical apparent radius smaller than the horizontal one.

knowledge_points.name: refraction gradient with altitude
knowledge_points.description: The amount of refraction depends on altitude above the horizon; rays from lower points on the Sun pass through denser, more refractive air and are bent more than rays from higher points.

knowledge_points.name: left-right symmetry of refraction
knowledge_points.description: Atmospheric refraction acts symmetrically in the horizontal direction, so the left and right apparent radii of the Sun remain equal.

sub_problems.problem: (b) What is the correction in the time of rise of the top edge of the disk as compared to the case without atmosphere? You may assume that typically atmospheric refraction near the horizon is $35^{\circ}$ . Please only consider the apparent diurnal motion.
sub_problems.solution: Atmospheric refraction near the horizon is $35'$ (arcminutes). The Sun's apparent diurnal motion angular speed is $\omega = \frac{360^\circ}{23^\text{h}56^\text{m}4^\text{s}} = \frac{21600'}{1436.0682^\text{m}} = 15.0411' / \text{min}$. The correction in rise time is the time for the Sun to move through the refraction angle projected onto the horizon. At latitude $\varphi = 40^\circ$, the effective angular speed along the horizon is $\omega \cos \varphi$. Thus $\Delta t = \frac{35'}{\omega \cos \varphi} = \frac{35'}{15.0411' \times \cos 40^\circ} = 3.04$ minutes.

knowledge_points.name: atmospheric refraction
knowledge_points.description: The bending of light rays from a celestial object as they pass through Earth's atmosphere, causing the object to appear higher in the sky than its true geometric position. The problem gives a typical horizon refraction value of 35 arcminutes.

knowledge_points.name: apparent diurnal motion
knowledge_points.description: The apparent daily motion of celestial objects across the sky due to Earth's rotation. The Sun's angular speed in this motion is needed to convert the refraction angle into a time correction.

knowledge_points.name: angular speed of Earth's rotation
knowledge_points.description: The rate at which the Earth rotates relative to the fixed stars, giving the Sun's apparent diurnal angular speed of approximately 15 degrees per hour (or 15.0411 arcminutes per minute as derived in the solution).

knowledge_points.name: projection of angular speed onto horizon
knowledge_points.description: At a given latitude, the effective angular speed of a rising object along the horizon is the full diurnal angular speed multiplied by the cosine of the latitude, because the diurnal circle is inclined relative to the horizon.

knowledge_points.name: vernal equinox sunrise geometry
knowledge_points.description: On the vernal equinox, the Sun rises due east and its diurnal path intersects the horizon at an angle equal to the co-latitude (90° minus latitude), which justifies the cos φ projection factor used in the solution.

knowledge_points.name: small refraction angle
knowledge_points.description: The atmospheric refraction of 35 arcminutes is small enough that the time correction can be computed simply as the refraction angle divided by the effective angular speed, without needing spherical trigonometry corrections.

title: Observe the Sun with FAST
problem:
The Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) is a single-dish radio telescope located in Guizhou Province, China. The physical diameter of the dish is $500\mathrm{m}$ , but during observations, the effective diameter of the collecting area is $300\mathrm{m}$ .

Consider observations of the thermal radio emission from the photosphere of the Sun at $3.0\mathrm{GHz}$ with this telescope and a receiver with bandwidth $0.3\mathrm{GHz}$ .

sub_problems.problem: (a) Calculate the total energy $(\mathrm{E}_{\odot})$ that the receiver will collect during 1 hour of observation.
sub_problems.solution:
Use the Rayleigh-Jeans law for thermal emission at $3\mathrm{GHz}$:
$$B_
u =  rac{2 k_B T}{c^2} 
u^2$$
This is the power per unit emitting area, per steradian, per unit frequency. The solar luminosity at 3 GHz is:
$$L_
u = B_
u \cdot 4\pi R_\odot^2$$
At Earth's distance (1 AU), the monochromatic flux from the Sun at 3 GHz is:
$$f_
u =  rac{L_
u}{4\pi D^2}$$
The energy flux received by FAST is:
$$F_
u = f_
u \cdot \Delta
u \cdot \pi  rac{d_c^2}{4}$$
where $d_c = 300\mathrm{m}$ is the effective diameter. The total energy collected in 1 hour is:
$$E_\odot = F_
u \Delta t =  rac{2 k_B T}{c^2} 
u^2  rac{R_\odot^2}{D^2} \cdot \pi  rac{d_c^2}{4} \Delta
u \Delta t$$
Using $T \approx 6000\mathrm{K}$, $R_\odot \approx 6.96	imes10^8\mathrm{m}$, $D \approx 1.5	imes10^{11}\mathrm{m}$, $
u = 3.0	imes10^9\mathrm{Hz}$, $\Delta
u = 0.3	imes10^9\mathrm{Hz}$, $\Delta t = 3600\mathrm{s}$, $k_B = 1.38	imes10^{-23}\mathrm{J/K}$, $c = 3.0	imes10^8\mathrm{m/s}$, we obtain:
$$E_\odot \approx 8.5	imes10^{-5}\mathrm{J}$$
