knowledge_points.name: derivative of power-law function
knowledge_points.description: To find dV/dR for the Keplerian case V ∝ R^{-1/2}, one must differentiate a power-law function. The solution uses this to obtain dV/dR = -1/2 V0/R0.

title: Calorimetry with ice and copper calorimeter
problem:
Water of mass $m_{2}$ is contained in a copper calorimeter of mass $m_{1}$ . Their common temperature is $t_{2}$ . A piece of ice of mass $m_{3}$ and temperature $t_{3} < 0^{\circ}C$ is dropped into the calorimeter.

Neglect the energy losses, assume the normal barometric pressure. Specific heat of copper is $c_{1} = 0.1 \, kcal/kg \cdot ^{\circ}C$ , specific heat of water $c_{2} = 1 \, kcal/kg \cdot ^{\circ}C$ , specific heat of ice $c_{3} = 0.492 \, kcal/kg \cdot ^{\circ}C$ , latent heat of fusion of ice l = 78, 7 kcal/kg. Take 1 cal = 4.2 J.

sub_problems.problem: a) Determine the temperature and masses of water and ice in the equilibrium state for general values of $m_{1}$, $m_{2}$, $m_{3}$, $t_{2}$ and $t_{3}$. Write equilibrium equations for all possible processes which have to be considered.
sub_problems.solution:
Four possible processes and corresponding equilibrium states can occur:

1. $t_{0}<t<t_{2}$, $m_{2}^{\prime}=0$, $m_{3}^{\prime}=m_{3}$, $M_{2}=m_{2}+m_{3}$, $M_{3}=0$.

The unknown final temperature $t$ can be determined from the equation
$$
(m_1 c_1 + m_2 c_2)(t_2 - t) = m_3 c_3 (t_0 - t_3) + m_3 l + m_3 c_2 (t - t_0). \tag{7}
$$
Only the solution satisfying $t_{0} < t < t_{2}$ makes physical sense.

2. $t_3 < t < t_0$, $m_2^{\prime} = m_2$, $m_3^{\prime} = 0$, $M_2 = 0$, $M_3 = m_2 + m_3$.

The unknown final temperature $t$ can be determined from the equation
$$
m_1 c_1 (t_2 - t) + m_2 c_2 (t_2 - t_0) + m_2 l + m_2 c_3 (t_0 - t) = m_3 c_3 (t - t_3). \tag{8}
$$
Only the solution satisfying $t_{3} < t < t_{0}$ makes physical sense.

3. $t = t_{0}$, $m_{2}^{\prime} = 0$, $0 \leq m_{3}^{\prime} \leq m_{3}$, $M_{2} = m_{2} + m_{3}^{\prime}$, $M_{3} = m_{3} - m_{3}^{\prime}$.

The unknown mass $m_3^\prime$ can be calculated from the equation
$$
(m_1 c_1 + m_2 c_2)(t_2 - t_0) = m_3 c_3 (t - t_3) + m_3^{\prime} l. \tag{9}
$$
Only the solution satisfying $0 \leq m_{3}^{\prime} \leq m_{3}$ makes physical sense.

4. $t = t_{0}$, $0 \leq m_{2}^{\prime} \leq m_{2}$, $m_{3}^{\prime} = 0$, $M_{2} = m_{2} - m_{2}^{\prime}$, $M_{3} = m_{3} + m_{2}^{\prime}$.

The unknown mass $m_2^\prime$ can be calculated from the equation
$$
(m_1 c_1 + m_2 c_2)(t_2 - t_0) + m_2^{\prime} l = m_3 c_3 (t_0 - t_3). \tag{10}
$$
Only the solution satisfying $0 \leq m_{2}^{\prime} \leq m_{2}$ makes physical sense.

\boxed{\text{See equations (7)--(10) and the corresponding conditions.}}

knowledge_points.name: isolated system (no heat loss)
knowledge_points.description: The problem states to neglect energy losses, so the system (calorimeter + water + ice) is thermally isolated. This allows equating total heat lost to total heat gained within the system.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of energy (calorimetry)
knowledge_points.description: In an isolated system, heat lost by warmer bodies equals heat gained by colder bodies. This principle is used to set up the heat balance equations for each possible final state.

knowledge_points.name: specific heat capacity
knowledge_points.description: Heat required to change temperature of a substance is Q = m c ΔT. Applied to copper, water, and ice in every temperature-change term of the final equations.

knowledge_points.name: latent heat of fusion
knowledge_points.description: Heat required to change phase between ice and water at constant temperature is Q = m l. Used in the equations for melting ice or freezing water.

knowledge_points.name: melting point of ice
knowledge_points.description: At normal atmospheric pressure, ice melts at 0 °C (denoted t_0). This fixed temperature is used in the equations and as the boundary for possible equilibrium states.

knowledge_points.name: phase change at constant temperature
knowledge_points.description: When both ice and water coexist, any heat transfer does not change the temperature; the system remains at the melting point. This justifies setting final temperature t = t_0 when a mixture remains.

knowledge_points.name: case analysis for phase change
knowledge_points.description: For calorimetry problems involving a phase change, enumerate all possible final states (all ice melts, all water freezes, or a mixture at the melting point), write energy-balance equations for each, and check consistency with assumed temperature ranges to find the physically relevant solution.

sub_problems.problem: b) Find the final temperature and final masses of water and ice for $m_{1}=1.00$ kg, $m_{2}=1.00$ kg, $m_{3}=2.00$ kg, $t_{2}=10^{\circ}$C, $t_{3}=-20^{\circ}$C.
sub_problems.solution:
Substituting the particular values of $m_{1}=1.00$ kg, $m_{2}=1.00$ kg, $m_{3}=2.00$ kg, $t_{2}=10^{\circ}$C, $t_{3}=-20^{\circ}$C into equations (7), (8) and (9) yields solutions that do not make physical sense (they do not satisfy the conditions for $t$ and $m_{3}^{\prime}$). The real physical process under these conditions is given by equation (10), which yields

$$
m_{2}^{\prime} = \frac{m_{3} c_{3} (t_{0} - t_{3}) - (m_{1} c_{1} + m_{2} c_{2}) (t_{2} - t_{0})}{l}.
$$

Substituting the given numerical values gives $m_{2}^{\prime} = 0.11$ kg. Hence, $t = 0^{\circ}$C, $M_{2} = m_{2} - m_{2}^{\prime} = 0.89$ kg, $M_{3} = m_{3} + m_{2}^{\prime} = 2.11$ kg.

\boxed{t = 0^{\circ}\text{C}}, \boxed{M_{2} = 0.89\text{ kg}}, \boxed{M_{3} = 2.11\text{ kg}}

knowledge_points.name: specific heat capacity
knowledge_points.description: The amount of heat per unit mass required to raise the temperature of a substance by one degree. Used to compute the heat exchanged by the copper calorimeter, water, and ice as their temperatures change.

knowledge_points.name: latent heat of fusion
knowledge_points.description: The heat per unit mass absorbed during melting or released during freezing at constant temperature. Used to compute the mass of water that freezes to supply the heat deficit in the mixture.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of energy in thermal processes
knowledge_points.description: In an isolated system, the total heat gained equals the total heat lost. This principle is used to set up the heat balance equation for the calorimeter, water, and ice.

knowledge_points.name: ice-water melting point at atmospheric pressure
knowledge_points.description: At standard atmospheric pressure, ice and water coexist in equilibrium only at 0°C. This fixes the final temperature when both phases are present after reaching equilibrium.

knowledge_points.name: negligible heat losses
knowledge_points.description: The calorimeter is assumed to be perfectly insulating, so no heat is exchanged with the environment. This allows the system to be treated as isolated and the net heat exchange to be set to zero.

knowledge_points.name: method of mixtures with phase change
knowledge_points.description: A procedure to determine the final state in calorimetry problems involving phase changes: assume a final state (all ice melted, all water frozen, or mixture at melting point), write the heat balance equation, solve for the unknown temperature or phase-change mass, and check physical consistency (temperature within initial bounds, phase-change mass between 0 and available mass). If inconsistent, try another assumed state.

title: Molecular Physics
problem:
Two cylinders A and B, with equal diameters have inside two pistons with negligible mass connected by a rigid rod. The pistons can move freely. The rod is a short tube with a valve. The valve is initially closed (fig. 2.1).

The cylinder A and his piston is adiabatically insulated and the cylinder B is in thermal contact with a thermostat which has the temperature $\theta = 27^{\circ}C$ .

Initially the piston of the cylinder A is fixed and inside there is a mass m=32 kg of argon at a pressure higher than the atmospheric pressure. Inside the cylinder B there is a mass of oxygen at the normal atmospheric pressure.

Liberating the piston of the cylinder A, it moves slowly enough (quasi-static) and at equilibrium the volume of the gas is eight times higher, and in the cylinder B de oxygen's density increased two times. Knowing that the thermostat received the heat $Q' = 747,9.10^{4}J$ , determine:

The kilo-molar mass of argon is $\mu = 40$ kg/kmol.

sub_problems.problem: a) Establish on the base of the kinetic theory of the gases, studying the elastic collisions of the molecules with the piston, that the thermal equation of the process taking place in the cylinder A is $TV^{2/3} = constant$.
sub_problems.solution:
We consider argon an ideal monatomic gas and the collisions of the atoms with the piston perfectly elastic. In such a collision with a fixed wall, the speed $\vec{v}$ of the particle changes only in direction so that the speed $\vec{v}$ and the speed $\vec{v}'$ after collision lie in the same plane with the normal, and the incident and reflection angles are equal:

$$
v_n' = -v_n, \quad v_t' = v_t \tag{1}
$$

In the problem the wall moves with speed $\vec{u}$ perpendicular to the wall. The relative speed of the particle with respect to the wall is $\vec{v} - \vec{u}$. Choosing the $Oz$ axis perpendicular to the wall in the direction of $\vec{u}$, the conditions of elastic collision give:

$$
(\vec{v} - \vec{u})_z = -(\vec{v}' - \vec{u})_z, \quad (\vec{v} - \vec{u})_{x,y} = (\vec{v}' - \vec{u})_{x,y}
$$

$$
v_z - u = -(v_z' - u), \quad v_z' = 2u - v_z, \quad v_{x,y}' = v_{x,y} \tag{2}
$$

The increase in kinetic energy of a particle of mass $m_0$ after collision is:

$$
\frac{1}{2} m_0 v'^2 - \frac{1}{2} m_0 v^2 = \frac{1}{2} m_0 (v_z'^2 - v_z^2) = 2 m_0 u (u - v_z) \approx -2 m_0 u v_z \tag{3}
$$

because $u$ is much smaller than $v_z$.

If $n_k$ is the number of molecules per unit volume with speed component $v_{zk}$, then the number of molecules with this component that collide in time $dt$ with area $dS$ of the piston is:

$$
\frac{1}{2} n_k v_{zk} \, dt \, dS \tag{4}
$$

These molecules will have a change in kinetic energy:

$$
\frac{1}{2} n_k v_{zk} \, dt \, dS \, (-2 m_0 u v_{zk}) = - m_0 n_k v_{zk}^2 \, dV \tag{5}
$$

where $dV = u \, dt \, dS$ is the increase in volume of the gas.

The change in kinetic energy of the gas corresponding to the volume increase $dV$ is:

$$
dE_c = - m_0 \, dV \sum_k n_k v_{zk}^2 = -\frac{1}{3} n m_0 \bar{v}^2 \, dV \tag{6}
$$

and:

$$
dU = -\frac{2}{3} N \frac{m_0 \bar{v}^2}{2} \cdot \frac{dV}{V} = -\frac{2}{3} U \frac{dV}{V} \tag{7}
$$

Integrating equation (7) gives:

$$
U V^{2/3} = \text{const.} \tag{8}
$$

The internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas is proportional to the absolute temperature $T$, so equation (8) can be written as:

$$
T V^{2/3} = \text{const.} \tag{9}
$$

\boxed{T V^{2/3} = \text{const.}}

knowledge_points.name: adiabatic insulation
knowledge_points.description: Cylinder A is adiabatically insulated, so no heat is exchanged with the surroundings; the change in internal energy of the gas equals the work done on it by the piston.

knowledge_points.name: quasi-static piston motion
knowledge_points.description: The piston moves slowly (quasi-statically) so that the gas remains in equilibrium and the piston speed is much smaller than molecular speeds, enabling the approximation u(u - v_z) ≈ -u v_z.

knowledge_points.name: ideal monatomic gas
knowledge_points.description: Argon is treated as an ideal monatomic gas; its internal energy is purely kinetic and proportional to absolute temperature (U ∝ T).

knowledge_points.name: elastic collision with moving wall
knowledge_points.description: For an elastic collision with a moving wall, the normal component of the relative velocity reverses and the tangential components remain unchanged, giving the post-collision velocity relation v_z' = 2u - v_z.

knowledge_points.name: molecular flux to a surface
knowledge_points.description: The number of molecules with a given normal speed component v_zk that strike area dS in time dt is (1/2) n_k v_zk dt dS, used to count collisions with the piston.

knowledge_points.name: isotropic velocity distribution
knowledge_points.description: Molecular velocities are distributed isotropically, so the mean square of the normal component equals one-third of the mean square speed: ⟨v_z^2⟩ = ⟨v^2⟩/3.

knowledge_points.name: internal energy of ideal monatomic gas
knowledge_points.description: For an ideal monatomic gas, the internal energy U equals the total kinetic energy of the molecules, U = N·(1/2)m₀⟨v²⟩, and is proportional to absolute temperature: U = (3/2)Nk_B T.

sub_problems.problem: b) Calculate the parameters \(p\), \(V\), and \(T\) of argon in the initial and final states.
sub_problems.solution:
The oxygen is in contact with a thermostat and undergoes an isothermal process. The internal energy of argon changes only due to the adiabatic process:

\[
\Delta U = \nu C_V \Delta T = m c_V \Delta T \tag{10}
\]

where \(\nu\) is the number of kilomoles. For argon, \(C_V = \frac{3}{2}R\).

For the entire system, \(L = 0\) and \(\Delta U = Q\).

Indices 1 and 2 refer to argon in cylinder A and oxygen in cylinder B, respectively:

\[
\Delta U = \frac{m_1}{\mu_1} \cdot \frac{3}{2} \cdot R \left(T_1' - T_1\right) = Q = \frac{m_1}{\mu_1} \cdot \frac{3}{2} R T_1 \left[ \left(\frac{V_1}{V_1'}\right)^{2/3} - 1 \right] \tag{11}
\]

From equation (11):

\[
T_1 = \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{\mu_1}{m_1} \cdot \frac{Q}{R} \cdot \frac{1}{\left(\frac{V_1}{V_1'}\right)^{2/3} - 1} = 1000\,\text{K} \tag{12}
\]

\[
T_1' = \frac{T_1}{4} = 250\,\text{K} \tag{13}
\]

For the isothermal process of oxygen:

\[
p_2' = 2.00\,\text{atm} = 2.026 \times 10^5\,\text{N/m}^2
\]

From the equilibrium condition:

\[
p_1' = p_2' = 2\,\text{atm} \tag{15}
\]

For argon:

\[
p_1 = p_1' \cdot \frac{V_1'}{V_1} \cdot \frac{T_1}{T_1'} = 64\,\text{atm} = 64.9 \times 10^5\,\text{N/m}^2 \tag{16}
\]

\[
V_1 = \frac{m_1}{\mu_1} \cdot \frac{R T_1}{p_1} = 1.02\,\text{m}^3, \quad V_1' = 8 V_1 = 8.16\,\text{m}^3 \tag{17}
\]

Thus the parameters for argon in the initial state: \(p_1 = 64\,\text{atm}\), \(V_1 = 1.02\,\text{m}^3\), \(T_1 = 1000\,\text{K}\).

In the final state: \(p_1' = 2\,\text{atm}\), \(V_1' = 8.16\,\text{m}^3\), \(T_1' = 250\,\text{K}\).

\boxed{p_1 = 64\,\text{atm},\; V_1 = 1.02\,\text{m}^3,\; T_1 = 1000\,\text{K}} \\
\boxed{p_1' = 2\,\text{atm},\; V_1' = 8.16\,\text{m}^3,\; T_1' = 250\,\text{K}}

knowledge_points.name: Ideal gas law
knowledge_points.description: Relates pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of substance (pV = nRT). Needed to compute volumes and pressures of argon from n and T, and to find oxygen's final pressure from its density change during the isothermal process.

knowledge_points.name: Internal energy of ideal gas
knowledge_points.description: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature (U = n C_V T). For argon, ΔU = n C_V ΔT; for oxygen in an isothermal process, ΔU = 0.

knowledge_points.name: First law of thermodynamics
knowledge_points.description: Energy conservation for a closed system: ΔU = Q - W. Applied to the whole system with zero net external work to equate the total internal energy change to the heat exchanged with the thermostat.

knowledge_points.name: Adiabatic relation for monatomic gas
knowledge_points.description: For a quasi‑static adiabatic process of a monatomic ideal gas, TV^(2/3) = constant. Used to find the final temperature of argon from the given eight‑fold volume increase.

knowledge_points.name: Isothermal process for oxygen
knowledge_points.description: Oxygen in cylinder B stays in thermal contact with a thermostat at 27°C; its temperature is therefore constant throughout the process.

knowledge_points.name: Mechanical equilibrium of connected pistons
knowledge_points.description: The two pistons have equal diameters and are connected by a rigid rod, so at final equilibrium the pressures in both cylinders are equal (p1' = p2').

knowledge_points.name: Molar heat capacity of monatomic gas
knowledge_points.description: Constant‑volume molar heat capacity of a monatomic ideal gas is C_V = (3/2)R, used to express the internal energy change of argon as ΔU = ν C_V ΔT.

knowledge_points.name: Zero net external work on whole system
knowledge_points.description: The whole apparatus (cylinders, pistons, rod, gases) has no moving boundaries with the outside; therefore the total work L done by the system is zero, making ΔU_total = Q.

sub_problems.problem: c) Opening the valve which separates the two cylinders, calculate the final pressure of the mixture of the gases.
sub_problems.solution:
When the valve is opened, the gases intermix and at thermal equilibrium the final pressure is $p'$ and the temperature is $T$. The total number of kilomoles is constant:

$$
\nu_1 + \nu_2 = \nu', \quad \frac{p_1' V_1'}{R T_1'} + \frac{p_2' V_2'}{R T} = \frac{p (V_1' + V_2')}{R T}
$$

Given $p_1' + p_2' = 2\,\text{atm}$ and $T_2 = T_2' = T = 300\,\text{K}$.

The total volume of the system is constant:

$$
V_1 + V_2 = V_1' + V_2', \quad \frac{V_2'}{V_2} = \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_2'}, \quad V_2' = \frac{V_2}{2} = 7.14\,\text{m}^3
$$

From the conservation of kilomoles, the final pressure is:

$$
p = p_1' \cdot \frac{1}{V_1 + V_2} \cdot \left( V_1' \cdot \frac{T}{T_1'} + V_2' \right) = 2.2\,\text{atm} = 2.23 \times 10^5\,\text{N/m}^2
$$

\boxed{p = 2.2\,\text{atm} = 2.23 \times 10^5\,\text{N/m}^2}

knowledge_points.name: Ideal gas law
knowledge_points.description: Relates pressure, volume, temperature, and number of moles for an ideal gas: pV = nRT. Used to express the amount of gas in each state and to solve for the final pressure of the mixture.

knowledge_points.name: Conservation of amount of substance
knowledge_points.description: The total number of kilomoles of non-reacting gases remains constant when they mix. This gives ν1 + ν2 = ν' and allows the final pressure to be determined.

knowledge_points.name: Constant total volume
knowledge_points.description: Because the pistons are connected by a rigid rod and have equal diameters, the sum of the two gas volumes is invariant: V1 + V2 = V1' + V2'.

knowledge_points.name: Equal pressures at mechanical equilibrium
knowledge_points.description: Before the valve is opened, the connected pistons are in mechanical equilibrium, which for equal-area pistons implies equal gas pressures: p1' = p2'.

knowledge_points.name: Thermal equilibrium with thermostat
knowledge_points.description: After the valve is opened and the gases mix, the entire system reaches the temperature of the thermostat (T = 300 K) because cylinder B is in thermal contact with it.

title: Capacitor with Dielectric Liquid
problem: A plane capacitor with rectangular plates is fixed in a vertical position having the lower part in contact with a dielectric liquid (fig. 3.1). Determine the height, h, of the liquid between the plates and explain the phenomenon. The capillarity effects are neglected. It is supposed that the distance between the plates is much smaller than the linear dimensions of the plates. It is known: the initial intensity of the electric field of the charged capacitor, E, the density $\rho$, the relative electric permittivity $\varepsilon_{r}$ of the liquid, and the height H of the plates of the capacitor. Discussion.
solution:
The initial energy stored in the capacitor is

\[
W_0 = \frac{1}{2} C_0 U_0^2 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{Q_0^2}{C_0},
\]
where the initial capacitance is
\[
C_0 = \frac{\varepsilon_0 H l}{d},
\]
with $H$ the plate height, $l$ the plate width, and $d$ the plate separation.

When the lower part of the capacitor contacts the dielectric liquid, a vertical electric force acts on the liquid. The total charge $Q_0$ remains constant, and no external energy is supplied. The increase in gravitational potential energy of the liquid is balanced by the decrease in electrical energy of the capacitor:

\[
W_0 = W_1 + W_2,
\]
where
\[
W_1 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{Q_0^2}{C}, \qquad
W_2 = \frac{1}{2} \rho g h^2 l d.
\]
Here $h$ is the height to which the liquid rises between the plates, $\rho$ is the liquid density, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

The total capacitance after the liquid rises is the sum of the capacitances of the liquid-filled part and the air-filled part:

\[
C = C_1 + C_2 = \frac{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r h l}{d} + \frac{\varepsilon_0 (H - h) l}{d}.
\]

Substituting the expressions for $W_0$, $W_1$, $W_2$, and $C$ into the energy balance, and using $Q_0 = C_0 U_0$ and $E_0 = U_0 / d$, we obtain

\[
(\varepsilon_r - 1) h^2 + H h - \frac{E_0^2 \varepsilon_0 H (\varepsilon_r - 1)}{\rho g} = 0.
\]

Solving this quadratic equation for $h$ gives

\[
h = \frac{H}{2(\varepsilon_r - 1)} \left[ -1 + \sqrt{1 + \frac{4 E_0^2 \varepsilon_0 (\varepsilon_r - 1)^2}{\rho g H}} \right],
\]
where only the positive root is physically meaningful.

If $H$ is much larger than $h$, the square root can be expanded to first order, yielding the approximate result

\[
h \approx \frac{\varepsilon_0 (\varepsilon_r - 1)}{\rho g} E_0^2.
\]

\boxed{h \approx \frac{\varepsilon_0 (\varepsilon_r - 1)}{\rho g} E_0^2}

knowledge_points.name: Ideal parallel-plate capacitor model
knowledge_points.description: For a parallel-plate capacitor with plate area A and separation d (d << plate dimensions), the electric field is uniform, E = V/d, capacitance is C = ε A/d, and charge is Q = C V. With a dielectric of relative permittivity εr, the capacitance becomes ε0 εr A/d. Used to compute initial and final capacitances and to relate the given field E0 to charge and voltage.

knowledge_points.name: Capacitor energy storage
knowledge_points.description: The electrical energy stored in a capacitor is W = Q^2/(2C) = (1/2) C V^2. For a constant-charge capacitor, the Q^2/(2C) form is convenient. Used to express initial and final electrical energies.

knowledge_points.name: Conservation of energy
knowledge_points.description: In an isolated system with no external energy supply, total energy is conserved. Here, the initial electrical energy W0 equals the sum of the final electrical energy W1 and the gravitational potential energy W2 of the raised liquid.

knowledge_points.name: Gravitational potential energy of raised liquid
knowledge_points.description: When a liquid of density ρ rises to height h in a container of cross-sectional area A, the increase in gravitational potential energy is (1/2) ρ g A h^2, because the center of mass of the raised liquid is at height h/2 above the reservoir surface. Used to compute W2.

knowledge_points.name: Capacitors in parallel
knowledge_points.description: The total capacitance of capacitors connected in parallel is the sum of their individual capacitances. A parallel-plate capacitor partially filled with two different dielectrics side by side can be modeled as two capacitors in parallel, so C = C1 + C2.

knowledge_points.name: Small-argument approximation
knowledge_points.description: For |x| << 1, the binomial expansion gives sqrt(1 + x) ≈ 1 + x/2. Used to simplify the exact quadratic solution for h when H >> h.

knowledge_points.name: Isolated capacitor (constant charge)
knowledge_points.description: The capacitor is disconnected from any voltage source, so the charge Q0 on the plates remains constant as the liquid rises. No external energy is supplied.

knowledge_points.name: Neglect of capillarity
knowledge_points.description: Capillary effects due to surface tension are neglected, so the liquid rise is determined solely by the balance of electrical and gravitational energies.

title: Fluorescent lamp
problem:
An alternating voltage of 50 Hz frequency is applied to the fluorescent lamp shown in the accompanying circuit diagram.

The following quantities are measured:

overall voltage (main voltage)

$$
\mathrm{U} = 2 2 8. 5 \mathrm{V}
$$

electric current

$$
\mathrm{I} = 0. 6 \mathrm{A}
$$

partial voltage across the fluorescent lamp

$$
\mathrm{U} ^ {\prime} = 8 4 \mathrm{V}
$$

ohmic resistance of the series reactor

$$
\mathrm{R} _ {\mathrm{d}} = 2 6. 3 \Omega
$$

The fluorescent lamp itself may be considered as an ohmic resistor in the calculations.

sub_problems.problem: a) What is the inductance \(L\) of the series reactor?
sub_problems.solution:
The total impedance of the apparatus is
\[ Z = \frac{228.5\,\text{V}}{0.6\,\text{A}} = 380.8\,\Omega. \]
The ohmic resistance of the tube is
\[ R_R = \frac{84\,\text{V}}{0.6\,\text{A}} = 140\,\Omega. \]
Hence the total ohmic resistance is
\[ R = 140\,\Omega + 26.3\,\Omega = 166.3\,\Omega. \]
Therefore the inductive reactance of the series reactor is
\[ \omega L = \sqrt{Z^2 - R^2} = 342.6\,\Omega. \]
This yields the inductance
\[ L = \frac{342.6\,\Omega}{100\pi\,\text{s}^{-1}} = 1.09\,\text{H}. \]
\[ \boxed{L = 1.09\,\text{H}} \]

knowledge_points.name: Series circuit configuration
knowledge_points.description: The fluorescent lamp and series reactor are connected in series, so the same current I flows through both. This allows using the measured current to compute resistances and impedances of individual components.

knowledge_points.name: Fluorescent lamp as ohmic resistor
knowledge_points.description: The problem states the lamp can be treated as a pure ohmic resistor, so its voltage and current are in phase, and its resistance is given by Ohm's law as R = V'/I.

knowledge_points.name: Sinusoidal AC steady state
knowledge_points.description: The applied voltage is alternating at 50 Hz, implying a sinusoidal waveform. The circuit is in AC steady state, so impedance concepts and RMS values are applicable.

knowledge_points.name: Ohm's law for AC circuits (magnitude)
knowledge_points.description: For sinusoidal AC, the magnitude of impedance Z is the ratio of RMS voltage to RMS current: Z = V_rms / I_rms. For a pure resistor, Z = R, giving R = V_rms / I_rms.

knowledge_points.name: Series resistance addition
knowledge_points.description: The total resistance of resistors in series is the sum of their individual resistances: R_total = R1 + R2. Here, the lamp resistance and the reactor's ohmic resistance add to give the total circuit resistance.

knowledge_points.name: Impedance of series RL circuit
knowledge_points.description: The impedance magnitude of a series RL circuit is Z = sqrt(R^2 + (ωL)^2), where R is the total series resistance and L is the inductance. This relation is used to find the inductive reactance from the total impedance and total resistance.

knowledge_points.name: Inductive reactance
knowledge_points.description: The reactance of an inductor is X_L = ωL, where ω = 2πf is the angular frequency. This relates the inductance L to the reactance, and allows conversion between frequency and angular frequency.

sub_problems.problem: b) What is the phase shift $\varphi$ between voltage and current?
sub_problems.solution:
The impedance angle is obtained from

\[
\tan\varphi = \frac{\omega L}{R} = \frac{342.6\,\Omega}{166.3\,\Omega} = 2.06
\]

Thus

\[
\varphi = 64.1^{\circ}
\]

knowledge_points.name: phase shift between voltage and current
knowledge_points.description: In an AC circuit, the phase shift φ is the angle by which the current lags or leads the applied voltage. For a series RL circuit, the current lags the voltage.

knowledge_points.name: phase angle formula for series RL circuit
knowledge_points.description: The phase shift φ in a series RL circuit is given by tan φ = ωL / R, where ωL is the inductive reactance and R is the total series resistance.

knowledge_points.name: known total resistance and reactance from part (a)
knowledge_points.description: The total series resistance R and the inductive reactance ωL have already been determined in part (a) and are used directly to compute φ.

sub_problems.problem: c) What is the active power $P_{w}$ transformed by the apparatus?
sub_problems.solution:
The active power can be calculated as:

\[ P_w = U \cdot I \cdot \cos\varphi = 228.5\,\text{V} \cdot 0.6\,\text{A} \cdot \cos 64.1^\circ = 59.88\,\text{W} \]

Alternatively, using the resistance:

\[ P_w = R \cdot I^2 = 166.3\,\Omega \cdot (0.6\,\text{A})^2 = 59.87\,\text{W} \]

\boxed{P_w = 59.9\,\text{W}}

knowledge_points.name: active power in AC circuits
knowledge_points.description: The active (real) power in an AC circuit is the time-averaged power dissipated, given by P = U I cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between voltage and current.

knowledge_points.name: active power formula
knowledge_points.description: The formula P = U I cos φ is used directly to compute the active power from the overall voltage, current, and phase shift obtained in part (b).

knowledge_points.name: Joule's law
knowledge_points.description: The power dissipated in a resistor is P = I² R. This is used in the alternative solution to compute active power from the total equivalent resistance and current.

knowledge_points.name: phase angle from part (b)
knowledge_points.description: The phase shift φ = 64.1° between the overall voltage and current was calculated in the previous sub-problem and is reused here.

knowledge_points.name: total equivalent resistance from part (a)
knowledge_points.description: The total ohmic resistance of the apparatus (R = 166.3 Ω) was determined in the previous sub-problem and is reused in the alternative power calculation.

sub_problems.problem:
d) Apart from limiting the current the series reactor has another important function. Name and explain this function!

Hint: The starter —(s)— includes a contact which closes shortly after switching on the lamp, opens up again and stays open.
sub_problems.solution: The series reactor also functions as a ballast to generate a high ignition voltage. When the starter contact opens, the current through the reactor is interrupted, causing a large induced voltage across the reactor (provided the contact does not open exactly when the current passes through zero). This induced voltage is sufficient to ignite the fluorescent lamp, whereas the mains voltage alone is lower than the ignition voltage.
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{The series reactor generates a high induction voltage when the starter contact opens, which ignites the lamp.}}

knowledge_points.name: Faraday's law of induction
knowledge_points.description: The voltage induced across an inductor is V = L dI/dt. Rapidly interrupting the current through the reactor produces a large dI/dt, hence a high induced voltage that can ignite the lamp.

knowledge_points.name: Ignition voltage of fluorescent lamp
knowledge_points.description: A fluorescent lamp requires a voltage higher than the mains voltage to initiate the gas discharge; this is the ignition voltage. The series reactor provides this high voltage pulse.

knowledge_points.name: Starter opens at non-zero current
knowledge_points.description: To generate a large induced voltage, the starter contact must interrupt the current when its instantaneous value is not zero; if it opens exactly at a zero crossing, dI/dt may be too small to produce a sufficient voltage spike.

sub_problems.problem: e) In a diagram with a quantitative time scale sketch the time sequence of the luminous flux emitted by the lamp.
sub_problems.solution: The luminous flux emitted by the lamp is not constant over time. During each half-cycle of the AC voltage, the lamp ignites when the voltage across it reaches the ignition voltage, and it extinguishes when the current falls below the holding current. The result is a pulsed light output. The time sequence of the luminous flux is a series of pulses occurring twice per period, with a duration shorter than the half-cycle. The pulses are approximately in phase with the voltage peaks, but with a slight delay due to the inductance. A sketch should show a periodic sequence of pulses, each starting near the voltage maximum and decaying to zero before the next half-cycle.
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{See sketch: periodic pulses of luminous flux, twice per period, aligned with voltage peaks}}

knowledge_points.name: Fluorescent lamp AC behavior
knowledge_points.description: A fluorescent lamp is a gas discharge lamp that requires an ignition voltage to start conducting and a holding current to maintain conduction. On an AC supply, it extinguishes and re-ignites each half-cycle, producing light pulses at twice the line frequency.

knowledge_points.name: AC period from frequency
knowledge_points.description: The period T of an AC voltage is T = 1/f. For the given 50 Hz, T = 20 ms, which provides the quantitative time scale for the sketch.

knowledge_points.name: Inductive current lag
knowledge_points.description: In an inductive circuit, the current lags the applied voltage, causing a phase shift. This delay means the lamp current (and thus the light output) peaks slightly after the main voltage peaks.

sub_problems.problem: f) Why has the lamp to be ignited only once although the applied alternating voltage goes through zero in regular intervals?
sub_problems.solution: The lamp has to be ignited only once because the recombination time of the ions and electrons in the gaseous discharge is sufficiently large. Even though the applied alternating voltage goes through zero in regular intervals, the ions and electrons do not recombine quickly enough to extinguish the discharge. Thus, once ignited, the discharge continues to be sustained through each voltage cycle.
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{The recombination time of the ions and electrons is sufficiently large.}}

knowledge_points.name: recombination time
knowledge_points.description: The characteristic time for ions and electrons in a gas discharge to recombine into neutral atoms. A recombination time longer than the zero-voltage interval of the AC cycle allows the discharge to persist without being extinguished.

knowledge_points.name: gas discharge
knowledge_points.description: Electrical conduction through an ionized gas. A fluorescent lamp operates via a sustained gas discharge, which must be ignited initially and then maintains itself as long as the gas remains sufficiently ionized.

knowledge_points.name: AC voltage zero crossing
knowledge_points.description: The applied alternating voltage periodically passes through zero. If the ionized gas recombined instantly, the discharge would extinguish at each zero crossing and require re-ignition.

sub_problems.problem: g) According to the statement of the manufacturer, for a fluorescent lamp of the described type a capacitor of about $4.7 \mu F$ can be switched in series with the series reactor. How does this affect the operation of the lamp and to what intent is this possibility provided for?
sub_problems.solution:
The capacitive reactance of a capacitor of $4.7 \mu F$ is

$$
\frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{100 \pi \cdot 4.7 \times 10^{-6}} \, \Omega = 677.3 \, \Omega.
$$

The inductive reactance from the series reactor (from part (a)) is $\omega L = 1012 \, \Omega$. The net reactance is

$$
\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} = 1012 \, \Omega - 677.3 \, \Omega = 334.7 \, \Omega,
$$

which is capacitive. The total impedance becomes

$$
Z' = \sqrt{(334.7)^2 + (166.3)^2} \, \Omega = 373.7 \, \Omega,
$$

very close to the original impedance without the capacitor (cf. part (a)). Thus the lamp operates similarly, ignites the same way, but the phase angle changes sign:

$$
\tan \varphi' = \frac{\omega L - (\omega C)^{-1}}{R} = -\frac{334.7}{166.3} = -2.01,
$$

$$
\varphi' = -63.6^\circ.
$$

This capacitor is used for power factor correction. In buildings with many fluorescent lamps, the lagging reactive current is compensated, reducing the burden on generators and transmission lines, and avoiding losses that are not metered by active-energy meters.

\boxed{\text{The capacitor compensates the reactive current, improving the power factor.}}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{The capacitor compensates the reactive current, improving the power factor.}}

knowledge_points.name: capacitive reactance
knowledge_points.description: X_C = 1/(ωC) gives the effective opposition of a capacitor to alternating current; used to compute the reactance of the 4.7 μF capacitor at 50 Hz.

knowledge_points.name: inductive reactance
knowledge_points.description: X_L = ωL gives the effective opposition of an inductor to alternating current; used to recall the inductive reactance of the series reactor from part (a).

knowledge_points.name: series RLC impedance magnitude
knowledge_points.description: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) is the total impedance magnitude for a series RLC circuit; used to compute the new impedance and show it is similar to the original, so lamp operation is largely unchanged.

knowledge_points.name: series RLC phase angle
knowledge_points.description: tan φ = (X_L - X_C)/R gives the phase angle between total voltage and current in a series RLC circuit; used to show the phase becomes negative (capacitive) with φ' ≈ -63.6°.

knowledge_points.name: power factor
knowledge_points.description: cos φ is the power factor, the ratio of active power to apparent power; a low power factor means a large reactive current that does not deliver useful work but causes line losses.

knowledge_points.name: power factor correction
knowledge_points.description: Adding capacitance in series with an inductive load compensates the inductive reactance, improving the power factor and reducing the reactive current drawn from the supply; this is the manufacturer's intent.

title: Mechanics - Problem I
problem:
A particle moves along the positive axis Ox (one-dimensional situation) under a force having a projection $F_{x} = F_{0}$ on Ox, as represented, as function of x, in the figure 1.1. In the origin of the Ox axis is placed a perfectly reflecting wall.

A friction force, with a constant modulus $F_{f} = 1,00 N$ , acts everywhere on the particle.

The particle starts from the point $x = x_{0} = 1,00 \, m$ having the kinetic energy $E_{c} = 10,0 \, J$ .

sub_problems.problem: a. Find the length of the path of the particle until its final stop.
sub_problems.solution:
The particle moves under a constant conservative force $F_x$ (directed toward the wall) and a constant friction force $F_f$.  The motion is analogous to a vertical elastic ball with weight $|F_x|$ and friction $F_f$.  The particle starts from $x_0$ with kinetic energy $E_c$ and potential energy $U(x_0)=|F_x|x_0$.  The total initial energy is $W(x_0)=|F_x|x_0+E_c$.  The particle eventually stops at the wall ($x=0$) because the friction force dissipates all mechanical energy.  The total distance $D$ travelled satisfies

$$
W(x_0) = D\,F_f \quad\Longrightarrow\quad |F_x|x_0+E_c = D\,F_f,
$$

so

$$
D = \frac{|F_x|x_0+E_c}{F_f}.
$$

Using the numerical data $|F_x|=10\,\text{N}$, $F_f=1\,\text{N}$, $x_0=1\,\text{m}$, $E_c=10\,\text{J}$,

$$
D = \frac{10\cdot1+10}{1}\,\text{m} = 20\,\text{m}.
$$

\boxed{D = 20\,\text{m}}

knowledge_points.name: conservative force
knowledge_points.description: The constant force F_x is conservative, meaning its work is path-independent and a potential energy can be defined. This is used to introduce potential energy U(x).

knowledge_points.name: potential energy of a constant force
knowledge_points.description: For a constant force of magnitude |F_x| directed toward the origin, the potential energy is U(x) = |F_x| x (with U(0)=0). This gives the initial potential energy U(x0) = |F_x| x0.

knowledge_points.name: mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: Total mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy. The initial mechanical energy is E_c + |F_x| x0.

knowledge_points.name: work-energy theorem
knowledge_points.description: The net work done by non-conservative forces equals the change in mechanical energy. Here, the friction force is non-conservative, and its work dissipates the initial mechanical energy.

knowledge_points.name: work done by kinetic friction
knowledge_points.description: The work done by a constant kinetic friction force of magnitude F_f over a total path length D is W = -F_f D, so the magnitude of work is F_f D.

knowledge_points.name: perfectly reflecting wall
knowledge_points.description: The wall at x=0 reflects the particle without energy loss, so mechanical energy is only reduced by friction.

knowledge_points.name: energy dissipation method for total distance
knowledge_points.description: Equating the initial mechanical energy to the total work done by friction (F_f D) yields the total distance traveled until the particle stops, avoiding the need to sum individual segments.

sub_problems.problem: b. Plot the potential energy $U(x)$ of the particle in the force field $F_{x}$.
sub_problems.solution:
The potential energy of the particle in the conservative force field $F_x$ is given by

$$
U(x) = |F_x| \, x
$$

This follows from the definition of potential energy as the work of the conservative force from the reference point $x=0$ (where $U(0)=0$) to the point $x$:

$$
U(x) - U(0) = -\int_0^x \vec{F}_x \cdot d\vec{x} = \int_0^x |F_x| \, dx = |F_x| \, x
$$

Thus $U(x)$ is a linear function of $x$ with slope $|F_x|$.  The graph is a straight line from the origin with positive slope.

If the motion occurs without friction, the particle starting from $x_0$ with kinetic energy $E_c$ reaches a maximum distance $\delta$ where the kinetic energy vanishes.  Energy conservation gives

$$
E_c + |F_x| x_0 = |F_x| \, \delta \quad \Rightarrow \quad \delta = x_0 + \frac{E_c}{|F_x|}
$$

With the given data $|F_x| = 10\,\text{N}$, $F_f = 1\,\text{N}$, $x_0 = 1\,\text{m}$, $E_c = 10\,\text{J}$, we obtain $\delta = 2\,\text{m}$.  The potential energy graph is the straight line $U(x)=10x$ for $0 \le x \le \delta$.

\boxed{U(x) = |F_x| \, x \quad \text{with } |F_x| = 10\,\text{N}}

knowledge_points.name: potential energy
knowledge_points.description: Energy associated with the position of a particle in a conservative force field. Required to interpret the request to plot U(x) and to connect it with the given force F_x.

knowledge_points.name: potential energy from conservative force
knowledge_points.description: U(x) - U(x_ref) = -∫_{x_ref}^{x} F(x') dx'.  This definition is used to compute U(x) directly from the constant force F_x.

knowledge_points.name: constant force field
knowledge_points.description: The force projection F_x is constant (as read from Figure 1.1).  The magnitude is 10 N and the direction is toward the wall (negative x), which makes U(x) = |F_x| x a linear function.

knowledge_points.name: zero potential at origin
knowledge_points.description: The reference point for the potential energy is chosen at the wall x=0 with U(0)=0.  This fixes the integration constant and gives the line through the origin.

sub_problems.problem: c. Qualitatively plot the dependence of the particle's speed as function of its x coordinate.
sub_problems.solution:
The speed of the particle as a function of its x-coordinate is shown qualitatively in the figure below. The motion consists of successive runs towards and away from the wall (x=0). During each run towards the wall the speed increases linearly with decreasing x (parabolic v² vs x), and during each run away from the wall the speed decreases linearly with increasing x. At the wall the speed reverses sign with unchanged magnitude. The maximum speed reached in each successive run decreases geometrically, and the turning points (where v=0) approach the wall geometrically. The qualitative shape is a sequence of parabolic arcs (in v vs x) that become smaller and closer to the origin.

![Qualitative plot of v vs x](images/0c4cc35da512a48b554c4325f5062db0dc9918b632cfce9769b3774b08570a77.jpg)

Figure: Speed v as a function of x for the particle. The solid lines show the motion: starting from x₀ with speed zero, the particle accelerates towards the wall (negative v), collides, then decelerates away from the wall (positive v) to a turning point x₁, then accelerates back to the wall, and so on. The pattern repeats with decreasing amplitudes.
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{See figure: a sequence of parabolic arcs with decreasing amplitude and decreasing turning points approaching } x=0}

knowledge_points.name: perfectly reflecting wall
knowledge_points.description: The wall at x=0 reverses the particle's velocity without energy loss, so the speed magnitude remains unchanged after collision; only the sign of the velocity changes.

knowledge_points.name: constant applied force
knowledge_points.description: The force F_x is constant (as shown in figure 1.1), leading to a piecewise constant net force when combined with the constant friction force.

knowledge_points.name: kinetic friction
knowledge_points.description: A force of constant magnitude that always opposes the direction of motion, causing the net force to differ between motion towards and away from the wall, and dissipating mechanical energy.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law
knowledge_points.description: F_net = ma relates net force to acceleration, allowing determination of the constant acceleration magnitude for each segment of motion.

knowledge_points.name: work-energy theorem for constant force
knowledge_points.description: ΔK = F_net Δx gives a linear relation between v² and x, resulting in parabolic v(x) arcs; equivalently, the kinematic equation v² = v₀² + 2aΔx.

knowledge_points.name: mechanical energy dissipation
knowledge_points.description: Friction does negative work, reducing total mechanical energy over time, so successive turning points (v=0) get closer to the wall and maximum speeds decrease.

title: Refraction in a medium with varying refractive index
problem:
b) Assume that you are standing in a large flat desert. At some distance you see what appears to be a water surface. When you approach the “water” is seems to move away such that the distance to the “water” is always constant. Explain the phenomenon.

c) Compute the temperature of the air close to the ground in b) assuming that your eyes are located 1.60 m above the ground and that the distance to the "water" is 250 m. The refractive index of the air at 15 °C and at normal air pressure (101.3 kPa) is 1.000276. The temperature of the air more than 1 m above the ground is assumed to be constant and equal to 30 °C. The atmospheric pressure is assumed to be normal. The refractive index, n, is such that n - 1 is proportional to the density of the air. Discuss the accuracy of your result.

sub_problems.problem: b) Assume that you are standing in a large flat desert. At some distance you see what appears to be a water surface. When you approach the “water” is seems to move away such that the distance to the “water” is always constant. Explain the phenomenon.
sub_problems.solution:
The phenomenon is due to total internal reflection in a warm layer of air. When the angle of incidence reaches the critical angle, the light from the sky is totally reflected, giving the appearance of a water surface. The condition for total reflection is that the angle of refraction is $90^{\circ}$, so by Snell's law:

$$
n_A \sin \alpha = n_B
$$

where $n_A$ is the refractive index of the cooler air near the ground, $n_B$ is the refractive index of the warmer air above, and $\alpha$ is the critical angle. This explains why the apparent water surface always remains at a constant distance as you approach it.

\boxed{\text{The phenomenon is a mirage caused by total internal reflection of light in a warm air layer.}}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{The phenomenon is a mirage caused by total internal reflection of light in a warm air layer.}}

knowledge_points.name: mirage
knowledge_points.description: The optical phenomenon where a virtual image of the sky appears on the ground, resembling water; caused by atmospheric refraction and total internal reflection of light due to a temperature‑dependent refractive index gradient.

knowledge_points.name: total internal reflection
knowledge_points.description: Complete reflection of light at a boundary from a higher to a lower refractive index medium when the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle; used here to explain why sky light is redirected upwards, creating the water‑like mirror effect.

knowledge_points.name: critical angle
knowledge_points.description: The minimum angle of incidence (measured from the normal) for which total internal reflection occurs, given by sin(θ_c) = n_lower / n_higher; the observed constant distance to the mirage corresponds to rays hitting the warm layer at exactly this angle.

knowledge_points.name: Snell's law
knowledge_points.description: Equation n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ relating angles and refractive indices at an interface; used here with θ₂ = 90° to derive the critical angle condition n_upper sin α = n_lower for the mirage.

knowledge_points.name: temperature-dependent refractive index of air
knowledge_points.description: In a desert the ground heats the air, creating a layer of warmer, less dense air near the surface that has a lower refractive index than the cooler air above (since n‑1 ∝ density ∝ 1/T). This refractive index gradient is necessary for total internal reflection of downward sky light.

sub_problems.problem: c) Compute the temperature of the air close to the ground in b) assuming that your eyes are located 1.60 m above the ground and that the distance to the "water" is 250 m. The refractive index of the air at 15 °C and at normal air pressure (101.3 kPa) is 1.000276. The temperature of the air more than 1 m above the ground is assumed to be constant and equal to 30 °C. The atmospheric pressure is assumed to be normal. The refractive index, n, is such that n - 1 is proportional to the density of the air. Discuss the accuracy of your result.
sub_problems.solution:
The refractive index of air satisfies $n-1 \propto \rho$, where $\rho$ is the density. For fixed pressure, $\rho \propto 1/T$, so

$$
n(T) = 1 + \frac{k}{T}
$$

Given $n(15^\circ\text{C}) = n(288\,\text{K}) = 1.000276$, we find

$$
k = (n-1)T = 0.000276 \times 288 = 0.0795\,\text{K}
$$

For total internal reflection, the critical condition is $n_{30}\sin\alpha = n_T$, where $n_{30}$ is the refractive index at $30^\circ\text{C} = 303\,\text{K}$, and $\alpha$ is the angle of incidence at the boundary. From the geometry, $\sin\alpha = L/\sqrt{h^2+L^2}$, with $h=1.60\,\text{m}$ and $L=250\,\text{m}$. Thus

$$
\left(1+\frac{k}{303}\right)\frac{L}{\sqrt{h^2+L^2}} = 1+\frac{k}{T}
$$

Since $h \ll L$, expand $1/\sqrt{1+h^2/L^2} \approx 1 - h^2/(2L^2)$. Solving for $T$:

$$
T = \frac{303}{\left(\frac{303}{k}+1\right)\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+h^2/L^2}} - \frac{303}{k}} \approx 303\left(1+\frac{303 h^2}{2k L^2}\right)
$$

Substituting values:

$$
T \approx 303\left(1+\frac{303 \times (1.60)^2}{2 \times 0.0795 \times (250)^2}\right) = 303\left(1+\frac{303 \times 2.56}{2 \times 0.0795 \times 62500}\right) = 303\left(1+\frac{775.68}{9937.5}\right) \approx 303 \times 1.0781 \approx 327\,\text{K} = 54^\circ\text{C}
$$

(Note: The exact calculation yields $T \approx 328\,\text{K} = 55^\circ\text{C}$; the slight difference arises from rounding.) The result is sensitive to the approximation $h \ll L$ and the assumption of constant pressure. The accuracy is limited because the temperature gradient near the ground may not be linear, and the refractive index formula is only approximate.

\boxed{T \approx 328\,\text{K} \approx 55^\circ\text{C}}

knowledge_points.name: ideal gas law at constant pressure
knowledge_points.description: To relate air density to temperature under constant pressure, giving ρ ∝ 1/T, which is needed to express n(T) from the given proportionality n−1 ∝ ρ.

knowledge_points.name: Snell's law for total internal reflection
knowledge_points.description: To set the critical condition n_30 sin α = n_T for the ray just undergoing total internal reflection at the boundary between the hot ground layer and the cooler air above.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation for geometry
knowledge_points.description: To simplify sin α = L/√(h²+L²) using h ≪ L, expanding 1/√(1+h²/L²) ≈ 1 − h²/(2L²) to solve for T analytically.

knowledge_points.name: constant atmospheric pressure
knowledge_points.description: The problem states normal atmospheric pressure and the solution assumes it is constant with height near the ground, which is needed to use ρ ∝ 1/T.

knowledge_points.name: n−1 proportional to density
knowledge_points.description: Given in the problem statement; used to write n(T) = 1 + k/T after combining with the ideal gas law at constant pressure.

knowledge_points.name: mirage geometry from part (b)
knowledge_points.description: The solution imports the total-internal-reflection interpretation of the mirage from part (b), where the apparent water surface corresponds to the critical ray from eye to ground.

title: Seiching in a rectangular container
problem:
Create a model of the movement of the water and derive a formula for the oscillation period T. The starting conditions are given in figure above. Assume that $\xi\ll h$. The table below shows experimental oscillation periods for different water depths in two containers of different lengths. Check in some reasonable way how well the formula that you have derived agrees with the experimental data. Give your opinion on the quality of your model.

Table 1. L = 479 mm

| h/ mm | 30 | 50 | 69 | 88 | 107 | 124 | 142 |
|-------|----|----|----|----|-----|-----|-----|
| T/ s  | 1.78 | 1.40 | 1.18 | 1.08 | 1.00 | 0.91 | 0.82 |

Table 2. L = 143 mm

| h/ mm | 31 | 38 | 58 | 67 | 124 |
|-------|----|----|----|----|-----|
| T/ s  | 0.52 | 0.52 | 0.43 | 0.35 | 0.28 |

The graph below shows results from measurements in lake Vättern in Sweden. This lake has a length of 123 km and a mean depth of 50 m. What is the time scale in the graph?
solution:
In the coordinate system of the figure, the centre of mass coordinates of the two triangular parts of the water are

$$
(x_1, y_1) = \left(\frac{L}{3}, \frac{h}{2} + \frac{\xi}{3}\right), \quad (x_2, y_2) = \left(-\frac{L}{3}, \frac{h}{2} - \frac{\xi}{3}\right).
$$

For the entire water mass, the centre of mass coordinates are

$$
(x_{\text{CoM}}, y_{\text{CoM}}) = \left(\frac{\xi L}{6h}, \frac{\xi^2}{6h}\right).
$$

The $y$ component is quadratic in $\xi$ and therefore much smaller than the $x$ component. The velocities of the water mass are

$$
(V_x, V_y) = \left(\frac{\dot{\xi} L}{6h}, \frac{\dot{\xi} \xi}{3h}\right),
$$

and again the vertical component is much smaller than the horizontal one. Neglecting the vertical components, the total energy (kinetic + potential) is

$$
W = W_K + W_P = \frac{1}{2} M \frac{\dot{\xi}^2 L^2}{36 h^2} + M g \frac{\xi^2}{6h}.
$$

For a harmonic oscillator,

$$
W = \frac{1}{2} m \dot{x}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2.
$$

Identifying terms gives

$$
\omega = \sqrt{\frac{12 g h}{L^2}} \quad \text{or} \quad T_{\text{model}} = \frac{\pi L}{\sqrt{3 g h}}.
$$

Comparing with the experimental data, we find $T_{\text{experiment}} \approx 1.1 \cdot T_{\text{model}}$, so the model gives a slight underestimation of the oscillation period. Applying the model to the Vättern data (length 123 km, mean depth 50 m) gives an oscillation period of about 3 hours.

\boxed{T = \frac{\pi L}{\sqrt{3 g h}}}
