sub_problems.problem:
(e) Taking Eqs. (5a) and (5b) into account, the surface charge density $\sigma$ on the lower electrode as a function of $x$ and $t$ is of the form,

$$
\sigma (x, t) = \left[ D_{1} \cos k \left(x - \frac{b}{2}\right) + D_{2} \right] \frac{V(t)}{h}
$$

where $k = \omega / u$. Find the expressions for $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$.
sub_problems.solution:
From Eqs. (5a) and (5b) in the question, the piezoelectric effect leads to the equations

$$
T = Y (S - d_p E) \tag{B15}
$$

$$
\sigma = Y d_p S + \varepsilon_T \left(1 - Y \frac{d_p^2}{\varepsilon_T}\right) E \tag{B16}
$$

Because $x = b/2$ must be a node of displacement for any longitudinal standing wave in the slab, the displacement $\xi$ and strain $S$ must have the form given in Eqs. (B6) and (B10), i.e., with $\omega = ku$,

$$
\xi(x, t) = \xi_m \sin k \left(x - \frac{b}{2}\right) \cos(\omega t + \phi) \tag{B17}
$$

$$
S(x, t) = k \xi_m \cos k \left(x - \frac{b}{2}\right) \cos(\omega t + \phi) \tag{B18}
$$

where a phase constant $\phi$ is now included in the time-dependent factors.

By assumption, the electric field $E$ between the electrodes is uniform and depends only on time:

$$
E(x, t) = \frac{V(t)}{h} = \frac{V_m \cos \omega t}{h} \tag{B19}
$$

Substituting Eqs. (B18) and (B19) into Eq. (B15), we have

$$
T = Y \left[ k \xi_m \cos k \left(x - \frac{b}{2}\right) \cos(\omega t + \phi) - \frac{d_p}{h} V_m \cos \omega t \right] \tag{B20}
$$

The stress $T$ must be zero at both ends ($x = 0$ and $x = b$) of the slab at all times because they are free. This is possible only if $\phi = 0$ and

$$
k \xi_m \cos \frac{k b}{2} = d_p \frac{V_m}{h} \tag{B21}
$$

Since $\phi = 0$, Eqs. (B16), (B18), and (B19) imply that the surface charge density must have the same dependence on time $t$ and may be expressed as

$$
\sigma(x, t) = \sigma(x) \cos \omega t \tag{B22}
$$

with the dependence on $x$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(x) &= Y d_p k \xi_m \cos k \left(x - \frac{b}{2}\right) + \varepsilon_T \left(1 - Y \frac{d_p^2}{\varepsilon_T}\right) \frac{V_m}{h} \\
&= \left[ Y \frac{d_p^2}{\cos \frac{k b}{2}} \cos k \left(x - \frac{b}{2}\right) + \varepsilon_T \left(1 - Y \frac{d_p^2}{\varepsilon_T}\right) \right] \frac{V_m}{h} \tag{B23}
\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing with the given form $\sigma(x, t) = \left[ D_1 \cos k \left(x - \frac{b}{2}\right) + D_2 \right] \frac{V(t)}{h}$, we identify

$$
D_1 = Y \frac{d_p^2}{\cos \frac{k b}{2}}, \quad D_2 = \varepsilon_T \left(1 - Y \frac{d_p^2}{\varepsilon_T}\right)
$$

\boxed{D_1 = Y \frac{d_p^2}{\cos \frac{k b}{2}}}, \quad \boxed{D_2 = \varepsilon_T \left(1 - Y \frac{d_p^2}{\varepsilon_T}\right)}

knowledge_points.description: The solution imports the spatial form ξ ∝ sin k(x - b/2) and S ∝ cos k(x - b/2) with ω = k u from earlier sub-problems (c) and (d), which are needed to express T and σ.

sub_problems.problem:
(f) The total surface charge $Q(t)$ on the lower electrode is related to $V(t)$ by

$$
Q(t) = \left[ 1 + \alpha^{2} \left(\frac{2}{k b} \tan \frac{k b}{2} - 1\right) \right] C_{0} V(t) \tag{6}
$$

Find the expression for $C_{0}$ and the expression and numerical value of $\alpha^{2}$.
sub_problems.solution:
The total surface charge $Q(t)$ on the lower electrode is obtained by integrating the surface charge density $\sigma(x,t)$ over the electrode area. Using the expression for $\sigma(x)$ from the problem, the result is

$$
\frac{Q(t)}{V(t)} = \frac{w}{h} \int_0^b \left[ Y d_p^2 \frac{\cos k\left(x - \frac{b}{2}\right)}{\cos \frac{kb}{2}} + \varepsilon_T \left(1 - \frac{Y d_p^2}{\varepsilon_T}\right) \right] dx
$$

Carrying out the integration yields

$$
\frac{Q(t)}{V(t)} = \varepsilon_T \frac{bw}{h} \left[ \frac{Y d_p^2}{\varepsilon_T} \left(\frac{2}{kb} \tan \frac{kb}{2}\right) + \left(1 - \frac{Y d_p^2}{\varepsilon_T}\right) \right]
$$

Comparing with the given form

$$
Q(t) = \left[ 1 + \alpha^2 \left(\frac{2}{kb} \tan \frac{kb}{2} - 1\right) \right] C_0 V(t)
$$

we identify

$$
C_0 = \varepsilon_T \frac{bw}{h}, \qquad \alpha^2 = \frac{Y d_p^2}{\varepsilon_T}
$$

In the static limit $k \to 0$, $\frac{2}{kb} \tan \frac{kb}{2} \to 1$, so $Q(t)/V(t) \to C_0$, confirming that $C_0$ is the capacitance of the parallel-plate capacitor formed by the electrodes (area $bw$) with the quartz slab (thickness $h$, permittivity $\varepsilon_T$).

Using the numerical values $d_p = 2.25 \times 10^{-2}$ (in appropriate units), $\varepsilon_T = 4.06$, and $Y = 1.27$ (from the problem context), we compute

$$
\alpha^2 = \frac{(2.25)^2 \times 10^{-2}}{1.27 \times 4.06} = 9.82 \times 10^{-3}
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{C_0 = \varepsilon_T \frac{bw}{h}}, \qquad \boxed{\alpha^2 = 9.82 \times 10^{-3}}
$$

title: An Ill Fated Satellite
problem:
The most frequent orbital manoeuvres performed by spacecraft consist of velocity variations along the direction of flight, namely accelerations to reach higher orbits or brakings done to initiate re-entering in the atmosphere. In this problem we will study the orbital variations when the engine thrust is applied in a radial direction.

To obtain numerical values use: Earth radius $R_{T} = 6.37 \cdot 10^{6}$ m, Earth surface gravity $g = 9.81 \, m/s^{2}$ , and take the length of the sidereal day to be $T_{0} = 24.0 \, h$ .

We consider a geosynchronous $^{1}$ communications satellite of mass m placed in an equatorial circular orbit of radius $r_{0}$ . These satellites have an apogee engine which provides the tangential thrusts needed to reach the final orbit.

Image: ESA

Marks are indicated at the beginning of each subquestion, in parenthesis.

Once this geosynchronous circular orbit has been reached (see Figure F-1), the satellite has been stabilised in the desired location, and is being readied to do its work, an error by the ground controllers causes the apogee engine to be fired again. The thrust happens to be directed towards the Earth and, despite the quick reaction of the ground crew to shut the engine off, an unwanted velocity variation $\Delta v$ is imparted on the satellite. We characterize this boost by the parameter $\beta = \Delta v / v_{0}$ . The duration of the engine burn is always negligible with respect to any other orbital times, so that it can be considered as instantaneous.

F-1

Under the action of central forces obeying the inverse-square law, bodies follow trajectories described by ellipses, parabolas or hyperbolas. In the approximation $m \ll M$ the gravitating mass M is at one of the focuses. Taking the origin at this focus, the general polar equation of these curves can be written as (see Figure F-3)

$$
r (\theta) = \frac {l}{1 - \varepsilon \cos \theta}
$$

where l is a positive constant named the semi-latus-rectum and $\varepsilon$ is the eccentricity of the curve. In terms of constants of motion:

$$
l = \frac {L ^ {2}}{G M m ^ {2}} \quad \text { and } \quad \varepsilon = \left(1 + \frac {2 E L ^ {2}}{G ^ {2} M ^ {2} m ^ {3}}\right) ^ {1 / 2}
$$

F-3

where G is the Newton constant, L is the modulus of the angular momentum of the orbiting mass, with respect to the origin, and E is its mechanical energy, with zero potential energy at infinity.

We may have the following cases:

i) If $0 \leq \varepsilon < 1$ , the curve is an ellipse (circumference for $\varepsilon = 0$ ).   
ii) If $\varepsilon = 1$ , the curve is a parabola.   
iii) If $\varepsilon > 1$ , the curve is a hyperbola.

sub_problems.problem: 1.1 Compute the numerical value of $r_0$.
sub_problems.solution:
The gravitational force provides the centripetal acceleration:

\[
G \frac{M_T m}{r_0^2} = m \frac{v_0^2}{r_0}
\]

The orbital speed is related to the period:

\[
v_0 = \frac{2 \pi r_0}{T_0}
\]

The surface gravity is:

\[
g = \frac{G M_T}{R_T^2}
\]

Combining these equations yields:

\[
r_0 = \left( \frac{g R_T^2 T_0^2}{4 \pi^2} \right)^{1/3}
\]

Substituting the known values gives:

\[
\boxed{r_0 = 4.22 \times 10^7 \, \mathrm{m}}
\]

sub_problems.problem: 1.2 Give the analytical expression of the velocity $v_{0}$ of the satellite as a function of $g$, $R_{T}$, and $r_{0}$, and calculate its numerical value.
sub_problems.solution:
The centripetal force is provided by the gravitational force:

\[
G \frac{M_T m}{r_0^2} = m \frac{v_0^2}{r_0}
\]

Using the relation for gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface:

\[
g = \frac{G M_T}{R_T^2}
\]

Eliminate \(G M_T\) to obtain:

\[
v_0 = R_T \sqrt{\frac{g}{r_0}}
\]

This is the analytical expression for the velocity \(v_0\) as a function of \(g\), \(R_T\), and \(r_0\).

To calculate the numerical value, substitute \(R_T = 6.37 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{m}\), \(g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), and \(r_0 = 4.22 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{m}\):

\[
v_0 = 6.37 \times 10^6 \sqrt{\frac{9.81}{4.22 \times 10^7}} \approx 3.07 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{m/s}
\]

\[
\boxed{v_0 = R_T \sqrt{\frac{g}{r_0}}}, \quad \boxed{v_0 = 3.07 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{m/s}}
\]

sub_problems.problem: 1.3 Obtain the expressions of its angular momentum $L_0$ and mechanical energy $E_0$, as functions of $v_0, m, g$ and $R_T$.
sub_problems.solution:
The angular momentum about the center of the Earth is

$$
L_0 = r_0 m v_0 = \frac{g R_T^2}{v_0^2} m v_0 = \frac{m g R_T^2}{v_0}.
$$

The mechanical energy is

$$
E_0 = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 - G \frac{M_T m}{r_0} = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 - \frac{g R_T^2 m}{r_0} = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 - m v_0^2 = -\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2.
$$

\boxed{L_0 = \frac{m g R_T^2}{v_0}} \quad \boxed{E_0 = -\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2}

sub_problems.problem: 2.1 Determine the parameters of the new orbit, semi-latus-rectum $l$ and eccentricity $\varepsilon$, in terms of $r_{0}$ and $\beta$.
sub_problems.solution:
The semi-latus-rectum $l$ is obtained from the conservation of orbital angular momentum. The angular momentum is the same in both orbits, so

$$
l = \frac{L_0^2}{G M_T m^2} = \frac{m^2 g^2 R_T^4}{v_0^2} \frac{1}{g R_T^2 m^2} = \frac{g R_T^2}{v_0^2} = r_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{l = r_0}
$$

The eccentricity is given by

$$
\varepsilon^2 = 1 + \frac{2 E L_0^2}{G^2 M_T^2 m^3}
$$

where $E$ is the new mechanical energy of the satellite:

$$
E = \frac{1}{2} m (v_0^2 + \Delta v^2) - G \frac{M_T m}{r_0} = \frac{1}{2} m \Delta v^2 + E_0 = \frac{1}{2} m \Delta v^2 - \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2
$$

that is

$$
E = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 \left( \frac{\Delta v^2}{v_0^2} - 1 \right) = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 (\beta^2 - 1)
$$

Combining both, one gets $\varepsilon = \beta$. This is an elliptical trajectory because $\varepsilon = \beta < 1$.

\boxed{\varepsilon = \beta}

knowledge_points.name: instantaneous velocity change
knowledge_points.description: The engine burn duration is negligible compared to orbital timescales, so the position r0 is unchanged during the impulse and the velocity change Δv is applied instantaneously.

knowledge_points.name: prior circular orbit results
knowledge_points.description: The solution reuses the previously derived expressions for v0, L0, E0, and the relation GM = g R_T² from the geosynchronous circular orbit analysis.

sub_problems.problem: 2.2 Calculate the angle $\alpha$ between the major axis of the new orbit and the position vector at the accidental misfire.
sub_problems.solution:
The initial and final orbits cross at P, where the satellite engine fired instantaneously. At this point

$$
r(\theta = \alpha) = r_0 = \frac{r_0}{1 - \beta \cos \alpha} \Rightarrow \boxed{\alpha = \frac{\pi}{2}}
$$

knowledge_points.name: polar equation of a conic section
knowledge_points.description: The general polar equation r(θ) = l / (1 - ε cos θ) describes the orbit with the origin at the focus. It is needed to relate the misfire position (r = r₀) to the angle α measured from the major axis.

knowledge_points.name: instantaneous velocity change
knowledge_points.description: The engine burn is treated as instantaneous, so the position r₀ does not change during the misfire. This allows equating the pre- and post-burn radial distance at the misfire point.

knowledge_points.name: misfire at orbital intersection
knowledge_points.description: The initial circular orbit and the new orbit intersect at the point P where the engine fired. This justifies setting r(θ=α) equal to the original orbital radius r₀.

knowledge_points.name: semi-latus rectum equals r₀
knowledge_points.description: From sub-problem 2.1, the semi-latus rectum l of the new orbit equals r₀. This result is imported to simplify the polar equation to r₀/(1 - β cos α).

knowledge_points.name: eccentricity equals β
knowledge_points.description: From sub-problem 2.1, the eccentricity ε of the new orbit equals β. This result is imported to write the denominator as (1 - β cos α).

sub_problems.problem: 2.3 Give the analytical expressions of the perigee $r_{min}$ and apogee $r_{max}$ distances to the Earth centre, as functions of $r_0$ and $\beta$, and calculate their numerical values for $\beta = 1/4$.
sub_problems.solution:
From the trajectory expression one immediately obtains that the maximum and minimum values of $r$ correspond to $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \pi$ respectively (see Figure 4). Hence, they are given by

$$
r_{\max} = \frac{l}{1 - \varepsilon}, \quad r_{\min} = \frac{l}{1 + \varepsilon}
$$

that is

$$
\boxed{r_{\max} = \frac{r_0}{1 - \beta}} \quad \text{and} \quad \boxed{r_{\min} = \frac{r_0}{1 + \beta}}
$$

For $\beta = 1/4$, one gets

$$
\boxed{r_{\max} = 5.63 \times 10^7 \, \mathrm{m}}, \quad \boxed{r_{\min} = 3.38 \times 10^7 \, \mathrm{m}}
$$

knowledge_points.name: perigee and apogee
knowledge_points.description: The perigee is the point of closest approach to Earth in an elliptical orbit, and the apogee is the farthest point. The problem asks for r_min and r_max, which correspond to these orbital extremes.

knowledge_points.name: polar equation of a conic section
knowledge_points.description: The general polar equation r(θ) = l / (1 - ε cos θ) describes the orbit. The extreme distances occur at θ = 0 and θ = π, giving r_max = l/(1-ε) and r_min = l/(1+ε).

knowledge_points.name: results from sub-problem 2.1
knowledge_points.description: The semi-latus rectum l and eccentricity ε for the new orbit were previously derived as l = r_0 and ε = β. These expressions are substituted directly to obtain r_max and r_min in terms of r_0 and β.

knowledge_points.name: numerical value of r_0
knowledge_points.description: The geosynchronous orbital radius r_0 was computed in sub-problem 1.1. Its numerical value is needed to evaluate r_max and r_min for β = 1/4.

sub_problems.problem: 2.4 Determine the period of the new orbit, $T$, as a function of $T_0$ and $\beta$, and calculate its numerical value for $\beta = 1/4$.
sub_problems.solution:
By Kepler's third law, the period $T$ in the new orbit satisfies

$$
\frac{T^2}{a^3} = \frac{T_0^2}{r_0^3}
$$

where $a$, the semi-major axis of the ellipse, is given by

$$
a = \frac{r_{\text{max}} + r_{\text{min}}}{2} = \frac{r_0}{1 - \beta^2}
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{T = T_0 \left(1 - \beta^2\right)^{-3/2}}
$$

For $\beta = 1/4$

$$
\boxed{T = T_0 \left(\frac{15}{16}\right)^{-3/2} = 26.4\,\mathrm{h}}
$$

knowledge_points.name: Kepler's third law
knowledge_points.description: Relates the orbital period squared to the semi-major axis cubed, allowing T to be expressed in terms of a and the known geosynchronous period T0 and radius r0.

knowledge_points.name: semi-major axis of ellipse
knowledge_points.description: The semi-major axis a is the average of perigee and apogee distances; needed to apply Kepler's third law to the new elliptical orbit.

knowledge_points.name: perigee and apogee from previous result
knowledge_points.description: The solution uses the expressions r_min = r0/(1+β) and r_max = r0/(1-β) derived in sub-problem 2.3 to compute the semi-major axis a.

knowledge_points.name: geosynchronous reference orbit
knowledge_points.description: The original circular orbit is geosynchronous with known period T0 and radius r0, providing the reference values for Kepler's third law scaling.

sub_problems.problem: 3.1 Calculate the minimum boost parameter, $\beta_{esc}$, needed for the satellite to escape Earth gravity.
sub_problems.solution:
The satellite escapes Earth gravity if its trajectory is open, i.e., the orbit eccentricity is at least one. The minimum boost corresponds to a parabolic trajectory with eccentricity $\varepsilon = 1$. Since $\varepsilon = \beta$, we obtain

$$
\beta_{\mathrm{esc}} = 1.
$$

Equivalently, the total energy of the satellite must be zero to reach infinity with zero residual kinetic energy:

$$
E = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 (\beta_{\mathrm{esc}}^2 - 1) = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \beta_{\mathrm{esc}} = 1.
$$

This also follows from requiring the orbital period $T \to \infty$ or the maximum distance $r_{\max} \to \infty$.

\boxed{\beta_{\mathrm{esc}} = 1}

knowledge_points.name: escape velocity
knowledge_points.description: The minimum speed needed for an object to escape a gravitational field, corresponding to a parabolic trajectory where total mechanical energy is zero.

knowledge_points.name: orbital eccentricity condition for escape
knowledge_points.description: A trajectory is open (escape) when eccentricity ε ≥ 1; the minimum escape case is the parabola with ε = 1.

knowledge_points.name: eccentricity equals beta
knowledge_points.description: From the previous sub-problem 2.1, the new orbit's eccentricity is ε = β, which is used directly to find the escape boost parameter.

knowledge_points.name: mechanical energy for escape
knowledge_points.description: Escape occurs when total mechanical energy E = 0, so the satellite reaches infinity with zero residual kinetic energy; used as an alternative derivation.

sub_problems.problem: 3.2 Determine in this case the closest approach of the satellite to the Earth centre in the new trajectory, $r_{min}'$, as a function of $r_0$.
sub_problems.solution:
For $\varepsilon = \beta_{\text{esc}} = 1$, the polar equation of the parabolic trajectory is

$$
r = \frac{l}{1 - \cos \theta}
$$

where the semi-latus rectum is $l = r_0$. The minimum distance from the Earth's centre occurs at $\theta = \pi$, giving

$$
\boxed{r_{\min}' = \frac{r_0}{2}}
$$

This result also follows from energy conservation (total energy $E = 0$) and the equality of angular momentum $L_0$ at the initial point $P$ and at the point of closest approach, where $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{v}$ are perpendicular.

knowledge_points.name: parabolic trajectory for escape
knowledge_points.description: For the minimum boost parameter that just allows escape, the eccentricity is exactly 1, so the new orbit is a parabola.

knowledge_points.name: polar equation of a parabola
knowledge_points.description: The general polar equation r = l/(1 - ε cos θ) reduces to r = l/(1 - cos θ) for ε = 1, which is needed to find the distance at θ = π.

knowledge_points.name: semi-latus rectum equals r0
knowledge_points.description: From the previous sub-problem 2.1, for the radial boost the semi-latus rectum l remains equal to the original orbital radius r0, which is used here.

knowledge_points.name: closest approach at θ = π
knowledge_points.description: For a parabola with the focus at the origin, the minimum radial distance occurs when the denominator 1 - cos θ is maximized, i.e., at θ = π.

sub_problems.problem: 4.1 Determine the residual velocity at the infinity, $v_{\infty}$, as a function of $v_{0}$ and $\beta$.
sub_problems.solution:
By energy conservation, the total energy of the satellite is

$$
E = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 (\beta^2 - 1) = \frac{1}{2} m v_\infty^2
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{v_\infty = v_0 \left(\beta^2 - 1\right)^{1/2}}
$$

knowledge_points.name: conservation of mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: The total mechanical energy E (kinetic plus potential) of the satellite is conserved after the impulsive burn, allowing the energy at the burn point to be equated to the energy at infinity.

knowledge_points.name: zero potential energy at infinity
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational potential energy is taken as zero at infinite distance, so the mechanical energy at infinity is purely kinetic (1/2 m v_infty^2).

knowledge_points.name: hyperbolic escape trajectory
knowledge_points.description: For beta > 1 the satellite escapes Earth, so the orbit is hyperbolic and the speed approaches a finite residual value v_infty at large distances.

knowledge_points.name: total energy after radial impulse
knowledge_points.description: The total mechanical energy after the radial impulse is E = (1/2) m v0^2 (beta^2 - 1), a result derived in an earlier sub-problem (2.1) and reused here.

sub_problems.problem: 4.3 Determine the angle $\phi$ of the asymptotic escape direction in terms of $\beta$. Calculate its numerical value for $\beta = \frac{3}{2}\beta_{esc}$.
sub_problems.solution:
The angle between each asymptote and the hyperbola axis is that appearing in its polar equation in the limit $r \to \infty$. This is the angle for which the equation denominator vanishes

$$
1 - \beta \cos \theta_{\text{asym}} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \theta_{\text{asym}} = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\beta}\right)
$$

According to Figure 5

$$
\phi = \frac{\pi}{2} + \theta_{\text{asym}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{\phi = \frac{\pi}{2} + \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\beta}\right)}
$$

For $\beta = \frac{3}{2}\beta_{\text{esc}} = \frac{3}{2}$, one gets $\boxed{\phi = 138^\circ = 2.41\,\text{rad}}$

knowledge_points.name: hyperbolic trajectory asymptotes
knowledge_points.description: For a hyperbolic orbit, the asymptotes are the straight lines the trajectory approaches as r → ∞. The angle between the asymptote and the major axis is found from the polar equation's denominator vanishing.

knowledge_points.name: polar equation of conic section
knowledge_points.description: The general polar equation r(θ) = l/(1 - ε cos θ) describes the orbit. Setting the denominator to zero gives the asymptotic angle θ_asym for ε > 1.

knowledge_points.name: eccentricity equals β for radial boost
knowledge_points.description: From the previous sub-problem 2.1, the new orbit's eccentricity is ε = β after a radial Δv at geosynchronous orbit. This result is reused here to express the asymptote condition.

knowledge_points.name: geometry of asymptote and escape angle
knowledge_points.description: The escape direction angle φ is related to the asymptote angle θ_asym by φ = π/2 + θ_asym, deduced from the geometry of the hyperbola and the initial radial direction.

knowledge_points.name: radial thrust at original orbit position
knowledge_points.description: The misfire occurs at the original geosynchronous position, so the initial position vector is perpendicular to the original velocity. This geometry sets the relation between φ and θ_asym.

title: Neutrons in a Gravitational Field
problem:
In the familiar classical world, an elastic bouncing ball on the Earth's surface is an ideal example for perpetual motion. The ball is trapped: it can not go below the surface or above its turning point. It will remain bounded in this state, turning down and bouncing up once and again, forever. Only air drag or inelastic bounces could stop the process and will be ignored in the following.

A group of physicists from the Institute Laue - Langevin in Grenoble reported $^{1}$ in 2002 experimental evidence on the behaviour of neutrons in the gravitational field of the Earth. In the experiment, neutrons moving to the right were allowed to fall towards a horizontal crystal surface acting as a neutron mirror, where they bounced back elastically up to the initial height once and again.

The setup of the experiment is sketched in Figure F-1. It consists of the opening W, the neutron mirror M (at height z = 0), the neutron absorber A (at height z = H and with length L) and the neutron detector D. The beam of neutrons flies with constant horizontal velocity component $v_{x}$ from W to D through the cavity between A and M. All the neutrons that reach the surface of A are absorbed and disappear from the experiment. Those that reach the surface of M are reflected elastically. The detector D counts the transmission rate $N(H)$ , that is, the total number of neutrons that reach D per unit time.

F-1

The neutrons enter the cavity with a wide range of positive and negative vertical velocities, $v_{z}$ . Once in the cavity, they fly between the mirror below and the absorber above.

sub_problems.problem: 1. Compute classically the range of vertical velocities $v_{z}(z)$ of the neutrons that, entering at a height $z$, can arrive at the detector D. Assume that $L$ is much larger than any other length in the problem.
sub_problems.solution:
The only neutrons that will survive absorption at A are those that cannot cross H. Their turning points will be below H. For a neutron entering the cavity at height z with vertical velocity $v_z$, conservation of energy implies

$$
\frac{1}{2} M v_z^2 + M g z \leq M g H \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{-\sqrt{2g(H-z)} \leq v_z(z) \leq \sqrt{2g(H-z)}}
$$

knowledge_points.name: conservation of mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: Used to relate the neutron's kinetic and potential energy at entry height z to its turning point, determining the maximum height it can reach.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface
knowledge_points.description: The potential energy is M g z, needed to write the energy conservation equation for the neutron in the uniform gravitational field.

knowledge_points.name: uniform gravitational field
knowledge_points.description: The problem assumes constant gravitational acceleration g near the Earth's surface, so potential energy is linear in height.

knowledge_points.name: elastic reflection at mirror
knowledge_points.description: Neutrons bounce elastically from the mirror M, so energy is conserved and the vertical speed magnitude is unchanged upon reflection.

knowledge_points.name: point particle
knowledge_points.description: Neutrons are treated as classical point particles with mass M, ignoring quantum effects for this classical part.

knowledge_points.name: absorber as perfect sink above height H
knowledge_points.description: Any neutron reaching height H is absorbed and lost; thus survival requires the turning point to be strictly below H.

knowledge_points.name: turning point condition
knowledge_points.description: The maximum height a particle reaches occurs when its vertical kinetic energy is zero; setting v_z=0 at height H gives the limiting inequality.

sub_problems.problem: 2. Calculate classically the minimum length $L_{c}$ of the cavity to ensure that all neutrons outside the previous velocity range, regardless of the values of $z$, are absorbed by A. Use $v_{x} = 10 \, \mathrm{m \, s^{-1}}$ and $H = 50 \, \mu\mathrm{m}$.
sub_problems.solution:
The cavity must be long enough to ensure that all neutrons with velocities outside the allowed range are absorbed. The longest required length corresponds to neutrons that enter at the top of the cavity ($z = H$) with zero vertical velocity ($v_z = 0$). These neutrons must reach their maximum height (the top) at least once within the cavity. Let $t_f$ be the time of fall from the top to the bottom. Then the horizontal distance traveled during the round trip (up and down) is $L_c = v_x \cdot 2 t_f$. The height $H$ is related to the fall time by $H = \frac{1}{2} g t_f^2$. Solving these equations gives $t_f = \sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}}$ and therefore $L_c = 2 v_x \sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}}$. Substituting $v_x = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $H = 50\,\mu\mathrm{m} = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}$ yields $L_c = 2 \cdot 10 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{2 \cdot 5.0 \times 10^{-5}}{9.8}} \approx 6.4 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m} = 6.4\,\mathrm{cm}$.

\boxed{L_c = 2 v_x \sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}} = 6.4\,\mathrm{cm}}

knowledge_points.name: worst-case neutron trajectory
knowledge_points.description: The longest required cavity length corresponds to neutrons entering at the top (z=H) with zero vertical velocity; these must complete at least one full bounce (up and down) before exiting.

knowledge_points.name: uniformly accelerated motion
knowledge_points.description: The vertical motion under constant gravitational acceleration g relates fall height H to fall time t_f via H = (1/2) g t_f^2.

knowledge_points.name: constant horizontal velocity
knowledge_points.description: The horizontal velocity component v_x remains constant throughout the motion, so horizontal distance traveled is v_x multiplied by time.

knowledge_points.name: round-trip time calculation
knowledge_points.description: The total horizontal distance L_c is computed as v_x times the round-trip time 2 t_f for a neutron to fall from top to bottom and bounce back to the top.

knowledge_points.name: elastic reflection at mirror
knowledge_points.description: Neutrons bounce elastically off the mirror at z=0, so the upward journey is symmetric to the downward fall and takes the same time t_f.

sub_problems.problem: 3. Compute the classical rate $N_{c}(H)$ assuming that neutrons arrive at the cavity with vertical velocity $v_{z}$ and at height $z$, being all the values of $v_{z}$ and $z$ equally probable. Give the answer in terms of $\rho$, the constant number of neutrons per unit time, per unit vertical velocity, per unit height, that enter the cavity with vertical velocity $v_{z}$ and at height $z$.
sub_problems.solution:
The rate of transmitted neutrons entering at a given height $z$, per unit height, is proportional to the range of allowed velocities at that height, $\rho$ being the proportionality constant:

$$
\frac{dN_c(z)}{dz} = \rho \left[ v_{z,\max}(z) - v_{z,\min}(z) \right] = 2\rho \sqrt{2g(H-z)}.
$$

The total number of transmitted neutrons is obtained by adding the neutrons entering at all possible heights. Let $y = z/H$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_c(H) &= \int_0^H dN_c(z) = \int_0^H 2\rho \sqrt{2g(H-z)} \, dz \\
&= 2\rho \sqrt{2g} \, H^{3/2} \int_0^1 (1-y)^{1/2} \, dy \\
&= 2\rho \sqrt{2g} \, H^{3/2} \left[ -\frac{2}{3} (1-y)^{3/2} \right]_0^1 \\
&= \frac{4}{3} \rho \sqrt{2g} \, H^{3/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

\boxed{N_c(H) = \frac{4}{3} \rho \sqrt{2g} \, H^{3/2}}

knowledge_points.name: uniform phase-space density
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that neutrons enter with all values of v_z and z equally probable, which justifies using a constant density ρ per unit height per unit vertical velocity.

knowledge_points.name: allowed velocity range from part 1
knowledge_points.description: The solution directly imports the result v_{z,max}(z) - v_{z,min}(z) = 2√(2g(H-z)) derived in sub-problem Q3(1) for neutrons that can reach the detector from height z.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: The allowed velocity range expression √(2g(H-z)) originates from energy conservation for a neutron in the uniform gravitational field between the mirror and absorber.

knowledge_points.name: integration over continuous distribution
knowledge_points.description: The total classical rate is obtained by integrating the differential rate dN_c(z)/dz over all entry heights from 0 to H, summing contributions from all z.

knowledge_points.name: change of variables in integration
knowledge_points.description: The substitution y = z/H is used to simplify the definite integral of (H-z)^{1/2} into a dimensionless form.

sub_problems.problem: 4. Compute the turning heights $H_{n}$ and energy levels $E_{n}$ (associated to the vertical motion) using the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization condition. Give the numerical result for $H_{1}$ in $\mu$m and for $E_{1}$ in eV.
sub_problems.solution:
For a neutron falling from a height $H$, the action over a bouncing cycle is twice the action during the fall or the ascent:

$$
S = 2 \int_0^H p_z \, dz = 2 M \sqrt{2g} H^{3/2} \int_0^1 (1-y)^{1/2} \, dy = \frac{4}{3} M \sqrt{2g} H^{3/2}
$$

Using the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization condition:

$$
S = \frac{4}{3} M \sqrt{2g} H^{3/2} = n h \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{H_n = \left( \frac{9 h^2}{32 M^2 g} \right)^{1/3} n^{2/3}}
$$

The corresponding energy levels (associated to the vertical motion) are:

$$
E_n = M g H_n \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{E_n = \left( \frac{9 M g^2 h^2}{32} \right)^{1/3} n^{2/3}}
$$

Numerical values for the first level:

$$
H_1 = \left( \frac{9 h^2}{32 M^2 g} \right)^{1/3} = 1.65 \times 10^{-5} \, \mathrm{m} \quad \boxed{H_1 = 16.5 \, \mu \mathrm{m}}
$$

$$
E_1 = M g H_1 = 2.71 \times 10^{-31} \, \mathrm{J} = 1.69 \times 10^{-12} \, \mathrm{eV} \quad \boxed{E_1 = 1.69 \, \mathrm{peV}}
$$

knowledge_points.name: Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization condition
knowledge_points.description: The action integral over one period of the vertical motion is quantized: S = ∮ p_z dz = n h. This is the central rule used to derive H_n and E_n.

knowledge_points.name: action variable
knowledge_points.description: The action S is defined as the integral of momentum over one complete cycle of the periodic vertical bouncing motion. The solution computes S = 2 ∫₀ᴴ p_z dz.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: For the vertical motion under gravity, total energy is conserved: E = p_z²/(2M) + Mgz. This gives p_z(z) = M√(2g(H−z)) used in the action integral.

knowledge_points.name: elastic reflection at mirror
knowledge_points.description: The neutron mirror at z=0 reflects neutrons elastically, making the vertical motion a periodic bouncing cycle between z=0 and the turning height H. This justifies the integral limits and the factor of 2.

knowledge_points.name: uniform gravitational field
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational acceleration g is constant near Earth's surface, giving linear potential Mgz. This is used in the energy relation and the momentum expression.

knowledge_points.name: definite integral evaluation
knowledge_points.description: The action integral ∫₀ᴴ √(H−z) dz is evaluated by substitution to obtain (2/3)H^(3/2), leading to S = (4/3)M√(2g)H^(3/2).

knowledge_points.name: turning height
knowledge_points.description: The maximum height H reached by a neutron with given vertical energy, where p_z = 0. The quantization condition directly yields discrete turning heights H_n.

sub_problems.problem: 5. Estimate the minimum time of flight $t_{q}$ and the minimum length $L_{q}$ of the cavity needed to observe the first sharp increase in the number of neutrons at D. Use $v_{x} = 10 \, m s^{-1}$.

knowledge_points.name: Heisenberg energy-time uncertainty principle
knowledge_points.description: Relates the minimum energy uncertainty ΔE to the minimum time uncertainty Δt via ΔE Δt ≥ ℏ, which is used to estimate the minimum time needed to resolve the first quantized energy level E₁.

knowledge_points.name: first quantized energy level E₁
knowledge_points.description: The minimum energy allowed in the cavity is the ground-state energy E₁ computed in the previous sub-problem using Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization; this value is used as ΔE in the uncertainty relation.

knowledge_points.name: uncertainty-based time estimation
knowledge_points.description: Using ΔE ≈ E₁, the minimum time is estimated as t_q ≈ ℏ / E₁, and the corresponding horizontal travel distance is L_q = v_x t_q.

knowledge_points.name: constant horizontal velocity
knowledge_points.description: The neutrons move with a constant horizontal velocity component v_x = 10 m/s, allowing the conversion of time uncertainty into a minimum cavity length via Δx = v_x Δt.

title: A Three-body Problem and LISA
problem:
Two gravitating masses M and m are moving in circular orbits of radii R and r, respectively, about their common centre of mass. A third body of infinitesimal mass  is placed in a coplanar circular orbit about the same centre of mass so that  remains stationary relative to both M and m as shown in Figure 1. Assume that the infinitesimal mass is not collinear with M and m.

The Laser Interferometry Space Antenna (LISA) is a group of three identical spacecrafts for detecting low frequency gravitational waves. Each of the spacecrafts is placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle as shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3. The sides (or arms) are about 5.0 million kilometres long. The LISA constellation is in an earth-like orbit around the Sun trailing the Earth by 20. Each of them moves on a slightly inclined individual orbit around the Sun. Effectively, the three spacecrafts appear to roll about their common centre one revolution per year.

They are continuously transmitting and receiving laser signals between each other. Overall, they detect the gravitational waves by measuring tiny changes in the arm lengths using interferometric means. A collision of massive objects, such as blackholes, in nearby galaxies is an example of the sources of gravitational waves.

sub_problems.problem: 1.1 Two gravitating masses M and m are moving in circular orbits of radii R and r, respectively, about their common centre of mass. Find the angular velocity 0 of the line joining M and m in terms of R, r, M, m and the universal gravitational constant G.
sub_problems.solution:
Let O be the centre of mass. Then

$$
M R - m r = 0 \tag{1}
$$

The centripetal force on each mass is provided by the gravitational attraction:

$$
m \omega_0^2 r = \frac{G M m}{(R + r)^2} \tag{2}
$$

$$
M \omega_0^2 R = \frac{G M m}{(R + r)^2}
$$

From Eq. (2), or using the reduced mass, we obtain

$$
\omega_0^2 = \frac{G(M + m)}{(R + r)^3}
$$

Thus the angular velocity is

$$
\boxed{\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{G(M + m)}{(R + r)^3}}}
$$

knowledge_points.name: Newton's law of universal gravitation
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational force between two point masses M and m separated by distance d is F = G M m / d^2. Here it provides the centripetal force on each mass, with d = R + r.

knowledge_points.name: centripetal force for uniform circular motion
knowledge_points.description: For a mass m moving in a circle of radius r with angular velocity ω, the centripetal force required is F = m ω^2 r. Applied to each mass about the CM.

knowledge_points.name: center of mass condition for two bodies
knowledge_points.description: For two masses M and m at distances R and r from their common center of mass, M R = m r. Used to relate the orbital radii.

knowledge_points.name: masses on opposite sides of CM
knowledge_points.description: The two masses are always on opposite sides of the center of mass, so the distance between them is the sum of their orbital radii, R + r. This is implicit in the circular orbit configuration about the CM.

knowledge_points.name: common angular velocity of the line
knowledge_points.description: Both masses orbit with the same angular velocity ω0, so the line joining them rotates rigidly. This is stated in the problem as the angular velocity of the line.

sub_problems.problem: 1.3 Consider the case \(M = m\). If \(\mu\) is now given a small radial perturbation (along \(O\mu\)), what is the angular frequency of oscillation of \(\mu\) about the unperturbed position in terms of \(\omega_0\)? Assume that the angular momentum of \(\mu\) is conserved.
sub_problems.solution:
For the case \(M = m\), the unperturbed configuration has \(r_1 = r_2 = \Re_0\) and \(ho_0 = \Re_0 \cos 30^\circ =  rac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\Re_0\).  The angular frequency of the system is \(\omega_0^2 =  rac{2GM}{\Re_0^3}\).  The energy of the mass \(\mu\) is

\[E = - rac{2GM\mu}{\Re} +  rac{1}{2}\mu\left[\left( rac{dho}{dt}ight)^2 +  rac{ho_0^4\omega_0^2}{ho^2}ight],
\]

where conservation of angular momentum has been used to replace \(ho^2\omega = ho_0^2\omega_0\).  Since energy is conserved, \( rac{dE}{dt}=0\).  Differentiating and using \( rac{d\Re}{dt} =  rac{d\Re}{dho} rac{dho}{dt} =  rac{ho}{\Re} rac{dho}{dt}\) gives

\[ rac{2GM\mu}{\Re^3}ho rac{dho}{dt} + \mu rac{dho}{dt} rac{d^2ho}{dt^2} - \mu rac{ho_0^4\omega_0^2}{ho^3} rac{dho}{dt} = 0.
\]

Dividing by \(\mu rac{dho}{dt}
eq 0\) yields

\[ rac{d^2ho}{dt^2} = - rac{2GM}{\Re^3}ho +  rac{ho_0^4\omega_0^2}{ho^3}.
\]

Now consider small perturbations: \(\Re = \Re_0(1+ rac{\Delta\Re}{\Re_0})\), \(ho = ho_0(1+ rac{\Deltaho}{ho_0})\).  Substituting and expanding to first order in the small quantities, using the binomial expansion \((1+\varepsilon)^n \approx 1+n\varepsilon\), we obtain

\[ rac{d^2\Deltaho}{dt^2} = - rac{2GM}{\Re_0^3}ho_0\left(1+ rac{\Deltaho}{ho_0} -  rac{3\Delta\Re}{\Re_0}ight) + ho_0\omega_0^2\left(1 -  rac{3\Deltaho}{ho_0}ight).
\]

From the geometry, \(\Delta\Re =  rac{\Re_0}{ho_0}\Deltaho\).  Using \(\omega_0^2 =  rac{2GM}{\Re_0^3}\) and simplifying,

\[ rac{d^2\Deltaho}{dt^2} = -\omega_0^2ho_0\left(1+ rac{\Deltaho}{ho_0} -  rac{3ho_0\Deltaho}{\Re_0^2}ight) + \omega_0^2ho_0\left(1 -  rac{3\Deltaho}{ho_0}ight) = -\omega_0^2\Deltaho\left(4 -  rac{3ho_0^2}{\Re_0^2}ight).
\]

With \( rac{ho_0^2}{\Re_0^2} =  rac{3}{4}\), this becomes

\[ rac{d^2\Deltaho}{dt^2} = -\omega_0^2\Deltaho\left(4 -  rac{9}{4}ight) = - rac{7}{4}\omega_0^2\Deltaho.
\]

This is the equation of simple harmonic motion with angular frequency \(\sqrt{ rac{7}{4}}\omega_0 =  rac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\omega_0\).

\boxed{\frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\omega_0}

sub_problems.problem: 1.4 In the plane containing the three spacecrafts, what is the relative speed of one spacecraft with respect to another?
sub_problems.solution:
Let $v$ be the speed of each spacecraft as it moves in a circle around the centre O. The period of circular motion is 1 year: $T = 365 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60$ s. The angular frequency is $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$. The speed is $v = \omega \frac{L}{2 \cos 30^{\circ}} = 575$ m/s. Since $v \ll c$, we use Galilean transformation.

In Cartesian coordinates, the velocities of B and C as observed by O are:
\[ \vec{v}_B = v \cos 60^{\circ} \hat{i} - v \sin 60^{\circ} \hat{j} \]
\[ \vec{v}_C = v \cos 60^{\circ} \hat{i} + v \sin 60^{\circ} \hat{j} \]
Hence the velocity of B as observed by C is:
\[ \vec{v}_{BC} = \vec{v}_B - \vec{v}_C = -2v \sin 60^{\circ} \hat{j} = -\sqrt{3} v \hat{j} \]
The speed of B as observed by C is $\sqrt{3} v \approx 996$ m/s.

\boxed{996 \text{ m/s}}

title: An Electrified Soap Bubble
problem:
A spherical soap bubble with internal air density $\rho_{i}$ , temperature $T_{i}$ and radius $R_{0}$ is surrounded by air with density $\rho_{a}$ , atmospheric pressure $P_{a}$ and temperature $T_{a}$ . The soap film has surface tension $\gamma$ , density $\rho_{s}$ and thickness t. The mass and the surface tension of the soap do not change with the temperature. Assume that $R_{0} \gg t$ .

The increase in energy, dE, that is needed to increase the surface area of a soap-air interface by dA, is given by $dE = \gamma dA$ where $\gamma$ is the surface tension of the film.

sub_problems.problem: 2.1 Find the ratio $\frac{\rho_{i}T_{i}}{\rho_{a}T_{a}}$ in terms of $\gamma$, $P_{a}$ and $R_{0}$.
sub_problems.solution:
Cutting the sphere in half and using the projected area to balance the forces gives

$$
P_i \pi R_0^2 = P_a \pi R_0^2 + 2 (2 \pi R_0 \gamma)
$$

$$
P_i = P_a + \frac{4 \gamma}{R_0} \quad \dots (1)
$$

The pressure and density are related by the ideal gas law:

$$
P V = n R T \quad \text{or} \quad P = \frac{\rho R T}{M},
$$

where $M$ is the molar mass of air. Apply the ideal gas law to the air inside and outside the bubble:

$$
\rho_i T_i = P_i \frac{M}{R}, \qquad \rho_a T_a = P_a \frac{M}{R}.
$$

Thus,

$$
\frac{\rho_i T_i}{\rho_a T_a} = \frac{P_i}{P_a} = 1 + \frac{4 \gamma}{R_0 P_a}.
$$

\boxed{\frac{\rho_i T_i}{\rho_a T_a} = 1 + \frac{4 \gamma}{R_0 P_a}}

knowledge_points.name: excess pressure in a soap bubble
knowledge_points.description: The pressure inside a spherical soap bubble exceeds the outside pressure by ΔP = 4γ/R, where γ is the surface tension and R is the radius. Used to relate the internal pressure P_i to the atmospheric pressure P_a and surface tension γ.

knowledge_points.name: ideal gas law
knowledge_points.description: PV = nRT, which can be expressed in terms of density as P = ρRT/M, where M is the molar mass. Used to relate the products ρ_i T_i and ρ_a T_a to the pressures P_i and P_a.

knowledge_points.name: spherical bubble
knowledge_points.description: The bubble is a perfect sphere, so the excess pressure formula 4γ/R applies with a single radius R0, and the geometry is well-defined.

knowledge_points.name: thin film
knowledge_points.description: The film thickness t is much smaller than the radius R0, so the inner and outer surfaces have approximately the same radius, allowing the use of a single radius R0 in the pressure difference formula.

sub_problems.problem:
2.2 Find the numerical value of $\frac{\rho_{i}T_{i}}{\rho_{a}T_{a}}-1$ using $\gamma=0.0250\ \mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$, $R_{0}=1.00\ \mathrm{cm}$, and

$$
P_{a}=1.013\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}.
$$
sub_problems.solution:
Using the given values:
\[
\gamma = 0.0250\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}},\quad R_0 = 1.00\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.0100\ \mathrm{m},\quad P_a = 1.013\times 10^5\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}.
\]
The required expression is
\[
\frac{\rho_i T_i}{\rho_a T_a} - 1 = \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}.
\]
Substituting the numbers:
\[
\frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a} = \frac{4 \times 0.0250}{0.0100 \times 1.013\times 10^5} = \frac{0.100}{1.013\times 10^3} \approx 9.87 \times 10^{-5}.
\]
Thus,
\[
\frac{\rho_i T_i}{\rho_a T_a} - 1 \approx 9.87 \times 10^{-5}.
\]
\boxed{9.87 \times 10^{-5}}

knowledge_points.name: Result from part 2.1
knowledge_points.description: The expression (ρ_i T_i)/(ρ_a T_a) - 1 = 4γ/(R_0 P_a) derived in the previous sub-problem is used directly to compute the numerical value.

knowledge_points.name: Unit conversion
knowledge_points.description: Convert the given radius from centimeters to meters (1 cm = 0.01 m) to ensure consistent SI units when substituting into the formula.

sub_problems.problem:
2.3 The bubble is initially formed with warmer air inside. Find the minimum numerical value of $T_{i}$ such that the bubble can float in still air. Use $T_{a} = 300 \, K$, $\rho_{s} = 1000 \, kgm^{-3}$,
$$
\rho_{a} = 1.30 \, \mathrm{kgm}^{-3}, t = 100 \, \mathrm{nm} \text{ and } g = 9.80 \, \mathrm{ms}^{-2}.
$$
sub_problems.solution:
Let $W$ be the total weight of the bubble and $F$ the buoyant force due to the surrounding air. The weight is the sum of the mass of the soap film and the mass of the air inside:

$$
W = \left(4\pi R_0^2 \rho_s t + \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_i\right) g
$$

Using the ideal gas law, the density of the air inside is related to the outside air density by

$$
\rho_i = \rho_a \frac{T_a}{T_i} \left(1 + \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}\right)
$$

so that

$$
W = 4\pi R_0^2 \rho_s t g + \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a \frac{T_a}{T_i} \left(1 + \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}\right) g
$$

The buoyant force is

$$
B = \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a g
$$

For the bubble to float in still air, we require $B \geq W$:

$$
\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a g \geq 4\pi R_0^2 \rho_s t g + \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a \frac{T_a}{T_i} \left(1 + \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}\right) g
$$

Dividing by $\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a g$ and rearranging gives

$$
1 \geq \frac{3\rho_s t}{R_0 \rho_a} + \frac{T_a}{T_i} \left(1 + \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}\right)
$$

or

$$
\frac{T_a}{T_i} \left(1 + \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}\right) \leq 1 - \frac{3\rho_s t}{R_0 \rho_a}
$$

Thus

$$
T_i \geq \frac{T_a \left(1 + \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}\right)}{1 - \frac{3\rho_s t}{R_0 \rho_a}}
$$

Substituting the given numerical values: $T_a = 300\,\mathrm{K}$, $\rho_s = 1000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\rho_a = 1.30\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $t = 100\,\mathrm{nm} = 1.00\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$, $g = 9.80\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, and using $R_0 = 1\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.01\,\mathrm{m}$, $\gamma = 0.025\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, $P_a = 1.013\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$, we compute:

$$
\frac{3\rho_s t}{R_0 \rho_a} = \frac{3 \times 1000 \times 1.00\times10^{-7}}{0.01 \times 1.30} \approx 0.02308
$$

$$
1 - \frac{3\rho_s t}{R_0 \rho_a} \approx 0.97692
$$

$$
\frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a} = \frac{4 \times 0.025}{0.01 \times 1.013\times10^5} \approx 9.87\times10^{-4}
$$

$$
1 + \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a} \approx 1.000987
$$

Therefore

$$
T_i \geq \frac{300 \times 1.000987}{0.97692} \approx 307.1\,\mathrm{K}
$$

So the minimum temperature of the air inside is $307.1\,\mathrm{K}$, which is about $7.1^\circ\mathrm{C}$ warmer than the surrounding air.

\boxed{T_i = 307.1\,\mathrm{K}}

knowledge_points.description: The buoyant force on an object submerged in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid displaced. Used to compute the upward force on the bubble as the weight of the displaced outside air.

knowledge_points.description: For an object to float in still air, the buoyant force must be at least equal to the total weight. This yields the inequality B ≥ W used to find the minimum internal temperature.

knowledge_points.description: The excess pressure inside a spherical soap bubble due to surface tension is ΔP = 4γ/R. Used to relate inside pressure to outside pressure via P_i = P_a + 4γ/R0.

knowledge_points.name: thin film approximation
knowledge_points.description: The soap film thickness t is much smaller than the bubble radius R0, so the film volume is approximately surface area times thickness. Used to compute the mass of the soap film as 4πR0^2 ρ_s t.

knowledge_points.description: The bubble is assumed to remain spherical, so its surface area and volume are given by 4πR^2 and 4/3 πR^3. Used for weight and buoyancy calculations.

knowledge_points.description: The surface tension γ does not change with temperature, as stated in the problem. This allows using the constant γ value given.

knowledge_points.name: parameters from previous parts
knowledge_points.description: The bubble radius R0 = 1.00 cm, surface tension γ = 0.0250 N/m, and atmospheric pressure P_a = 1.013×10^5 Pa are taken from earlier sub-problems, as they are not re-specified in 2.3.

sub_problems.problem: 2.4 Find the minimum velocity $u$ of an updraught (air flowing upwards) that will keep the bubble from falling at thermal equilibrium. Give your answer in terms of $\rho_s$, $R_0$, $g$, $t$ and the air's coefficient of viscosity $\eta$. You may assume that the velocity is small such that Stokes's law applies, and ignore the change in the radius when the temperature lowers to the equilibrium. The drag force from Stokes' Law is $F = 6\pi \eta R_0 u$.
sub_problems.solution:
The drag force from Stokes' law is $F = 6\pi \eta R_0 u$.  For the bubble to float in the updraught, the drag force must balance the net downward force (weight minus buoyancy):

$$
F \geq W - B
$$

$$
6\pi \eta R_0 u \geq \left(4\pi R_0^2 \rho_s t + \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_i\right) g - \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a g
$$

At thermal equilibrium, $T_i = T_a$, and using the ideal gas law for the internal air density $\rho_i = \rho_a \left(1 + \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}\right)$ (from the Laplace pressure correction), we have:

$$
6\pi \eta R_0 u \geq \left(4\pi R_0^2 \rho_s t + \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a \left[1 + \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}\right]\right) g - \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a g
$$

Simplifying:

$$
6\pi \eta R_0 u \geq 4\pi R_0^2 \rho_s t g + \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a g \cdot \frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}
$$

Dividing both sides by $6\pi \eta R_0$:

$$
u \geq \frac{4 R_0 \rho_s t g}{6 \eta} + \frac{\frac{4}{3} R_0^2 \rho_a g \left(\frac{4\gamma}{R_0 P_a}\right)}{6 \eta}
$$

Thus the minimum updraught velocity is:

$$
u_{\text{min}} = \frac{2 R_0 \rho_s t g}{3 \eta} + \frac{8 \gamma \rho_a g R_0}{9 \eta P_a}
$$

\boxed{u = \frac{2 R_0 \rho_s t g}{3 \eta} + \frac{8 \gamma \rho_a g R_0}{9 \eta P_a}}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{u = \frac{2 R_0 \rho_s t g}{3 \eta} + \frac{8 \gamma \rho_a g R_0}{9 \eta P_a}}

sub_problems.problem: 2.6 If this spherical bubble is now electrified uniformly with a total charge $q$, find an equation describing the new radius $R_{1}$ in terms of $R_{0}, P_{a}, q$ and the permittivity of free space $\varepsilon_{0}$.
sub_problems.solution:
When the bubble is electrified, the electrical repulsion causes it to expand. The electric field on the surface of the soap film is found using Gauss's law. Consider a thin pill box on the soap surface. The total field just outside the pill box is

$$E_q = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R_1^2} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$$

where $\sigma = q/(4\pi R_1^2)$ is the surface charge density. This field is the sum of the field $E$ from all other parts of the film (excluding the charge inside the pill box) and the field $E_\sigma$ from the surface charge inside the pill box. By Gauss's law, $E_\sigma = \sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$ perpendicular to the film. Hence

$$E = E_q - E_\sigma = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} - \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{1}{2\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{4\pi R_1^2}$$

The repulsive force per unit area on the surface is

$$\left(\frac{q}{4\pi R_1^2}\right) E = \frac{(q/(4\pi R_1^2))^2}{2\varepsilon_0}$$

Let $P_i'$ be the new internal pressure when the bubble is electrified. The gas inside obeys the ideal gas law at constant temperature (isothermal process), so

$$P_i' \frac{4}{3}\pi R_1^3 = P_i \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3$$

where $P_i$ is the original internal pressure. For a soap bubble, the surface tension term is ignored in this part, so $P_i = P_a$ (the external atmospheric pressure). Thus

$$P_i' = \left(\frac{R_0}{R_1}\right)^3 P_a$$

Balancing forces on a half-sphere projected area (again ignoring surface tension) gives

$$P_i' + \frac{(q/(4\pi R_1^2))^2}{2\varepsilon_0} = P_a$$

Substituting $P_i'$:

$$P_a \left(\frac{R_0}{R_1}\right)^3 + \frac{q^2}{32\pi^2 \varepsilon_0 R_1^4} = P_a$$

Rearranging:

$$\left(\frac{R_1}{R_0}\right)^4 - \left(\frac{R_1}{R_0}\right) - \frac{q^2}{32\pi^2 \varepsilon_0 R_0^4 P_a} = 0$$

This is the equation for $R_1$ in terms of $R_0$, $P_a$, $q$, and $\varepsilon_0$.

\boxed{\left(\frac{R_1}{R_0}\right)^4 - \frac{R_1}{R_0} - \frac{q^2}{32\pi^2 \varepsilon_0 R_0^4 P_a} = 0}

knowledge_points.name: Gauss's law
knowledge_points.description: Used to find the electric field just outside a uniformly charged spherical shell: E = q/(4πε₀R₁²), which gives the relation between total charge and surface charge density.

knowledge_points.name: Electrostatic pressure on a charged surface
knowledge_points.description: The outward pressure on a charged surface is P_elec = σ²/(2ε₀) = (1/2)ε₀E². This is used to model the repulsive force per unit area that expands the bubble.

knowledge_points.name: Ideal gas law

knowledge_points.name: Pressure balance on a spherical shell

knowledge_points.name: Neglect of surface tension

sub_problems.problem:
2.7 Assume that the total charge is not too large (i.e. $\frac{q^{2}}{\varepsilon_{0}R_{0}^{4}} \ll P_{a}$ ) and the bubble only experiences a small increase in its radius, find $\Delta R$ where $R_{1}=R_{0}+\Delta R$ .

Given that $(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx$ where $x \ll 1$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Write $R_1 = R_0 + \Delta R$, with $\Delta R \ll R_0$. Then

$$
\frac{R_1}{R_0} = 1 + \frac{\Delta R}{R_0}, \quad \left(\frac{R_1}{R_0}\right)^4 \approx 1 + 4\frac{\Delta R}{R_0}.
$$

Using the equilibrium condition (Eq. (17)), we obtain

$$
\Delta R \approx \frac{q^2}{96 \pi^2 \varepsilon_0 R_0^3 P_a}.
$$

Thus

$$
R_1 \approx R_0 + \frac{q^2}{96 \pi^2 \varepsilon_0 R_0^3 P_a} = R_0 \left(1 + \frac{q^2}{96 \pi^2 \varepsilon_0 R_0^4 P_a}\right).
$$

\boxed{\Delta R = \frac{q^2}{96 \pi^2 \varepsilon_0 R_0^3 P_a}}

knowledge_points.name: equilibrium condition from Q2(2.6)
knowledge_points.description: The equation relating the new radius R1 to R0, Pa, q, and ε0 derived in sub-problem 2.6 is used as the starting point for this sub-problem.

knowledge_points.name: binomial approximation for small exponent
knowledge_points.description: The approximation (1+x)^n ≈ 1+nx for x≪1 is applied to (R1/R0)^4 to linearize the equilibrium equation and solve for ΔR.

knowledge_points.name: small radius increment
knowledge_points.description: The new radius is expressed as R1 = R0 + ΔR with ΔR ≪ R0, defining the quantity to be found.

knowledge_points.name: small charge assumption
knowledge_points.description: The condition q²/(ε0 R0⁴) ≪ Pa ensures the radius change is small, justifying the use of the binomial approximation and the perturbation approach.

sub_problems.problem: 2.8 What must be the magnitude of this charge \(q\) in terms of \(t, \rho_{a}, \rho_{s}, \varepsilon_{0}, R_{0}, P_{a}\) in order that the bubble will float motionlessly in still air? Calculate also the numerical value of \(q\). The permittivity of free space \(\varepsilon_{0} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\) farad/m.
sub_problems.solution:
The bubble will float motionlessly if the buoyant force equals the total weight.  The buoyant force is the weight of displaced air, and the weight includes the mass of the soap film and the mass of the air inside.  Initially the inside and outside temperatures are equal, so the density of the inside air equals the ambient density \(\rho_a\) (for \(\gamma \to 0\)).  The condition is

\[
\frac{4}{3}\pi R_1^3 \rho_a g = 4\pi R_0^2 \rho_s t g + \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a g
\]

where \(R_1 = R_0 + \Delta R\).  Substituting and expanding to first order in \(\Delta R\):

\[
\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \left(1 + \frac{\Delta R}{R_0}\right)^3 \rho_a g \approx \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \left(1 + 3\frac{\Delta R}{R_0}\right) \rho_a g
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a g + 4\pi R_0^2 \Delta R \rho_a g = 4\pi R_0^2 \rho_s t g + \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \rho_a g
\]

Cancelling the common term gives

\[
4\pi R_0^2 \Delta R \rho_a g = 4\pi R_0^2 \rho_s t g
\]

so

\[
\Delta R = \frac{\rho_s t}{\rho_a}
\]

From the result of part 2.7, the change in radius due to the charge is

\[
\Delta R = \frac{q^2}{96\pi^2 \varepsilon_0 R_0 P_a}
\]

Equating the two expressions for \(\Delta R\):

\[
\frac{q^2}{96\pi^2 \varepsilon_0 R_0 P_a} = \frac{\rho_s t}{\rho_a}
\]

Solving for \(q\):

\[
q^2 = \frac{96\pi^2 R_0^3 \rho_s t \varepsilon_0 P_a}{\rho_a}
\]

\[
q = \sqrt{\frac{96\pi^2 R_0^3 \rho_s t \varepsilon_0 P_a}{\rho_a}}
\]

Using the numerical values: \(R_0 = 0.10\,\text{m}\), \(\rho_s = 1.0\times10^3\,\text{kg/m}^3\), \(t = 1.0\times10^{-7}\,\text{m}\), \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\,\text{F/m}\), \(P_a = 1.0\times10^5\,\text{Pa}\), \(\rho_a = 1.2\,\text{kg/m}^3\).  Then

\[
q \approx 256 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{C} = 256\,\text{nC}
\]

\[
\boxed{q = \sqrt{\frac{96\pi^2 R_0^3 \rho_s t \varepsilon_0 P_a}{\rho_a}}}
\]
\[
\boxed{q \approx 256\,\text{nC}}
\]
