title: Scattering of an Ion by a Neutral Atom
problem:
An ion of mass m, charge Q, is moving with an initial non-relativistic speed $v_{0}$ from a great distance towards the vicinity of a neutral atom of mass M >> m and of electrical polarisability $\alpha$ . The impact parameter is b as shown in Figure 1.

The atom is instantaneously polarised by the electric field $\vec{E}$ of the in-coming (approaching) ion. The resulting electric dipole moment of the atom is $\vec{p} = \alpha\vec{E}$ . Ignore any radiative losses in this problem.

sub_problems.problem: 3.2 Find the expression for the force $\vec{f}$ acting on the ion due to the polarised atom. Show that this force is attractive regardless of the sign of the charge of the ion.
sub_problems.solution:
The electric field seen by the atom from the ion is

$$
\vec{E}_{ion} = -\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} \hat{r}
$$

The induced dipole moment is

$$
\vec{p} = \alpha \vec{E}_{ion} = -\frac{\alpha Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} \hat{r}
$$

From the expression for the field of a dipole,

$$
\vec{E}_p = \frac{2p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3} \hat{r}
$$

Substituting the induced dipole moment,

$$
\vec{E}_p = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3} \left[ -\frac{2\alpha Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} \hat{r} \right] = -\frac{\alpha Q}{8\pi^2 \varepsilon_0^2 r^5} \hat{r}
$$

The force acting on the ion is

$$
\vec{f} = Q \vec{E}_p = -\frac{\alpha Q^2}{8\pi^2 \varepsilon_0^2 r^5} \hat{r}
$$

The negative sign indicates that the force is attractive, and the presence of $Q^2$ shows that the force is attractive regardless of the sign of $Q$.

\boxed{\vec{f} = -\frac{\alpha Q^2}{8\pi^2 \varepsilon_0^2 r^5} \hat{r}}

knowledge_points.name: Coulomb's law (electric field of a point charge)
knowledge_points.description: Gives the electric field of the ion at the atom's location: E = (1/(4πε₀)) Q/r² radially. Used to compute the field that polarises the atom.

knowledge_points.name: Induced dipole moment (polarisability)
knowledge_points.description: The relation p = α E, where α is the polarisability. The problem states that the atom acquires a dipole moment proportional to the applied field. Used to find the dipole moment of the polarised atom.

knowledge_points.name: Electric field of a point dipole on its axis
knowledge_points.description: The electric field at a point on the axis of a point dipole is E = (1/(4πε₀)) (2p/r³) along the axis (direction depends on orientation). Used to compute the field of the polarised atom at the ion's position.

knowledge_points.name: Lorentz force law (electric force)
knowledge_points.description: The force on a point charge in an electric field is f = q E. Used to compute the force on the ion from the dipole field.

sub_problems.problem: 3.3 What is the electric potential energy of the ion-atom interaction in terms of $\alpha, Q$ and $r$?
sub_problems.solution:
The electric potential energy of the ion-atom interaction is obtained by integrating the force from infinity to a distance $r$:

$$U = \int_{r}^{\infty} \vec{f} \cdot d\vec{r}$$

Carrying out the integration yields:

$$U = -\frac{\alpha Q^{2}}{32\pi^{2}\varepsilon_{0}^{2} r^{4}}$$

\boxed{U = -\frac{\alpha Q^{2}}{32\pi^{2}\varepsilon_{0}^{2} r^{4}}}

knowledge_points.name: Conservative force
knowledge_points.description: The ion-atom interaction force is conservative, depending only on distance r, so a potential energy function U(r) can be defined.

knowledge_points.name: Potential energy from force integral
knowledge_points.description: The potential energy U(r) of a conservative central force F(r) is obtained by integrating the radial force component from r to infinity, with U(∞)=0: U(r) = ∫_r^∞ F(r') dr'.

knowledge_points.name: Force expression from sub-problem 3.2
knowledge_points.description: The attractive force on the ion due to the polarised atom has magnitude f = α Q^2/(8 π^2 ε0^2 r^5) and is radial inward. This result is imported from the previous sub-problem.

sub_problems.problem: 3.5 If the impact parameter $b$ is less than a critical value $b_{0}$, the ion will descend along a spiral to the atom. In such a case, the ion will be neutralized, and the atom is, in turn, charged. This process is known as the “charge exchange” interaction. What is the cross sectional area $A = \pi b_{0}^{2}$ of this “charge exchange” collision of the atom as seen by the ion?

knowledge_points.name: real minimum distance condition
knowledge_points.description: The result from the previous sub-problem that a real distance of closest approach exists only if 1 ≥ α Q² / (4π² ε₀² m v₀² b⁴); failure of this inequality leads to a spiral trajectory and charge exchange.

knowledge_points.name: collision cross-section
knowledge_points.description: The cross-sectional area for a collision process is A = π b₀², where b₀ is the maximum impact parameter that leads to the specified outcome (here, charge exchange).

title: Motion on a horizontal surface
problem:
Force of friction is not always isotropic. Often the magnitude and direction of a friction force depend on the direction of body motion. For example, friction anisotropy can arise in the presence of "grooves" of a certain orientation on the contact surface of bodies (it is known that the coefficient of friction of oak against oak along and across the grain is equal to 0.48 and 0.34, respectively). Friction anisotropy can lead to unusual properties of motion which are studied in this problem.

# What you need to know about anisotropic friction

Suppose that a surface is made of an anisotropic material. One of the most popular models of anisotropic friction suggests that there are perpendicular axes $X$ and $Y$ (they are called primary) so that the friction force $\vec{F}$ acting on a body will depend on the direction of the body motion as

$$F_{x} = - \frac{| N |}{\left| v \right|} \mu_{x} v_{x} \tag{1}$$

$$F_{y} = - \frac{\frac{| v |}{| N |}}{| v |} \mu_{y} v_{y}$$

where $F_{x}$ and $F_{y}$ are the friction force components, $N$ is a normal reaction force acting on the body, $v_{x}$ and $v_{y}$ are components of the velocity vector $\vec{v} ,$ , and $\mu_{x}$ and $\mu_{y}$ are the friction coefficients along the primary axes.

Hereinafter, it is understood that the coordinate axes on the plane coincide with the primary axes. The friction coefficients are $\mu_{x} =0,75$ and $\mu_{y} =0 {,} 5$ unless otherwise stated.

In parts A and B a body can be considered as point-like. The plane, on which the bodies move, is horizontal in all parts of the problem.

Provide a numerical answer wherever possible.

# Part A. Motion on a horizontal surface

sub_problems.problem: (1) At what angle $\alpha_{1}$ to the $X$ axis should the body velocity vector be for the absolute value of the power of the friction force be at maximum?
sub_problems.solution:
For motion with velocity making an angle \(\alpha\) to the \(X\)-axis, we have
\[v_x = v\cos\alpha, \qquad v_y = v\sin\alpha.
\]
The friction force does negative work, so its power is
\[
P = \vec F\cdot \vec v = -mg\left(\mu_x\cos^2\alpha + \mu_y\sin^2\alpha\right)v.
\]
Hence the absolute value of the power is
\[
|P| = mgv\left(\mu_x\cos^2\alpha + \mu_y\sin^2\alpha\right).
\]
Since \(\mu_x=0.75 > \mu_y=0.5\), this expression is maximal when \(\cos^2\alpha=1\), i.e. when the velocity is directed along the \(X\)-axis.

Therefore,
\[
\boxed{\alpha_1 = 0}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Anisotropic friction model
knowledge_points.description: Friction force components along primary axes are given by F_x = -μ_x |N| v_x/|v|, F_y = -μ_y |N| v_y/|v|; this model is applied to compute the friction power.

knowledge_points.name: Normal force on horizontal surface
knowledge_points.description: On a horizontal plane the normal force magnitude equals the weight mg, allowing replacement of |N| in the friction law with mg.

knowledge_points.name: Power as dot product
knowledge_points.description: Instantaneous mechanical power of a force is P = F·v, used to compute the rate of work done by friction and its magnitude.

knowledge_points.name: Velocity component decomposition
knowledge_points.description: Resolve velocity into components v_x = v cosα, v_y = v sinα to express the friction force components and power in terms of the angle α to the X‑axis.

sub_problems.problem: (2) At what angle $\alpha_{2}$ to the $X$ axis should the body velocity vector be for the absolute value of the power of the friction force be 1.2 times less than maximum?
sub_problems.solution:
The power of the friction force is
\[
P=\vec F\cdot \vec v.
\]
For a velocity making an angle \(\alpha\) with the \(X\)-axis, \(v_x=v\cos\alpha\) and \(v_y=v\sin\alpha\). Hence the magnitude of the friction power is
\[
|P|=mgv\bigl(\mu_x\cos^2\alpha+\mu_y\sin^2\alpha\bigr).
\]
Since \(\mu_x>\mu_y\), the maximum occurs when the motion is along the \(X\)-axis:
\[
|P|_{\max}=mgv\mu_x.
\]
We need the power to be 1.2 times less than the maximum, i.e.
\[
|P|=\frac{1}{1.2}|P|_{\max}=\frac56\,mgv\mu_x.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mu_x\cos^2\alpha+\mu_y\sin^2\alpha=\frac56\mu_x.
\]
Substitute \(\mu_x=0.75\) and \(\mu_y=0.5\):
\[
0.75\cos^2\alpha+0.5\sin^2\alpha=0.625.
\]
Using \(\sin^2\alpha=1-\cos^2\alpha\),
\[
0.75\cos^2\alpha+0.5(1-\cos^2\alpha)=0.625,
\]
\[
0.25\cos^2\alpha=0.125,
\]
\[
\cos^2\alpha=\frac12.
\]
Thus
\[
\cos\alpha=\pm\frac1{\sqrt2},
\]
so the possible angles are
\[
\alpha_2=\pm\frac\pi4,\ \pm\frac{3\pi}{4}.
\]
Final answer: \(\boxed{\alpha_2=\pm\frac\pi4,\ \pm\frac{3\pi}{4}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Power as dot product of force and velocity
knowledge_points.description: The instantaneous power of a force is P = F·v, used to calculate the friction power magnitude from the given friction force.

knowledge_points.name: Anisotropic friction force model
knowledge_points.description: Friction force components along primary axes X and Y are given by F_x = -|N|/|v| μ_x v_x and F_y = -|N|/|v| μ_y v_y, as stated in the problem introduction.

knowledge_points.name: Normal force equals weight on horizontal surface
knowledge_points.description: On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration, the normal reaction force magnitude |N| equals the weight mg, allowing substitution into the friction law.

knowledge_points.name: Resolution of velocity into components
knowledge_points.description: Velocity components are expressed as v_x = v cos α, v_y = v sin α, where α is the angle with the X-axis, to substitute into the power expression.

knowledge_points.name: Maximum friction power result from part A(1)
knowledge_points.description: From the previous sub-problem, the maximum absolute friction power is |P|_max = mgv μ_x and occurs when motion is along the X-axis (α = 0), used to set up the 1.2‑times‑less condition.

knowledge_points.name: Point-like body approximation
knowledge_points.description: The body is treated as a point particle, so its translational velocity uniquely defines the friction force direction without rotational complications.

sub_problems.problem: (3) Let the initial velocity have components $v_{0 x} =1 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ and $v_{0 y} =1 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ . After some time the velocity component along the $Y$ axis equals $v_{1 y} = \mathrm{0,25 m / s}$ . What is the velocity magnitude at this moment?
sub_problems.solution:
Newton’s equations for the velocity components are

\[
\begin{cases}
 m\dfrac{d v_x}{dt} = -\mu_x m g \dfrac{v_x}{v}, \\
 m\dfrac{d v_y}{dt} = -\mu_y m g \dfrac{v_y}{v},
\end{cases}
\]
where \(v=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}\).

Dividing the first equation by the second gives

\[
\frac{d v_x}{d v_y} = \frac{\mu_x v_x}{\mu_y v_y}.
\]

Integrating, we obtain the invariant

\[
\frac{v_x^{\mu_y}}{v_y^{\mu_x}}=\text{const}.
\]

Using the initial conditions \(v_{0x}=1\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and \(v_{0y}=1\,\mathrm{m/s}\), we get

\[
\frac{v_x^{0.5}}{v_y^{0.75}}=1,
\]
so

\[
 v_x = v_y^{\mu_x/\mu_y}=v_y^{3/2}.
\]

At the moment when \(v_y=0.25\,\mathrm{m/s}\),

\[
 v_x = (0.25)^{3/2} = 0.125\,\mathrm{m/s}.
\]

Therefore the speed is

\[
 v = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2} = \sqrt{0.125^2+0.25^2} \approx 0.28\,\mathrm{m/s}.
\]

Final answer: \(\boxed{0.28\,\mathrm{m/s}}\).

knowledge_points.name: anisotropic friction force
knowledge_points.description: The friction force components are given by F_x = -μ_x N v_x / |v|, F_y = -μ_y N v_y / |v|, with different coefficients μ_x, μ_y along primary axes. Needed to write the equations of motion.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law
knowledge_points.description: The net force on a particle equals mass times acceleration. Used in component form m dv_x/dt = F_x and m dv_y/dt = F_y to obtain the differential equations for the velocity components.

knowledge_points.name: normal force equals weight on horizontal plane
knowledge_points.description: On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration, the magnitude of the normal reaction force N equals mg. This replaces N in the friction force expressions.

knowledge_points.name: eliminating time by dividing differential equations
knowledge_points.description: Dividing the two autonomous equations of motion for v_x and v_y eliminates dt, yielding dv_x/dv_y = F_x/F_y. This transforms the system into a single relation between velocity components that can be integrated without solving for time evolution.

knowledge_points.name: constant of motion (invariant)
knowledge_points.description: A function of dynamical variables that remains constant during motion. Integration gives the invariant v_x^{μ_y} / v_y^{μ_x} = const, enabling one velocity component to be found from the other without solving the full time dependence.

knowledge_points.name: separation of variables for first-order ODE
knowledge_points.description: The ODE dv_x/dv_y = (μ_x/μ_y)(v_x/v_y) is separable. Integrating dv_x/v_x = (μ_x/μ_y) dv_y/v_y gives the logarithmic solution and the power‑law relation v_x = v_y^{μ_x/μ_y}.

sub_problems.problem: (4) Let the velocity be $v_{2} =1.0 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ . At what angle $\alpha_{3}$ to the $X$ axis should the velocity vector be for the radius of curvature of the trajectory be minimum? What is this radius equal to? The free fall acceleration is $\dot{g} =9,8 \mathrm{{m} / \mathrm{{s}^{2}}}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The radius of curvature is determined by the component of the friction force perpendicular to the velocity. For a velocity making an angle \(\alpha\) with the \(X\)-axis, this component is

\[
F_n = mg(\mu_x-\mu_y)\sin\alpha\cos\alpha.
\]

Using Newton’s second law in the normal direction to the trajectory,

\[
\frac{mv^2}{R}=mg(\mu_x-\mu_y)\sin\alpha\cos\alpha.
\]

Hence

\[
R=\frac{v^2}{g(\mu_x-\mu_y)\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}
=\frac{2v^2}{g(\mu_x-\mu_y)\sin 2\alpha}.
\]

The radius is minimal when \(\sin 2\alpha\) is maximal, i.e. when

\[
2\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \alpha=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]

Then

\[
R_{\min}=\frac{2v^2}{g(\mu_x-\mu_y)}.
\]

With \(v=1.0\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), \(\mu_x=0.75\), and \(\mu_y=0.50\),

\[
R_{\min}=\frac{2\cdot 1.0^2}{9.8\cdot(0.75-0.50)}\approx 0.82\,\mathrm{m}.
\]

Thus the minimum radius occurs for \(\alpha_3=\frac{\pi}{4}\), and the minimum radius is \(0.82\,\mathrm{m}\).

knowledge_points.name: Anisotropic friction force law
knowledge_points.description: The friction force components along primary axes X and Y are given by F_x = - μ_x |N| v_x/|v|, F_y = - μ_y |N| v_y/|v|. This model is needed to compute the friction force vector for any velocity direction.

knowledge_points.name: Normal force equals weight on horizontal plane
knowledge_points.description: For a point mass on a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration, the magnitude of the normal reaction force equals mg. This replaces |N| in the friction law.

knowledge_points.name: Normal acceleration and radius of curvature
knowledge_points.description: For motion along any curved path, the instantaneous normal acceleration is a_n = v^2/R, where R is the local radius of curvature. This kinematic relation connects path geometry to the centripetal acceleration.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law in normal direction
knowledge_points.description: Applying Newton's second law along the normal to the trajectory gives m v^2/R = F_n, where F_n is the net force component perpendicular to the velocity. This equation yields the radius of curvature from the normal force.

knowledge_points.name: Resolving friction force into normal component
knowledge_points.description: To find the friction force component perpendicular to velocity, project the given X-Y components onto a unit vector orthogonal to the velocity direction (e.g., (-v_y, v_x)/|v|). This technique isolates the part of the friction that causes centripetal acceleration.

sub_problems.problem: (5) In a single diagram on the $X Y$ plane, sketch the trajectories of the body launched at the angles $\alpha_{4} = \pi /6$ and $\alpha_{5} = \pi /3$ for the friction coefficients specified above. The magnitudes of initial velocities are the same. Solve the same problem for the friction coefficients $\mu_{x} =0,4$ and $\mu_{y} =0 {,} 7$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For anisotropic friction, the decelerations along the coordinate axes are determined separately by the coefficients \(\mu_x\) and \(\mu_y\). The trajectory is straight only in the special isotropic case \(\mu_x=\mu_y\), because then both velocity components decrease in the same proportion.

For the given coefficients \(\mu_x=0.75\) and \(\mu_y=0.5\), we have \(\mu_x>\mu_y\). Therefore the \(x\)-component of velocity decreases faster than the \(y\)-component, so the trajectory bends away from the straight line in the same sense for both launch angles \(\alpha_4=\pi/6\) and \(\alpha_5=\pi/3\). In a single \(XY\)-diagram, both paths should start from the origin with the corresponding initial directions, and then curve so that the motion becomes progressively more aligned with the \(y\)-axis.

For the second set \(\mu_x=0.4\) and \(\mu_y=0.7\), we have \(\mu_x<\mu_y\). The bending is then in the opposite sense: the \(y\)-component decreases faster than the \(x\)-component, so both trajectories curve toward the \(x\)-axis. Again, the direction of deflection does not depend on the initial launch angle, only on whether \(\mu_x\) is greater or smaller than \(\mu_y\).

Final answer: \(\boxed{\text{For }\mu_x>\mu_y\text{ both trajectories bend toward the }y\text{-axis; for }\mu_x<\mu_y\text{ both bend toward the }x\text{-axis.}}\)
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{For }\mu_x>\mu_y\text{ both trajectories bend toward the }y\text{-axis; for }\mu_x<\mu_y\text{ both bend toward the }x\text{-axis.}}

knowledge_points.name: anisotropic friction force law
knowledge_points.description: The friction force components are given by Fx = -(|N|/|v|) μx vx and Fy = -(|N|/|v|) μy vy, where μx and μy are the primary friction coefficients. This law governs the motion on the anisotropic surface and is used to determine the acceleration components and the resulting trajectory curvature.

knowledge_points.name: point particle approximation
knowledge_points.description: The body is treated as a point mass, neglecting its size and rotational dynamics, so only translational motion under the given friction law is considered. This justifies applying the friction law directly to the body's velocity.

knowledge_points.name: normal force equals weight on horizontal plane
knowledge_points.description: On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration, the normal reaction force N equals the weight mg, so |N| = mg is constant. This determines the magnitude of the friction force and, together with the friction coefficients, sets the deceleration along each axis.

title: Conditions for the beginning of body movement
problem:
Force of friction is not always isotropic. Often the magnitude and direction of a friction force depend on the direction of body motion. For example, friction anisotropy can arise in the presence of "grooves" of a certain orientation on the contact surface of bodies (it is known that the coefficient of friction of oak against oak along and across the grain is equal to 0.48 and 0.34, respectively). Friction anisotropy can lead to unusual properties of motion which are studied in this problem.

# What you need to know about anisotropic friction

Suppose that a surface is made of an anisotropic material. One of the most popular models of anisotropic friction suggests that there are perpendicular axes $X$ and $Y$ (they are called primary) so that the friction force $\vec{F}$ acting on a body will depend on the direction of the body motion as

$$F_{x} = - \frac{| N |}{\left| v \right|} \mu_{x} v_{x} \tag{1}$$

$$F_{y} = - \frac{\frac{| v |}{| N |}}{| v |} \mu_{y} v_{y}$$

where $F_{x}$ and $F_{y}$ are the friction force components, $N$ is a normal reaction force acting on the body, $v_{x}$ and $v_{y}$ are components of the velocity vector $\vec{v} ,$ , and $\mu_{x}$ and $\mu_{y}$ are the friction coefficients along the primary axes.

Hereinafter, it is understood that the coordinate axes on the plane coincide with the primary axes. The friction coefficients are $\mu_{x} =0,75$ and $\mu_{y} =0 {,} 5$ unless otherwise stated.

In parts A and B a body can be considered as point-like. The plane, on which the bodies move, is horizontal in all parts of the problem.

Provide a numerical answer wherever possible.

# Part B. Conditions for the beginning of body movement

A body of mass $m$ is at rest at the origin. A force has been applied to it at an angle $\alpha$ to the $X$ axis. The force magnitude $F ( t ) = \gamma t$ linearly grows with time. Find the dependence of the moment the body starts moving on $\alpha$ . Ignore the stagnation phenomenon.
solution:
At the instant the body is just about to start moving, the applied force balances the maximal static friction force in the direction of impending motion. Since the body may start moving in a direction making an angle \(\varphi\neq \alpha\) with the \(X\)-axis, the friction components at threshold satisfy
\[
\left\{
\begin{array}{l}F_{\mathrm{fr},x}=\mu_x m g\cos\varphi=\gamma t\cos\alpha,\\ F_{\mathrm{fr},y}=\mu_y m g\sin\varphi=\gamma t\sin\alpha.
\end{array}
\right.
\]
Divide the first equation by \(\mu_x m g\) and the second by \(\mu_y m g\), then square and add:
\[
\left(\frac{\gamma t\cos\alpha}{\mu_x m g}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\gamma t\sin\alpha}{\mu_y m g}\right)^2=1.
\]
Hence
\[
(mg)^2=(\gamma t)^2\left[\left(\frac{\cos\alpha}{\mu_x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\mu_y}\right)^2\right],
\]
so the time when motion starts is
\[
\boxed{t(\alpha)=\frac{\mu_x\mu_y\,mg}{\gamma\sqrt{\mu_y^2\cos^2\alpha+\mu_x^2\sin^2\alpha}}}.
\]

sub_problems.problem:
Force of friction is not always isotropic. Often the magnitude and direction of a friction force depend on the direction of body motion. For example, friction anisotropy can arise in the presence of "grooves" of a certain orientation on the contact surface of bodies (it is known that the coefficient of friction of oak against oak along and across the grain is equal to 0.48 and 0.34, respectively). Friction anisotropy can lead to unusual properties of motion which are studied in this problem.

# What you need to know about anisotropic friction

Suppose that a surface is made of an anisotropic material. One of the most popular models of anisotropic friction suggests that there are perpendicular axes $X$ and $Y$ (they are called primary) so that the friction force $\vec{F}$ acting on a body will depend on the direction of the body motion as

$$F_{x} = - \frac{| N |}{\left| v \right|} \mu_{x} v_{x} \tag{1}$$

$$F_{y} = - \frac{\frac{| v |}{| N |}}{| v |} \mu_{y} v_{y}$$

where $F_{x}$ and $F_{y}$ are the friction force components, $N$ is a normal reaction force acting on the body, $v_{x}$ and $v_{y}$ are components of the velocity vector $\vec{v} ,$ , and $\mu_{x}$ and $\mu_{y}$ are the friction coefficients along the primary axes.

Hereinafter, it is understood that the coordinate axes on the plane coincide with the primary axes. The friction coefficients are $\mu_{x} =0,75$ and $\mu_{y} =0 {,} 5$ unless otherwise stated.

In parts A and B a body can be considered as point-like. The plane, on which the bodies move, is horizontal in all parts of the problem.

Provide a numerical answer wherever possible.

# Part B. Conditions for the beginning of body movement

A body of mass $m$ is at rest at the origin. A force has been applied to it at an angle $\alpha$ to the $X$ axis. The force magnitude $F ( t ) = \gamma t$ linearly grows with time. Find the dependence of the moment the body starts moving on $\alpha$ . Ignore the stagnation phenomenon.
sub_problems.solution:
At the instant the body is just about to start moving, the applied force balances the maximal static friction force in the direction of impending motion. Since the body may start moving in a direction making an angle \(\varphi\neq \alpha\) with the \(X\)-axis, the friction components at threshold satisfy
\[
\left\{
\begin{array}{l}F_{\mathrm{fr},x}=\mu_x m g\cos\varphi=\gamma t\cos\alpha,\\ F_{\mathrm{fr},y}=\mu_y m g\sin\varphi=\gamma t\sin\alpha.
\end{array}
\right.
\]
Divide the first equation by \(\mu_x m g\) and the second by \(\mu_y m g\), then square and add:
\[
\left(\frac{\gamma t\cos\alpha}{\mu_x m g}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\gamma t\sin\alpha}{\mu_y m g}\right)^2=1.
\]
Hence
\[
(mg)^2=(\gamma t)^2\left[\left(\frac{\cos\alpha}{\mu_x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\mu_y}\right)^2\right],
\]
so the time when motion starts is
\[
\boxed{t(\alpha)=\frac{\mu_x\mu_y\,mg}{\gamma\sqrt{\mu_y^2\cos^2\alpha+\mu_x^2\sin^2\alpha}}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: anisotropic static friction threshold
knowledge_points.description: The maximum static friction force in a direction making an angle φ to the X-axis is assumed to follow the same anisotropic law as kinetic friction: the components are F_fr,x = μ_x N cos φ, F_fr,y = μ_y N sin φ, where N is the normal force.

knowledge_points.name: impending motion direction in anisotropy
knowledge_points.description: In anisotropic friction, the direction of impending motion φ is generally not aligned with the applied force direction α; the body chooses the direction in which the friction threshold is lowest relative to the applied force components.

knowledge_points.name: force equilibrium at motion threshold
knowledge_points.description: Just before motion starts, the body is in translational equilibrium: the vector sum of the applied force and the static friction force is zero, i.e., F_app = -F_fr.

knowledge_points.name: normal force equals weight on horizontal plane
knowledge_points.description: Since the surface is horizontal and there is no vertical acceleration, the normal reaction N equals the weight mg.

title: Circular motion
problem:
Force of friction is not always isotropic. Often the magnitude and direction of a friction force depend on the direction of body motion. For example, friction anisotropy can arise in the presence of "grooves" of a certain orientation on the contact surface of bodies (it is known that the coefficient of friction of oak against oak along and across the grain is equal to 0.48 and 0.34, respectively). Friction anisotropy can lead to unusual properties of motion which are studied in this problem.

# What you need to know about anisotropic friction

Suppose that a surface is made of an anisotropic material. One of the most popular models of anisotropic friction suggests that there are perpendicular axes $X$ and $Y$ (they are called primary) so that the friction force $\vec{F}$ acting on a body will depend on the direction of the body motion as

$$F_{x} = - \frac{| N |}{\left| v \right|} \mu_{x} v_{x} \tag{1}$$

$$F_{y} = - \frac{\frac{| v |}{| N |}}{| v |} \mu_{y} v_{y}$$

where $F_{x}$ and $F_{y}$ are the friction force components, $N$ is a normal reaction force acting on the body, $v_{x}$ and $v_{y}$ are components of the velocity vector $\vec{v} ,$ , and $\mu_{x}$ and $\mu_{y}$ are the friction coefficients along the primary axes.

Hereinafter, it is understood that the coordinate axes on the plane coincide with the primary axes. The friction coefficients are $\mu_{x} =0,75$ and $\mu_{y} =0 {,} 5$ unless otherwise stated.

In parts A and B a body can be considered as point-like. The plane, on which the bodies move, is horizontal in all parts of the problem.

Provide a numerical answer wherever possible.

# Part C. Circular motion

Two identical point-like masses $m$ are connected with a weightless inextensible rod of length $L =1 \mathrm{m}_{\iota}$ the system lies on a surface with anisotropic friction. The rod is aligned with the $Y$ axis and does not touch the surface. One of the masses is given an initial velocity perpendicular to the rod.

sub_problems.problem: (1) For a given initial velocity $v_{0}$ find the dependence of its velocity $v$ on the angle of rotation of the rod $\varphi$ assuming that the other body remains at rest.
sub_problems.solution:
Let the moving mass have velocity magnitude $v$. The rod makes an angle $\varphi$ with the $X$ axis, so the velocity components are proportional to the instantaneous direction of motion. The friction force components are therefore

$$F_x=-mg\,\mu_x\frac{v_x}{v},\qquad F_y=-mg\,\mu_y\frac{v_y}{v}.$$
\nProjecting Newton’s second law onto the direction of motion gives

$$m\frac{dv}{dt}=-mg\left(\mu_x\cos^2\varphi+\mu_y\sin^2\varphi\right).$$
\nSince the moving mass is constrained by the rigid rod, its speed is related to the angular velocity by

$$v=L\dot\varphi.$$
\nHence

$$L\ddot\varphi=-g\left(\mu_x\cos^2\varphi+\mu_y\sin^2\varphi\right).$$
\nMultiply by $\dot\varphi$:

$$L\dot\varphi\,\ddot\varphi=-g\left(\mu_x\cos^2\varphi+\mu_y\sin^2\varphi\right)\dot\varphi.$$
\nUsing $v=L\dot\varphi$, this becomes

$$v\,dv=-gL\left(\mu_x\cos^2\varphi+\mu_y\sin^2\varphi\right)d\varphi.$$
\nIntegrating from the initial state $(v_0,\varphi=0)$ to $(v,\varphi)$,

$$\frac{v^2-v_0^2}{2}=-gL\int_0^{\varphi}\left(\mu_x\cos^2\phi+\mu_y\sin^2\phi\right)d\phi.$$
\nEvaluating the integral,

$$v^2=v_0^2-gL\left[(\mu_x+\mu_y)\varphi+(\mu_x-\mu_y)\frac{\sin 2\varphi}{2}\right].$$
\nTherefore the dependence of the speed on the rotation angle is

$$\boxed{v(\varphi)=\sqrt{\,v_0^2-gL\left[(\mu_x+\mu_y)\varphi+(\mu_x-\mu_y)\frac{\sin 2\varphi}{2}\right]\,}}.$$

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law
knowledge_points.description: The net force on a particle equals its mass times acceleration: F = m a. Used to relate the tangential friction force to the rate of change of speed.

knowledge_points.name: Tangential acceleration
knowledge_points.description: For a particle moving along a path, the component of acceleration along the tangent is a_t = dv/dt, where v is speed. Used to project Newton's second law onto the direction of motion.

knowledge_points.name: Circular motion kinematics
knowledge_points.description: For a particle constrained to a circle of radius L, its speed v is related to the angular velocity by v = L dφ/dt, and its velocity is tangential to the circle. Used to relate v and φ and to express the velocity direction.

knowledge_points.name: Normal force equals weight
knowledge_points.description: On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration, the normal reaction force N equals the weight mg. Used to replace |N| with mg in the friction force formula.

knowledge_points.name: Stationary second mass
knowledge_points.description: The other point mass remains at rest, so the moving mass is effectively attached to a fixed pivot by the rod, resulting in circular motion.

knowledge_points.name: Chain rule for acceleration
knowledge_points.description: To integrate the equation of motion with respect to angle, use the chain rule dv/dt = (dv/dφ)(dφ/dt) = (v/L) dv/dφ, or equivalently multiply by v dt = ds to obtain v dv = a_t ds. Used to derive a differential equation relating v and φ.

sub_problems.problem: (2) Find the maximum value of the initial velocity $v_{\mathrm{0 max}}$ at which the other body will remain at rest.
sub_problems.solution:
Let the tension in the rod be $T$. For the moving mass, the component of Newton’s second law along the rod gives

$$T + F_{\mathrm{fr}}\sin\beta = m\dot{\varphi}^{2}L,$$
\nwhere $\beta$ is the angle between the friction force and the velocity direction.
\nUsing the result from part C1, the tension can be written as

$$T = \frac{m v_0^2}{L} - mg(\mu_x+\mu_y)\varphi - mg(\mu_x-\mu_y)\sin 2\varphi.$$
\nUsing the result from part B1, the condition for the other mass to remain at rest is

$$\frac{m v_0^2}{L} - mg(\mu_x+\mu_y)\varphi - mg(\mu_x-\mu_y)\sin 2\varphi \le \frac{\mu_x\mu_y}{\sqrt{\mu_y^2\sin^2\varphi+\mu_x^2\cos^2\varphi}}\,mg.$$
\nAs $\varphi$ increases, the left-hand side decreases while the right-hand side increases, so the limiting case occurs at $\varphi=0$. Therefore

$$v_{0\max}=\sqrt{\mu_y g L}.$$
\nWith $\mu_y=0.5$ and $L=1\,\mathrm{m}$, this gives

$$v_{0\max}=2.2\,\mathrm{m/s}.$$
\nFinal answer: $\boxed{2.2\,\mathrm{m/s}}$

knowledge_points.name: centripetal force equation
knowledge_points.description: The radial component of net force acting on a point mass in circular motion equals m ω² r; used to relate tension and friction along the rod to the centripetal acceleration of the moving mass.

knowledge_points.name: massless inextensible rod
knowledge_points.description: The rod connecting the two masses transmits equal and opposite tension forces along its length, with no mass or stretching, so tension is uniform and acts axially.

knowledge_points.name: tension expression from rotating anisotropic friction
knowledge_points.description: The tension in the rod as a function of rotation angle φ, obtained from solving the moving mass's dynamics under anisotropic friction in part C1: T = m v₀²/L − mg(μₓ+μᵧ)φ − mg(μₓ−μᵧ) sin 2φ.

knowledge_points.name: static friction limit for anisotropic surface
knowledge_points.description: The inequality T ≤ (μₓ μᵧ / √(μᵧ² sin²φ + μₓ² cos²φ)) mg that must hold for the second mass to remain at rest under the applied rod tension, derived from the anisotropic friction model in part B1.

sub_problems.problem: (3) What distance will the body travel until it stops completely if the initial velocity is $v_{0\mathrm{max}}$?
sub_problems.solution:
Substituting the value of \(v_{0\max}\) found in the previous part into the stopping condition from part C1, we obtain an equation for the angle \(\varphi\) at which the motion ends:\
\[\ngL\left[(\mu_x+\mu_y)\varphi + (\mu_x-\mu_y)\frac{\sin 2\varphi}{2}\right]=\mu_y gL.
\]\nWith \(\mu_x=0.75\) and \(\mu_y=0.5\), this becomes
\[
1.25\,\varphi + 0.125\,\sin 2\varphi = 0.5.
\]\nSolving numerically gives \(\varphi \approx 0.34\,\text{rad}\).
\nThe travelled distance is the arc length
\[\ns=L\varphi.
\]\nSince \(L=1\,\text{m}\),
\[\ns\approx 0.34\,\text{m}.
\]\nTherefore, the body travels \(\boxed{0.34\,\text{m}}\) before stopping completely.

knowledge_points.name: circular path of the moving mass
knowledge_points.description: With the other mass at rest and the rod inextensible, the moving mass follows a circular arc of radius equal to the rod length L.

knowledge_points.name: arc length formula
knowledge_points.description: The distance traveled along a circular arc is s = L φ, where φ is the angular displacement in radians.

knowledge_points.name: stopping condition from part C1
knowledge_points.description: The relation derived in part C1 that determines the stopping angle φ by setting v(φ) = 0. For v_0 = v_0max it reduces to L[(μ_x+μ_y)φ + (μ_x-μ_y)(sin 2φ)/2] = v_0max²/g.

knowledge_points.name: maximum initial velocity v_0max
knowledge_points.description: The result from part C2: the largest initial speed for which the second mass stays at rest is v_0max = √(μ_y g L).

knowledge_points.name: numerical root-finding
knowledge_points.description: The transcendental equation from the stopping condition must be solved numerically (e.g., by iteration) to obtain the stopping angle φ, as no closed-form solution exists.

title: The ring as a capacitor
problem:
Consider a uniformly charged metallic ring of radius $R$ and total charge $q$ . The ring is a hollow toroid of thickness $2a \ll R$ . This thickness can be neglected in parts A, B, C, and E. The $xy$ plane coincides with the plane of the ring, while the $z$ -axis is perpendicular to it, as shown in Figure 1. In parts A and B you might need to use the formula (Taylor expansion)

$$(1+ x)^{\varepsilon} \approx 1+ \varepsilon x + \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon (\varepsilon -1) x^{2}, \mathrm{when} | x | \ll 1.$$

Figure 1. A charged ring of radius $R$ .

# Part D. The ring as a capacitor

The model considered above was idealized and we assumed that the ring charged instantaneously. In reality charging is non-instantaneous, as the ring is a capacitor with a finite capacitance $C$ . In this part we will analyze the properties of this capacitor. You might need the following integrals:

$$\int \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\sin x} = - \ln \left| \frac{\cos x +1}{\sin x} \right| + \text{const}$$

and

$$\int \frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\sqrt{1+ x^{2}}} = \ln \left| x + \sqrt{1+ x^{2}} \right| + \mathrm{const .}$$

sub_problems.problem:
(1) Calculate the capacitance $C$ of the ring. Consider that the ring has a finite width $2a$ , but remember that $a \ll R$ .

When electrons reach the "active region", the ring is connected to a source of voltage $V_{0}$ (Figure 3). When electrons pass the "active region", the ring is connected to the ground. The resistance of contacts is $R_{0}$ and the resistance of the ring itself can be neglected.

Figure 3. Charging of the electrostatic lens.
sub_problems.solution:
Let the ring have total charge $q$ uniformly distributed along its circumference, so the linear charge density is
\[
\lambda=\frac{q}{2\pi R}.
\]\nSince the ring has a small but finite thickness $2a\ll R$, we may model it as a thin torus of minor radius $a$.
\nTo find its capacitance, compute the electrostatic potential of the charged ring relative to infinity. Split the ring into two parts:

1. a small arc of angular size $2\alpha\ll 1$, and
2. the rest of the ring.
\nChoose the field point $K$ on the ring surface where the potential is evaluated.
\nFor the small arc, curvature can be neglected because $\alpha\ll 1$, so this part is approximated by a straight charged segment of length $2\alpha R$. Its contribution is
\[
\Phi_1=2\cdot \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{2\pi R}\int_0^{\alpha R}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}.
\]\nUsing
\[
\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}=\ln\left|x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\right|+\text{const},
\]\nwe get
\[
\Phi_1=\frac{q}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha R}{a}+\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\alpha R}{a}\right)^2}\right)
\approx \frac{q}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R}\ln\left(\frac{2\alpha R}{a}\right),
\]\nwhere $\alpha R\gg a$ was used.
\nFor the rest of the ring, the thickness may be neglected. If the angular coordinate from the nearby point is $\phi$, then the distance from the field point to the source element is
\[
|KL|=2R\sin\frac{\phi}{2}.
\]\nHence
\[
\Phi_2=2\cdot \frac{q}{2\pi}\cdot \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_\alpha^\pi \frac{d\phi}{2R\sin(\phi/2)}
=\frac{q}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R}\int_{\alpha/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{d\chi}{\sin\chi}.
\]\nUsing
\[
\int \frac{d\chi}{\sin\chi}=-\ln\left|\frac{\cos\chi+1}{\sin\chi}\right|+\text{const},
\]\nwe obtain
\[
\Phi_2=\frac{q}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R}\ln\left(\frac{\cos(\alpha/2)+1}{\sin(\alpha/2)}\right)
\approx \frac{q}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R}\ln\left(\frac{4}{\alpha}\right),
\]\nfor $\alpha\ll 1$.
\nAdding both contributions,
\[
\Phi=\Phi_1+\Phi_2
=\frac{q}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R}\ln\left(\frac{2\alpha R}{a}\right)+\frac{q}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R}\ln\left(\frac{4}{\alpha}\right)
=\frac{q}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R}\ln\left(\frac{8R}{a}\right).
\]\nThe arbitrary parameter $\alpha$ cancels, as it must.
\nTherefore the capacitance is
\[\nC=\frac{q}{\Phi}=\frac{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R}{\ln(8R/a)}.
\]\nFinal answer: \boxed{C=\dfrac{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R}{\ln(8R/a)}}

knowledge_points.name: Capacitance of an isolated conductor
knowledge_points.description: The capacitance C of an isolated conductor is defined as C = Q/Φ, where Q is its net charge and Φ its electrostatic potential relative to infinity. Used to obtain the final capacitance from the computed potential.

knowledge_points.name: Electric potential of a continuous charge distribution
knowledge_points.description: The electrostatic potential at a point is given by the superposition integral Φ = (1/(4π ε₀)) ∫ dq/r, where dq is an infinitesimal charge element and r is the distance to the field point. Used to set up the potential integrals for the ring.

knowledge_points.name: Uniform charge distribution on the ring
knowledge_points.description: The net charge q is uniformly distributed along the circumference of the ring, so the linear charge density λ = q/(2π R) is constant. This allows expressing dq = λ dl in the integrals.

knowledge_points.name: Ring as a thin torus
knowledge_points.description: The ring is modelled as a thin torus of major radius R and minor radius a with a circular cross‑section; a ≪ R. The finite thickness a is used to regularize the self‑potential: distances from a point on the surface to nearby points include a (e.g., √(x²+a²)).

knowledge_points.name: Equipotential surface of a conductor
knowledge_points.description: In electrostatic equilibrium a conductor is an equipotential body. The potential is the same everywhere on its surface, so the value computed at one point K is taken as the potential Φ of the whole ring, which enters the capacitance formula.

knowledge_points.name: Splitting method for self-potential regularization
knowledge_points.description: To handle the singular self‑potential of a thin ring, the integration domain is split into a small near arc (where curvature can be neglected, allowing a straight‑segment approximation) and the remainder of the ring (where the thickness a can be neglected). This regularizes the integral and leads to a cancellation of the arbitrary splitting parameter α.

knowledge_points.name: Small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: For small angles, sin θ ≈ θ and cos θ ≈ 1. Used to simplify the expression for the potential from the remainder of the ring to a form that is free of the auxiliary angle α.

sub_problems.problem:
(2) Determine the dependence of the charge on the ring as a function of time, $q(t)$ ,

and make a schematic plot of this dependence. $t =0$ corresponds to a time moment when electrons are in the plane of the ring. What is the charge on the ring $q_{0}$ when the absolute value $q(t)$ is maximal? The capacitance of the ring is $C$ (i.e., you do not have to use the actual expression found in D.1).

Remark: the drawn polarity in Figure 3 is for indicative purposes only. The sign should be chosen so that the lens is focusing.
sub_problems.solution:
Let $q(t)$ be the charge on the ring at time $t$. Since the ring has capacitance $C$, its potential is $q(t)/C$. The current through the charging resistance is
\[
I(t)=\frac{dq}{dt},
\]
so the voltage drop across the resistor is $R_0 I(t)=R_0\,dq/dt$.

While the external charging voltage $V_0$ is applied, the circuit equation is
\[
\frac{q(t)}{C}+R_0\frac{dq}{dt}=V_0.
\]
This applies for
\[
-\frac{d}{2v}<t<\frac{d}{2v}.
\]

Using the initial condition that the charge is zero when the electrons are in the plane of the ring at the beginning of charging, we take
\[
q\!\left(-\frac{d}{2v}\right)=0.
\]
Solving the differential equation gives
\[
q(t)=CV_0\left(1-e^{-\frac{d}{2vR_0C}}e^{-\frac{t}{R_0C}}\right),
\qquad -\frac{d}{2v}<t<\frac{d}{2v}.
\]

The charge reaches its largest absolute value at the end of the charging interval,
\[
t=\frac{d}{2v},
\]
so
\[
q_0=q\!\left(\frac{d}{2v}\right)=CV_0\left(1-e^{-\frac{d}{vR_0C}}\right).
\]

After the electrons have left the plane of the ring, the capacitor discharges through the resistor, so for
\[
t>\frac{d}{2v},
\]
the circuit equation becomes
\[
\frac{q(t)}{C}+R_0\frac{dq}{dt}=0.
\]
Hence
\[
q(t)=q_0\,e^{-\frac{t-\frac{d}{2v}}{R_0C}}
=CV_0\left(e^{\frac{d}{2vR_0C}}-e^{-\frac{d}{2vR_0C}}\right)e^{-\frac{t}{R_0C}}.
\]

Therefore the full time dependence is
\[
q(t)=
\begin{cases}
0, & t<-\dfrac{d}{2v},\[6pt]
CV_0\left(1-e^{-\frac{d}{2vR_0C}}e^{-\frac{t}{R_0C}}\right), & -\dfrac{d}{2v}<t<\dfrac{d}{2v},\[8pt]
CV_0\left(e^{\frac{d}{2vR_0C}}-e^{-\frac{d}{2vR_0C}}\right)e^{-\frac{t}{R_0C}}, & t>\dfrac{d}{2v}.
\end{cases}
\]

The schematic plot is: zero before charging, then a rise during the charging interval, reaching its extremum at $t=d/(2v)$, followed by an exponential decay.

For the lens to be focusing, the charge must have the appropriate sign, so the polarity is chosen such that
\[
V_0<0,
\]
and the maximal charge is correspondingly negative if focusing requires negative charge.

knowledge_points.name: self-capacitance relation
knowledge_points.description: For an isolated conductor with capacitance C, the potential is V = q/C. Used to relate the ring's charge to its voltage in the circuit equation.

knowledge_points.name: Ohm's law
knowledge_points.description: The voltage drop across a resistor of resistance R carrying current I is V = IR. Applied to the contact resistance R0.

knowledge_points.name: Kirchhoff's voltage law
knowledge_points.description: The sum of voltage drops around a closed loop equals the applied electromotive force. Used to write the circuit equation: q/C + R0 dq/dt = V0 (charging) and = 0 (discharging).

knowledge_points.name: electric current definition
knowledge_points.description: Electric current is the rate of change of charge, I = dq/dt. Used to express the resistor current in terms of the ring's charge.

knowledge_points.name: solving first-order linear ODE
knowledge_points.description: Technique to solve differential equations of the form dq/dt + a q = b, yielding exponential solutions. Used to find q(t) for both charging and discharging phases.

knowledge_points.name: initial uncharged ring
knowledge_points.description: The ring is assumed to have zero charge at the moment the electrons enter the active region (t = -d/(2v)). This provides the integration constant for the charging phase.

knowledge_points.name: charging interval timing
knowledge_points.description: The active region has length d and electrons move at speed v (from earlier parts), so the charging occurs only for -d/(2v) < t < d/(2v). After this, the ring is grounded (applied voltage zero). Defines the piecewise time domains.

title: Interaction of magnets
problem:
Strong permanent magnets are made from NdFeB alloy which obeys a very wide hysteresis loop so that the magnetization $J$ can be assumed to be constant over a wide range of applications; in what follows, we assume that $J \equiv 1.5\mathrm{T} / \mu_0$ , where $\mu_0=4\pi \times 10^{-7}\mathrm{N / A^2}$ , and the magnetization of all the permanent magnets is homogeneous. Magnetization is defined as the volume density of the magnetic dipole moment of the matter.

Hint 1. The following equality might be useful:

$$\sum_{n =1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^{4}} = \frac{\pi^{4}}{90}.$$

Hint 2. The magnetic field created by a spherical magnet is identical to that of a point dipole. The magnetic fields created by magnets of other shapes become equivalent to a point dipole fields only at distances much larger than their diameter.
Hint 3. Electric and magnetic fields of electric and magnetic point dipoles as functions of coordinates and of the corresponding dipole moment are similar, i.e. one can be obtained from the other by multiplying it by a constant factor.
Hint 4. The induced field due to a boundary condition can always be replaced by some configuration of field sources outside the given boundaries.

# Part A. Interaction of magnets

When the distance to a magnet is much larger than its size, the magnetic field created by it can be approximated with the magnetic field of its dipole moment $\vec{m}$ ,

$$\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_{0}}{4 \pi r^{3}} (2 \vec{m}_{\parallel} - \vec{m}_{\perp}).$$

Here $r = |\vec{r}|$ , and we have decomposed the dipole moment into components parallel and perpendicular to the radius vector $\vec{r}$ drawn from the dipole to the observation point, $\vec{m} = \vec{m}_{\perp} + \vec{m}_{\parallel}$ .

sub_problems.problem: (1) Find the magnitude of the interaction force between two coaxially placed cylind- drical magnets of diameter $d =20\mathrm{mm}$ and thickness $h =2\mathrm{mm}$ , magnetized parallel to their axis, if the distance between the centres of the magnets is $L =20\mathrm{cm}$ . You may assume that $L \gg d,h$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Since the distance between the magnets is much larger than their size, each cylindrical magnet can be treated as a point dipole.
\nThe magnetic moment of one uniformly magnetized cylinder is its volume times the magnetization:
\[\nm = J V = J\left(\frac{\pi d^2}{4}h\right).
\]\nWith \(J=1.5\,\mathrm{T}/\mu_0\), \(d=20\,\mathrm{mm}=2.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}\), and \(h=2\,\mathrm{mm}=2.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\), this gives
\[\nm=\frac{\pi}{4}d^2 h J \approx 0.75\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}.
\]
\nFor two coaxial dipoles with moments parallel to the separation vector, the magnetic field of one at the position of the other is
\[\nB = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{L^3},
\]\nso the interaction energy is
\[\nW = -mB = -\frac{\mu_0 m^2}{2\pi L^3}.
\]\nThe force magnitude follows from
\[\nF = \left|\frac{dW}{dL}\right| = \frac{3\mu_0 m^2}{2\pi L^4}.
\]\nUsing \(L=20\,\mathrm{cm}=0.20\,\mathrm{m}\),
\[\nF \approx \frac{3(4\pi\times10^{-7})(0.75)^2}{2\pi(0.20)^4}
\approx 2.1\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{N}
= 0.21\,\mathrm{mN}.
\]\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{0.21\,\mathrm{mN}}\).

knowledge_points.name: point dipole approximation
knowledge_points.description: When the distance between magnets is much larger than their size, each magnet can be treated as a point magnetic dipole, allowing use of the dipole field formula instead of a full magnetostatic calculation.

knowledge_points.name: magnetic dipole moment
knowledge_points.description: The vector quantity m that characterizes the strength and orientation of a magnetic dipole; for a uniformly magnetized body, m = J V where J is magnetization.

knowledge_points.name: magnetic moment from magnetization and volume
knowledge_points.description: For a homogeneously magnetized material, the total magnetic dipole moment is m = J V, with J given and V = (π d²/4) h for the cylinder.

knowledge_points.name: magnetic field of a point dipole on the axis
knowledge_points.description: Along the axis of a magnetic dipole, the field is B = (μ₀/(4π)) (2m/r³), used for two coaxial magnets with moments parallel to the separation vector.

knowledge_points.name: potential energy of a magnetic dipole in an external field
knowledge_points.description: The interaction energy is U = − m·B, which here gives W = −m B for parallel alignment.

knowledge_points.name: force from gradient of interaction energy
knowledge_points.description: The conservative force magnitude is F = |dW/dL| in the coaxial geometry, converting the energy dependence on separation into the force expression F = (3μ₀ m²)/(2π L⁴).

sub_problems.problem: (2) At distances much larger than $\frac{h}{2}$ , the field created by the magnet from task A.1 is the same as that created by a circular current $I$ . Find $I$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a uniformly magnetized permanent magnet, the bound volume currents cancel in the bulk. The only remaining current is a bound surface current on the side surface of the cylinder.
\nFor magnetization parallel to the cylinder axis, the bound surface current density on the side wall has magnitude
\[\nK_b = J.
\]\nIf the cylinder height is \(h\), this surface current sheet is equivalent, when viewed from distances much larger than the size of the magnet, to a circular current loop with current
\[\nI = K_b h = Jh.
\]
\nAn equivalent way to see this is to match magnetic dipole moments. The dipole moment of a current loop is
\[
 m = IA,
\]\nwhile the dipole moment of a uniformly magnetized cylinder is
\[
 m = JV = JAh.
\]\nEquating them gives again
\[\nI = Jh.
\]\nUsing the given value of \(J\) and the height from task A.1 gives
\[\nI \approx 2.4\,\mathrm{kA}.
\]\nTherefore the equivalent current is \(\boxed{2.4\,\mathrm{kA}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Magnetic dipole moment of a current loop
knowledge_points.description: The magnetic dipole moment of a planar current loop is m = I A, with direction normal to the plane. Used in the solution to express the moment of the equivalent circular current.

knowledge_points.name: Total dipole moment from uniform magnetization
knowledge_points.description: Since magnetization J is the volume density of magnetic dipole moment, a uniformly magnetized body of volume V has total magnetic moment m = J V. Applied to the cylinder (V = A h) to get the magnet's moment.

knowledge_points.name: Far-field magnetic dipole equivalence
knowledge_points.description: At distances much larger than the source size, the magnetic field is determined solely by the total magnetic dipole moment. The problem hints state this, and it justifies equating the moments to match the fields.

knowledge_points.name: Matching dipole moments
knowledge_points.description: To find the equivalent current, the magnetic dipole moment of the magnet is set equal to that of the current loop, ensuring the same far-field behaviour.

sub_problems.problem: (3) Find the interaction force between the magnets for the setup of task A.1 if instead $L =5\mathrm{mm}$ . You may assume that $d\gg L\gg h$
sub_problems.solution:
For $d\gg L\gg h$, the two magnets may be treated as two long, straight, parallel current-carrying segments of length $\pi d$ separated by the distance $L$. The force between two parallel currents is
\[
\frac{F}{\ell}=\frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi L}.
\]\nTherefore, for the effective interacting length $\ell=\pi d$,
\[\nF_2=\frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi L}\,(\pi d)=\frac{\mu_0 I^2 d}{2L}.
\]\nUsing the current $I$ from the setup of part A.1 and $L=5\,\mathrm{mm}$ gives
\[\nF_2\approx 14\,\mathrm{N}.
\]\nSo the interaction force is \(\boxed{14\,\mathrm{N}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Force between parallel currents
knowledge_points.description: The force per unit length between two parallel infinite straight wires carrying currents I1 and I2 separated by distance r is F/L = μ0 I1 I2 / (2π r). This formula is used to compute the interaction force between the equivalent current segments of the magnets.

knowledge_points.name: Magnet as equivalent current loop
knowledge_points.description: The cylindrical magnet magnetized along its axis can be represented by a circular current I flowing around its circumference; the value of I is known from part A.2 (or can be computed from the magnetization and geometry). This allows the magnets to be treated as current-carrying loops in the force calculation.

knowledge_points.name: Straight wire approximation for close loops
knowledge_points.description: When two coaxial circular current loops have diameter d much larger than their separation L (d >> L), the interaction force can be approximated by treating the loops as straight parallel wires of length equal to the circumference πd. This approximation is applied to use the parallel wire force formula.

sub_problems.problem: (4) Identical spherical magnets of diameter $\delta =5\mathrm{mm}$ , bound together by magnetic attraction, form a chain. What is the maximal length $l$ for such a chain which does not break under its own weight when hanging beneath the topmost magnet? The density of NdFeB magnets $\rho =7500\mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The chain will break first just below the topmost magnet, because there the magnetic attraction must support the weight of the largest possible number of magnets below.
\nLet the chain contain $N+1$ identical spherical magnets of diameter $\delta$. The mass of one magnet is
\[\nM=\frac{\pi}{6}\rho\delta^3.
\]\nThe magnetic moment of one uniformly magnetized sphere is
\[\nm=J\,\frac{\pi}{6}\delta^3.
\]
\nThe force between two dipoles aligned along the line joining them scales as the inverse fourth power of the distance. Therefore, the upward magnetic force on the top magnet from all the others is
\[\nF=\frac{3\mu_0 m^2}{2\pi\delta^4}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{n^4}.
\]\nUsing
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^4}=\frac{\pi^4}{90},
\]\nand taking $N\gg 1$, we get
\[\nF=\frac{3\mu_0 m^2}{2\pi\delta^4}\cdot\frac{\pi^4}{90}
=\frac{\mu_0 m^2\pi^3}{60\,\delta^4}.
\]\nAt the breaking threshold this balances the weight of the $N$ magnets below:
\[\nMgN=\frac{\mu_0 m^2\pi^3}{60\,\delta^4}.
\]\nHence
\[\nN=\frac{\mu_0 m^2\pi^3}{60Mg\delta^4}.
\]\nSubstituting $\delta=5\text{ mm}$, $\rho=7500\,\text{kg/m}^3$, and $J=1.5\text{ T}/\mu_0$ gives
\[\nM\approx 0.5\text{ g},\qquad m\approx 78\,\text{mA m}^2,
\]\nso
\[\nN\approx 1320.
\]\nTherefore the maximal chain length is
\[\nl\approx N\delta \approx 1320\times 5\text{ mm} = 6.6\text{ m}.
\]\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{6.6\text{ m}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Magnetization
knowledge_points.description: Magnetization J is the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume. For a uniformly magnetized object, the total magnetic moment is m = J V, where V is the volume.

knowledge_points.name: Spherical magnet dipole field
knowledge_points.description: The external magnetic field of a uniformly magnetized sphere is exactly that of a point dipole at its center, valid at all distances outside the sphere, not just the far field. This justifies the dipole force formula even when magnets are in contact.

knowledge_points.name: Dipole-dipole force (coaxial)
knowledge_points.description: The force between two identical magnetic dipoles with moments m aligned along the line joining their centers, separated by distance r, is attractive and given by F = (3 μ₀ m²)/(2π r⁴).

knowledge_points.name: Infinite series truncation
knowledge_points.description: For a large number N of magnets, the finite sum ∑_{n=1}^N 1/n⁴ can be approximated by the given infinite sum ∑_{n=1}^∞ 1/n⁴ = π⁴/90 (Hint 1).

knowledge_points.name: Force balance at breaking
knowledge_points.description: At the maximum chain length before breaking, the upward magnetic force on the top magnet from all magnets below exactly balances their total weight, i.e., static equilibrium at the threshold of failure.

knowledge_points.name: Gravitational acceleration g
knowledge_points.description: The weight of an object is mg, with standard gravitational acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface. This value, though not given, is needed to compute the weight.

sub_problems.problem: (5) Consider the chain from part A.4. Obtain an expression for the magnitude of the magnetic $B$ -field at such a point $P$ which is at distance $r$ from one of the chain's endpoint $O$ , and the angle between the chain and the line $OP$ is $\theta$ (cf. figure below), assuming that $l \gg r$ and $r \sin \theta \gg \delta$
sub_problems.solution:
Since the observation point is far from each individual magnet, each ball of the chain can be treated as a point dipole. A dipole of moment \(m\) is equivalent to two fictitious magnetic charges \(\pm q\) separated by a small distance \(s\) such that \(m = q s\). Choosing \(s = \delta\), we get \(q = m/\delta\). For the long chain, the contributions of neighboring opposite charges cancel, and only the charge at the near endpoint \(O\) remains relevant at point \(P\); the other endpoint is far away and gives a negligible contribution under the conditions \(l \gg r\) and \(r\sin\theta \gg \delta\).
\nThus the magnetic field at \(P\) is just the field of a magnetic charge \(q\) at distance \(r\):
\[\nB = \frac{\mu_0 q}{4\pi r^2}.
\]\nUsing \(q = m/\delta\),
\[\nB = \frac{\mu_0 m}{4\pi \delta r^2}.
\]\nFor one magnet ball of diameter \(\delta\) and homogeneous magnetization \(J\), its dipole moment is
\[\nm = J V = J \cdot \frac{\pi}{6}\delta^3.
\]\nSubstituting this into the field gives
\[\nB = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r^2\delta}\,J\frac{\pi}{6}\delta^3
= \frac{J\mu_0\delta^2}{24r^2}.
\]\nSo the magnetic field magnitude at point \(P\) is
\[
\boxed{B = \frac{J\mu_0\delta^2}{24r^2}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Far-field dipole approximation for magnets
knowledge_points.description: At distances much larger than the magnet's size, its magnetic field is well approximated by that of a point dipole with the same magnetic moment. This justifies treating each spherical magnet as a point dipole because the observation point P satisfies r sin θ ≫ δ.

knowledge_points.name: Magnetic dipole moment from magnetization and volume
knowledge_points.description: For a uniformly magnetized object, the total magnetic dipole moment m is the product of magnetization J and volume V: m = J V. Used to find the moment of each sphere from the given J and diameter δ.

knowledge_points.name: Magnetic charge representation of a dipole chain
knowledge_points.description: A magnetic dipole can be modeled as two equal and opposite fictitious magnetic charges ±q separated by a distance s, with m = q s. For a linear chain of aligned dipoles, the interior opposite charges cancel, leaving only the charges at the ends. Choosing s equal to the sphere diameter δ gives q = m/δ, and the field near one end is approximately that of a single charge q.

knowledge_points.name: Magnetic field of a point magnetic charge
knowledge_points.description: The magnetic field B at a distance r from a point magnetic charge q is radial and has magnitude B = (μ0 / 4π) q / r^2, in analogy with Coulomb's law for electric charges.

knowledge_points.name: Neglect of far endpoint and chain thickness
knowledge_points.description: The conditions l ≫ r and r sin θ ≫ δ imply that the other endpoint of the chain is too far to contribute significantly and that the chain's finite diameter can be ignored, so the field at P is dominated by the nearest endpoint charge.

title: Electrophoresis
problem:
Colloidal science is useful to characterize soil particles because many of them can be regarded as colloidal particles of micrometer size. For example, Brownian motion (random motion of colloidal particles) can be used to measure particle sizes.

# Part C. Electrophoresis

Here we discuss electrophoresis, i.e., transport of charged particles by an electric field. Suspension of colloidal particles with mass $M$ and charge $Q (> 0)$ is put in a narrow channel with a cross-section $A$ (Fig.1(a)). We ignore the interaction between particles, effects of the wall, the fluid, the ions therein, and gravity.

(a)

(b)

(c)
Fig.1: Setting for Part C.

By applying a uniform electric field $E$ in the $x$ -direction, particles are transported and their concentration $n(x)$ (particle number per unit volume) becomes non-uniform (Fig.1(b)). When $E$ is removed, this non-uniformity gradually disappears. This is due to Brownian motion of particles. If $n(x)$ is not uniform, the numbers of right-going and left-going particles may differ (Fig.1(c)). This generates a particle flux $J_{D}(x)$ , the mean number of particles flowing at $x$ along the $x$ -axis per unit cross-sectional area and unit time. This flux is known to satisfy

$$J_{D} (x) = - D \frac{d n}{d x} (x), \tag{4}$$

where $D$ is called the diffusion coefficient.

Now let's assume, for simplicity, that half of the particles have velocity $+v$ and the other half have velocity $-v$ . Let $N_{+}(x_0)$ be the number of particles with velocity $+v$ that cross $x_0$ from left to right per unit cross-sectional area and unit time. For particles with velocity $+v$ to cross $x_0$ in the time interval $\delta$ , they should be in the shaded region of Fig.1(c). Since $\delta$ is small, we have $n(x) \simeq n(x_0) + (x - x_0)\frac{dn}{dx}(x_0)$ in this region.

sub_problems.problem:
(1) Express $N_{+}(x_{0})$ using necessary quantities from $v, \delta, n(x_0)$ , and $\frac{dn}{dx} (x_0)$ .

We define $N_{-}(x_0)$ as the counterpart of $N_{+}(x_0)$ for the velocity $-v$ . With this, we have $J_{D}(x_{0}) = \langle N_{+}(x_{0}) - N_{-}(x_{0})\rangle$ . According to Eq.(3), we have $\langle v^2\rangle = C$
sub_problems.solution:
For particles with velocity $+v$, only those initially located in the interval $x_0-v\delta\le x\le x_0$ can cross the point $x_0$ during the time interval $\delta$. Since half of the particles have velocity $+v$, the flux is

$$N_{+}(x_0)=\frac{1}{\delta}\int_{x_0-v\delta}^{x_0}\frac12\,n(x)\,dx.$$
\nFor small $\delta$, expand the density near $x_0$:

$$n(x)\simeq n(x_0)+(x-x_0)\frac{dn}{dx}(x_0).$$
\nSubstituting this into the integral gives

$$N_{+}(x_0)=\frac{1}{\delta}\int_{x_0-v\delta}^{x_0}\frac12\left[n(x_0)+(x-x_0)\frac{dn}{dx}(x_0)\right]dx.$$
\nEvaluating the integral,

$$N_{+}(x_0)=\frac12 n(x_0)v-\frac14\frac{dn}{dx}(x_0)v^2\delta.$$
\nTherefore, the required expression is

$$\boxed{N_{+}(x_0)=\frac12 n(x_0)v-\frac14\frac{dn}{dx}(x_0)v^2\delta}.$$

knowledge_points.name: half of particles move at +v
knowledge_points.description: The model explicitly assumes exactly half the particles have velocity +v (and half -v), which supplies the factor 1/2 in the expression for N_+.

knowledge_points.name: ballistic motion during short time δ
knowledge_points.description: Particles travel with constant speed v and do not undergo collisions or direction changes during the small time interval δ, so the distance each particle can cover is exactly vδ, setting the integration limits.

knowledge_points.name: one-way particle number flux N_+
knowledge_points.description: N_+(x0) is defined as the number of particles with velocity +v crossing x0 from left to right per unit cross‑sectional area per unit time; this definition is used to relate the flux to an integral over particle density in the approach region.

knowledge_points.name: flux from density integral over capture region
knowledge_points.description: By equating N_+(x0) to (1/δ) times the number of particles initially within distance vδ to the left of x0 (per unit area), the one-way particle flux is expressed as an integral of the number density over the interval [x0 - vδ, x0].

knowledge_points.name: first-order Taylor expansion of density
knowledge_points.description: In the small‑δ limit, the number density is approximated near x0 as n(x) ≈ n(x0) + (x - x0) dn/dx(x0), which linearizes the integrand and yields the final expression to first order in δ.

sub_problems.problem:
(2) Determine $J_{D}(x_{0})$ using necessary quantities from $C, \delta, n(x_{0})$ , and $\frac{dn}{dx}(x_{0})$ . Using this and Eq.(4), express $D$ in terms of $C$ and $\delta$ , and $\langle \Delta x(t)^2 \rangle$ in terms of $D$ and $t$ .

Now we discuss the effect of osmotic pressure $\Pi$ . It is given by $\Pi = \frac{n}{N_A} RT = nkT$ with the Avogadro constant $N_{A}$ , the gas constant $R$ , temperature $T$ , and the Boltzmann constant $k = \frac{R}{N_A}$ . Let us consider the non-uniform concentration formed under the electric field $E$ (Fig.1(b)). Since $n(x)$ depends on $x$ , so does $\Pi(x)$ . Then the forces due to $\Pi(x)$ and $\Pi(x + \Delta x)$ must be balanced with the total force from the field $E$ acting on the particles (Fig.2). Here we consider small $\Delta x$ , so that $n(x)$ can be regarded as constant over this range, while $n(x + \Delta x) - n(x) \simeq \Delta x \frac{dn}{dx}(x)$ .

Fig.2: Force balance.
sub_problems.solution:
Let $N_{-}(x_0)$ be the number of particles with velocity $-v$ crossing $x_0$ from right to left per unit cross-sectional area and unit time. Then, by the same reasoning as for $N_{+}(x_0)$, one finds

$$N_{-}(x_0)=\frac{1}{2}n(x_0)v+\frac{1}{4}\frac{dn}{dx}(x_0)v^2\delta.$$ 
\nUsing the corresponding expression for $N_{+}(x_0)$ and the definition

$$J_D(x_0)=N_{+}(x_0)-N_{-}(x_0),$$
\nwe obtain

$$J_D(x_0)=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{dn}{dx}(x_0)\langle v^2\rangle\delta.$$
\nSince $\langle v^2\rangle=C$, this becomes

$$J_D(x_0)=-\frac{1}{2}C\delta\frac{dn}{dx}(x_0).$$
\nComparing with Fick’s law

$$J_D(x)=-D\frac{dn}{dx}(x),$$
\nwe identify

$$D=\frac{1}{2}C\delta.$$
\nFrom the result for one-dimensional diffusion,

$$\langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle = 2Dt,$$
\nso the mean square displacement is

$$\langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle = 2Dt = C\delta\, t.$$ 
\nFinal answer: $\boxed{J_D(x_0)=-\frac{1}{2}C\delta\,\frac{dn}{dx}(x_0),\; D=\frac{1}{2}C\delta,\; \langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle=2Dt=C\delta\, t}$.

knowledge_points.name: One-sided flux expressions from part (1)
knowledge_points.description: The solution uses the previously derived formulas for the right-going and left-going particle fluxes N_+(x0) and N_-(x0) in terms of n(x0), dn/dx, v, and δ.

knowledge_points.name: Net diffusion flux
knowledge_points.description: The net particle flux J_D is defined as the difference between the right-going and left-going fluxes: J_D = N_+ - N_-.

knowledge_points.name: Mean square velocity relation
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that the mean square velocity ⟨v^2⟩ equals a given constant C (from Eq.3).

knowledge_points.name: Fick's first law of diffusion
knowledge_points.description: The diffusive flux is proportional to the concentration gradient: J_D = -D dn/dx (Eq.4).

knowledge_points.name: Einstein relation for 1D diffusion
knowledge_points.description: The mean square displacement of a particle undergoing one-dimensional diffusion is related to the diffusion coefficient by ⟨Δx(t)^2⟩ = 2Dt.

sub_problems.problem:
(3) Express $\frac{dn}{dx}(x)$ using $n(x), T, Q, E,$ and $k$ .

Let us discuss the balance of the flux now. Besides the flux $J_{D}(x)$ due to the Brownian motion, there is also a flux due to the electric field, $J_{Q}(x)$ . It is given by

$$J_{Q} (x) = n (x) u, \tag{5}$$

where $u$ is the terminal velocity of particles driven by the field.
sub_problems.solution:
Using the osmotic pressure of the colloidal particles,
\[
\Pi(x)=n(x)kT,
\]\nwe balance the pressure difference against the electric force on the particles in a thin slab of width \(\Delta x\). The pressure at the left face is \(\Pi(x)\), and at the right face it is \(\Pi(x+\Delta x)\). The electric force acting on the particles inside the slab is \(n(x)A\Delta x\,QE\), so the balance is
\[
\Pi(x)A+n(x)A\Delta x\,QE=\Pi(x+\Delta x)A.
\]\nExpanding \(\Pi(x+\Delta x)\) to first order,
\[
\Pi(x+\Delta x)=\Pi(x)+\Delta x\,\frac{d\Pi}{dx},
\]\nand canceling \(A\), we get
\[
\Pi(x)+n(x)\Delta x\,QE=\Pi(x)+\Delta x\,\frac{d\Pi}{dx}.
\]\nHence
\[
\frac{d\Pi}{dx}=n(x)QE.
\]\nSince \(\Pi=nkT\),
\[\nkT\,\frac{dn}{dx}=n(x)QE,
\]\nso
\[
\frac{dn}{dx}=\frac{n(x)}{kT}QE.
\]\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{\frac{dn}{dx}=\frac{n(x)QE}{kT}}\).

knowledge_points.name: osmotic pressure of ideal solution
knowledge_points.description: Relates osmotic pressure Π to particle concentration n and temperature T via Π = nkT (van 't Hoff law). This is needed to connect the pressure gradient to the concentration gradient.

knowledge_points.name: static mechanical equilibrium of slab
knowledge_points.description: The system is in steady state, so the net force on a thin slab of particles vanishes; the pressure difference across the faces balances the total electric force. The problem statement explicitly imposes this force balance.

knowledge_points.name: electric force on point charge
knowledge_points.description: A particle of charge Q in an electric field E experiences a force F = QE. Required to compute the total electric force on all particles inside the slab.

knowledge_points.name: pressure as force per unit area
knowledge_points.description: Pressure Π applied over an area A produces a normal force of magnitude ΠA. Used to translate osmotic pressure at the slab faces into mechanical forces.

knowledge_points.name: first-order Taylor expansion
knowledge_points.description: For small displacements Δx, approximate Π(x+Δx) ≈ Π(x) + Δx dΠ/dx. This is used to linearize the pressure difference across the thin slab.

sub_problems.problem: (4) To determine $u$ , we use Eq.(1) with $F_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) = QE$ . Since $v(t)$ is fluctuating, we consider $\langle v(t)\rangle$ . Assuming $\langle v(0)\rangle =0$ and using $\langle F(t)\rangle =0$ , evaluate $\langle v(t)\rangle$ and obtain $u = \lim_{t\to \infty}\langle v(t)\rangle$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Taking the average of the equation of motion under the constant external force \(F_{\mathrm{ext}}(t)=QE\), and using \(\langle F(t)\rangle=0\), the mean velocity satisfies

\[\nM \frac{d\langle v(t)\rangle}{dt}=-\gamma \langle v(t)\rangle + QE.
\]
\nWith the initial condition \(\langle v(0)\rangle=0\), this first-order linear differential equation gives

\[
\langle v(t)\rangle=\frac{QE}{\gamma}\left(1-e^{-t/\tau}\right),
\]
\nwhere \(\tau=M/\gamma\). Therefore, the long-time drift velocity is

\[\nu=\lim_{t\to\infty}\langle v(t)\rangle=\frac{QE}{\gamma}.
\]
\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{u=\frac{QE}{\gamma}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Langevin equation
knowledge_points.description: The equation of motion for a Brownian particle, M dv/dt = -γ v + F(t) + F_ext(t), used here with the external electric force F_ext = QE.

knowledge_points.name: zero mean of random force
knowledge_points.description: The random thermal force F(t) has ensemble average zero, ⟨F(t)⟩ = 0, so it does not contribute to the mean drift velocity.

knowledge_points.name: ensemble averaging of Langevin equation
knowledge_points.description: Taking the expectation value of both sides of the Langevin equation yields a deterministic ordinary differential equation for the mean velocity.

knowledge_points.name: terminal velocity
knowledge_points.description: The long‑time drift velocity under a constant force, obtained when acceleration is zero or from the limit t→∞; here u = QE/γ balances drag and electric force.

sub_problems.problem: (5) The flux balance reads $J_{D}(x) + J_{Q}(x) =0$ . Express the diffusion coefficient $D$ in terms of $k, \gamma,$ and $T$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Using the results obtained in the preceding parts, the diffusion flux is
\[\nJ_D(x)=-\frac{DQE}{kT}\,n(x),
\]\nand the electric-field-driven flux is
\[\nJ_Q(x)=\frac{QE}{\gamma}\,n(x).
\]\nIn steady state the flux balance condition is
\[\nJ_D(x)+J_Q(x)=0.
\]\nSubstituting the two expressions gives
\[
-\frac{DQE}{kT}\,n(x)+\frac{QE}{\gamma}\,n(x)=0.
\]\nSince this must hold for nonzero \(n(x)\) and \(E\), we obtain
\[\nD=\frac{kT}{\gamma}.
\]\nTherefore, the diffusion coefficient is \(\boxed{D=\frac{kT}{\gamma}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Steady-state flux balance
knowledge_points.description: In steady state, the total particle flux is zero: J_D(x) + J_Q(x) = 0. This condition is given in the problem and is the starting point for finding D.

knowledge_points.name: Diffusion flux in electric field
knowledge_points.description: From previous parts, the diffusion flux is J_D(x) = - (D Q E / k T) n(x). This expression combines Fick's law and the concentration gradient from the osmotic-electric force balance.

knowledge_points.name: Electrophoretic drift flux
knowledge_points.description: From previous parts, the electric-field-driven flux is J_Q(x) = (Q E / γ) n(x), where u = QE/γ is the terminal velocity of a charged particle under electric field and linear drag.

title: Mean square displacement
problem:
Colloidal science is useful to characterize soil particles because many of them can be regarded as colloidal particles of micrometer size. For example, Brownian motion (random motion of colloidal particles) can be used to measure particle sizes. # Part D. Mean square displacement Suppose we observed the Brownian motion of an isolated, spherical colloidal particle with radius $a =5.0 \mu \mathrm{m}$ in water. Figure 3 shows the histogram of displacements $\Delta x$ measured in the $x$ -direction at every interval $\Delta t =60$ s. The friction coefficient is given by $\gamma =6\pi a\eta$ with water viscosity $\eta =8.9 \times 10^{-4}$ Pa·s and the temperature was $T =25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Fig.3: Histogram of displacements.
