sub_problems.problem:
(1) Estimate the value of $N_{A}$ without using the fact that it is the Avogadro constant, up to two significant digits from the data in Fig.3. The gas constant is $R =8.31 \, \text{J/K} \cdot \text{mol}$ . Do not use the value of the Boltzmann constant $k$ given in General Instructions. As for the Avogadro constant, you might obtain a value different from that in General Instructions.

Now we extend the model in Part B to describe the motion of a particle with charge $Q$ under an electric field $E$ . The particle velocity $v(t)$ considered in Eq.(2) should be replaced by $v(t) = u + v_{n}$ ( $t_{n-1} < t \leq t_{n}$ ) with $v_{n}$ satisfying Eq. (3) and $u$ being the terminal velocity considered in Eq.(5).
sub_problems.solution:
For Brownian motion in one dimension, the mean square displacement over time \(\Delta t\) is
\[
\langle \Delta x^2\rangle = 2D\Delta t,
\]\nwhere the diffusion constant is given by the Einstein relation
\[\nD=\frac{kT}{\gamma}.
\]\nWith \(k=R/N_A\) and \(\gamma=6\pi a\eta\), this becomes
\[
\langle \Delta x^2\rangle = \frac{2RT\Delta t}{6\pi a\eta N_A}
=\frac{RT\Delta t}{3\pi a\eta N_A}.
\]
\nFrom the histogram in Fig. 3, the mean square displacement is estimated as
\[
\langle \Delta x^2\rangle \approx 6.34\,\mu\mathrm{m}^2.
\]\nUsing
\[\na=5.0\,\mu\mathrm{m},\quad \eta=8.9\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s},\quad T=25^\circ\mathrm{C}=298\,\mathrm{K},\quad R=8.31\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}},
\]\nwe solve for \(N_A\):
\[\nN_A=\frac{RT\Delta t}{3\pi a\eta\langle \Delta x^2\rangle}.
\]\nSubstituting the numbers gives
\[\nN_A \approx 5.6\times 10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}.
\]
\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{5.6\times 10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}}\).

knowledge_points.name: 1D mean square displacement relation
knowledge_points.description: For one-dimensional Brownian motion, the mean square displacement after time interval Δt is ⟨Δx²⟩ = 2DΔt, where D is the diffusion constant. This is used to relate the measured displacements to D.

knowledge_points.name: Einstein relation
knowledge_points.description: Connects the diffusion constant D to the thermal energy kT and the friction coefficient γ: D = kT/γ. This allows the mean square displacement to be expressed in terms of temperature and friction.

knowledge_points.name: Stokes' law
knowledge_points.description: The friction coefficient for a sphere of radius a moving through a fluid of viscosity η is γ = 6πηa. Given in the problem statement; needed to relate the friction to the particle size.

knowledge_points.name: Boltzmann constant from gas constant
knowledge_points.description: The Boltzmann constant k is related to the gas constant R and Avogadro's number N_A by k = R/N_A. Required to eliminate k and solve for N_A using the given value of R.

knowledge_points.name: mean square displacement from histogram
knowledge_points.description: Estimate the mean square displacement from a histogram of displacements by computing the weighted average Σᵢ (Δxᵢ)² Nᵢ / Σᵢ Nᵢ, where Nᵢ are the counts for each bin.

knowledge_points.name: one-dimensional Brownian motion
knowledge_points.description: The analysis uses displacements only along the x-axis, so the motion is treated as one-dimensional; the formula ⟨Δx²⟩ = 2DΔt applies to the observed component.

sub_problems.problem:
(2) Express the MSD $\langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle$ in terms of $u$ , $D$ , and $t$ . Obtain approximate power laws for small $t$ and large $t$ , as well as the characteristic time $t_*$ where this change occurs. Draw a rough graph of MSD in a log-log plot, indicating the approximate location of $t_*$ .

Next, we consider swimming microbes (Fig.4(a)), in one dimension for simplicity (Fig.4(b)). These are spherical particles with radius $a$ . They swim at velocity either $+u_{0}$ or $-u_{0}$ , the sign chosen randomly at every time interval $\delta_{0}$ without correlation. The observed motion is a combination of displacements due to swimming and those due to the Brownian motion of a spherical particle.

(b)

Fig.4: (a) Motion of microbes. (b) Its one-dimensional version.
sub_problems.solution:
For a particle moving with constant drift speed $u$ and Brownian diffusion coefficient $D$, the displacement after time $t$ can be written as
\[
\Delta x(t)=ut+\Delta x_B(t),
\]\nwhere $\Delta x_B$ is the Brownian contribution. Since the Brownian part has zero mean and variance
\[
\langle \Delta x_B^2\rangle = 2Dt,
\]\nwe obtain
\[
\langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle = \langle (ut+\Delta x_B)^2\rangle = u^2 t^2 + 2Dt.
\]\nThis may be written as
\[
\langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle = 2Dt\left(1+\frac{t}{t_*}\right),
\qquad t_* = \frac{2D}{u^2}.
\]\nTherefore, the two limiting behaviors are
\[
\langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle \propto t \qquad (t\ll t_*),
\]\nand
\[
\langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle \propto t^2 \qquad (t\gg t_*).
\]\nOn a log-log plot, the MSD is a straight line of slope 1 for small $t$, crosses over around $t=t_*$, and becomes a straight line of slope 2 for large $t$.
\nFinal answer: \boxed{\langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle = u^2 t^2 + 2Dt},\ \boxed{\langle \Delta x^2\rangle \propto t\ (t\ll t_*)\ \text{and}\ \propto t^2\ (t\gg t_*)},\ \boxed{t_* = 2D/u^2}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle = u^2 t^2 + 2Dt}, \boxed{\langle \Delta x^2\rangle \propto t\ (t\ll t_*)\ \text{and}\ \propto t^2\ (t\gg t_*)}, \boxed{t_* = \frac{2D}{u^2}}

knowledge_points.name: Mean square displacement
knowledge_points.description: The mean square displacement (MSD) is the ensemble average of the squared displacement of a particle from its initial position, ⟨Δx(t)²⟩. The problem asks to express this quantity.

knowledge_points.name: 1D Brownian motion displacement statistics
knowledge_points.description: For a free Brownian particle in one dimension, the displacement Δx_B over time t has zero mean (⟨Δx_B⟩ = 0) and variance given by the Einstein relation ⟨Δx_B²⟩ = 2Dt, where D is the diffusion coefficient. The solution uses both properties to compute the total MSD.

knowledge_points.name: Drift-diffusion superposition
knowledge_points.description: When a particle undergoes both constant drift (velocity u) and Brownian motion, the total displacement can be written as the sum Δx = ut + Δx_B. Because the Brownian part has zero mean, the cross term vanishes and the MSD is the sum of the individual contributions: u²t² + 2Dt.

knowledge_points.name: Crossover time analysis
knowledge_points.description: The characteristic time t_* = 2D/u² is found by equating the diffusive (2Dt) and ballistic (u²t²) contributions to the MSD, or by rewriting the MSD as 2Dt(1 + t/t_*). For t ≪ t_* the motion is predominantly diffusive (MSD ∝ t), and for t ≫ t_* it is predominantly ballistic (MSD ∝ t²).

knowledge_points.name: Log-log plot interpretation
knowledge_points.description: On a log-log plot, a power law MSD ∝ t^α appears as a straight line with slope α. The problem asks for such a plot, showing slope 1 for t ≪ t_*, slope 2 for t ≫ t_*, and the crossover near t_*.

sub_problems.problem:
(3) Figure 5 displays the MSD $\langle \Delta x(t)^2\rangle$ of those microbes, showing different power laws for small, large, and intermediate $t$ , as indicated by dashed lines. Obtain the power law for each time range and express it using necessary quantities from $D, u_0, \delta_0$ , and $t$ .
Fig.5: Mean square displacement of the microbes.
sub_problems.solution:
For the mean square displacement (MSD), the motion has three regimes:

1. **Small $t$**: ordinary Brownian motion dominates, so the displacement is diffusive:
\[
\langle \Delta x(t)^2 \rangle \propto t.
\]\nUsing the diffusion coefficient $D$,
\[
\langle \Delta x(t)^2 \rangle = 2Dt.
\]

2. **Intermediate $t$**: the microbe moves almost straight with typical speed $u_0$, so the displacement grows linearly in time and the MSD is ballistic:
\[
\langle \Delta x(t)^2 \rangle \propto t^2,
\]\nthus
\[
\langle \Delta x(t)^2 \rangle = u_0^2 t^2.
\]

3. **Large $t$**: the direction of motion is randomized after a persistence time $\delta_0$, so the motion becomes an effective random walk with step length $u_0\delta_0$. The number of steps in time $t$ is $t/\delta_0$, hence
\[
\langle \Delta x(t)^2 \rangle \sim (u_0\delta_0)^2\frac{t}{\delta_0}=u_0^2\delta_0 t.
\]
\nTherefore the MSD is
\[
\boxed{\langle \Delta x(t)^2 \rangle =
\begin{cases}
2Dt, & \text{small } t,\\
 u_0^2 t^2, & \text{intermediate } t,\\
 u_0^2\delta_0 t, & \text{large } t.
\end{cases}}
\]
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\langle \Delta x(t)^2 \rangle = \begin{cases} 2Dt, & \text{small } t,\\ u_0^2 t^2, & \text{intermediate } t,\\ u_0^2\delta_0 t, & \text{large } t. \end{cases}}

knowledge_points.name: Einstein relation for Brownian motion
knowledge_points.description: In one dimension, the mean square displacement of a Brownian particle is ⟨Δx^2⟩ = 2Dt, where D is the diffusion coefficient. This gives the diffusive scaling for the small-t regime.

knowledge_points.name: Ballistic motion scaling
knowledge_points.description: For motion with constant speed u0, the displacement is Δx = u0 t, so the mean square displacement is ⟨Δx^2⟩ = u0^2 t^2. This gives the ballistic scaling for the intermediate-t regime.

knowledge_points.name: Random walk mean square displacement
knowledge_points.description: For a 1D random walk with step length L and step time τ, after N = t/τ steps, the mean square displacement is ⟨Δx^2⟩ = N L^2 = (L^2/τ) t. Applied here with L = u0 δ0 and τ = δ0 to obtain the large-t diffusive scaling.

knowledge_points.name: Persistence time
knowledge_points.description: The time interval δ0 over which a microbe maintains its swimming direction before randomly reversing. For t < δ0 the motion is approximately ballistic; for t > δ0 it becomes a random walk with step time δ0.

title: A vertically placed board
problem:
In this problem, we consider the phenomena caused by the interaction between water and objects, related to surface tension. Part A treats motion, while Parts B and C are regarding static situations.

If necessary, you can use the fact that if the function $y(x)$ satisfies the differential equation $y''(x) = ay(x)$ ( $a$ is a positive constant), then its general solution is $y(x) = Ae^{\sqrt{a} x} + Be^{-\sqrt{a} x}$ , where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants.

# Part B. A vertically placed board

A flat board is immersed vertically in water. Figures 2(a) and 2(b) respectively show water surface forms for the hydrophilic (attractive) and hydrophobic board materials. We neglect the thickness of the board.

The board surface is on the $yz$ plane, and the horizontal water surface far away from the board is on the $xy$ plane with $z =0$ . The surface shape does not depend on the $y$ -coordinate. Let $\theta(x)$ be the angle between the water surface and the horizontal plane at a point $(x,z)$ on the water surface in the $xz$ plane. Here $\theta(x)$ is measured with respect to the positive $x$ axis and the counterclockwise rotation is taken as positive. Let $\theta(x)$ be $\theta_0$ at the point of contact between the board and the water surface ( $x =0$ ). In the following, $\theta_0$ is fixed by the properties of the board material.

Water density $\rho$ is constant and water surface tension $\gamma$ is uniform. The gravitational acceleration constant is given by $g$ . The atmospheric pressure, $P_0$ , is assumed to be always uniform. Let us determine the water surface form in the following steps. Note that the unit of surface tension is $\mathrm{J} / \mathrm{m}^2$ as well as N/m.

(a)

(b)
Fig. 2: Boards vertically immersed in the water. (a) hydrophilic board case; (b) hydrophobic board case.

sub_problems.problem: (1) We consider a hydrophilic board case, as shown in Fig.2(a). We note that the water pressure, $P$ , satisfies the conditions $P < P_0$ for $z > 0$ and $P = P_0$ for $z =0$ . Then, express $P$ at $z$ in terms of $\rho, g, z,$ and $P_0$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Consider a vertical column of water of height $z$ and unit cross-sectional area. The pressure at the bottom of the column is $P$, while the pressure at the top, at the free surface $z=0$, is $P_0$. Force balance in the vertical direction gives
\[P + \rho g z = P_0.
\]
Therefore,
\[P = P_0 - \rho g z.
\]
Final answer: \(\boxed{P = P_0 - \rho g z}\).

knowledge_points.name: Hydrostatic pressure equation
knowledge_points.description: In a static fluid of constant density ρ under uniform gravity g, the pressure P at a vertical height z above a reference level where the pressure is P0 is P = P0 − ρ g z. This relation is used directly to express the water pressure in terms of the given quantities.

sub_problems.problem:
(2) We consider a water block whose cutout is shown as shaded in Fig.3(a). Its $xz$ plane cross-section is shown in a hatched area in Fig.3(b). Let $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ respectively be the left and right edge coordinates of the boundary (water surface) between the water block and the air. Obtain a horizontal component ( $x$ component) of the net force per unit length along the $y$ -axis, $f_{x}$ , which is exerted on the water block due to the pressure, in terms of $\rho, g, z_{1}$ , and $z_{2}$ . Note that $P_{0}$ results in no net horizontal force on the water block.

(a)

Fig. 3: Cutout form of water block on the water surface. (a) Bird's eye view and (b) cross-sectional view.
sub_problems.solution:
The atmospheric pressure \(P_0\) gives no net horizontal force on the water block, so only the hydrostatic part contributes. At height \(z\), the pressure relative to \(P_0\) is \(-\rho g z\). Therefore, the horizontal force per unit length along the \(y\)-axis is
\[
 f_x=\int_{z_2}^{z_1}(-\rho g z)\,dz
 =\frac{1}{2}\rho g\left(z_2^2-z_1^2\right).
\]
This force acts leftward.
Thus, \(\boxed{f_x=\frac{1}{2}\rho g\left(z_2^2-z_1^2\right)}\).

knowledge_points.name: Hydrostatic pressure equation
knowledge_points.description: In a static fluid under gravity, pressure varies linearly with height: P = P0 - ρ g z, where z is upward from the undisturbed surface. This gives the water pressure at any point needed to compute the force.

knowledge_points.name: Uniform atmospheric pressure cancellation
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that the uniform atmospheric pressure P0 results in no net horizontal force on the water block, so only the gauge pressure (relative to P0) contributes to f_x.

knowledge_points.name: Pressure force integration on a vertical surface
knowledge_points.description: The horizontal force per unit length on a vertical surface due to fluid pressure is the integral of pressure over the vertical coordinate: f = ∫ P dz. For the water block, the net force is obtained by integrating the gauge pressure from the right edge height z2 to the left edge height z1.

sub_problems.problem: (3) Surface tension acting on the water block is balanced with the force $f_{x}$ discussed in B.2. We respectively define $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ as the angles between the water surface and the horizontal plane at the left and right edges. Express $f_{x}$ in terms of $\gamma$ , $\theta_{1}$ , and $\theta_{2}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The horizontal components of the surface tension forces acting at the left and right edges of the water block are, respectively, $\gamma\cos\theta_1$ and $\gamma\cos\theta_2$, with opposite directions. Therefore the net horizontal force from surface tension is $\gamma\cos\theta_2-\gamma\cos\theta_1$. 
For equilibrium, this must be balanced by the force $f_x$:
\[f_x + \gamma\cos\theta_2 - \gamma\cos\theta_1 = 0.
\]
Hence,
\[f_x = \gamma\cos\theta_1 - \gamma\cos\theta_2.
\]
Final answer: \(\boxed{f_x = \gamma\cos\theta_1 - \gamma\cos\theta_2}\).

knowledge_points.name: surface tension
knowledge_points.description: Surface tension exerts a force per unit length of magnitude γ along the liquid surface, directed tangentially to the surface. In this sub-problem, the horizontal component per unit length at each edge is γ cos θ, where θ is the local inclination of the surface to the horizontal.

knowledge_points.name: static force equilibrium
knowledge_points.description: For a fluid element at rest, the net force acting on it must be zero. This sub-problem uses this condition to balance the horizontal pressure force fx with the horizontal components of the surface tension forces.

sub_problems.problem:
(4) The following equation holds at an arbitrary point $(x, z)$ on the water surface,

$$\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{z}{\ell}\right)^{a} + \cos \theta (x) = \text{constant}. \tag{1}$$

Determine the exponent $a$ and express the constant $\ell$ in terms of $\gamma$ and $\rho$ . Note that this equation holds regardless of hydrophilic or hydrophobic board materials.
sub_problems.solution:
From the results of B.2 and B.3, we have

\[
\frac{1}{2}\rho g z_1^{2}+\gamma \cos\theta_1
=
\frac{1}{2}\rho g z_2^{2}+\gamma \cos\theta_2.
\]
Since this relation holds for any two points on the water surface, it follows that at an arbitrary point \((x,z)\) on the surface,

\[
\frac{1}{2}\rho g z^{2}+\gamma \cos\theta = \text{constant}.
\]
Comparing this with

\[
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{z}{\ell}\right)^{a}+\cos\theta(x)=\text{constant},
\]
we identify

\[a=2,
\qquad
\ell=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{\rho g}}.
\]
Thus the constant \(\ell\) is the capillary length.
Final answer: \(\boxed{a=2}\), \(\boxed{\ell=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{\rho g}}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Capillary force balance equation
knowledge_points.description: For a static water meniscus, the balance of hydrostatic pressure and surface tension yields (1/2)ρg z^2 + γ cosθ = constant along the surface. This relation is imported from the force balances in parts B.2 and B.3 and is used to match the given equation.

sub_problems.problem: (5) In Eq. (1) in B.4, we assume that variation of the water surface is slow, i.e., $|z'(x)| \ll 1$ , so that we can expand $\cos \theta(x)$ with respect to $z'(x)$ up to the second order. Then, differentiating the resultant equation with respect to $x$ , we obtain the differential equation satisfied by $z(x)$ . Solve this differential equation and determine $z(x)$ for $x \geq 0$ in terms of $\tan \theta_0$ and $\ell$ . Note that the vertical directions of Figs. 2 and 3 are exaggerated for better view and they do not satisfy the condition, $|z'(x)| \ll 1$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For the water surface profile \(z(x)\), the slope is related to the local inclination angle by
\[
z'(x)=\tan\theta(x).
\]
Hence
\[
\cos\theta(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(z')^2}} \simeq 1-\frac12(z')^2
\]
using \(|z'(x)|\ll 1\).
Substituting this approximation into Eq. (1) from B.4 gives
\[
\frac{z^2}{\ell^2}-(z')^2=\text{const}.
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(x\), we obtain
\[
\frac{2z}{\ell^2}z'-2z'z''=0,
\]
and for nontrivial slope this yields
\[
z''=\frac{z}{\ell^2}.
\]
This is a linear differential equation with general solution
\[
z(x)=Ae^{x/\ell}+Be^{-x/\ell}.
\]
Since the water surface must approach the flat level far from the board,
\[
z(\infty)=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad A=0.
\]
Also, at the contact point \(x=0\),
\[
z'(0)=\tan\theta_0.
\]
Because \(z'(x)=-(B/\ell)e^{-x/\ell}\), this gives
\[
-\frac{B}{\ell}=\tan\theta_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad B=-\ell\tan\theta_0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
z(x)=-\ell\tan\theta_0\,e^{-x/\ell}\qquad (x\ge 0).
\]
Final answer: \(\boxed{z(x)=-\ell\tan\theta_0\,e^{-x/\ell}}\).

knowledge_points.name: slope as tangent of angle
knowledge_points.description: The derivative of the surface profile z'(x) equals tanθ(x), where θ is the local inclination angle measured from the horizontal. This relation connects the geometric definition of θ to the calculus of the surface shape and is used to express cosθ in terms of z' and to impose the contact-angle boundary condition.

knowledge_points.name: small-slope expansion of cosθ
knowledge_points.description: Under the slow-variation assumption |z'|≪1, cosθ = 1/√(1+z'²) is expanded to second order as 1 − ½(z')². This linearises the meniscus equation and yields a tractable differential equation.

knowledge_points.name: Meniscus profile equation (B.4 result)
knowledge_points.description: The force-balance equation from part B.4, with the exponent determined as a=2 and the capillary length ℓ = √(γ/(ρg)), reads (1/2)(z/ℓ)² + cosθ = constant. This is the starting point for finding z(x).

knowledge_points.name: exponential solution of y''=a y
knowledge_points.description: The ODE z'' = (1/ℓ²)z is of the form y'' = a y with a>0. The general solution is a linear combination of exponentials, A e^{x/ℓ} + B e^{-x/ℓ}, as quoted in the problem header. This allows solving for the meniscus shape.

knowledge_points.name: far-field water surface flat
knowledge_points.description: Far from the board (x→∞) the water surface returns to the undisturbed horizontal level z = 0 and the slope vanishes. This provides the boundary condition z(∞)=0, eliminating the growing exponential term.

knowledge_points.name: contact angle boundary condition
knowledge_points.description: At the board (x=0) the water surface meets the material with a prescribed angle θ₀. Using z'(0) = tanθ₀ fixes the remaining integration constant.

title: Interaction between two rods
problem:
In this problem, we consider the phenomena caused by the interaction between water and objects, related to surface tension. Part A treats motion, while Parts B and C are regarding static situations.

If necessary, you can use the fact that if the function $y(x)$ satisfies the differential equation $y''(x) = ay(x)$ ( $a$ is a positive constant), then its general solution is $y(x) = Ae^{\sqrt{a} x} + Be^{-\sqrt{a} x}$ , where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants.

# Part C. Interaction between two rods

The identical rods A and B made of the same material floating in parallel on the water surface are placed at the same distance away from the $y$ -axis (Fig.4).

Fig. 4: Two rods A and B floating on the water surface.

sub_problems.problem:
(1) At the contact points of the rod B and the water surface, we define the $z-$ coordinates $z_{\mathrm{a}}$ and $z_{\mathrm{b}}$ , and the angles $\theta_{\mathrm{a}}$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{b}}$ , as shown in Fig.5. Determine the horizontal force component, $F_{x}$ , on the rod B per unit length along the $y$ -axis in terms of $\theta_{\mathrm{a}}, \theta_{\mathrm{b}}, z_{\mathrm{a}}, z_{\mathrm{b}}, \rho, g,$ and $\gamma$ .

Fig. 5: Vertical cross-sectional view of two rods floating on the water surface.
sub_problems.solution:
The horizontal force on rod B per unit length along the $y$-axis has two contributions: the hydrostatic pressure from the water and the surface-tension forces at the contact points.

For the pressure contribution, the horizontal component is

$$
F_x^{(p)}=\int_{z_a}^{z_b} \rho g z\,dz
=\frac12\rho g\left(z_b^2-z_a^2\right).
$$

The surface tension at the two contact points contributes horizontal components of magnitude $\gamma\cos\theta_a$ and $\gamma\cos\theta_b$, with opposite signs according to their directions. Therefore,

$$
F_x = F_x^{(p)} + \gamma(\cos\theta_b-\cos\theta_a).
$$

So the horizontal force component on rod B per unit length is

$$
\boxed{F_x=\frac12\rho g\left(z_b^2-z_a^2\right)+\gamma\left(\cos\theta_b-\cos\theta_a\right)}.
$$

knowledge_points.name: Hydrostatic pressure
knowledge_points.description: In a static fluid, gauge pressure increases linearly with depth below the free surface: p = ρ g z. Needed to express the pressure acting on the rod as a function of z.

knowledge_points.name: Horizontal force on curved surface
knowledge_points.description: The horizontal component of the pressure force on a curved surface per unit width equals the integral of pressure over the vertical projection of the surface, i.e., ∫ p dz from the lowest to the highest point. Used to compute the pressure contribution to F_x.

knowledge_points.name: Surface tension force
knowledge_points.description: Surface tension exerts a force per unit length γ tangent to the liquid surface at the contact line. The horizontal component is γ cosθ, where θ is the angle between the tangent and the horizontal. At the two contact points these forces act in opposite directions, giving a net contribution γ(cosθ_b - cosθ_a).

knowledge_points.name: Force superposition
knowledge_points.description: The total horizontal force is the algebraic sum of the independent force contributions (here, pressure force and surface tension forces). Used to combine the two physical effects.

sub_problems.problem: (2) We define the $z$ -coordinate of the water surface, $z_0$ , at the midpoint of two rods in the $xz$ plane. Express the force $F_x$ obtained in C.1 without using $\theta_{a}, \theta_{b}, z_{a}$ , and $z_b$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For the meniscus shape, the quantity
\[
\frac{1}{2}\rho g z^2+\gamma\cos\theta
\]
has the same value at points connected by the surface profile. Applying this at the two rods and at the midpoint gives
\[
\frac{1}{2}\rho g z_a^2+\gamma\cos\theta_a=\frac{1}{2}\rho g z_0^2+\gamma,
\]
\[
\frac{1}{2}\rho g z_b^2+\gamma\cos\theta_b=\gamma.
\]
Subtracting the first relation from the second eliminates \(\theta_a,\theta_b,z_a\), and \(z_b\), so the horizontal force becomes
\[
F_x=-\frac{1}{2}\rho g z_0^2.
\]
Therefore, the attractive force between the rods is
\[
\boxed{F_x=-\frac{1}{2}\rho g z_0^2}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: first integral of meniscus equation
knowledge_points.description: The quantity (1/2)ρg z² + γ cosθ is constant along a static 2D meniscus. This invariant is used to relate conditions at the rods and the midpoint.

knowledge_points.name: force from meniscus invariant
knowledge_points.description: The horizontal force per unit length on a rod from a meniscus equals the value of the invariant (1/2)ρg z² + γ cosθ at the contact line. The net force F_x from C.1 is the difference between the invariants on the two sides of rod B.

knowledge_points.name: midpoint symmetry
knowledge_points.description: At the midpoint between the two identical rods, the meniscus is symmetric, so the slope is zero (θ=0) and the height is z₀. This gives the invariant for the inner meniscus as (1/2)ρg z₀² + γ.

knowledge_points.name: flat surface at infinity
knowledge_points.description: Far from the rods, the water surface is flat (θ=0) and at the reference level z=0, so the invariant for the outer meniscus equals γ.

knowledge_points.name: inner and outer menisci
knowledge_points.description: The water surface consists of an inner meniscus between the rods and separate outer menisci outside each rod, each with its own invariant constant. This allows assigning different constants to the two sides of rod B.

sub_problems.problem: (3) Let $x_{\mathrm{a}}$ be the $x$ -coordinate of the contact point between the water surface and the left side of the rod B. Using the differential equation obtained in B.5, express the water level coordinate $z_{0}$ of the midpoint of these two rods A and B in terms of $x_{\mathrm{a}}$ and $z_{\mathrm{a}}$ . You can use the constant $\ell$ introduced in B.4.
sub_problems.solution:
For the water surface profile, the differential equation from B.5 gives
\[
z(x)=A e^{x/\ell}+B e^{-x/\ell}.
\]
Since rods A and B are placed symmetrically with respect to the \(y\)-axis, the surface profile is symmetric about \(x=0\). Hence
\[
A=B.
\]
Let \(z_0\) be the water level at the midpoint, i.e. at \(x=0\). Then
\[
z(0)=A+B=z_0,
\]
so
\[
A=B=\frac{z_0}{2}.
\]
At the left contact point of rod B, \(x=x_a\) and \(z(x_a)=z_a\). Therefore
\[
z_a=\frac{z_0}{2}\left(e^{x_a/\ell}+e^{-x_a/\ell}\right).
\]
Solving for \(z_0\),
\[
\boxed{z_0=\frac{2z_a}{e^{x_a/\ell}+e^{-x_a/\ell}}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: linearized capillary surface equation
knowledge_points.description: The water surface profile z(x) satisfies z'' = z/ℓ², where ℓ is the capillary length constant from B.4. This yields exponential solutions with decay length ℓ, used directly to write the general solution z(x) = A e^{x/ℓ} + B e^{-x/ℓ}.

knowledge_points.name: symmetry of water surface
knowledge_points.description: Identical rods placed symmetrically about the y‑axis imply a symmetric water surface profile, z(x)=z(‑x). This forces A=B in the general exponential solution.

knowledge_points.name: midpoint water level definition
knowledge_points.description: The water surface height at the midpoint (x=0) is defined as z₀, giving the boundary condition z(0)=z₀.

knowledge_points.name: contact point boundary condition
knowledge_points.description: At the left contact point of rod B, x = xₐ and the water surface height is zₐ, providing the condition z(xₐ)=zₐ.

title: Tully-Fisher relation and MOND theory
problem:
This problem aims to study the peculiar physics of galaxies, such as their dynamics and structure. In particular, we explain how to measure the mass distribution of our galaxy from the inside. For this we will focus on hydrogen, its main constituent.

Throughout this problem we will only use $\hbar$ , defined as $\hbar = h /2\pi$ .

# Part D. Tully-Fisher relation and MOND theory

The flat external velocity curve of NGC 6946 in Fig. 1 is a common property of spiral galaxies, as can be seen in Fig. 4 (left). Plotting the external constant velocity value $\nu_{c,\infty}$ as a function of the measured total mass $M_{\mathrm{tot}}$ of each galaxy gives an interesting correlation called the Tully-Fischer relation, see Fig. 4 (right).

Fig. 4. Left: Rotation curves for typical spiral galaxies - Right: $\log_{10}(M_{\mathrm{tot}})$ as a function of $\log_{10}(\nu_{c,\infty})$ on linear scales. Colored dots correspond to different galaxies and different surveys. The green line is the Tully-Fischer relation which is in very good agreement with the best fit line of the data (in black).

sub_problems.problem: (4) Considering relevant cases, determine $\nu_{c}(r)$ for all values of $r$ in the MOND theory in the case of a gravitational field due to a homogeneously distributed mass $M$ with radius $R_{b}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Using the MOND modified second law with circular acceleration \(a=v_c^2/r\) and interpolation function \(\mu(x)=\frac{x}{1+x}\), we have
\[
\mu\!\left(\frac{a}{a_0}\right)a=g_N(r),
\qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \frac{a^2}{a+a_0}=g_N(r),
\]\nwhere \(g_N(r)=|\mathcal G(r)|\) is the Newtonian gravitational field.
\nFor a homogeneous sphere of mass \(M\) and radius \(R_b\), Gauss’ theorem gives
\[
 g_N(r)=
\begin{cases}
 \dfrac{GM}{r^2}, & r>R_b,\\[1ex]
 \dfrac{GMr}{R_b^3}, & r\le R_b.
\end{cases}
\]\nThe equation for \(a\) is quadratic:
\[\na^2-g_N a-g_N a_0=0,
\]\nso the physical (positive) root is
\[\na=\frac{g_N}{2}\left(1+\sqrt{1+\frac{4a_0}{g_N}}\right).
\]\nSince \(a=v_c^2/r\),
\[\nv_c^2(r)=\frac{g_N(r)\,r}{2}\left(1+\sqrt{1+\frac{4a_0}{g_N(r)}}\right).
\]\nSubstituting the two expressions for \(g_N(r)\):
\[
\boxed{
 v_c(r)=
\begin{cases}
 \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{2r}\left(1+\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4a_0 r^2}{GM}}\right)}, & r>R_b,\\[2ex]
 \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{2r}\left(\dfrac{r}{R_b}\right)^3\left[1+\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4a_0 r^2}{GM}\left(\dfrac{R_b}{r}\right)^3}\right]}, & r\le R_b.
 \end{cases}
}
\]\nFor \(r\to\infty\), \(v_c\to (GMa_0)^{1/4}\), giving the flat Tully–Fisher scaling. For \(r\to 0\), \(v_c\to 0\).

knowledge_points.name: MOND equation with simple interpolation function
knowledge_points.description: In MOND, the true acceleration a is related to the Newtonian gravitational field g_N by μ(a/a0) a = g_N. The problem uses the interpolation function μ(x)=x/(1+x), giving a^2/(a+a0)=g_N. This is the fundamental law to solve for v_c(r).

knowledge_points.name: centripetal acceleration formula
knowledge_points.description: For circular motion, the centripetal acceleration is a = v^2/r, linking orbital speed v to radius r. Used to replace a in the MOND equation.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational field of a uniform sphere
knowledge_points.description: The Newtonian gravitational field inside a homogeneous sphere of mass M and radius R_b is g_N = GMr/R_b^3, and outside it is g_N = GM/r^2. This provides the right-hand side of the MOND equation for the two regions.

knowledge_points.name: circular orbits
knowledge_points.description: The rotation curve v_c(r) assumes that the gas/stars move in circular orbits around the galactic center, allowing the use of the centripetal acceleration formula.

title: Two-part barometric tube
problem:
In 1765, British clockmaker James Cox invented a clock whose only source of energy is the fluctuations in atmospheric pressure. Cox's clock used two vessels containing mercury. Changes in atmospheric pressure caused mercury to move between the vessels, and the two vessels to move relative to each other. This movement acted as an energy source for the actual clock.

We propose an analysis of this device. Throughout, we assume that

- the Earth's gravitational field $\overrightarrow{g} = -g\overrightarrow{u_z}$ is uniform with $g =9.8\mathrm{m}\cdot \mathrm{s}^{-2}$ and $\overrightarrow{u_z}$ a unit vector;
- all liquids are incompressible and their density is denoted $\rho$ ;
- no surface tension effects will be considered;
- the variations of atmospheric pressure with altitude are neglected;
- the surrounding temperature $T_{\mathrm{a}}$ is uniform and all transformations are isothermal.

Fig. 1. Artistic view of Cox's clock

# Part B. Two-part barometric tube

From now on, we work with mercury (density $\rho =13.5\times 10^{3}\mathrm{kg}\cdot \mathrm{m}^{-3})$ at the ambient temperature $T_{\mathrm{a}} =20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and we take $P_{\mathrm{sat}} =0$

Let us consider a tube with a reservoir on top, modeled as two superposed cylinders of different dimensions, as shown in Fig. 3.

- the bottom part (still called the tube) has cross-sectional area $S_{t}$ and height $H_{t} =80 \mathrm{~cm}$ ;
- the top part (called the bulb) has cross-sectional area $S_{\mathrm{b}} > S_{\mathrm{t}}$ and height $H_{\mathrm{b}} =20\mathrm{cm}$ .

This two-part tube is dipped into a semi-infinite liquid bath.

Fig. 3. Sketch of the two-part barometric tube

As in Part A, the system is prepared such that the tube contains no air. We identify the vertical position of the tube by the altitude $h_{\mathrm{t}}$ of the junction between the tube and the bulb. The height of the column of mercury is again denoted $z_{\ell}$ . The force $\overrightarrow{F}$ that must be exerted to maintain the tube in equilibrium in the configuration shown in Fig. 3 can now be written as

$$\overrightarrow{F} = \left(m_{\mathrm{tb}} + m_{\mathrm{add}}\right) g \overrightarrow{u_{z}} \tag{1}$$

where $m_{\mathrm{tb}}$ is the total mass of the two-part tube (when empty of mercury).

sub_problems.problem:
(2) Sketch the evolution of the mass $m_{\mathrm{add}}$ as a function of $h_{\mathrm{t}}$ for $h_{\mathrm{t}} \in [-H_{\mathrm{b}}, H_{\mathrm{t}}]$ . On the graph, provide the expression for the slopes of the different segments, as well as the $h_{\mathrm{t}}$ analytical value of any angular points, in terms of $P_{0}, \rho, g, S_{\mathrm{b}}, S_{\mathrm{t}}, H_{\mathrm{b}}$ and $H_{\mathrm{t}}$ .

As the system is lifted while $P_{\mathrm{a}} = P_{0} =10^{5}\mathrm{Pa}$ , we stop when the free surface of the liquid is in the middle of the bulb. The value of $h_{\mathrm{t}}$ is fixed and then we observe variations in the mass $m_{\mathrm{add}}$ due to variations in the atmospheric pressure described by

$$P_{\mathrm{a}} (t) = P_{0} + P_{1} (t) \tag{2}$$

where $P_0$ designates the average value and $P_{1}$ is a perturbative term. We model $P_{1}$ by a periodic triangular function of amplitude $A =5\times 10^{2}\mathrm{Pa}$ and period $\tau_{1}$ of 1 week.

Fig. 4. Simplified model of the perturbative term $P_{1}(t)$
sub_problems.solution:
At atmospheric pressure $P_0$, the mercury free surface in the tube is at the barometric height
\[\nz_\ell^*=\frac{P_0-P_{\rm sat}}{\rho g}=\frac{P_0}{\rho g}.
\]\nWith $P_0=10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$, this gives $z_\ell^*=76\,\mathrm{cm}$.
\nThe quantity $m_{\rm add}$ is the mass of mercury that effectively lies above the bath surface in the two-part tube. Since the mercury below the bath surface is exchanged with the bath mercury of the same density, it does not contribute to the additional mass.
\nWe therefore distinguish the positions of the junction $h_t$ relative to the bath surface ($z=0$), to the point where the free surface reaches the top of the bulb, and to the point where it reaches the junction:

1. **$-H_b\le h_t\le 0$**: the junction is below the bath surface, so the part above the bath is only the portion of the bulb. Hence
   \[
   m_{\rm add}=\rho S_b(h_t+H_b),
   \]
   with slope $\rho S_b$.

2. **$0\le h_t\le z_\ell^*-H_b$**: the whole bulb is above the bath surface, and the free surface is still above the bulb. Thus
   \[
   m_{\rm add}=\rho\bigl(S_t h_t+S_b H_b\bigr),
   \]
   with slope $\rho S_t$.

3. **$z_\ell^*-H_b\le h_t\le z_\ell^*$**: the free surface lies inside the bulb. The mercury above the bath consists of the tube part up to $h_t$ and the bulb part from $h_t$ up to $z_\ell^*$. Thus
   \[
   m_{\rm add}=\rho\bigl(S_t h_t+S_b(z_\ell^*-h_t)\bigr)
   =\rho\bigl(S_b z_\ell^*+(S_t-S_b)h_t\bigr),
   \]
   with slope $\rho(S_t-S_b)$.

4. **$z_\ell^*\le h_t\le H_t$**: the free surface lies in the tube. Then only the tube section up to height $z_\ell^*$ contributes, so
   \[
   m_{\rm add}=\rho S_t z_\ell^*,
   \]
   with slope $0$.
\nThe angular points are therefore at
\[
 h_t=0,\qquad h_t=z_\ell^*-H_b=\frac{P_0}{\rho g}-H_b,\qquad h_t=z_\ell^*=\frac{P_0}{\rho g}.
\]\nNumerically, these are $0$, $56\,\mathrm{cm}$, and $76\,\mathrm{cm}$.
\nSo the graph is a continuous broken line: increasing with slope $\rho S_b$, then with slope $\rho S_t$, then decreasing with slope $\rho(S_t-S_b)$, and finally flat.
\nFinal answer:
\[
\boxed{m_{\rm add}(h_t)=\rho\begin{cases}\nS_b(h_t+H_b), & -H_b\le h_t\le 0,\\[2mm]\nS_t h_t+S_b H_b, & 0\le h_t\le \dfrac{P_0}{\rho g}-H_b,\\[3mm]\nS_t h_t+S_b\!\left(\dfrac{P_0}{\rho g}-h_t\right), & \dfrac{P_0}{\rho g}-H_b\le h_t\le \dfrac{P_0}{\rho g},\\[3mm]\nS_t\dfrac{P_0}{\rho g}, & \dfrac{P_0}{\rho g}\le h_t\le H_t.
\end{cases}}
\]

knowledge_points.name: ideal barometer vacuum
knowledge_points.description: The tube contains no air and the vapor pressure of mercury is negligible (P_sat = 0), so the pressure at the top of the mercury column is zero. This simplifies the barometric height to h = P_atm/(ρg).

knowledge_points.name: hydrostatic pressure equation
knowledge_points.description: In a static fluid, the pressure difference between two points separated by height Δh is ΔP = ρ g Δh. Used to relate the atmospheric pressure P0 to the height of the mercury column: P0 = ρ g z_ℓ*.

knowledge_points.name: barometric height
knowledge_points.description: The height of a liquid column in a barometer is determined solely by the atmospheric pressure and the liquid density, independent of the tube's cross-sectional shape or position. Here it gives the fixed free surface height z_ℓ* = P0/(ρg) above the bath surface.

knowledge_points.name: effective additional mass of immersed tube
knowledge_points.description: For a tube open at the bottom and dipped in a liquid bath, the additional mass m_add that appears in the force balance equals the mass of the liquid inside the tube that lies above the external liquid surface. The liquid below the bath surface is supported by the bath and does not contribute to the net weight that must be supported externally.

knowledge_points.name: mass from density and volume
knowledge_points.description: The mass of a homogeneous liquid is m = ρ V. For a cylindrical column of cross-sectional area A and height h, V = A h, so m = ρ A h. Used to compute the mass of mercury in each segment of the two-part tube.

sub_problems.problem: (3) Given that $S_{\mathrm{t}} =5 \, \mathrm{cm}^2$ and $S_{\mathrm{b}} =200 \, \mathrm{cm}^2$ , express the amplitude $\Delta m_{\mathrm{add}}$ of the variations of the mass $m_{\mathrm{add}}$ over time, then give its numerical value. Assume that the liquid surface always stays in the bulb.
sub_problems.solution:
The free surface in the tube is at altitude
\[\nz_\ell(t)=\frac{P_a(t)}{\rho g}=\frac{P_0}{\rho g}+\frac{P_1(t)}{\rho g}=z_{\ell,0}+\frac{P_1(t)}{\rho g},
\]\nso the amount of mercury above the junction contributes to the added mass
\[\nm_{\mathrm{add}}(t)=\rho\Big[S_t h_t+S_b\big(z_\ell(t)-h_t\big)\Big].
\]\nThe time-dependent part is therefore
\[
\delta m_{\mathrm{add}}(t)=\rho S_b\frac{P_1(t)}{\rho g}=\frac{S_b}{g}P_1(t).
\]\nHence the amplitude of the variations is
\[
\Delta m_{\mathrm{add}}=\frac{S_b}{g}A.
\]\nWith \(S_b=200\,\mathrm{cm}^2=2.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}^2\) and \(A=5.0\times10^2\,\mathrm{Pa}\),
\[
\Delta m_{\mathrm{add}}=\frac{2.0\times10^{-2}\times 5.0\times10^2}{9.8}\approx 1.0\,\mathrm{kg}.
\]\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{\Delta m_{\mathrm{add}}=\dfrac{S_bA}{g}\approx 1.0\,\mathrm{kg}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Hydrostatic equilibrium (barometric formula)
knowledge_points.description: Relates the height of a liquid column in a barometer to the external pressure when the space above is vacuum: P_a = ρ g z_ℓ. Used to convert the pressure variation P1(t) into the height variation of the mercury column.

knowledge_points.name: Vacuum above mercury column
knowledge_points.description: The tube contains no air and the saturated vapour pressure P_sat is zero, so the full atmospheric pressure is balanced by the weight of the mercury column. This justifies the direct proportionality z_ℓ = P_a/(ρ g).

knowledge_points.name: Added mass for two-part tube
knowledge_points.description: When the free surface lies in the bulb, the mass of mercury inside the tube is m_add = ρ [S_t h_t + S_b (z_ℓ − h_t)]. This expression, derived earlier, is required to compute how m_add varies with z_ℓ.

knowledge_points.name: Fixed tube position h_t
knowledge_points.description: The junction altitude h_t is held constant after positioning the free surface in the middle of the bulb. Consequently, the time dependence of m_add comes only from changes in z_ℓ(t).

knowledge_points.name: Free surface remains in bulb
knowledge_points.description: The problem explicitly instructs to assume the liquid surface always stays inside the bulb, ensuring the added mass formula with S_b (not S_t alone) remains applicable throughout the pressure cycle.

title: Volleyball
problem: Consider a simplified model of a volleyball: a thin spherical envelope filled with air. The envelope material is non-stretchable, easily foldable. The excess pressure inside the ball $\Delta p =20\mathrm{kPa}$ , the ball radius $R =10\mathrm{cm}$ and mass $m =400\mathrm{g}$ (the air mass inside the ball is negligible). You can neglect the dependence of the excess pressure on the deformation of the ball.

sub_problems.problem: (1) The ball is pressed between two parallel rigid plates, the distance between of which is $2R -2h$ (so that the height of the deformed segments is $h =1\mathrm{cm}$ ). Find the force between the ball and a plate $N$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The force on one plate equals the pressure difference times the area of contact:

\[N=\Delta p\,S,
\]
where \(S=\pi r^2\) is the area of the circular contact region.
From the geometry of a spherical cap of height \(h\), the radius \(r\) of its base satisfies

\[r^2=(2R-h)h.
\]
Therefore,

\[N=\Delta p\,\pi(2R-h)h.
\]
Substituting \(\Delta p=20\,\mathrm{kPa}\), \(R=10\,\mathrm{cm}\), and \(h=1\,\mathrm{cm}\),

\[N=2.0\times 10^4\,\mathrm{Pa}\cdot \pi \cdot (0.20-0.01)\,\mathrm{m}\cdot 0.01\,\mathrm{m}
\approx 1.2\times 10^2\,\mathrm{N}.
\]
So the force between the ball and one plate is \(\boxed{120\,\mathrm{N}}\).

knowledge_points.name: pressure force relation
knowledge_points.description: The force exerted by a uniform pressure on a surface is the product of the pressure and the area of the surface (F = p A). Here it is used to relate the contact force N to the excess pressure Δp and the contact area S.

knowledge_points.name: spherical cap geometry
knowledge_points.description: The radius r of the base of a spherical cap of height h cut from a sphere of radius R satisfies r² = (2R - h)h. This is needed to compute the circular contact area from the given deformation h.

knowledge_points.name: constant excess pressure
knowledge_points.description: The excess pressure Δp inside the ball is assumed independent of the deformation, as stated in the problem. This allows using the given Δp directly without corrections for volume change.

knowledge_points.name: flat circular contact region
knowledge_points.description: The contact region between the spherical ball and the rigid flat plate is assumed to be a flat circle of radius r, so its area is simply πr².

sub_problems.problem: (2) Ball moves with velocity $v_{0} =2 \, \mathrm{m/s}$ and hits a rigid wall. Find the maximal height of the deformed segment $h_{m}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
During the collision the ball is deformed by the wall. Since the envelope is non-stretchable, the undeformed part remains spherical, and the contact force comes from the excess pressure acting over the deformed area.
For a deformation height \(h \ll R\), the contact area is approximately a circular cap, and the force is linear in \(h\):
\[F(h) \approx 2\pi R\Delta p\, h.
\]Thus the ball behaves like a spring with effective stiffness
\[k = 2\pi R\Delta p.
\]At maximal deformation the ball momentarily stops, so its initial kinetic energy is fully converted into elastic deformation energy:
\[
\frac12 m v_0^2 = \frac12 k h_m^2.
\]Substituting \(k\) gives
\[
\frac12 m v_0^2 = \frac12 (2\pi R\Delta p) h_m^2,
\]so
\[h_m = v_0\sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi R\Delta p}}.
\]With \(v_0=2\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(m=0.40\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(R=0.10\,\mathrm{m}\), and \(\Delta p=2.0\times 10^4\,\mathrm{Pa}\),
\[h_m \approx 1.1\times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m} = 11\,\mathrm{mm}.
\]Final answer: \boxed{11\,\mathrm{mm}}

knowledge_points.name: non-stretchable envelope
knowledge_points.description: The envelope material is non-stretchable, so the undeformed part of the ball remains spherical during deformation, and the contact area is a flat circular cap.

knowledge_points.name: constant excess pressure
knowledge_points.description: The excess pressure inside the ball is assumed constant and independent of deformation, so the force on the contact area is simply Δp times the area.

knowledge_points.name: small deformation approximation
knowledge_points.description: The deformation height h is much smaller than the radius R, allowing the use of the linearized force-deformation relation and the approximate contact area 2πRh.

knowledge_points.name: force-deformation relation for pressurized sphere
knowledge_points.description: For a pressurized thin spherical shell pressed against a rigid plane, the force is F ≈ 2πRΔp h for small h, acting like a spring with stiffness k = 2πRΔp.

knowledge_points.name: effective spring constant
knowledge_points.description: The linear force-deformation relation implies the ball behaves as a spring with effective stiffness k = 2πRΔp, allowing the use of spring energy formulas.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: During the collision, the initial kinetic energy of the ball is converted entirely into elastic potential energy at maximum deformation, with no energy losses.

knowledge_points.name: elastic potential energy of a spring
knowledge_points.description: The elastic potential energy stored in a spring with stiffness k compressed by distance x is U = (1/2) k x^2.

sub_problems.problem: (3) ...and the collision time $\tau$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The collision can be modeled as half of a harmonic oscillation of the balls radial deformation. For a small compression \(x\), the restoring force is proportional to the excess pressure acting over the contact area, giving an effective spring constant
\[k = 2\pi R\Delta p.
\]Hence the oscillation period is
\[T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi R\Delta p}}.
\]The collision time is half a period:
\[
\tau = \frac{T}{2} = \pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi R\Delta p}} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi m}{2R\Delta p}}.
\]Substituting \(m=0.40\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(R=0.10\,\mathrm{m}\), and \(\Delta p=2.0\times 10^4\,\mathrm{Pa}\),
\[
\tau \approx \sqrt{\frac{\pi\cdot 0.40}{2\cdot 0.10\cdot 2.0\times 10^4}} \approx 1.8\times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}.
\]Therefore, the collision time is \(\boxed{\tau \approx 18\,\mathrm{ms}}\).

knowledge_points.name: constant excess pressure
knowledge_points.description: The excess pressure inside the ball remains constant during deformation, as stated in the problem, so the restoring force depends only on the contact area.

knowledge_points.name: collision as half-period SHM
knowledge_points.description: The collision is modeled as half a period of a simple harmonic oscillator, with the ball's centre of mass moving against a linear restoring force.

knowledge_points.name: period of mass-spring system
knowledge_points.description: The period of a mass m on a spring of constant k is T = 2π√(m/k); used to find the full oscillation period from which the collision time is derived.

knowledge_points.name: effective spring constant of ball
knowledge_points.description: For small deformations, the restoring force from the constant excess pressure gives an effective spring constant k = 2πRΔp, as derived from the contact area.

knowledge_points.name: pressure force relation
knowledge_points.description: Force exerted by a pressure difference Δp over an area A is F = Δp A; used to relate the excess pressure to the restoring force on the contact area.

sub_problems.problem: (4) For small excess pressures, the ball can lose its spherical shape even in those points, which are not in touch with the wall. Which condition between the quantities $\Delta p$ , $R$ , $m$ and $h$ has to be satisfied in order to ensure that such a loss of sphericity is negligible?
sub_problems.solution:
In the reference frame of the ball, the ball as a whole accelerates with acceleration
\[a=\frac{\Delta p\,\pi h(2R-h)}{m}.
\]A small surface element \(dS\) of the spherical envelope contains the mass
\[dm=\frac{m}{4\pi R^2}\,dS,
\]so the corresponding inertial force is
\[dF_i=dm\,a=\frac{m}{4\pi R^2}dS\cdot \frac{\Delta p\,\pi h(2R-h)}{m}
=\Delta p\,\frac{h(2R-h)}{4R^2}\,dS.
\]To keep the ball spherical, the restoring force due to the excess pressure,
\[dF_r=\Delta p\,dS,
\]must be larger than this inertial force. Therefore we need
\[
\Delta p\,\frac{h(2R-h)}{4R^2}\,dS < \Delta p\,dS,
\]which reduces to
\[h(2R-h)<4R^2.
\]Since physically \(0\le h\le 2R\), this inequality is always satisfied, so no additional constraint is needed.
Final answer: \(\boxed{h(2R-h)<4R^2}\).

knowledge_points.name: acceleration from contact force
knowledge_points.description: The ball's center-of-mass acceleration during impact is a = (Δp π h (2R-h))/m, a result imported from earlier sub-problems that combines the contact force N = Δp π h (2R-h) with Newton's second law.

knowledge_points.name: surface mass density
knowledge_points.description: For a thin spherical shell of mass m and radius R, the mass of a surface element dS is dm = (m/(4πR²)) dS, assuming uniform mass distribution.

knowledge_points.name: inertial force in accelerating frame
knowledge_points.description: In the non-inertial frame of the accelerating ball, each mass element experiences a fictitious force dF_i = dm a opposite to the acceleration direction.

knowledge_points.name: pressure force on area element
knowledge_points.description: The force exerted by a pressure p on a surface element dS is dF = p dS, directed normal to the surface. Here the excess pressure Δp provides the restoring force.

knowledge_points.name: force comparison for shape stability
knowledge_points.description: To ensure negligible loss of sphericity, the restoring force (from excess pressure) on any surface element must exceed the deforming inertial force; comparing their magnitudes yields a condition on the parameters.

knowledge_points.name: constant excess pressure
knowledge_points.description: The excess pressure Δp inside the ball is assumed constant and independent of the deformation, as stated in the problem's main text.

title: Loop of wire
problem: Consider a rectangular loop of wire with dimensions $a =0.03\mathrm{m}$ and $b =1.0\mathrm{m}$ , one side of which is parallel to another long straight wire carrying current $I_0=1000\mathrm{A}$ , at distance $l =0,01\mathrm{m}$ , see figure. The magnetic inductance of such current is plotted as a function of the distance from the wire in attached graph. The Ohmic resistance of the loop is $R =1,0\Omega$ , the inductance is negligible.

sub_problems.problem: (1) Calculate the magnetic flux $\Phi$ through the loop .
sub_problems.solution:
For a long straight wire, the magnetic field at distance \(r\) is
\[B(r)=\frac{\mu_0 I_0}{2\pi r}.\]
The rectangular loop has side length \(b\) parallel to the wire, and spans distances from \(r=l\) to \(r=l+a\) away from the wire. Therefore the magnetic flux through the loop is
\[
\Phi=\int_l^{l+a} B(r)\,b\,dr
=\int_l^{l+a} \frac{\mu_0 I_0}{2\pi r}\,b\,dr
=\frac{\mu_0 I_0 b}{2\pi}\ln\!\left(\frac{l+a}{l}\right).
\]
Substitute the given values \(a=0.03\,\mathrm{m}\), \(l=0.01\,\mathrm{m}\), \(b=1.0\,\mathrm{m}\), \(I_0=1000\,\mathrm{A}\):
\[
\Phi=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\cdot 1000\cdot 1.0}{2\pi}\ln\!\left(\frac{0.04}{0.01}\right)
=2.0\times10^{-4}\ln 4
\approx 2.8\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Wb}.
\]
Thus the magnetic flux through the loop is \(\boxed{2.8\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Wb}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Magnetic field of a long straight wire
knowledge_points.description: The magnitude of the magnetic field at distance r from an infinitely long straight wire carrying current I is B = μ0 I / (2π r). This formula is used to compute the flux through the loop.

knowledge_points.name: Magnetic flux
knowledge_points.description: Magnetic flux Φ through a surface is the surface integral of the magnetic field component normal to the surface: Φ = ∫ B·dA. The problem asks for this quantity.

knowledge_points.name: Flux integration for rectangular loop
knowledge_points.description: For a rectangular loop with side b parallel to the wire and radial extent from l to l+a, with B perpendicular to the loop and varying only with r, the flux is computed as Φ = ∫_l^{l+a} B(r) b dr.

knowledge_points.name: Infinite straight wire approximation
knowledge_points.description: The wire is treated as infinitely long, so its magnetic field is purely azimuthal and depends only on radial distance, justifying the use of B = μ0 I/(2π r).

knowledge_points.name: Loop plane contains wire
knowledge_points.description: The rectangular loop lies in the same plane as the wire, so the magnetic field (which circles the wire) is perpendicular to the loop's plane, making the flux integral simply ∫ B dA.

sub_problems.problem: (3) What is the net momentum $p$ given to the loop during the switch-off of the current (express it in terms of $Q$ and the given quantities, if you were unable to calculate $Q$ ) ?
sub_problems.solution:
The magnetic field of the long straight wire at the two sides of the loop is
\[B_1=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi l},\qquad B_2=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi (l+a)}.\]
So the net magnetic force on the loop is the difference of the forces on the two parallel sides:
\[F=b\,i\,(B_1-B_2)
=b\,i\,\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi}\left(\frac1l-\frac1{l+a}\right)
=b\,i\,\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi}\frac{a}{l(l+a)}.\]
The induced current is related to the changing flux by Faraday’s law:
\[i=-\frac1R\frac{d\Phi}{dt},
\qquad
\Phi=\frac{b\mu_0 I}{2\pi}\ln\frac{l+a}{l}.\]
Hence
\[i\,dt=-\frac{b\mu_0}{2\pi R}\ln\frac{l+a}{l}\,dI.\]
The impulse given to the loop is
\[p=\int F\,dt
=\frac{ab\mu_0}{2\pi l(l+a)}\int I\,i\,dt.\]
Substituting the expression for \(i\,dt\) and integrating from \(I_0\) to 0 gives
\[p=\left(\frac{b\mu_0}{2\pi}\right)^2\frac{a}{Rl(l+a)}\ln\frac{l+a}{l}\int_0^{I_0} I\,dI
=\frac{a(b\mu_0 I_0)^2}{8\pi^2 Rl(l+a)}\ln\frac{l+a}{l}.\]
If the total charge that flowed in the loop during the switch-off is \(Q\), then this can also be written as
\[p=\frac{ab\mu_0 I_0}{4\pi l(l+a)}\,Q.\]
For the given values, this evaluates to
\[p\approx 2.08\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}.\]
Thus the momentum given to the loop is \(\boxed{\frac{ab\mu_0 I_0}{4\pi l(l+a)}Q}\), or numerically \(\boxed{2.08\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Magnetic field of a long straight wire
knowledge_points.description: The magnetic field at distance r from a long straight wire carrying current I is B = μ0 I / (2π r). Used to compute B1 and B2 at the two parallel sides of the loop.

knowledge_points.name: Magnetic force on a current-carrying wire
knowledge_points.description: A straight wire of length L carrying current i in a uniform magnetic field B experiences a force of magnitude F = i L B (when perpendicular). Used to compute forces on the loop's sides and the net force.

knowledge_points.name: Faraday's law of induction
knowledge_points.description: The induced electromotive force in a loop equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through the loop, emf = -dΦ/dt. Used to relate the induced current to the changing flux.

knowledge_points.name: Ohm's law
knowledge_points.description: The current through a resistor is proportional to the voltage across it, i = V/R. Used to relate the induced emf to the induced current in the loop.

knowledge_points.name: Impulse-momentum theorem
knowledge_points.description: The impulse (integral of force over time) equals the change in momentum, p = ∫ F dt. Used to compute the net momentum imparted to the loop from the time-varying magnetic force.

knowledge_points.name: Magnetic flux through loop from part (1)
knowledge_points.description: The magnetic flux through the rectangular loop due to the long straight wire is Φ = (b μ0 I)/(2π) ln((l+a)/l), as derived in part (1). This expression is used to relate i dt to dI.

knowledge_points.name: Negligible self-inductance
knowledge_points.description: The loop's self-inductance is negligible, so the induced emf is solely due to the changing external flux, with no back-emf from the loop's own current.

knowledge_points.name: Negligible loop displacement during switch-off
knowledge_points.description: During the short switch-off time, the loop's displacement is negligible, so the distances l and l+a remain constant in the force and flux expressions.

title: Sucking
problem: Let a large vessel be filled with an incompressible dielectric liquid of density of mass density $\rho_{m}$ (the relative dielectric permeability $\varepsilon \approx 1$ ). This liquid carries homogeneous volume charge of density $\rho_{e}$ which is so small that the electric field $E_0$ created by it is negligible: $E_0\rho_e\ll g\rho_m$ where $g$ is the free fall acceleration. Surface tension can be also neglected. All the heights will be measured from the unperturbed height of the liquid surface. A point charge $-q$ of opposite sign is brought to the height $H$ , due to which a kink is formed on the liquid surface.

sub_problems.problem: (1) Determine the height of the kink $a$ .
sub_problems.solution:
At equilibrium the free energy density at the liquid surface is constant. Taking the unperturbed surface as zero level, the balance between gravitational and electrostatic contributions gives
\[
\rho_m g\,\chi - \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho_e q}{r}=0,
\]
where
\[
r=\sqrt{x^2+(\chi-H)^2}
\]
is the distance from the point charge.
The maximum deformation occurs directly below the charge, so at the kink apex we set \(x=0\) and \(\chi=a\). Then
\[
r=H-a,
\]
so the equilibrium condition becomes
\[
\rho_m g\,a-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho_e q}{H-a}=0.
\]
Multiplying by \(H-a\) gives
\[
a(H-a)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho_e q}{\rho_m g}.
\]
Define
\[
A=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho_e q}{\rho_m g}.
\]
Then
\[
a^2-Ha+A=0,
\]
whose solutions are
\[
a=\frac{H\pm\sqrt{H^2-4A}}{2}.
\]
The physical solution is the smaller root, since the deformation must vanish as \(q\to 0\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{a=\frac{H-\sqrt{H^2-\frac{4}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho_e q}{\rho_m g}}}{2}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: constant free energy density at liquid surface
knowledge_points.description: At equilibrium the total free energy density (gravitational plus electrostatic) at the liquid surface is constant; this condition replaces direct pressure balance when the interface is free to deform under external body forces.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational potential energy density in a fluid
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational potential energy per unit volume of a fluid element lifted by height χ in a uniform gravitational field is ρ_m g χ, which is needed here to form the gravitational contribution to the free energy density.
keywords: gravitational potential energy per unit volume

knowledge_points.name: electrostatic interaction energy density in point-charge field
knowledge_points.description: The potential energy per unit volume of a continuous volume charge density ρ_e in the electric potential of a point charge -q is -ρ_e q/(4πε₀ r), combining Coulomb's potential with the definition of electrostatic energy of a charge in an external potential.

knowledge_points.name: incompressible dielectric liquid with ε ≈ 1
knowledge_points.description: The liquid is incompressible (constant mass density ρ_m) and its relative permittivity is ε ≈ 1, so the electric field can be treated as in vacuum and the gravitational energy density uses the undisturbed density.

knowledge_points.name: negligible surface tension
knowledge_points.description: Surface tension effects are ignored, so the interface shape is determined solely by volumetric energy densities without curvature‑related pressure jumps.

knowledge_points.name: negligible self-field of volume charge
knowledge_points.description: The condition E₀ρ_e ≪ gρ_m ensures that the electric field created by the volume charge itself is so weak that it can be omitted; only the field of the external point charge matters for the interaction energy.

knowledge_points.name: maximum deformation directly below point charge
knowledge_points.description: By symmetry the kink apex (highest point of the deformed surface) lies on the vertical line through the point charge (x = 0), so the apex coordinate a satisfies r = H − a.

knowledge_points.name: physical root selection by limiting case
knowledge_points.description: When solving the quadratic for a, the physical solution is the one that vanishes as the perturbation q → 0 (a → 0), i.e. the smaller root; this is chosen by taking the limit A → 0 or by requiring consistency with the unperturbed state.

sub_problems.problem: (2) If the height of the charge is slowly decreased, at which height $h$ the liquid will start flowing to the point charge?
sub_problems.solution:
Flow begins when the highest point of the liquid surface becomes unstable with respect to motion toward the charge. Let that point have height \(\chi_0\) above the unperturbed surface, and let the charge be at height \(h\). The potential energy per unit volume of liquid at height \(y\) is
\[
\Pi(y)=\rho_m g y-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho_e q}{h-y},
\]
where the first term is gravitational energy and the second is the electrostatic contribution.
At the threshold of motion, \(\Pi(y)\) has a maximum at \(y=\chi_0\), so
\[
\rho_m g \chi_0-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho_e q}{h-\chi_0}=0,
\]
\[
\rho_m g-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho_e q}{(h-\chi_0)^2}=0.
\]
From the second equation,
\[
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\rho_e q=\rho_m g\,(h-\chi_0)^2.
\]
Substitute this into the first equation:
\[
\rho_m g\chi_0-\rho_m g\,(h-\chi_0)=0,
\]
so
\[
\chi_0=h-\chi_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad h=2\chi_0.
\]
Using \(h-\chi_0=h/2\) in the second condition gives
\[
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\rho_e q=\rho_m g\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
h^2=\frac{\rho_e q}{\pi\varepsilon_0\rho_m g},
\]
so the liquid starts flowing when the charge is lowered to
\[
\boxed{h=\sqrt{\frac{\rho_e q}{\pi\varepsilon_0\rho_m g}}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: gravitational potential energy per unit volume
knowledge_points.description: The potential energy per unit volume of a liquid of density ρ_m in a gravitational field g is ρ_m g y, where y is the height above a reference. This appears as the first term in the energy density Π(y).

knowledge_points.name: electrostatic interaction energy per unit volume
knowledge_points.description: For a continuous charge distribution with charge density ρ_e placed in an external electric potential φ, the interaction energy per unit volume is ρ_e φ. This gives the electrostatic contribution to Π(y).

knowledge_points.name: Coulomb potential of a point charge
knowledge_points.description: The electric potential at distance r from a point charge -q in vacuum (or with ε≈1) is φ = –(1/(4πε₀)) q/r. With r = h – y, this is used to construct the electrostatic term in Π(y).

knowledge_points.name: energy‑barrier instability condition
knowledge_points.description: The onset of flow (‘sucking’) occurs when the potential‑energy profile Π(y) develops a maximum that just reaches the reference energy level (taken as zero), i.e. Π(χ₀)=0 and Π′(χ₀)=0 simultaneously. This condition yields the critical height.

knowledge_points.name: negligible electric field from volume charge
knowledge_points.description: The electric field produced by the volume charge density ρ_e is so small that only the field of the external point charge needs to be considered. This justifies ignoring ρ_e in the electric potential expression.

knowledge_points.name: incompressible liquid with dielectric constant ≈1
knowledge_points.description: The liquid is incompressible (constant ρ_m and ρ_e) and its relative permittivity is approximately 1, allowing the use of vacuum permittivity ε₀ in Coulomb’s law.

knowledge_points.name: surface tension neglected
knowledge_points.description: Surface tension is negligible, so energy contributions from the liquid‑air interface can be omitted in the energy‑barrier balance.

title: Pencil
problem:
Equipment: pencil, paper, ruler.

Determine the coefficient of friction of the pencil's graphite core against the paper. Estimate the uncertainty.
solution:
Place the graphite end of the pencil on the paper and push on the other end with a fingertip so that the pencil is not bent. Then the pencil is in pure compression, and the force transmitted to the contact point must be along the pencil axis.
\nAt the graphite-paper contact, the normal reaction \(N\) and friction force \(f\) must therefore combine into a resultant along the pencil. If the pencil makes an angle \(\alpha\) with the vertical, this is possible only if
\[
\tan\alpha \le \mu,
\]\nwhere \(\mu\) is the coefficient of static friction between graphite and paper. At the threshold of slipping,
\[
\mu = \tan\alpha_0.
\]
\nNow measure the pencil length \(l\) and the horizontal projection \(x\) of the pencil when it is just about to slide. From the right triangle formed by the pencil,
\[
\sin\alpha_0 = \frac{x}{l},
\qquad
\cos\alpha_0 = \frac{\sqrt{l^2-x^2}}{l}.
\]\nHence
\[
\mu = \tan\alpha_0 = \frac{\sin\alpha_0}{\cos\alpha_0} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{l^2-x^2}}.
\]
\nTo estimate the uncertainty, measure \(x\) and \(l\) several times and use the spread of the resulting \(\mu\) values, or propagate the ruler uncertainties \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta l\):
\[
\Delta\mu \approx \sqrt{\left(\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial x}\Delta x\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial l}\Delta l\right)^2}
=\frac{\sqrt{l^4(\Delta x)^2+x^2l^2(\Delta l)^2}}{(l^2-x^2)^{3/2}}.
\]\nThus the coefficient of friction is determined from the slipping angle, with uncertainty obtained from repeated measurements or error propagation. Final answer: \(\boxed{\mu=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{l^2-x^2}}}\), with uncertainty \(\boxed{\Delta\mu\approx\dfrac{\sqrt{l^4(\Delta x)^2+x^2l^2(\Delta l)^2}}{(l^2-x^2)^{3/2}}}\).
