knowledge_points.name: pure compression along pencil axis
knowledge_points.description: The pencil is pushed without bending so the internal force is purely axial; this guarantees the resultant of normal and friction forces at the tip is collinear with the pencil.

knowledge_points.name: static friction threshold
knowledge_points.description: The maximum static friction force is proportional to the normal force, and slipping occurs when the required friction-to-normal ratio equals the coefficient of static friction.

knowledge_points.name: force equilibrium at a point
knowledge_points.description: At the threshold of slipping, the vector sum of normal reaction and friction force must balance the applied force along the pencil axis, leading to tan(alpha) = mu.

knowledge_points.name: trigonometric ratio from geometry
knowledge_points.description: The tangent of the angle is expressed as the ratio of the horizontal projection x to the vertical projection sqrt(l^2 - x^2) using the measured pencil length l.

knowledge_points.name: error propagation formula
knowledge_points.description: The uncertainty in mu is estimated by propagating the measurement uncertainties in x and l through the functional dependence mu(x,l) using partial derivatives.

title: Thermos bottle
problem: In order to study the thermal properties of a thermos bottle, let us model it as two concentric spherical vessels, with radii $R_{1} =7\mathrm{cm}$ and $R_{2} =10\mathrm{cm}$ . The gap between the walls of the vessels contains vacuum (hence, the heat conductivity can be neglected).

sub_problems.problem: (1) (3,) Find the radiative heat flux (i.e. transmitted heat per unit time) between the walls of the bottle, assuming that the ambient temperature is $T_{2} =293\mathrm{K}$ and the inner sphere is filled with liquid nitrogen at the boiling temperature $T_{1} =77\mathrm{K}$ . The emissivities of all the surfaces are equal to that of stainless steel: $\varepsilon =0.1$ . Remark: The emitted heat flux per unit area is given Stefan-Boltzmann's law $P = \varepsilon \sigma T^4$ , where $\sigma =5.67\times 10^{-8}\mathrm{W / m^2K^4}$ (assuming that $\varepsilon$ is independent of the wavelength.
sub_problems.solution:
For two concentric spherical shells with vacuum between them, heat transfer occurs only by radiation. Let
\[S_1=4\pi R_1^2,\qquad S_2=4\pi R_2^2.
\]
Because a ray leaving the outer sphere reaches the inner one only for a fraction
\[
\kappa=\frac{S_1}{S_2}=\frac{R_1^2}{R_2^2},
\]
of the emitted power, multiple reflections must be taken into account.

A convenient way to sum the radiative exchange is to use the standard result for two diffuse gray concentric spheres:
\[
P=\frac{\sigma\,(T_2^4-T_1^4)}{\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon S_1}+\frac{1}{S_1}+\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon S_2}}^{-1},
\]
which simplifies here to
\[
P=\frac{\varepsilon\,\sigma\,S_1\,(T_2^4-T_1^4)}{1+(1-\varepsilon)\,S_1/S_2}
=\frac{\varepsilon\,\sigma\,4\pi R_1^2\,(T_2^4-T_1^4)}{1+(1-\varepsilon)R_1^2/R_2^2}.
\]

Now insert the numbers:
\[
R_1=0.07\,\text{m},\qquad R_2=0.10\,\text{m},\qquad \varepsilon=0.1,
\]
\[
T_2^4-T_1^4=293^4-77^4,
\qquad \sigma=5.67\times 10^{-8}\,\text{W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4}.
\]
Hence
\[
P\approx \frac{0.1\cdot 5.67\times 10^{-8}\cdot 4\pi(0.07)^2\,(293^4-77^4)}{1+0.9\,(0.07^2/0.10^2)}\approx 1.8\,\text{W}.
\]
Therefore the radiative heat flux into the liquid nitrogen is \(\boxed{1.8\,\text{W}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
knowledge_points.description: Relates the radiative power emitted per unit area of a surface to its temperature: P/A = ε σ T⁴. The net radiation formula used in the solution is built on this law.

knowledge_points.name: Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation
knowledge_points.description: For an opaque surface in thermal equilibrium, absorptivity equals emissivity (α = ε). For a gray surface, reflectivity is 1 – ε. Needed to account for reflected radiation in the net heat transfer.

knowledge_points.name: View factor for concentric spheres
knowledge_points.description: The fraction of radiation leaving the outer sphere that directly intercepts the inner sphere is the ratio of their surface areas: F₂→₁ = A₁/A₂ = (R₁/R₂)². The inner sphere sees only the outer sphere (F₁→₂ = 1). Essential for setting up the radiation balance.

knowledge_points.name: Net radiation formula for concentric gray spheres
knowledge_points.description: For two diffuse gray concentric spheres with equal emissivity ε, the net radiative heat transfer rate is P = ε σ A₁ (T₂⁴ – T₁⁴) / [1 + (1 – ε) A₁/A₂], where A₁ is the inner area. This formula accounts for multiple reflections and is used directly to compute the heat flux.

knowledge_points.name: Vacuum gap: no conduction or convection
knowledge_points.description: The space between the walls is evacuated, so heat transfer occurs solely by radiation; conduction and convection are negligible.

knowledge_points.name: Diffuse gray surfaces
knowledge_points.description: The surfaces are assumed to be gray (emissivity independent of wavelength) and diffuse (emission and reflection are isotropic). This justifies using the simple view factor and the standard net radiation formula.

sub_problems.problem: (2) (2,) Estimate, how long time does it take for a full vaporization of the liquid nitrogen (the vapor escapes through an over pressure valve). For the liquid nitrogen, density $\rho =810\mathrm{g / l}$ and latent heat for vaporization $\lambda =5.580\mathrm{kJ / mol})$ . NB! If you were unable to find $P$ (for question i), express the evaporation time symbolically (i.e. using the symbol $P$ ).
sub_problems.solution:
The heat flow \(P\) into the inner vessel is used entirely to vaporize the liquid nitrogen, so the total energy balance is
\[
\tau P = \lambda m,
\]
where \(m\) is the mass of liquid nitrogen.

Treating the liquid nitrogen as filling a sphere of radius \(R\), its mass is
\[
 m = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho.
\]
Since \(\lambda\) is given per mole, we convert mass to moles using the molar mass \(\mu\):
\[
 n = \frac{m}{\mu} = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \frac{\rho}{\mu}.
\]
Thus
\[
\tau = \frac{n\lambda}{P} = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \frac{\rho\lambda}{\mu P}.
\]
Using the numerical values gives approximately
\[
\tau \approx 36\,\mathrm{h}.
\]
Therefore, the evaporation time is \(\boxed{36\,\mathrm{h}}\).

knowledge_points.name: energy balance for phase change
knowledge_points.description: The total heat energy supplied equals the latent heat required to vaporize the entire mass: τ P = λ n (or τ P = L m). This is the fundamental relation linking heat flow, time, and vaporization energy.

knowledge_points.name: latent heat of vaporization
knowledge_points.description: The energy per mole (or per mass) required to convert liquid to gas at constant temperature. The problem gives λ in kJ/mol, so the student must know to multiply by number of moles to get total energy.

knowledge_points.name: mass from density and volume
knowledge_points.description: The mass of liquid nitrogen is obtained from its density and the volume of the inner sphere: m = ρ V. This is needed to convert the given density into a mass, then into moles.

knowledge_points.name: mass-to-mole conversion
knowledge_points.description: The number of moles n is obtained by dividing the mass m by the molar mass μ. This is required because the latent heat λ is given per mole.

knowledge_points.name: liquid nitrogen fills inner sphere
knowledge_points.description: The liquid nitrogen is assumed to occupy the entire volume of the inner sphere of radius R₁, so its volume is (4/3)πR₁³. This is used to compute the mass.

knowledge_points.name: all heat goes to vaporization
knowledge_points.description: The radiative heat flow P into the inner vessel is assumed to be used entirely for vaporizing the liquid nitrogen, with no other heat losses or temperature changes of the liquid.

title: Elastic thread
problem:
Equipment: ruler, tape, an elastic thread, a wooden rod, marker, a known weight.
The purpose of this problem is to study the elastic properties of an elastic thread for large relative deformations $\varepsilon = (l - l_0) / l_0$ , where $l_0$ and $l$ are the lengths in initial and stretched states, respectively. If the Hooke's law were valid, the ratio $F / \varepsilon$ of the elastic force $F$ and $\varepsilon$ would be constant: $F / \varepsilon = SE$ , where $S$ is the cross-section area of the thread and $E$ — the Young modulus of the thread material.

sub_problems.problem: (1) Collect the data needed to plot the ratio $F / \varepsilon$ as a function $\varepsilon$ , up to $\varepsilon \approx 4$ . Plot the appropriate graph, and indicate the uncertainties.
sub_problems.solution:
Measure the unstretched length of the elastic thread, \(l_0\). Then, for a chosen placement of the thread along the wooden rod, fix its ends at two points \(A\) and \(B\) and hang the known mass so that it acts at the midpoint-like point \(C\) of the stretched thread segment.
\nMeasure the stretched length \(l\) of the thread and compute the relative deformation
\[
\varepsilon=\frac{l-l_0}{l_0}.
\]
\nTo determine the tensile force in the thread, use equilibrium of the hanging load. If \(D\) is the midpoint of the segment \(AB\), then the two equal thread tensions have vertical components balancing the weight, so
\[\nF=T=\frac12 mg\,\frac{AC}{CD}.
\]
\nBy changing the placement of the thread and its pre-stretch, one can obtain data points over a wide range, up to about \(\varepsilon\approx 4\). For each measurement, plot the quantity \(F/\varepsilon\) versus \(\varepsilon\). The uncertainties should be indicated by the measurement errors of the ruler/tape readings for \(l_0\), \(l\), \(AC\), and \(CD\), propagated to 
\(\varepsilon\) and \(F\).
\nThus the required quantities are
\[
\boxed{\varepsilon=\frac{l-l_0}{l_0},\qquad F=\frac12 mg\,\frac{AC}{CD}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Relative deformation (strain)
knowledge_points.description: Defined as ε = (l - l0)/l0, where l0 is the original length and l is the stretched length. Needed to compute ε from the measured lengths of the thread.

knowledge_points.name: Static equilibrium of a point mass
knowledge_points.description: The net force on a stationary point mass is zero. Used to equate the vertical components of the two thread tensions to the weight of the hanging mass.

knowledge_points.name: Tension in a string
knowledge_points.description: The pulling force transmitted along a string or thread. The elastic force F in the thread equals the tension T acting on the hanging mass.

knowledge_points.name: Force resolution using geometry
knowledge_points.description: Resolving a force into components using the geometry of the setup, e.g., the vertical component of tension is T·(CD/AC) from the right triangle ACD. This yields F = (1/2)mg·(AC/CD).

knowledge_points.name: Uncertainty propagation
knowledge_points.description: Calculating the uncertainties in derived quantities (ε and F) from the measurement uncertainties of directly measured lengths, using error propagation formulas.

knowledge_points.name: Symmetric loading
knowledge_points.description: The mass is hung at the midpoint of the stretched thread, so the two segments have equal length and tension, and the geometry is symmetric about the vertical. This simplifies the force balance to a single equation.

knowledge_points.name: Massless thread
knowledge_points.description: The thread's mass is negligible, so tension is uniform along each segment and no additional gravitational or inertial forces from the thread need to be considered.

sub_problems.problem: (2) By making assumption that the Young modulus $E = F / S\varepsilon$ remains constant, study, how does the volume of the thread depend on $\varepsilon$ . Plot the appropriate graph.
sub_problems.solution:
Assuming the Young modulus stays constant, we have
\[\nE=\frac{F}{S\varepsilon},
\]\nso the cross-sectional area of the thread at strain \(\varepsilon\) is
\[\nS(\varepsilon)=\frac{F}{E\varepsilon}.
\]\nThe stretched length is
\[\nl=l_0(1+\varepsilon).
\]\nTherefore the volume of the thread is
\[\nV(\varepsilon)=lS=l_0(1+\varepsilon)\frac{F}{E\varepsilon}
=\frac{F l_0}{E}\left(1+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right).
\]\nSo the volume depends on \(\varepsilon\) as a decreasing hyperbola shifted upward by a constant. The graph of \(V\) versus \(\varepsilon\) has a vertical asymptote at \(\varepsilon=0\) and approaches the horizontal asymptote \(V=\frac{F l_0}{E}\) as \(\varepsilon\to\infty\).
\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{V(\varepsilon)=\frac{F l_0}{E}\left(1+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)}\).

knowledge_points.name: Strain (relative deformation)
knowledge_points.description: Defined as ε = (l - l0)/l0, which gives the stretched length l = l0(1+ε). Needed to express the thread's length in terms of its original length and strain.

knowledge_points.name: Young modulus
knowledge_points.description: Defined as E = (F/S)/ε, relating tensile stress to strain. Used to find the cross-sectional area S = F/(Eε) from the measured force F and constant E.

knowledge_points.name: Volume of a prism
knowledge_points.description: The volume V of a uniform thread is the product of its cross-sectional area S and its length l: V = S l. Needed to combine the expressions for S and l into V(ε).

knowledge_points.name: Constant Young modulus
knowledge_points.description: The problem instructs to assume that the Young modulus E remains constant even at large strains, so the relation E = F/(Sε) holds with a fixed E for all data points.

title: Charged cylinder
problem: Dielectric cylinder of radius $r$ carries a charge of surface density $\sigma$ on its cylindrical surface and rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ .

sub_problems.problem: (1) Determine the magnetic induction $B$ inside the cylinder. Remark: if you wish, you can use the expression for the inductance $L = \mu_0 N^2 S / l$ of a solenoidal coil of radius $r$ , length $l \gg r$ , area of cross-section $S$ and number of loops $N$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The rotating surface charge corresponds to a surface current. A point on the cylindrical surface moves with tangential speed
\[v=\omega r,
\]\nso the surface current density is
\[j=\sigma v=\sigma \omega r.
\]\nThis is equivalent to a long solenoid carrying a surface current density \(j\). For a long solenoid, Ampres law gives a uniform magnetic field inside,
\[B=\mu_0 j.
\]\nTherefore,
\[B=\mu_0 \sigma \omega r.
\]\nThe magnetic induction inside the cylinder is
\[
\boxed{B=\mu_0\sigma\omega r}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: surface current density from moving surface charge
knowledge_points.description: A surface charge density σ moving with tangential velocity v gives a surface current density K = σ v. This converts the rotating charged cylinder into a static current distribution.

knowledge_points.name: tangential speed in circular motion
knowledge_points.description: For a point at distance r from the rotation axis, the linear speed is v = ω r. Used to find the speed of the surface charge.

knowledge_points.name: magnetic field inside a long solenoid
knowledge_points.description: Applying Ampère's law to an ideal solenoid with surface current density K yields a uniform interior magnetic field B = μ₀ K. This directly gives the magnetic induction inside the cylinder.

knowledge_points.name: long solenoid approximation
knowledge_points.description: The rotating cylinder is treated as an infinitely long solenoid, so end effects are ignored and the field inside is uniform. The problem hints at this by referencing the inductance of a long solenoid.

sub_problems.problem: (2) A radial conducting wire connects the axis of the cylinder with the cylindrical surface (it rotates together with the cylinder). Find the electromotive force (voltage) $\mathcal{E}$ between the ends of the wire.
sub_problems.solution:
The rotating charged cylindrical surface acts like a surface current. At radius $r$, the charges move with speed $v=\omega r$, so the surface current density is
\[K=\sigma v=\sigma \omega r.
\]\nFor an infinitely long cylindrical shell, the magnetic field inside is
\[B=\mu_0 K=\mu_0 \sigma \omega r.
\]\nNow consider the radial wire. In a time interval $dt$, its outer end moves through an arc length $r\omega\,dt$, so the wire sweeps out a thin sector of area
\[dS=\frac12 r(r\omega\,dt)=\frac12 r^2\omega\,dt.
\]\nThe magnetic flux through this swept area changes by
\[d\Phi = B\,dS,
\]\nso the induced electromotive force is
\[
\mathcal{E}=\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=B\frac{dS}{dt}=B\frac12 r^2\omega.
\]\nSubstituting $B=\mu_0\sigma\omega r$ gives
\[
\mathcal{E}=\frac12\mu_0\sigma\omega^2 r^3.
\]\nTherefore, the voltage between the ends of the wire is \(\boxed{\mathcal{E}=\frac12\mu_0\sigma\omega^2 r^3}\).

knowledge_points.name: surface current density
knowledge_points.description: The rotating charged cylindrical surface is equivalent to a surface current with density K = σ v, where σ is the surface charge density and v is the tangential speed of the charges.

knowledge_points.name: tangential velocity in circular motion
knowledge_points.description: For a point at radius r rotating with angular velocity ω, the linear speed is v = ω r, used to express the surface current density as K = σ ω r.

knowledge_points.name: Ampere's law
knowledge_points.description: Applied to an infinite cylindrical shell with surface current K, it gives the uniform magnetic field inside as B = μ0 K, which here becomes B = μ0 σ ω r.

knowledge_points.name: Faraday's law of induction
knowledge_points.description: The induced electromotive force equals the rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit, E = dΦ/dt, used to find the voltage between the ends of the moving wire.

knowledge_points.name: flux calculation via swept area
knowledge_points.description: For a rotating radial wire, the area swept in time dt is a sector of area dS = (1/2) r^2 ω dt, allowing the flux change to be written as dΦ = B dS.

knowledge_points.name: steady uniform magnetic field
knowledge_points.description: The magnetic field inside the cylinder is constant in time and spatially uniform, so the flux change is simply dΦ = B dS with B constant.

sub_problems.problem: (3) Suppose that the wire connecting the axis of the cylinder with the cylindrical surface is not radial and has an arbitrary shape (still, there are no segments protruding outside the cylinder). Show that $\mathcal{E}$ does not depend on the shape of the wire.
sub_problems.solution:
The induced emf is proportional to the rate at which the wire sweeps area in the rotating field. We show that this sweep rate is independent of the wire shape.
\nBecause the cylinder rotates uniformly and the setup is rotationally symmetric, the swept area rate cannot depend on the absolute rotation angle; therefore it is a constant, \(\dot S\).
\nNow consider one full rotation of the cylinder, during which the wire goes through angle \(2\pi\). Since the wire connects the axis to the cylindrical surface and does not extend outside the cylinder, the set of points swept by the wire over one full turn covers the entire disk of radius \(r\). Hence the total swept area after one revolution is
\[
\dot S \cdot \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \pi r^2.
\]\nSolving for \(\dot S\) gives
\[
\dot S = \frac{r^2\omega}{2}.
\]\nThus the emf \(\mathcal{E}\) does not depend on the shape of the wire, only on the endpoints and the rotation rate. Final answer: \(\boxed{\mathcal{E}\text{ is independent of the wire shape}}\).
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\mathcal{E}\text{ is independent of the wire shape}}

knowledge_points.name: Motional emf (flux cutting rule)
knowledge_points.description: In a uniform magnetic field, the emf induced in a moving conductor equals the magnetic field strength times the rate at which the conductor sweeps area perpendicular to the field. This relation is used to connect the unknown emf to the area sweep rate of the wire.

knowledge_points.name: Uniform internal magnetic field
knowledge_points.description: The magnetic induction inside the rotating charged cylinder is uniform and axial, as derived in part (1). This uniformity is essential for the simple proportionality between emf and swept area rate.

knowledge_points.name: Rotational symmetry argument
knowledge_points.description: Because the system is rotationally symmetric and the rotation is uniform, the rate at which the wire sweeps area cannot depend on the rotation angle, so it is constant. This allows the total swept area over one revolution to be equated to the constant rate times the period.

knowledge_points.name: Area swept by rotating curve
knowledge_points.description: Any curve connecting the center to the rim of a disk, when rotated through a full turn, sweeps out the entire disk area. This geometric fact is used to compute the total swept area as πr².

title: FRCTION OF A STRING
problem:
Measure the dynamic coefficient of friction $\mu_{1}$ between the ballpoint pen and the string. Estimate the uncertainty. It might help that the dynamic coefficient of friction between the pencil and the same string was measured beforehand and $\mu_{2} =0.20\pm 0.01$ was obtained.

Equipment: dynamometer, string, ballpoint pen, pencil and weight.

# Estonian-Finnish Olympiad 2013
solution:
For a string sliding over a cylindrical object, consider a small segment that subtends an angle $d\alpha$.
The friction force on this segment is
\[dF_f = \mu\, dR,
\]\nwhere $dR$ is the normal reaction.
\nFor a short arc, the two end tensions differ by $dT$, and their radial components give
\[dR \approx T\, d\alpha.
\]\nHence
\[dT = \mu T\, d\alpha,
\]\nso that
\[
\frac{dT}{T} = \mu\, d\alpha.
\]\nIntegrating from $\alpha=0$ to $\alpha$ gives the capstan law
\[T = T_0 e^{\mu\alpha},
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\ln T = \ln T_0 + \mu\alpha.
\]\nTherefore, to measure the friction coefficient of the ballpoint pen, wrap the string around it at different angles $\alpha$, measure the tension $T$ with the dynamometer, and plot $\ln T$ versus $\alpha$. The slope of the straight line is $\mu_1$.
The uncertainty is obtained from the uncertainty of the fitted slope, or equivalently from repeated measurements of $T$ and $\alpha$.
Thus the result is
\[
\boxed{\mu_1 = \frac{d\ln T}{d\alpha} = \frac{1}{\alpha}\ln\!\left(\frac{T}{T_0}\right)}.
\]

sub_problems.problem:
Measure the dynamic coefficient of friction $\mu_{1}$ between the ballpoint pen and the string. Estimate the uncertainty. It might help that the dynamic coefficient of friction between the pencil and the same string was measured beforehand and $\mu_{2} =0.20\pm 0.01$ was obtained.

Equipment: dynamometer, string, ballpoint pen, pencil and weight.

# Estonian-Finnish Olympiad 2013
sub_problems.solution:
For a string sliding over a cylindrical object, consider a small segment that subtends an angle $d\alpha$.
The friction force on this segment is
\[dF_f = \mu\, dR,
\]\nwhere $dR$ is the normal reaction.
\nFor a short arc, the two end tensions differ by $dT$, and their radial components give
\[dR \approx T\, d\alpha.
\]\nHence
\[dT = \mu T\, d\alpha,
\]\nso that
\[
\frac{dT}{T} = \mu\, d\alpha.
\]\nIntegrating from $\alpha=0$ to $\alpha$ gives the capstan law
\[T = T_0 e^{\mu\alpha},
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\ln T = \ln T_0 + \mu\alpha.
\]\nTherefore, to measure the friction coefficient of the ballpoint pen, wrap the string around it at different angles $\alpha$, measure the tension $T$ with the dynamometer, and plot $\ln T$ versus $\alpha$. The slope of the straight line is $\mu_1$.
The uncertainty is obtained from the uncertainty of the fitted slope, or equivalently from repeated measurements of $T$ and $\alpha$.
Thus the result is
\[

\]

knowledge_points.name: dynamic coefficient of friction
knowledge_points.description: The ratio of kinetic friction force to normal contact force, quantifying sliding resistance. The sub-problem explicitly asks to measure this quantity for a ballpoint pen on a string.

knowledge_points.name: Coulomb friction law
knowledge_points.description: The kinetic friction force is proportional to the normal force: F_f = μ N. This law is used in the differential force balance for each string element, dF_f = μ dR.

knowledge_points.name: normal force on curved string segment
knowledge_points.description: When a tensioned string wraps around a cylinder, the radial components of tension produce a normal force dR ≈ T dα on an angular segment dα. This relation is essential to derive the capstan equation.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: Approximations sin(dα/2) ≈ dα/2 and cos(dα/2) ≈ 1 are used to simplify the radial force balance on an infinitesimal string element, yielding dR = T dα.

knowledge_points.name: capstan equation
knowledge_points.description: For a string wrapped over a cylinder with friction, the tension varies exponentially with wrap angle: T = T₀ e^{μα}. This equation directly relates μ to the measured tension and angle.

knowledge_points.name: linearization by semi-log plot
knowledge_points.description: Taking the natural logarithm, ln T = ln T₀ + μα, transforms the exponential relation into a straight line with slope μ. Plotting ln T vs. α allows μ to be measured as the slope.

knowledge_points.name: uncertainty estimation from linear fit
knowledge_points.description: The uncertainty in μ is obtained from the uncertainty of the fitted slope, e.g., using the standard error of the regression or error propagation from repeated measurements of T and α.

title: GLASS PLATE
problem: Rasmus Kisel and Mibkel Heidelberg. Light from a laser with a wavelength of $\lambda$ and power of $P$ falls perpendicularly on to a thin glass plate of thickness $a = (100.25\lambda) / n$ where $n$ is the index of refraction of glass. The reflection coefficient of the glass surfaces is $r$ , which can be interpreted as the probability for a photon to be reflected from a single glass surface.

sub_problems.problem: (1) Calculate the force $F_{a}$ applied to the glass by the laser light when the incident side of the glass is painted totally black.
sub_problems.solution:
For a photon, the energy and momentum are related by
\[\nE=pc.
\]\nIf the incident side of the glass is painted black, the incoming photons are absorbed there, so their momentum is transferred to the glass.
\nThe laser power is the energy delivered per unit time, so the rate of momentum transfer is
\[
\frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{1}{c}\frac{dE}{dt}=\frac{P}{c}.
\]\nThis rate of momentum transfer equals the force on the glass:
\[\nF_a=\frac{P}{c}.
\]\nTherefore, the force applied to the glass is \(\boxed{\frac{P}{c}}\).

knowledge_points.name: normal incidence
knowledge_points.description: Laser light falls perpendicularly on the glass, so all photon momentum is along the normal, simplifying force calculation to a single direction.

knowledge_points.name: perfectly absorbing surface
knowledge_points.description: The incident side is painted totally black, absorbing all incoming photons, so no reflection contributes to momentum transfer.

knowledge_points.name: photon energy-momentum relation
knowledge_points.description: For a photon, energy E and momentum p are related by E = pc, allowing conversion between laser power and momentum flux.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of momentum
knowledge_points.description: When a photon is absorbed, its momentum is transferred to the absorbing object, so the rate of momentum transfer equals the force.

knowledge_points.name: power as energy flux
knowledge_points.description: Laser power P is the rate of energy delivery, dE/dt, used to relate photon energy rate to momentum rate.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law (momentum form)
knowledge_points.description: Force equals rate of change of momentum, F = dp/dt, used to equate momentum transfer rate to the force on the glass.

sub_problems.problem: (2) Calculate the force $F_{b}$ applied to the glass by the laser light when the opposite side of the glass is painted totally black.
sub_problems.solution:
A fraction $r$ of the photons is reflected from the front surface. Each reflected photon reverses its momentum, so the momentum transfer is twice that of absorption, giving a force contribution

$$F_{\text{refl}}=2r\frac{P}{c}.$$ 
\nThe remaining fraction $1-r$ enters the glass and is absorbed by the blackened back side. Absorption transfers momentum $P/c$ per unit time, so this contributes

$$F_{\text{abs}}=(1-r)\frac{P}{c}.$$ 
\nAdding both contributions,

$$F_b=2r\frac{P}{c}+(1-r)\frac{P}{c}=(1+r)\frac{P}{c}.$$ 
\nTherefore, the force applied to the glass is \boxed{F_b=(1+r)\frac{P}{c}}.

knowledge_points.name: reflection coefficient
knowledge_points.description: The reflection coefficient r is the probability that a photon is reflected from a single glass surface, as stated in the problem. It determines the fraction of incident photons reflected at the front surface.

knowledge_points.name: perfectly absorbing back surface
knowledge_points.description: The opposite side of the glass is painted totally black, so it absorbs all photons that reach it without reflection. This ensures the transmitted fraction contributes a force from absorption.

knowledge_points.name: transparent glass bulk
knowledge_points.description: The glass plate itself does not absorb or scatter light, so all photons not reflected at the front surface reach the back surface. This makes the transmitted fraction exactly 1-r.

knowledge_points.name: force from absorbed light
knowledge_points.description: When light of power P is completely absorbed, the force exerted is F = P/c. Used for the (1-r) fraction of power absorbed at the black back surface.

knowledge_points.name: force from reflected light
knowledge_points.description: When light of power P is perfectly reflected, the force exerted is F = 2P/c because the photon momentum reverses. Used for the r fraction of power reflected at the front surface.

sub_problems.problem: (3) Calculate the force $F_{c}$ applied to the glass by the laser light when neither of the sides is painted.
sub_problems.solution:
Because the plate thickness satisfies
\[
2nd=200.5\lambda,
\]\nthe phase accumulated in one round trip inside the glass is an odd multiple of \(\pi\). Thus successive transmitted waves interfere alternately in sign.
\nIf the reflection coefficient of one glass surface is \(r\), then the amplitude transmission factor at one surface is \(\sqrt{1-r}\), and the reflected amplitude factor is \(\sqrt{r}\). The first transmitted wave has amplitude
\[\nE_0=(1-r)E_i.
\]\nAfter one additional round trip inside the plate, the wave acquires an extra factor \(-r\), so the transmitted amplitudes form the geometric series
\[\nE_t=(1-r)E_i\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-r)^k
= (1-r)E_i\,\frac{1}{1+r}
=\frac{1-r}{1+r}E_i.
\]\nTherefore the transmitted power is
\[
\frac{P_t}{P}=\left(\frac{E_t}{E_i}\right)^2
=\left(\frac{1-r}{1+r}\right)^2.
\]\nThe remaining power \(P-P_t\) is reflected back, so the force on the plate equals twice the momentum flux of that part:
\[\nF_c=2\frac{P-P_t}{c}
=\frac{2P}{c}\left(1-\left(\frac{1-r}{1+r}\right)^2\right)
=\frac{8Pr}{c(1+r)^2}.
\]\nHence the force is
\[
\boxed{F_c=\frac{8Pr}{c(1+r)^2}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: round-trip phase shift in a thin film
knowledge_points.description: The phase accumulated in one round trip inside the glass is Δφ = 2kd = 4πnd/λ. For the given thickness 2nd = 200.5λ, this phase is an odd multiple of π, causing a sign flip (factor -1) in the amplitude after each round trip, which leads to alternating signs in the multiple-beam interference.

knowledge_points.name: amplitude coefficients from power reflection coefficient
knowledge_points.description: For a lossless interface at normal incidence, the amplitude reflection coefficient is √r and the amplitude transmission coefficient is √(1-r), where r is the power (intensity) reflection coefficient. This is used to express the amplitude of each transmitted wave in terms of r and the incident amplitude.

knowledge_points.name: multiple-beam interference summation
knowledge_points.description: The total transmitted amplitude is obtained by summing the amplitudes of all waves that emerge after multiple internal reflections. Each subsequent wave is multiplied by an additional factor of -r per round trip, forming a geometric series.

knowledge_points.name: geometric series sum
knowledge_points.description: The infinite sum ∑_{k=0}^∞ (-r)^k equals 1/(1+r) for |r|<1, which is used to evaluate the total transmitted amplitude.

knowledge_points.name: intensity-amplitude relation
knowledge_points.description: The power (intensity) of a light wave is proportional to the square of its electric field amplitude, so the transmitted power ratio is (E_t/E_i)^2.

knowledge_points.name: radiation pressure force from momentum flux
knowledge_points.description: The force exerted by light on an object equals the net rate of change of momentum of the light. For normal incidence, the momentum flux is power/c. For a non-absorbing plate, the net force is F = 2(P_incident - P_transmitted)/c, which is twice the momentum flux of the reflected part.

knowledge_points.name: no absorption
knowledge_points.description: The glass plate does not absorb light, so the incident power equals the sum of reflected and transmitted powers. This allows the reflected power to be expressed as P - P_t.

knowledge_points.name: normal incidence
knowledge_points.description: The laser light falls perpendicularly on the plate, so all momentum vectors are collinear and the force is along the beam direction, simplifying the force calculation to a scalar equation.

knowledge_points.name: coherent monochromatic light
knowledge_points.description: The laser provides coherent, monochromatic light, enabling stable interference. The plate thickness is specified to a fraction of a wavelength, so the phase condition is well-defined and amplitudes (not intensities) are summed.

title: DRAGON
problem: — Aigar Vaigu. Here is a photo of a dragon under water (there is a larger photo on a separate sheet). The length of the dragon is $l =8\mathrm{cm}$ and its height is $h =3\mathrm{cm}$ . The diameter of the bottom of the bowl is $d =10\mathrm{cm}$ and the angle between the table and the side of the bowl is $\alpha =60^\circ$ . The refractive index of water is $n =1.33$ . The photo has been taken so that the camera was pointing directly along the water surface. In the following questions the angle between the horizon when looking at some point on the image of the dragon is defined as the angle between the horizontal water surface (or any other horizontal surface) and the straight line from the eye to that point on the image.

sub_problems.problem: (1) What is the largest angle below the horizon from which the reflection of the dragon from the water surface can be seen?
sub_problems.solution:
To see the reflection of the dragon in the water surface, the ray inside the water must reach the water–air interface with an incidence angle at least equal to the critical angle for total internal reflection. The largest viewing angle below the horizon corresponds to the limiting case when the reflected ray is just totally internally reflected at the water surface.
\nFor the water–air boundary,
\[
\sin \gamma_1 = \frac{1}{n},
\]\nso
\[
\gamma_1 = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{1}{1.33}\right) \approx 48.8^\circ.
\]
\nThe bowl wall makes an angle \(\alpha=60^\circ\) with the table, so the normals to the water surface and to the bowl wall differ by \(60^\circ\). Therefore the ray inside the bowl makes the angle
\[
\gamma_2 = 60^\circ - \gamma_1 \approx 11.2^\circ
\]\nwith the normal to the bowl wall.
\nApplying Snell’s law at the bowl wall (air to water or vice versa, depending on the ray path),
\[
\sin \gamma_3 = n\sin \gamma_2,
\]\nwhich gives
\[
\gamma_3 = \arcsin\bigl(1.33\sin 11.2^\circ\bigr) \approx 15.0^\circ.
\]
\nThe normal to the bowl wall is \(30^\circ\) from the horizontal, so the emerging ray makes an angle
\[
30^\circ + \gamma_3 \approx 45.0^\circ
\]\nbelow the horizon.
\nThus the largest angle below the horizon from which the reflection can be seen is \(\boxed{45^\circ}\).

knowledge_points.name: total internal reflection
knowledge_points.description: The reflection of the dragon from the water surface is only visible when the ray inside the water strikes the water-air interface at an angle greater than or equal to the critical angle.

knowledge_points.name: Snell's law
knowledge_points.description: Used to relate the angle of incidence and refraction at the water-air interface (for critical angle) and at the bowl wall (air to water transition).

knowledge_points.name: critical angle formula
knowledge_points.description: The critical angle for total internal reflection at the water-air boundary is given by sin(gamma) = 1/n, which determines the limiting ray path.

knowledge_points.name: planar water surface
knowledge_points.description: The water surface is treated as a flat horizontal plane, so the normal to the water surface is vertical.

knowledge_points.name: bowl wall geometry
knowledge_points.description: The bowl wall makes a 60-degree angle with the table, so its normal is 30 degrees from the horizontal; this geometry is used to relate angles inside and outside the bowl.

title: SATELLITE
problem: Taavet Kalda. A solar powered satellite with starting velocity $v_{0}$ is launched from Earth onto an elliptical heliocentric orbit with the intent of gathering as much solar energy as possible. The angle of departure can be freely changed.

sub_problems.problem: (1) What is the minimal required launching speed $\mathbf{v}_m$ for the satellite to reach any heliocentric orbit?
sub_problems.solution:
Using conservation of mechanical energy, the minimal launch speed is obtained when the satellite just reaches zero speed at infinity. Then its initial kinetic energy equals the magnitude of Earths gravitational potential energy:

$$\frac{m v_m^2}{2} - \frac{G M_\oplus m}{r_\oplus} = 0.$$
\nSolving for $v_m$ gives

$$v_m = \sqrt{\frac{2 G M_\oplus}{r_\oplus}}.$$
\nThus the minimal required launching speed is \(\boxed{\sqrt{\frac{2 G M_\oplus}{r_\oplus}}}\).

knowledge_points.name: escape velocity
knowledge_points.description: The minimum speed needed for an object to escape a gravitational field, reaching zero speed at infinity. In this sub-problem, the minimal launch speed to reach a heliocentric orbit is Earth's escape velocity.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: In the absence of non-conservative forces, the total mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) remains constant. Used to equate initial kinetic energy at Earth's surface to the magnitude of gravitational potential energy at infinity.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational potential energy formula
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational potential energy of a mass m at distance r from a point mass M is U = -GMm/r. Used to express Earth's potential energy at the surface.

knowledge_points.name: kinetic energy formula
knowledge_points.description: The kinetic energy of a mass m moving at speed v is K = (1/2)mv^2. Used to express the initial kinetic energy at launch.

knowledge_points.name: launch from Earth's surface
knowledge_points.description: The satellite is launched from the surface of the Earth, so the initial distance from Earth's center is Earth's radius r_⊕.

knowledge_points.name: Earth escape leads to heliocentric orbit
knowledge_points.description: The minimal speed to reach any heliocentric orbit is the speed needed to escape Earth's gravitational field; the Sun's gravity and Earth's orbital motion are not considered during the launch phase.

sub_problems.problem: (2) What is the speed of the satellite just after exiting Earth's gravitational field?
sub_problems.solution:
Let the speed of the satellite just after leaving Earths gravitational field be $v_{1}$. By conservation of mechanical energy, the initial kinetic energy minus the gravitational potential energy at Earths surface equals the kinetic energy after escape:

$$\frac{m v_{0}^{2}}{2} - \frac{G M_{\oplus} m}{r_{\oplus}} = \frac{m v_{1}^{2}}{2}.$$
\nSolving for $v_{1}$ gives

$$v_{1} = \sqrt{v_{0}^{2} - \frac{2 G M_{\oplus}}{r_{\oplus}}}.$$
\nUsing $g = \frac{G M_{\oplus}}{r_{\oplus}^{2}}$, this can also be written as

$$v_{1} = \sqrt{v_{0}^{2} - 2 g r_{\oplus}}.$$
\nTherefore, the speed of the satellite just after exiting Earths gravitational field is $\boxed{\sqrt{v_{0}^{2} - 2 g r_{\oplus}}}$.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: Total mechanical energy (kinetic plus gravitational potential) is conserved for the satellite after launch, assuming no non-conservative forces act during escape.

knowledge_points.name: Newtonian gravitational potential energy
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational potential energy of a point mass m at distance r from Earth's center is -GMm/r, with the zero of potential at infinity.

knowledge_points.name: escape to infinity
knowledge_points.description: Exiting Earth's gravitational field means the satellite reaches a distance where the gravitational potential energy is negligible (taken as zero).

knowledge_points.name: kinetic energy formula
knowledge_points.description: The translational kinetic energy of a mass m moving with speed v is (1/2)mv^2.

knowledge_points.name: surface gravity relation
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational acceleration at Earth's surface is g = GM/r^2, used to express the final speed in terms of g and Earth's radius.

sub_problems.problem: (3) Express the long-time-average solar irradiance of the satellite in terms of its semi-major axis $\alpha$ , angular momentum $J$ , orbital period $T$ and mass $m$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The long-time-average solar irradiance is

$$I_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T I(t)\,dt,$$
\nwith the instantaneous irradiance from the Sun

$$I(t)=\frac{L_{\odot}}{4\pi r(t)^2}.$$
\nTo evaluate the time average, change variables from time to the orbital angle $\alpha$:

$$dt=\frac{d\alpha}{\omega},$$
\nso that

$$I_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{L_{\odot}}{4\pi r^2}\frac{d\alpha}{\omega}
=\frac{L_{\odot}}{4\pi T}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\alpha}{\omega r^2}.$$
\nUsing conservation of angular momentum,

$$J=mvr=m\omega r^2,$$
\nhence

$$\frac{1}{\omega r^2}=\frac{m}{J}.$$
\nTherefore the integrand is constant and

$$I_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{L_{\odot}}{4\pi T}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{m}{J}\,d\alpha
=\frac{L_{\odot}m}{4\pi TJ}(2\pi).
$$
\nSo the long-time-average solar irradiance is

$$\boxed{I_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{L_{\odot}m}{2TJ}}.$$

knowledge_points.name: time average
knowledge_points.description: The long-time average of a periodic quantity is defined as the integral over one period divided by the period, I_avg = (1/T) ∫_0^T I(t) dt.

knowledge_points.name: inverse-square law of irradiance
knowledge_points.description: The instantaneous solar irradiance at distance r from the Sun is I = L_sun/(4π r^2), where L_sun is the solar luminosity.

knowledge_points.name: change of integration variable to angle
knowledge_points.description: To integrate over time, use dt = dα/ω where α is the orbital angle and ω = dα/dt is the angular velocity, converting the time integral to an angular integral.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of angular momentum
knowledge_points.description: For a central force, angular momentum J = m r^2 ω is constant, allowing the substitution 1/(ω r^2) = m/J, which simplifies the integral.

knowledge_points.name: elliptical orbit
knowledge_points.description: The satellite is in a bound Keplerian orbit around the Sun, so the orbital angle α runs from 0 to 2π over one period, making the angular integration straightforward.

sub_problems.problem:
(4) What is the maximal average solar irradiance the satellite can gather and what is the needed launch angle relative to Earth's motion?

The Sun's mass is $M_{\odot}$ , Earth's orbital radius $R_{\oplus}$ , free fall acceleration on Earth $\pmb{g}$ , Earth's radius $\pmb{r}_{\oplus}$ and Sun's luminosity $L_{\odot}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a Keplerian ellipse, the time-averaged solar irradiance is proportional to
\[
\left\langle \frac{1}{r^2} \right\rangle
= \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T \frac{dt}{r^2}
= \frac{2\pi}{T h},
\]\nwhere \(T\) is the orbital period and \(h\) is the specific angular momentum. Thus maximizing the average irradiance is equivalent to minimizing \(T h\).
\nLet the speed acquired after escaping Earths gravity be
\[\nu=\sqrt{v_0^2-2 g r_\oplus}.
\]\nThe heliocentric speed at launch depends on the launch angle. The smallest possible heliocentric speed is obtained when the satellite is launched directly opposite to Earths motion, so that the speeds subtract.
\nDenote Earths orbital speed by
\[\nv_\oplus=\sqrt{\frac{G M_\odot}{R_\oplus}}.
\]\nThen the heliocentric launch speed is
\[\nv=v_\oplus-\nu,
\qquad x\equiv \frac{v}{v_\oplus}.
\]\nUsing the orbital energy at \(r=R_\oplus\),
\[
-\frac{G M_\odot m}{2a}=\frac{m v^2}{2}-\frac{G M_\odot m}{R_\oplus},
\]\nso
\[
\frac{R_\oplus}{a}=2-\frac{v^2 R_\oplus}{G M_\odot}=2-x^2.
\]\nKeplers third law gives
\[\nT=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{a^3}{G M_\odot}}
=\frac{2\pi R_\oplus^{3/2}}{\sqrt{G M_\odot}}\,(2-x^2)^{-3/2}.
\]\nSince the launch is tangential in the optimal case, the specific angular momentum is
\[\nh=R_\oplus v=R_\oplus v_\oplus x.
\]\nTherefore
\[
\left\langle I\right\rangle
=\frac{L_\odot}{4\pi}\frac{2\pi}{T h}
=\frac{L_\odot}{4\pi R_\oplus^2}\,\frac{(2-x^2)^{3/2}}{x}.
\]\nThis is maximized by the smallest allowed \(x\), which is achieved by launching directly opposite Earths motion.
\nWith
\[\nx=1-\sqrt{\frac{R_\oplus}{G M_\odot}}\sqrt{v_0^2-2 g r_\oplus},
\]\nthe maximal average irradiance is
\[
\boxed{\left\langle I\right\rangle_{\max}
=\frac{L_\odot}{4\pi R_\oplus^2}\,
\frac{\left[2-\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{R_\oplus}{G M_\odot}}\sqrt{v_0^2-2 g r_\oplus}\right)^2\right]^{3/2}}
{1-\sqrt{\frac{R_\oplus}{G M_\odot}}\sqrt{v_0^2-2 g r_\oplus}}}
\]
(and equivalently \(\boxed{\langle I\rangle_{\max}=\frac{L_\odot}{4\pi R_\oplus^2}\frac{(2-x^2)^{3/2}}{x}}\) with the above \(x\)).
\nThe required launch direction is
\[
\boxed{180^\circ\ \text{relative to Earths motion}}.
